root.title: Approximation Conversion Algorithm Family
root.top_down_role: Approximation methods that convert relaxations, dual certificates, or local optimality into discrete solutions. Exact combinatorial algorithms, general convex optimization, approximation hardness, and standalone approximation schemes are owned elsewhere.

children.title: Relaxation-Certificate Quality Interface
children.top_down_role: Common navigation for comparing relaxation strength and the certificate types used by the method families that follow.

assumptions_latex: The instance \(I\) is a minimization problem with a nonempty feasible set \(F_I\subseteq X_I\), objective \(c_I:X_I\to\mathbb{R}\), and attained finite optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{x\in F_I}c_I(x)\).
The relaxation region \(R_I\subseteq X_I\) satisfies \(F_I\subseteq R_I\), and \(L(I)=\inf_{x\in R_I}c_I(x)\) is finite.

notation.meaning: attained integral optimum of instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention with an attained integral optimum; the bound direction reverses for maximization.

source_refs.locator: Section 5.6. Lagrangean Relaxation p. 124

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every minimization instance \(I\) satisfying \(F_I\subseteq R_I\), the relaxation value \(L(I)=\inf_{x\in R_I}c_I(x)\) is an instancewise lower bound on the attained integral optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{x\in F_I}c_I(x)\), namely \(L(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every minimization instance whose integral optimum is attained, optimizing over a relaxation containing all integral feasible solutions gives an instancewise lower bound on the integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Instancewise Relaxation Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5.6. Lagrangean Relaxation p. 124

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori quality certificate from any feasible solution and a valid relaxation lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every feasible \(z\in F_I\), \[L(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\leq c_I(z),\qquad 0\leq c_I(z)-\operatorname{OPT}(I)\leq c_I(z)-L(I).\] If \(L(I)>0\), then \(c_I(z)/L(I)\) is an upper bound on \(c_I(z)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\); in particular, \(c_I(z)\leq\alpha L(I)\) certifies an \(\alpha\)-approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any feasible solution and relaxation lower bound enclose the optimum and certify absolute or, with a positive lower bound, multiplicative quality.
knowledge_statements.title: Instancewise Upper–Lower Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent zero-gap conditions when an integral optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(F_I\subseteq R_I\) and let \(x^\star\in F_I\) attain the integral optimum. Then \[L(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)\] if and only if \(x^\star\) is also optimal over \(R_I\). In particular, if an attained relaxation minimizer \(\bar x\in R_I\) belongs to \(F_I\), then the relaxation is exact and \(\bar x\) is integrally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation has zero instancewise gap exactly when an integral optimum is also relaxation-optimal; an integral relaxation minimizer certifies this condition.
assumptions_latex: An integral optimum \(x^\star\in F_I\) is attained.
For the sufficient test, a relaxation minimizer \(\bar x\) is attained and belongs to \(F_I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)\iff x^\star\in\arg\min_{x\in R_I}c_I(x)\), and \(\bar x\in F_I\cap\arg\min_{R_I}c_I\) certifies equality.
knowledge_statements.title: Instancewise Relaxation Exactness

children.title: Dual Relaxation Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds obtained from dual representations of the governing relaxation.

assumptions_latex: The minimization instance \(I\) has integral feasible set \(F_I\subseteq X_I\), relaxation region \(R_I\subseteq X_I\) with \(F_I\subseteq R_I\), objective \(c_I:X_I\to\mathbb{R}\), relaxation value \(L(I)=\inf_{x\in R_I}c_I(x)\), and integral optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\inf_{x\in F_I}c_I(x)\).
A dual feasible set \(D_I\) and objective \(b_I:D_I\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(b_I(y)\leq c_I(x)\) for every \(y\in D_I\) and \(x\in R_I\).

notation.meaning: dual-feasible point and its objective value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificate for a minimization relaxation.

source_refs.locator: Section 5.3. Total Dual Integrality p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization relaxation satisfying weak duality, every dual-feasible point \(y\in D_I\) supplies the checkable lower-bound certificate \(b_I(y)\leq L(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a minimization relaxation satisfying weak duality, every feasible dual solution certifies a lower bound on both the relaxation value and the integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Relaxation Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5.3. Total Dual Integrality p. 111

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori absolute and multiplicative guarantees from an integral feasible solution and a dual lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in F_I\) be integral feasible and \(y\in D_I\) dual feasible. Then \[0\leq c_I(z)-\operatorname{OPT}(I)\leq c_I(z)-b_I(y).\] If \(b_I(y)>0\), then \[\frac{c_I(z)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}\leq\frac{c_I(z)}{b_I(y)}.\] Consequently, \(c_I(z)\leq\alpha b_I(y)\) certifies that \(z\) is an \(\alpha\)-approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible integral upper bound and dual lower bound enclose the optimum and certify absolute or multiplicative approximation quality.
assumptions_latex: \(z\in F_I\) is feasible for the minimization problem.
\(y\in D_I\) is dual feasible and weak duality holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Approximation Interval

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation of the relaxation value by an attained dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If weak duality holds and some \(y^\star\in D_I\) satisfies \(b_I(y^\star)=L(I)\), then \[L(I)=\max_{y\in D_I}b_I(y)=b_I(y^\star)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I).\] Thus an attained strong-dual solution certifies the exact relaxation value, although equality with the integral optimum additionally requires zero integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under attained strong duality, an optimal dual solution certifies the exact relaxation value but not automatically the integral optimum.
assumptions_latex: Weak duality holds between \(D_I\) and the primal relaxation.
A dual point \(y^\star\) is attained and satisfies \(b_I(y^\star)=L(I)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Attained Strong-Dual Representation

children.title: Lagrangean Relaxation Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds obtained by pricing selected constraints through Lagrangean relaxation.

assumptions_latex: For an instance \(I\), let \(X_I\) be a nonempty set, let \(c_I:X_I\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(g_I:X_I\to\mathbb{R}^m\).
The minimization problem has feasible set \(F_I=\{x\in X_I:g_I(x)\leq0\}\) and finite value \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\inf_{x\in F_I}c_I(x)\).
For every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m_+\), the value \(q_I(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X_I}(c_I(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g_I(x))\) is well-defined in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inequality-constrained minimization in the sign convention \(g_I(x)\leq0\) with nonnegative multipliers.

source_refs.locator: Section 5.6. Lagrangean Relaxation p. 124

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization problem with constraints \(g_I(x)\leq0\), the Lagrangean lower-bound family is \(q_I(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X_I}(c_I(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g_I(x))\) for \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m_+\), and its strongest bound is \[L_{\mathrm{Lag}}(I)=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m_+}q_I(\lambda)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a minimization problem written with constraints no greater than zero, nonnegative Lagrangean multipliers define lower bounds, and their supremum is the strongest bound in this family.
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangean Relaxation Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: Section 5.6. Lagrangean Relaxation p. 124

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient exactness test using an attained Lagrangean subproblem minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda\geq0\) and let \(x_\lambda\) attain \(q_I(\lambda)\). If \(g_I(x_\lambda)\leq0\) and \(\lambda^{\mathsf T}g_I(x_\lambda)=0\), then \[q_I(\lambda)=c_I(x_\lambda)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)=L_{\mathrm{Lag}}(I).\] Thus primal feasibility and complementarity certify zero Lagrangean duality gap and optimality of \(x_\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangean subproblem minimizer that is feasible and complementary to its multiplier certifies exactness and primal optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Complementary Lagrangean Exactness Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity and Supergradients of the Lagrangean Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural shape of the multiplier-dependent lower-bound function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(q_I(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X_I}(c_I(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g_I(x))\) is concave on \(\mathbb R_+^m\). If \(x_\lambda\) attains the infimum at \(\lambda\), then for every \(\mu\in\mathbb R_+^m\), \[q_I(\mu)\leq q_I(\lambda)+g_I(x_\lambda)^{\mathsf T}(\mu-\lambda),\] so \(g_I(x_\lambda)\) is a supergradient of \(q_I\) at \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrangean lower-bound function is concave, and the constraint vector of an optimal subproblem solution is a supergradient.
assumptions_latex: \(q_I\) is the infimum of functions affine in \(\lambda\).
For the supergradient statement, an infimum minimizer \(x_\lambda\) exists.

notation.meaning: superdifferential of the concave Lagrangean function
Lagrangean subproblem minimizer at multiplier lambda

knowledge_statements.title: Concavity and Supergradients of the Lagrangean Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization-form integer programs in which selected inequalities are priced instead of explicitly enforced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax\le b\}\), and suppose linear objectives can be optimized over \(Q\). For \[z:=\max\{c^\top x:A'x\le b',\ x\in Q\},\] define, for each \(\lambda\ge0\), \[LR(\lambda):=\max_{x\in Q}\bigl\{c^\top x+\lambda^\top(b'-A'x)\bigr\}.\] This is the Lagrangean relaxation, and the components of \(\lambda\) are Lagrange multipliers. Moreover, \(LR(\lambda)\ge z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The selected inequalities are removed and their nonnegative multiplier-weighted slacks are added to the objective. Maximizing the modified objective over the easier integer set defines the Lagrangean relaxation and gives an upper bound on the original maximization value.
assumptions_latex: \text{Linear objective functions can be optimized over }Q
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: LR(\lambda):=\max_{x\in Q}\{c^\top x+\lambda^\top(b'-A'x)\}\ge\max\{c^\top x:A'x\le b',\ x\in Q\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the best Lagrangean upper bound and the stated feasibility condition for attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Lagrangean dual of \(\max\{c^\top x:A'x\le b',\ x\in Q\}\) is \[\min_{\lambda\ge0}LR(\lambda).\] In the stated integer-programming setting, if \[\{x:Ax\le b,\ A'x\le b'\}\ne\varnothing,\] then this minimum is attained. The extract makes no attainment assertion when this continuous constraint system is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrangean dual minimizes the relaxation value over nonnegative multipliers to obtain the best upper bound. The source guarantees attainment when the combined continuous constraint system is nonempty and excludes the empty-system case from that guarantee.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangean dual equals the constrained convex-hull relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and exact value of the Lagrangean dual when the convex hull of the easy set is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A'\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b'\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), where \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) is a polyhedron. Suppose \[\max\{c^\top x:A'x\le b',\ x\in\operatorname{conv}(Q)\}\] has an optimal solution, and define \[LR(\lambda):=\max_{x\in Q}\{c^\top x+\lambda^\top(b'-A'x)\}.\] Then the infimum over \(\lambda\ge0\) is attained and \[\min_{\lambda\ge0}LR(\lambda)=\max\{c^\top x:A'x\le b',\ x\in\operatorname{conv}(Q)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the convex hull of the easy set is polyhedral and its constrained linear optimization problem has an optimal solution, an optimal nonnegative Lagrange multiplier exists. The best Lagrangean bound equals the optimum over the constrained convex hull of Q.
assumptions_latex: \max\{c^\top x:A'x\le b',\ x\in\operatorname{conv}(Q)\}\text{ has an optimal solution}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gap Monotonicity Under Stronger Positive Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of pointwise lower-bound dominance on multiplicative minimization gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0<L_2(I)\leq L_1(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), then \[\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{L_1(I)}\leq\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{L_2(I)}\] instancewise and therefore \[\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{L_1(I)}\leq\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{L_2(I)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise stronger positive minimization lower bound cannot have a worse multiplicative integrality gap.

notation.meaning: positive lower-bound functions on the same instances

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise comparison of minimization lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower bound \(L_1\) is at least as strong as \(L_2\), written \(L_1\succeq L_2\), precisely when \(L_1(I)\geq L_2(I)\) for every common instance \(I\). It is strictly stronger when this inequality holds for every instance and is strict for at least one instance. If there exist instances \(I\) and \(J\) with \(L_1(I)>L_2(I)\) and \(L_1(J)<L_2(J)\), the bounds are incomparable under pointwise dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One minimization lower bound is stronger when it is never smaller on any common instance; crossing values make the bounds incomparable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative worst-case gap for positive-valued maximization relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem whose relaxation is an upper bound \(U(I)\geq\operatorname{OPT}(I)>0\), define \(\gamma_{\max}(I)=U(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) and \[\operatorname{gap}_{\max}(\mathcal I,U)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\gamma_{\max}(I).\] A worst-case family has ratios converging to this supremum. This orientation keeps every gap ratio at least one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximization, the multiplicative gap is the relaxation upper bound divided by the positive integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximization Worst-Case Gap Convention

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Witness Characterization of a Finite Worst-Case Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment and nonattainment of the supremal minimization gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite number \(G\) equals \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\gamma(I)\) if and only if \(\gamma(I)\leq G\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\) and, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), some \(I_\varepsilon\in\mathcal I\) satisfies \(\gamma(I_\varepsilon)>G-\varepsilon\). The supremum need not be attained; choosing witnesses for \(\varepsilon=1/k\) yields a sequence whose ratios converge to \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite worst-case gap is a uniform upper bound approached arbitrarily closely, even when no single instance attains it.
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Witness Characterization of a Finite Worst-Case Gap

assumptions_latex: Each instance \(I\) has positive finite relaxation value \(L(I)\) and finite integral optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
The family of instances under consideration is \(\mathcal I\).

notation.meaning: worst-case gap of the relaxation over the family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative gap for positive-valued minimization instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization relaxation \(L\) on an instance family \(\mathcal I\), with \(0<L(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)<\infty\), the instancewise integrality ratio is \(\gamma(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)/L(I)\). The worst-case integrality gap is \[\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal I,L)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\gamma(I).\] A sequence \((I_k)_{k\geq1}\subseteq\mathcal I\) is a worst-case gap family with limiting value \(g\) when \(\gamma(I_k)\to g\); it is gap-witnessing when \(g=\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal I,L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A worst-case gap family is a sequence of instances whose integral-to-relaxation ratios approach the supremal ratio of the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Gap Families

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-and-lower certificate that an algorithm exactly matches a relaxation's worst-case gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization family \(\mathcal I\), let \(0<L(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), and let algorithm \(A\) return a feasible solution. Define \(\gamma=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\operatorname{OPT}(I)/L(I)\) and \(\rho_A=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}c_I(A(I))/L(I)\). Feasibility gives \(\gamma\le\rho_A\). Consequently, if \(c_I(A(I))\le gL(I)\) for every instance and some sequence \(I_m\) satisfies \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_m)/L(I_m)\to g\), then \(\gamma=\rho_A=g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A universal algorithmic upper bound and relaxation-gap instances approaching the same factor certify exact gap matching.
assumptions_latex: There is a sequence with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_m)/L(I_m)\to g\).

notation.meaning: worst-case integrality gap of the relaxation
worst-case relaxation-relative cost ratio of algorithm A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation-relative approximation guarantee for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm family \(A\) matches a relaxation gap bound \(g\geq1\) on \(\mathcal I\) when, for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), it outputs \(A(I)\in F_I\) satisfying \(c_I(A(I))\leq gL(I)\). Because \(L(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), the same output is a \(g\)-approximation. If additionally \(\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal I,L)=g\), then the relaxation-relative factor is tight: no universal assertion \(c_I(A(I))\leq g'L(I)\) with \(g'<g\) can hold for all feasible-output algorithms and all instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm matches a gap when its solution costs at most that gap times the relaxation value; the resulting approximation factor is then tight for that relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Matching Algorithm Families

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between geometric strictness and strict objective-value dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=R_1=\{(0,0)\}\), let \(R_2=\{(0,t):0\le t\le1\}\), and minimize \(c(x)=x_1\). Then \(F\subseteq R_1\subsetneq R_2\), but \(\min_{R_1}c=\min_{R_2}c=0\). Hence proper projected-region containment need not give a strictly better bound for a particular objective and instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometrically stricter relaxation can have the same optimum because its extra fractional points need not improve the chosen objective.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instancewise and family-wise effect of containment on minimization bounds and ratio gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F_I\subseteq R_1(I)\subseteq R_2(I)\), then \(L_1(I)\ge L_2(I)\). With positive finite relaxation values, \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)/L_1(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)/L_2(I)\). Uniform containment over an instance family therefore makes the worst-case integrality gap of formulation 1 no larger than that of formulation 2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger minimization formulation gives a no-weaker lower bound and, for positive values, a no-larger ratio integrality gap.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_1\subseteq R_2\iff \min_{x\in R_1}c^{\mathsf T}x\ge\min_{x\in R_2}c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\forall c.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-wise characterization of geometric strength for compact convex projected relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty compact convex regions \(R_1,R_2\) in a common variable space, \(R_1\subseteq R_2\) if and only if \(\min_{x\in R_1}c^{\mathsf T}x\ge\min_{x\in R_2}c^{\mathsf T}x\) for every linear minimization objective \(c\). Dominance for only one chosen objective is weaker and does not imply containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For compact convex relaxations, containment is equivalent to giving a no-weaker bound for every linear minimization objective, not merely one objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Wise Characterization of Formulation Strength

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1(I)\) and \(R_2(I)\) be relaxation regions expressed, or projected, in the same variable space. If \(F_I\subseteq R_1(I)\subseteq R_2(I)\), then minimization over the smaller region gives \[L_1(I)=\inf_{x\in R_1(I)}c_I(x)\geq\inf_{x\in R_2(I)}c_I(x)=L_2(I).\] Thus formulation \(1\) is at least as strong as formulation \(2\) on instance \(I\). Uniform containment over an instance family implies uniform bound dominance; lack of containment alone does not establish incomparability of objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, a relaxation contained in another is at least as strong because optimizing over the smaller feasible region gives a no-smaller lower bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract criterion for a gap-witnessing construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integrality-gap construction against a proposed factor \(g'<g\) is an explicit sequence \((I_k)_{k\geq1}\) for which both \(L(I_k)\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_k)\) are established and \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I_k)}{L(I_k)}\geq g.\] For every \(g'<g\), some constructed instance then satisfies \(\operatorname{OPT}(I_k)>g'L(I_k)\). Consequently the relaxation cannot support a universal integrality-gap bound below \(g\), regardless of the rounding procedure applied after solving that relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit instance sequence disproves every smaller gap factor when its integral-to-relaxation ratios approach or exceed the claimed boundary.

children.title: Relaxation Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where the selected relaxation loses approximation strength.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization boundary for multiplicative relaxation quality on a fixed instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), and add the same constant \(a\) to every feasible objective value, giving \(L_a(I)=L(I)+a\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_a(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)+a\). When \(L_a(I)>0\), \[\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_a(I)}{L_a(I)}=1+\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)-L(I)}{L(I)+a}.\] Hence a common additive shift preserves the additive gap but generally changes the multiplicative ratio; if the additive gap is positive, the ratio is unbounded as \(L(I)+a\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common additive objective shift preserves additive relaxation error but can arbitrarily change the multiplicative gap ratio.
assumptions_latex: The same constant \(a\) is added to every feasible objective value.
The shifted ratio is used only when \(L(I)+a>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_a(I)/L_a(I)=1+(\operatorname{OPT}(I)-L(I))/(L(I)+a)\), so multiplicative gap claims require a fixed normalization.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Shift Instability of Multiplicative Gaps

assumptions_latex: A minimization relaxation has value \(L(I)\geq0\) and integral optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\operatorname{OPT}(I)/L(I)=\infty\) whenever positive denominators are used and the ratios are unbounded.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for multiplicative guarantees derived solely from a relaxation value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A relaxation is in a multiplicative failure regime on \(\mathcal I\) if either some instance has \(L(I)=0<\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), or for every finite \(g\geq1\) there exists \(I\in\mathcal I\) with \(L(I)>0\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)>gL(I)\). In either case, no finite constant \(g\) can certify \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\leq gL(I)\) uniformly over \(\mathcal I\). A finite multiplicative approximation guarantee therefore cannot be inferred from the relaxation value alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation fails multiplicatively when it can be zero below a positive optimum or when its integral-to-relaxation ratios are unbounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly identifies both zero-denominator and unbounded-positive-ratio failure regimes, and `failure_boundary` is the right kind. children.title: Rounding Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-cost and almost-sure-feasibility boundary for randomized minimization rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(I,x)\) be randomized, let integral costs be nonnegative, and require \(R(I,x)\in F_I\) almost surely and \(\mathbb E[c_I(R(I,x))]\leq g c_I(x)\) for every admissible \((I,x)\). The factor-\(g\) guarantee fails if some admissible pair satisfies \(\Pr[R(I,x)\notin F_I]>0\) or \(\mathbb E[c_I(R(I,x))]>g c_I(x)\). An expectation guarantee alone does not imply a pointwise or high-probability cost bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomized rounding fails its expected factor guarantee if it can be infeasible with positive probability or its expected cost exceeds the claimed factor.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a target factor \(g\geq1\), a rounding map \(R\) is valid on a domain \(\mathcal D\) only if every \((I,x)\in\mathcal D\), with \(x\in R_I\), produces \(R(I,x)\in F_I\) and satisfies \(c_I(R(I,x))\leq g c_I(x)\). The rounding guarantee fails beyond its boundary when an admissible pair yields an infeasible output or violates this inequality. Such failure concerns the particular map and domain; it does not by itself prove that every rounding algorithm fails or that the relaxation has gap exceeding \(g\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between certifying an exact relaxation value and certifying integer optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min x_1+x_2+x_3\) subject to \(x_1+x_2\ge1\), \(x_2+x_3\ge1\), \(x_1+x_3\ge1\), and \(x\in\{0,1\}^3\). Its relaxation \(0\le x\le1\) has exact value \(3/2\), attained at \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\), whereas every integral feasible solution has value at least \(2\). Thus an exact relaxation-value certificate alone neither certifies integer optimality nor eliminates an integrality gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A relaxation-value certificate for instance \(I\) is a polynomially checkable witness \(z\) establishing both a relaxation-feasible solution of value \(v(z)\) and a valid relaxation lower bound of the same value. These two checks imply \(L(I)\leq v(z)\) and \(v(z)\leq L(I)\), hence \(v(z)=L(I)\). Since the relaxation is valid for minimization, \(v(z)=L(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). A primal-dual optimal pair with equal objectives is a canonical realization of such a certificate.

assumptions_latex: \(A\), \(b\), and \(c\) define the displayed primal minimization relaxation and its dual.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled dual feasibility certifies an approximation ratio for a minimization relaxation.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal relaxation \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge 0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c,\ y\ge 0\}\). A dual-fitting certificate for an integral feasible solution \(\bar x\) with factor \(\alpha\ge 1\) is a vector \(y\ge 0\) satisfying \(c^{\mathsf T}\bar x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le \alpha c\). Then \(y/\alpha\) is dual feasible, and weak duality gives \(c^{\mathsf T}\bar x\le \alpha b^{\mathsf T}(y/\alpha)\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{IP}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearly feasible dual whose value pays for the integral solution certifies an approximation ratio after scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Fitting Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Client charges provide a lower bound that can pay for an approximate solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization instance with client set \(U\), let \(F\) be a feasible solution of cost \(C(F)\). Nonnegative shares \((\xi_j)_{j\in U}\) form an \(\alpha\)-cost-sharing certificate when \(\sum_{j\in U}\xi_j\le \operatorname{OPT}\) and \(C(F)\le \alpha\sum_{j\in U}\xi_j\). The first inequality makes the aggregate charge a valid lower bound, while the second shows that this charge covers a \(1/\alpha\) fraction of the constructed cost. Consequently, \(C(F)\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative client charges certify approximation when their sum lower-bounds optimum and approximately covers the constructed solution's cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{y\ge 0:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\) be the feasible region of a packing dual with objective \(b^{\mathsf T}y=\sum_{j\in U}b_jy_j\). For any \(y\in D\), define the client share \(\xi_j=b_jy_j\). Then \(\sum_{j\in U}\xi_j=b^{\mathsf T}y\le \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\). Conversely, shares having a representation \(\xi_j=b_jy_j\) for some \(y\ge 0\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\) inherit this lower-bound property. If only \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le \alpha c\) holds, the scaled shares \(\xi_j/\alpha\) correspond to the feasible dual \(y/\alpha\).

assumptions_latex: One-run success probability is at least \(p>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amplification of a certified one-run approximation-success probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one randomized run returns a feasible \(\alpha\)-approximation with probability at least \(p>0\), then \(r\) independent runs followed by selection of the cheapest feasible output succeed with probability at least \(1-(1-p)^r\). Failure probability at most \(\delta\) is ensured by \(r\ge\lceil\ln(1/\delta)/(-\ln(1-p))\rceil\); the simpler bound \(r\ge\lceil p^{-1}\ln(1/\delta)\rceil\) also suffices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent repetition amplifies success from p to at least one minus (1-p) to the r, with linear runtime overhead.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Repetition Amplification

assumptions_latex: Both possible outputs are feasible and the lower-cost output is optimal.

notation.meaning: probability of the high-cost feasible output

review_flags: Corrects the Builder's invalid zero-cost construction, which contradicted positive optimal value and feasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for expectation-only conversion when every output is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q=\delta-\varepsilon\). Return an optimal solution of cost \(\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability \(1-q\), and a feasible solution of cost \([1+(\beta-1)/q]\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability \(q\). The expectation is \(\beta\operatorname{OPT}\), while the high-cost value exceeds \([1+(\beta-1)/\delta]\operatorname{OPT}\) and occurs with probability \(\delta-\varepsilon\). Hence the adjusted failure bound can be approached arbitrarily closely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid two-point distribution over feasible outputs makes the feasibility-adjusted expectation bound essentially sharp.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Feasibility-Adjusted Bound

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is feasible almost surely for a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharper expectation-to-success conversion using the lower bound satisfied by every feasible minimization output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Almost-sure feasibility implies \(C(X)\ge\operatorname{OPT}\). Therefore, for every \(t>1\), \[\Pr\{C(X)>t\operatorname{OPT}\}\le\frac{\beta-1}{t-1}.\] Equivalently, for every \(\delta\in(0,1)\), the output is a \([1+(\beta-1)/\delta]\)-approximation with probability at least \(1-\delta\). This dominates the seed's generic \(\beta/\delta\) Markov factor when feasibility is almost sure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because every feasible minimization output costs at least optimum, applying Markov to excess cost gives a sharper high-probability ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Adjusted Expectation Conversion

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is generated by a specified probability distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(E_\alpha)\ge p\); under the stated expectation bound, \((\alpha,p)=(\beta/\delta,1-\delta)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct application of Markov's inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A probability bound certifies the success rate and approximation quality of randomized conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a randomized conversion return \(X\), and define the success event \(E_\alpha=\{X\text{ is feasible and }C(X)\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}\}\). A probabilistic success certificate with parameters \((\alpha,p)\) is a verifiable derivation of \(\Pr(E_\alpha)\ge p\). In particular, if feasibility holds almost surely, \(C(X)\ge 0\), and \(\mathbb E[C(X)]\le \beta\operatorname{OPT}\), then for every \(\delta\in(0,1)\), Markov's inequality certifies \(\Pr\{C(X)\le (\beta/\delta)\operatorname{OPT}\}\ge 1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified lower bound on the probability of producing a feasible approximate solution constitutes a probabilistic success certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Success Certificates

assumptions_latex: Only feasibility, nonnegative cost, and local optimality are assumed.
No exchange theorem or locality-gap inequality is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup C(S)/\operatorname{OPT}=\infty\text{ over locally optimal instances under these assumptions}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary separating a neighborhood check from a global approximation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(M>1\), consider a finite minimization problem with feasible solutions \(S,O\), costs \(C(S)=M\), \(C(O)=1\), and \(N(S)=\{S\}\). Then \(S\) has no improving neighbor but \(C(S)/\operatorname{OPT}=M\). Thus no finite approximation factor follows from local optimality without a valid structural bound for the specified neighborhood and problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A no-improving-move check has no approximation meaning unless a structural locality-gap theorem connects the neighborhood to global solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Optimality Alone Has No Global Ratio
knowledge_statements.title: Local Optimality Alone Has No Global Ratio

assumptions_latex: The neighborhood \(N(S)\) is finitely enumerable or has a separation oracle.
The stated exchange inequality is valid for the problem class.
review_flags: approximation factor and exchange inequality depend on the selected problem and neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checked neighborhood inequalities certify approximation when a structural exchange bound is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be the feasible solutions, let \(C:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) be the objective, and let \(N(S)\subseteq\mathcal F\) be a specified neighborhood. A local-optimality certificate for \(S\) consists of the verifiable inequalities \(C(S)\le C(T)\) for every \(T\in N(S)\), together with a valid exchange inequality for this neighborhood stating that every locally optimal \(S\) satisfies \(C(S)\le \alpha C(O)\) for every global optimum \(O\). These two components certify \(C(S)\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No improving local move certifies a global approximation only when paired with a neighborhood-specific exchange bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Optimality Certificates

children.title: Sweep-Based Rounding
children.top_down_role: Rounding families organized by ordered sweeps through candidate thresholds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison-model cost of maintaining every distinct coordinate-threshold set incrementally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given x\in[0,1]^n, sorting indices by nonincreasing x_i costs O(n\log n) comparisons. Batching equal positive values and inserting each index once maintains all m distinct nonempty sweep sets in O(n) additional update time. If feasibility and objective evaluation on the maintained set costs at most T per candidate, total time is O(n\log n+mT), where m\le n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After one sort, all distinct sweep sets can be maintained with linear update work; candidate evaluation determines the remaining cost.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ bounds evaluation of one incrementally maintained candidate}

Worst-case evaluation time per maintained candidate

assumptions_latex: The objective and feasibility predicate are evaluable on each sweep set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sweep examines every distinct set \(\{i:x_i\ge \tau\}\) for \(\tau\in(0,1]\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sweep examines every distinct coordinate level without redundantly testing equivalent thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(x\in[0,1]^n\), an objective \(C\), and a feasibility predicate \(\Phi\). Sort the distinct positive coordinate values as \(1\ge v_1>\cdots>v_m>0\). Starting with the empty set, sweep downward through these values, adding every index \(i\) satisfying \(x_i=v_r\) at step \(r\). The step-\(r\) candidate is \(S_r=\{i:x_i\ge v_r\}\). Evaluate each feasible \(S_r\) and output one minimizing \(C(S_r)\); report failure if none is feasible.

children.title: Threshold-Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Deterministic, adaptive, plus objective-sensitive choices among candidate thresholds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a deterministic threshold matching an average performance guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mu be a probability measure on thresholds and let h\ge0 be measurable with \mathbb E_{\tau\sim\mu}[h(\tau)]\le B<\infty. Then some threshold in the support of \mu satisfies h(\tau)\le B. If the support is finite and every value is computable, exhaustive selection returns a supported threshold of value at most B.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected threshold-rounding bound guarantees a deterministic threshold no worse than the mean; finite support permits exhaustive derandomization.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaging Derandomization for Threshold Choice

assumptions_latex: For randomized selection, \(R_x\) and \(g\circ R_x\) are measurable.
For exhaustive selection, the finite candidate set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Randomized threshold selection satisfies \(\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\mu}[g(R_x(\tau))]=\int_{(0,1]}g(R_x(t))\,d\mu(t)\), whereas exhaustive finite selection evaluates all thresholds in its support rather than sampling from that measure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: probability measures represent deterministic and randomized threshold choices
exhaustive finite threshold search is distinct from sampling a finite-support measure
source connecting these regimes to approximation rounding required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic, exhaustive, and randomized threshold choices admit related but distinct representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_x:(0,1]\to\mathcal F\cup\{\bot\}\) be a threshold-dependent rounding map. A randomized threshold-selection regime is a probability measure \(\mu\) on \((0,1]\). Deterministic selection is represented by a point mass \(\mu=\delta_\tau\), while randomized selection may use a finite-support measure or a continuous distribution. For any measurable nonnegative performance function \(g\), its expected performance is \(\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\mu}[g(R_x(\tau))]=\int_{(0,1]}g(R_x(t))\,d\mu(t)\), with \(g(\bot)=+\infty\) when infeasibility counts as failure. By contrast, exhaustive multi-threshold selection evaluates every threshold in a finite candidate set and returns the best feasible outcome; it is not equivalent to sampling from a finite-support measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed and randomized threshold choices can be represented by probability measures, while exhaustive multi-threshold search is a distinct regime that evaluates every candidate.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Selection Regimes

Define the retained set \(L_\tau=\{e\in E:x_e\ge \tau\}\) and the filtered vector by \(x'_e=x_e\) for \(e\in L_\tau\) and \(x'_e=0\) otherwise. Selecting every retained coordinate gives the incidence vector \(z_e=\mathbf 1\{e\in L_\tau\}\). For every nonnegative weight vector \(c\), \(c^{\mathsf T}z\le \tau^{-1}c^{\mathsf T}x\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) satisfy \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\) for every client \(j\), and let \(d_{ij}\ge 0\) be assignment distances. Define \(\bar d_j=\sum_i d_{ij}x_{ij}\). For a filtering parameter \(\rho>1\), discard every pair with \(d_{ij}>\rho\bar d_j\) and retain \(N_j=\{i:d_{ij}\le \rho\bar d_j\}\). Then \(\sum_{i\notin N_j}x_{ij}\le 1/\rho\), so the retained assignment mass is at least \(1-1/\rho\). Normalizing the retained assignments multiplies each retained mass by at most \(\rho/(\rho-1)\).

Facility-Clustering Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy clustering of fractionally served clients in a metric facility-location relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given facilities \(F\), clients \(D\), metric distances \(d\), and a feasible fractional solution \((x,y)\), define each client's average radius by \(r_j=\sum_{i\in F}d(i,j)x_{ij}\). Process clients in nondecreasing order of \(r_j\). When an unassigned client \(j\) is encountered, declare it a center and assign to its cluster every unassigned client \(k\) satisfying \(d(j,k)\leq \tau(r_j+r_k)\), where \(\tau\geq1\). Reassign each clustered client's fractional facility mass to facilities represented by its center, using a separately specified aggregation rule. Output the centers, clusters, and aggregated fractional instance for subsequent facility selection.

children.title: Capacity Filtering
children.top_down_role: Filtering interfaces for fractional assignments subject to capacity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold predicate separating facilities with sufficient fractional capacity support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For facility capacities \(u_i>0\), fractional openings \(y_i\in[0,1]\), and assigned loads \(\ell_i=\sum_j d_jx_{ij}\), fix \(\alpha\in(0,1]\). The capacity-filtered facility set is \[F_{\mathrm{cap}}(\alpha)=\{i:\ell_i\leq \alpha u_i y_i\}.\] Facilities outside this set are rejected or handled by a separate exceptional-set rule. Thus every retained facility has fractional utilization \(\ell_i/(u_i y_i)\leq\alpha\), with zero-opening facilities retained only when their load is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep precisely the facilities whose assigned fractional load is at most an alpha fraction of their fractionally available capacity.

children.title: Load Filtering
children.top_down_role: Filtering interfaces for controlling machine, facility, route, or resource load.

knowledge_statements.title: Load Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Markov-style removal of assignments whose facility load exceeds a chosen multiple of average load.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonnegative weights \(w_i\) satisfy \(W=\sum_iw_i>0\), and let \(\ell_i\geq0\) be facility loads. Define the weighted average \(\bar\ell=W^{-1}\sum_iw_i\ell_i\). For \(\beta>1\), retain \(G_\beta=\{i:\ell_i\leq\beta\bar\ell\}\) and remove the remaining facilities from the ordinary rounding instance. Then \[\sum_{i\notin G_\beta}w_i<\frac{W}{\beta}.\] The algorithm outputs the retained instance together with the removed weighted mass, which must be reassigned or charged separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard facilities loaded above beta times the weighted average; less than a 1/beta fraction of total facility weight is discarded.

notation.meaning: Facilities retained by the load filter

children.title: Capacity-Violation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes separating strict capacity preservation from bounded capacity violation.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Violation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative violation incurred when fractional capacity is normalized by scaling openings upward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a fractional solution obeys \(\ell_i\leq u_i y_i\). Fix \(\gamma\in(0,1]\), retain only facilities with \(y_i\geq\gamma\), and normalize their openings to one while preserving their assigned loads. Every retained facility then satisfies \(\ell_i\leq u_i\), so no capacity violation occurs. If instead assignments are scaled upward by at most \(1/\gamma\) while capacities remain unchanged, the only generally valid guarantee is \[\ell_i'\leq \frac{u_i}{\gamma}.\] Without additional redistribution structure, the factor \(1/\gamma\) cannot be improved from the inequality \(\ell_i\leq u_i y_i\) alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opening normalization is capacity-safe if loads stay fixed; scaling assignments by 1/gamma can force the same multiplicative capacity violation.
review_flags: The algebraic boundary is standard, but no supplied source identifies this as the intended capacity-violation regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf and the displayed upper bound follows from the listed assumptions. However, the statement alternates between scaling loads by 1/gamma and the distinct assumption ell_i' <= ell_i/(gamma y_i), while the claimed unimprovability is unsupported. A source specifying the intended scaling regime is required.

children.title: Scaling-Based Fractional Normalization
children.top_down_role: Scaling transformations used to normalize fractional mass, costs, capacities, or distances before rounding.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact behavior of homogeneous linear quantities before unit-box capping or coordinate deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For z\in\mathbb R_+^E and \alpha>0, define N_\alpha(z)=\alpha z. For every compatible matrix M and vector c, MN_\alpha(z)=\alpha Mz and c^{\mathsf T}N_\alpha(z)=\alpha c^{\mathsf T}z. Coordinatewise capping or deletion generally destroys these equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform uncapped scaling multiplies every linear load and cost exactly by the scale factor; capping or deletion generally leaves only inequality-based bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M(\alpha z)=\alpha Mz,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}(\alpha z)=\alpha c^{\mathsf T}z

Scaling-Based Fractional Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalize retained fractional coordinates by a common threshold and record the induced scaling factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z\in[0,1]^E\) and a threshold \(\gamma\in(0,1]\), retain \(E_\gamma=\{e:z_e\geq\gamma\}\) and define \(\widehat z_e=z_e/\gamma\) for retained coordinates, capped at one when unit-box feasibility is required: \[\widetilde z_e=\min\{1,z_e/\gamma\}.\] Delete or separately charge coordinates outside \(E_\gamma\). Any nonnegative linear cost satisfies \(c^\top\widetilde z\leq c^\top z/\gamma\). Output \(\widetilde z\), the discarded coordinates, and the scale factor \(1/\gamma\) for feasibility and approximation accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Filter small coordinates, divide retained values by gamma, cap at one if necessary, and charge at most a 1/gamma increase in nonnegative linear cost.

children.title: Scale-Sensitive Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasibility plus approximation effects arising from aggressive or nonuniform scaling.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary feasibility behavior under uniform coordinate downscaling in a nonnegative mixed packing-covering system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P=\{z\in[0,1]^E:Az\le b,\ Cz\ge d\}, where A,C are entrywise nonnegative. If z\in P and 0\le\lambda\le1, then z'=\lambda z satisfies Az'=\lambda Az\le\lambda b\le b and Cz'=\lambda Cz\ge\lambda d. Thus packing feasibility is preserved, while only a factor-\lambda covering guarantee is universal. Both factors are attained by one-variable constraints with equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Downscaling preserves nonnegative packing constraints but generally retains only a lambda fraction of a covering requirement; these bounds are sharp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(\lambda z)\le b,\qquad C(\lambda z)\ge\lambda d
knowledge_statements.title: Downscaling Feasibility Regime
Scale-Sensitive Feasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes which linear constraints survive coordinate scaling and optional capping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{z\in[0,1]^E:Az\leq b,\ Cz\geq d\}\), where \(A,C\) are entrywise nonnegative, and define \(S_\lambda(z)=\min\{\mathbf1,\lambda z\}\) componentwise for \(\lambda\geq1\). Upper-bound feasibility is guaranteed only under the relaxed right-hand side \(Az'\leq\lambda b\). Covering feasibility is preserved, because \(CS_\lambda(z)\geq Cz\geq d\). Consequently, scaling yields a mixed regime: packing constraints require a factor-\(\lambda\) resource augmentation, whereas nonnegative covering constraints remain feasible without augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling up preserves nonnegative covering constraints but may multiply packing loads by lambda, so packing feasibility needs matching resource augmentation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Select an integral constituent from an explicit convex decomposition of a fractional solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}(X)\) for a finite set \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), and suppose \(x=\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_kx^k\), where \(x^k\in X\), \(\lambda_k\geq0\), and \(\sum_k\lambda_k=1\). The deterministic output satisfies \(c^\top x^{k^*}\leq c^\top x\); randomized selection satisfies \(\mathbb E[x^k]=x\) and \(\mathbb E[c^\top x^k]=c^\top x\).

children.title: Flow Decomposition Rounding
children.top_down_role: Rounding based on decomposing fractional solutions into flow-supported components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination and output-size bound for bottleneck flow decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every bottleneck subtraction along a positive-support path or cycle makes at least one positive residual edge zero. Hence at most \(|E|\) components are extracted. Repeated support searches and residual updates give a polynomial-time decomposition algorithm with a polynomial-size explicit component list.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginal-preservation boundary when circulation is discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f=\sum_k\lambda_k\chi^{P_k}+g\) with a nonzero nonnegative circulation \(g\), then sampling only the paths with probabilities \(\lambda_k\) gives \[\Pr[e\in P_K]=f_e-g_e\] for every edge. Thus it cannot preserve the complete edge-marginal vector of \(f\) on edges with \(g_e>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact marginals and linear-cost preservation for a circulation-free unit-flow decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f=\sum_k\lambda_k\chi^{P_k}\) is a circulation-free decomposition of a unit \(s\)-\(t\) flow and \(\Pr[K=k]=\lambda_k\), then \[\Pr[e\in P_K]=f_e\quad(e\in E),\qquad \mathbb E[c(P_K)]=c^\top f.\] Consequently some constituent path has cost at most \(c^\top f\).

This produces paths with positive weights summing to one and \[f=\sum_k\lambda_k\chi^{P_k}+g,\] where \(g\) is a nonnegative circulation. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite bipartite graph \(G=(L\cup R,E)\) with \(|L|=|R|\), edge costs \(c\in\mathbb R^E\), and a doubly stochastic matrix \(X=(x_{ij})\) supported on \(E\), initialize the residual matrix \(R=X\). While \(R\neq0\), find a perfect matching \(M_k\) in its positive support, set \(\lambda_k=\min_{(i,j)\in M_k}R_{ij}\), and replace \(R\) by \(R-\lambda_k\chi^{M_k}\). The process terminates with \(X=\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_k\chi^{M_k}\), where \(\lambda_k>0\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_k=1\). Selecting \(k^*\in\arg\min_k c^\top\chi^{M_k}\) gives \(c^\top\chi^{M_{k^*}}\leq c^\top X\); alternatively, sampling \(M_k\) with probability \(\lambda_k\) preserves all edge marginals.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=\sum_k\lambda_kx^k\) be an explicit convex decomposition and suppose \(T(x^k)\in Y\) for every \(k\) with \(\lambda_k>0\). If \(\Pr[K=k]=\lambda_k\), then \(T(x^K)\in Y\) almost surely and, for every linear target observable \(a\), \[\mathbb E[a^\top T(x^K)]=\sum_k\lambda_k a^\top T(x^k).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constituent-wise feasible transfer guarantees target feasibility; linear target values average according to the decomposition weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(x^K)\in Y\text{ almost surely, and }\mathbb E[a^\top T(x^K)]=\sum_k\lambda_ka^\top T(x^k).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible fractional average can consist entirely of constituents whose transferred images are infeasible.

Decomposition-Transfer Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a decomposition preserves feasibility, marginals, and linear objective guarantees after transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\to Y\) map integral auxiliary solutions into feasible target solutions, and suppose an auxiliary fractional point has a decomposition \(x=\sum_k\lambda_kx^k\), with \(x^k\in X\). If a linear observable satisfies \(a^\top T(x^k)=b^\top x^k\) for every constituent, then sampling \(x^k\) with probability \(\lambda_k\) gives \[\mathbb E[a^\top T(x^k)]=b^\top x.\] If instead \(a^\top T(x^k)\leq\rho b^\top x^k+\delta\) for every constituent, some constituent satisfies \(a^\top T(x^k)\leq\rho b^\top x+\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constituent-wise feasible transfer preserves decomposed linear expectations; uniform affine bounds also guarantee one comparably good deterministic constituent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[a^\top T(x^k)]=b^\top x\quad\text{or}\quad \exists k:\ a^\top T(x^k)\leq\rho b^\top x+\delta

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical slot-matching rounding for a fractional generalized assignment with an additive one-job load guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each machine \(i\), order the jobs with \(x_{ij}>0\) by nonincreasing \(p_{ij}\), place their fractional masses consecutively into \(k_i=\lceil\sum_jx_{ij}\rceil\) unit slots, and join job \(j\) to every slot containing some of its mass, assigning that edge cost \(c_{ij}\). A minimum-cost matching covering all jobs produces an integral assignment \(\sigma\) with cost at most \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\). If \(L_i=\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\) and \(P_i=\max(\{p_{ij}:\sigma(j)=i\}\cup\{0\})\), then \(L_i\leq T+P_i\). In particular, if every eligible pair satisfies \(p_{ij}\leq T\), then \(L_i\leq2T\). The slot graph has polynomial size and the construction is polynomial-time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pack each machine's fractional job mass into ordered unit slots and find a minimum-cost job-to-slot matching. Cost does not increase, and each machine exceeds its fractional load bound by at most its largest assigned job.

notation.meaning: Fraction of job j assigned to machine i
Size of job j on machine i
Largest size assigned to machine i, or zero if it receives no job

knowledge_statements.title: Shmoys–Tardos Slot-Matching Rounding Theorem
Shmoys–Tardos Assignment Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slot-matching rounding for the generalized assignment LP with additive one-job load overflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each machine \(i\), order jobs by nonincreasing size \(p_{ij}\), partition its fractional assignment mass into consecutive unit-capacity slots, and connect every job to each slot containing some of its mass. Give such an edge the job's assignment cost. Compute a minimum-cost matching that covers every job, and assign each job to the machine owning its matched slot. If the fractional solution assigns every job completely and has machine load at most \(T\), then the integral assignment has cost no greater than the fractional cost and each machine's load is at most \(T+\max\{p_{ij}:j\text{ assigned to }i\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pack fractional job mass into machine slots and match jobs to slots, preserving cost while adding at most one assigned job size to each load.

notation.meaning: Fraction of job j assigned to machine i

review_flags: The named theorem is standard, but no supplied locator supports the Shmoys–Tardos load and cost guarantees.

children.title: Configuration-Based Rounding
children.top_down_role: Rounding from local or resource-specific configuration representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of independent local configuration sampling to enforce global item uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two resources independently select a configuration containing the same item \(j\), each with probability \(p>0\). Then both select \(j\) with probability \(p^2>0\), so the raw selections need not form a globally feasible allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent locally feasible configuration choices can select the same item twice.
assumptions_latex: Two resources can select configurations containing the same item.
Their selections are independent and each has positive probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Configuration Contention Failure
Configuration-Based Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round a configuration-LP solution by selecting integral local configurations and reconciling shared items.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For resources \(i\in I\), let \(\mathcal C_i\) be feasible local configurations and let \(y_{iC}\geq0\) satisfy \(\sum_{C\in\mathcal C_i}y_{iC}=1\). Select one configuration \(C_i\) for each resource, either independently with probability \(y_{iC}\) or through a dependent-rounding procedure preserving these marginals. If an item appears in several selected configurations, retain at most one copy according to a specified contention-resolution rule. Output the resulting integral allocation. Before contention resolution, every item \(j\) has expected multiplicity \(\sum_i\sum_{C\ni j}y_{iC}\); feasibility follows locally from \(C_i\in\mathcal C_i\) and globally from the contention rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one feasible configuration per resource from LP marginals, then resolve duplicate items to obtain a globally feasible integral allocation.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal C_i\text{ contains only locally feasible configurations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_i\in\mathcal C_i\text{ for all }i,\quad \text{and each item is retained at most once}

children.title: Pattern-Based Rounding
children.top_down_role: Rounding from pattern variables encoding admissible combinatorial choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input- and output-sensitive complexity of coordinatewise pattern ceiling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicitly stored vector \(x\in\mathbb R_+^q\), computing \(z_p=\lceil x_p\rceil\) for every coordinate uses \(O(q)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(q)\) storage. Explicitly listing every copy additionally requires time proportional to \(\sum_pz_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ceiling an explicit pattern vector is linear-time; expanding all copies is output-sensitive.
assumptions_latex: The fractional vector has \(q\) explicitly represented coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Pattern-Rounding Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between the seed's additive guarantee and multiplicative approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take one pattern of cost \(1\), supply vector \(a>0\), fractional multiplicity \(x=\varepsilon\), and demand \(d=\varepsilon a\), where \(0<\varepsilon<1\). The fractional cost is \(\varepsilon\), while ceiling returns one copy of cost \(1\), giving ratio \(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrarily small positive pattern fraction shows that coordinatewise ceiling has no generic multiplicative cost guarantee.

notation.meaning: fractional multiplicity of the sole pattern

knowledge_statements.title: No Generic Multiplicative Ceiling Bound
Pattern-Based Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise ceiling for a finite nonnegative covering-pattern LP; the guarantee is additive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\), set \(z_p:=\lceil x_p\rceil\) for every \(p\in\mathcal P\) and output \(z_p\) copies of pattern \(p\). Then \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}a^p z_p\ge d\) and \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}c_pz_p\le\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}c_px_p+\sum_{p:x_p\notin\mathbb Z}c_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round each pattern multiplicity upward. This preserves all nonnegative covering constraints and increases cost by at most the total cost of the fractionally used patterns.
assumptions_latex: The pattern family \(\mathcal P\) is finite and \(a^p\in\mathbb R_+^m\) for every \(p\in\mathcal P\).
The vector \(x\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal P}\) satisfies \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}a^p x_p\ge d\).
The costs satisfy \(c_p\ge0\) for every \(p\in\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer multiplicities cover \(d\) and satisfy the stated additive cost bound.

notation.meaning: nonnegative vector supplied by pattern p
rounded integer multiplicity of pattern p

children.title: Representation-Strength Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparisons of formulation strength, representation size, plus rounding compatibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Information Loss Within a Fiber
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal witness that aggregation can lose configuration-specific information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let distinct configurations \(C_1,C_2\) satisfy \(\pi(C_1)=\pi(C_2)\), with \(q_{C_1}=0\) and \(q_{C_2}=1\). Their unit vectors have the same aggregate but different values under \(q\), so the aggregate vector cannot recover every configuration-specific linear observable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Configurations in one aggregation fiber become indistinguishable even when their configuration-specific values differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Information Loss Within a Fiber

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strength Does Not Determine Computational Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit-size and oracle-access boundary for the representation comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Projection can reduce the number of named variables while producing exponentially many projected inequalities, and either representation may contain exponentially many columns. Efficient use therefore requires a polynomial explicit description or suitable separation and pricing oracles; representational strength alone does not imply computational tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregation may reduce visible variables without producing a compact or efficiently accessible formulation.
assumptions_latex: Configuration or pattern families may be implicitly represented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Projection size and computational accessibility require separate analysis.}
knowledge_statements.title: Strength Does Not Determine Computational Size

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact projection relation between linked configuration and pattern relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=A(Q)\), where \((A\lambda)_p=\sum_{C:\pi(C)=p}\lambda_C\). Then \(y\in P\) exactly when some \(\lambda\in Q\) satisfies \(A\lambda=y\). Every valid inequality \(u^\top y\le\gamma\) for \(P\) pulls back to \(u^\top A\lambda\le\gamma\) for \(Q\), and objectives factoring through \(A\) have equal optima over the linked formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pattern region is the configuration region's projection; aggregate objectives are preserved and a configuration lift certifies aggregate membership.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection and Exact Liftability
Representation-Strength Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional comparison of configuration variables with their pattern aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P:=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal P}:\exists\lambda\in Q,\ y_p=\sum_{C:\pi(C)=p}\lambda_C\}\). For coefficients satisfying \(q_C=\bar q_{\pi(C)}\), every such pair obeys \(\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}q_C\lambda_C=\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\bar q_p y_p\). Thus aggregation preserves linear data constant on each fiber of \(\pi\), but \(y\) does not determine configuration-specific data that vary within a fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pattern aggregation exactly preserves linear information constant on each aggregation fiber, while configuration-specific information varying within a fiber cannot be recovered from the aggregate variables alone.
assumptions_latex: The families \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal P\) are finite.
The map \(\pi:\mathcal C\to\mathcal P\) aggregates configurations into patterns.
The set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R_+^{\mathcal C}\) is a configuration relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregation is exact for linear data factoring through \(\pi\), whereas data varying within a fiber are not determined by \(y\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: linear projection preserves data factoring through its aggregation map

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Rank-Based Large-Coordinate Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that the sigma-over-r guarantee cannot be improved using only rank and total fractional mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let r\ge1 and 0<\sigma<r. Put a=\sigma/r, A=I_r, and b=a\mathbf1. The boxed equality polytope P=\{x\in[0,1]^r:Ax=b\} has the unique extreme point x=a\mathbf1. All r coordinates are fractional, their sum is \sigma, and \max_i x_i=\sigma/r.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r singleton polytope can have r equal fractional coordinates of total mass sigma, so the sigma-over-r guarantee is tight.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Rank-Based Large-Coordinate Bound
Large-Coordinate Phenomena
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-based large-coordinate consequence for boxed equality polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:0<x_i<1\}\). Then \(|F|\le r\), and if \(\sum_{i\in F}x_i\ge\sigma>0\), then \(\max_{i\in F}x_i\ge\sigma/r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme point has at most rank-many fractional coordinates. If their total mass is at least sigma, one of them is at least sigma divided by the rank.
assumptions_latex: The vector \(x\) is an extreme point of \(P\).

notation.meaning: positive lower bound on total fractional mass

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fractional columns at a boxed-polyhedron extreme point are linearly independent

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is extreme in }P\iff \operatorname{rank}\!\begin{pmatrix}A\\ I_{B(x)}\end{pmatrix}=n\iff \{A_i:i\in F(x)\}\text{ is linearly independent};\quad |F(x)|\le\operatorname{rank}(A),\text{ and the bound is sharp}.

notation.meaning: indices strictly between their box bounds
identity rows indexed by active bound coordinates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent active-constraint rank test and sharpness of the boxed-equality support bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following are equivalent: \(x\) is an extreme point of \(P\); the equality rows together with the active box-bound rows have rank \(n\); and the columns \(\{A_i:i\in F(x)\}\) are linearly independent. Hence \(|F(x)|\le\operatorname{rank}(A)\). Equality is possible: if \(A=I_r\) and \(b\in(0,1)^r\), then \(P=\{b\}\) and \(|F(b)|=r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boxed-equality feasible point is extreme exactly when its equalities and active bounds have full rank, equivalently when its fractional columns are independent. The resulting rank bound is best possible.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an extreme point of a boxed equality polyhedron, the columns associated with fractional variables are independent, so the fractional support has size at most the matrix rank.
assumptions_latex: The vector \(x\) is an extreme point of \(P\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point structure of the weakly supermodular cut relaxation used by Jain's method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph, \(m=|E(G)|\), and let \(f:2^{V(G)}\to\mathbb Z_+\) be weakly supermodular. If \(x\) is a basic solution of the cut LP and \(0<x_e<1\) for every \(e\in E(G)\), then there is a laminar family \(\mathcal B\subseteq2^{V(G)}\) of \(m\) tight sets such that \(\{\chi^B:B\in\mathcal B\}\) is linearly independent in \(\mathbb R^{E(G)}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservation law underlying token-counting contradiction certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A valid token assignment conserves nonnegative source mass: \(\sum_La_{iL}=w_i\) for every source. If receiver \(L\) receives at most \(u_L\), total source mass cannot exceed total receiver capacity. Thus \(\sum_iw_i>\sum_Lu_L\) refutes at least one asserted conservation or capacity condition. The inference is not valid if mass may be lost, duplicated, or assigned with unrestricted sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A token argument conserves nonnegative mass from sources to receivers. Receiver capacities must cover all source mass, so a strict deficit is a contradiction; lost, duplicated, or signed mass invalidates the inference.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist nonempty \(P\subseteq[0,1]^U\) and \(x\in P\) with \(0<x_i<1\) for which both binary faces are empty. In particular, for \(P=\{x\in[0,1]:x=\tfrac12\}\), \(P\cap\{x=0\}=P\cap\{x=1\}=\varnothing\).

assumptions_latex: Fixings are restricted to values in \(\{0,1\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records objective preservation when an optimal LP coordinate is fixed at its current integral value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\in\arg\min\{c^\top x:x\in P\subseteq[0,1]^U\}\) and \(x_i^*\in\{0,1\}\). For \(P'=\{z:(z,x_i^*)\in P\}\), \(x^*_{U\setminus\{i\}}\) minimizes \(c_{U\setminus\{i\}}^\top z\) over \(P'\), and \[\min_{x\in P}c^\top x=c_ix_i^*+\min_{z\in P'}c_{U\setminus\{i\}}^\top z.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing an integral coordinate at its value in an optimal LP solution preserves a residual optimum and the optimum value after accounting for the fixed cost.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is optimal for the current LP.

notation.meaning: fixed face projected onto the remaining coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Preservation by Integral Fixing
Variable Fixing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One iterative-rounding update fixing a coordinate already integral in the current solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(i\in U_t\) with \(x_i^t\in\{0,1\}\), set \(\bar x_i:=x_i^t\), define \(U_{t+1}:=U_t\setminus\{i\}\), and set \(P_{t+1}:=\{x_{U_{t+1}}:(x_{U_{t+1}},\bar x_i)\in P_t\}\). Then \(x^t_{U_{t+1}}\in P_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix a coordinate already equal to zero or one, substitute its value, and continue with the projected relaxation on one fewer undecided coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixing update preserves the current vector's feasibility and reduces \(|U_t|\) by one.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixing an integral coordinate preserves the current feasible solution

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\subseteq P',\quad \inf_{x\in P'}c^Tx\le\inf_{x\in P}c^Tx,\quad \sup_{x\in P'}c^Tx\ge\sup_{x\in P}c^Tx;\text{ deletion alone gives no bound on }g_k.
review_flags: finite-step bound applies only when no constraints are reintroduced
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective monotonicity, finite pure-deletion progress, and the absence of a feasibility guarantee from deletion alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dropping \(k\) gives \(P\subseteq P'\), so a minimization infimum cannot increase and a maximization supremum cannot decrease. A sequence that only deletes members of an initial finite active set \(J_0\) has at most \(|J_0|\) dropping steps. Containment gives no violation bound: dropping \(x\le0\) from \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}\) yields \(P'=\mathbb R\), on which the discarded-constraint violation is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping enlarges the relaxation, weakens its objective bound, and gives finite progress when constraints are only deleted. It provides no control over the discarded constraint without a separate certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Dropping Monotonicity and Uncertified-Loss Boundary
Constraint Dropping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic iterative-relaxation deletion rule requiring an explicit terminal-loss certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select \(k\in J_t\) only with a certificate that every permitted terminal continuation either satisfies \(g_k(z)\le\Delta_k\) or admits a repair of loss at most \(\Delta_k\). Set \(J_{t+1}:=J_t\setminus\{k\}\) and \(P_{t+1}:=\{x\in B_t:g_j(x)\le0\text{ for every }j\in J_{t+1}\}\). Then \(P_t\subseteq P_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Drop a constraint only when a certificate bounds either its terminal violation or the loss of repairing it. Removing the constraint enlarges the current relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The current relaxation is \(P_t=\{x\in B_t:g_j(x)\le0\text{ for every }j\in J_t\}\).
A certificate supplies either a terminal violation bound or a repair-loss bound \(\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dropping \(k\) enlarges the relaxation, and its terminal effect is controlled in the specific sense certified by \(\Delta_k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: iterative relaxation couples constraint deletion with a bounded-loss certificate

assumptions_latex: P_0\subseteq P_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq P_m\text{ are the feasible regions produced by a finite sequence of weakening modifications}.
R_t:P_t\to P_{t-1}\text{ is a repair map for }t=1,\ldots,m.
\ell(R_t(z))\le\ell(z)+\Delta_t\text{ for every }z\in P_t,\text{ where }\Delta_t\ge0\text{ and }\ell\text{ is a common additive loss measure}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_0\subseteq P_m\quad\text{and}\quad R_1\circ R_2\circ\cdots\circ R_m:P_m\to P_0\text{ has loss at most }\sum_{t=1}^m\Delta_t.

certified loss increment for modification t

modification alone does not imply termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition invariant for a finite sequence of certified constraint modifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Valid weakening modifications compose to give \(P_0\subseteq P_m\). If each step has a repair map \(R_t:P_t\to P_{t-1}\) increasing a common loss measure by at most \(\Delta_t\), the composed repair returns any terminal point in \(P_m\) to \(P_0\) with total loss at most \(\sum_t\Delta_t\). Without the weakening implication, previously feasible points may be removed; without composable repairs, per-step terminal bounds cannot in general be added.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakening modifications preserve nested feasible regions. Compatible repair maps compose and their additive losses sum; containment or loss aggregation can fail when the corresponding hypotheses are absent.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Certified Modifications
Constraint Modification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic iterative-relaxation rule replacing one constraint by a weaker constraint with a terminal certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace constraint \(g_k^t(x)\le0\) by \(\widetilde g_k(x)\le0\) only if \(g_k^t(x)\le0\) implies \(\widetilde g_k(x)\le0\) for every \(x\in B_t\). Define \(P_{t+1}:=\{x\in B_t:\widetilde g_k(x)\le0,\ g_j^t(x)\le0\text{ for every }j\in J_t\setminus\{k\}\}\). Then \(P_t\subseteq P_{t+1}\), while the retained certificate controls either terminal violation or repair loss by \(\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a constraint by a weaker one on the common domain, preserving all currently feasible points, and retain a certificate bounding terminal violation or repair loss.
assumptions_latex: The current feasible region is \(P_t=\{x\in B_t:g_j^t(x)\le0\text{ for every }j\in J_t\}\).
A terminal violation or repair-loss certificate with bound \(\Delta_k\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The modified relaxation contains \(P_t\) and retains the separately specified terminal-loss guarantee.

assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\widetilde C\text{ are nonempty feasible sets}.
\text{Infima and suprema are interpreted in the extended-real sense}.
