review_flags: elementary optimization monotonicity under set inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of constraint relaxation on minimization and maximization values, including the strictness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\widetilde C\), relaxation can only decrease a minimization infimum and increase a maximization supremum. Strict containment alone does not imply strict change: for \(C=\{0\}\), \(\widetilde C=[0,1]\), and objective \(x\), both minimization optima equal \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation can only weaken the corresponding optimization bound. Even a strict enlargement can leave the optimum unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Value Monotonicity
Constraint Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-set inclusion definition, including additive right-hand-side relaxation as a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:=\{x\in B:g(x)\le b\}\) and \(\widetilde C:=\{x\in B:\widetilde g(x)\le\widetilde b\}\). The second constraint is a relaxation of the first on \(B\) exactly when \(C\subseteq\widetilde C\), and it is strict when \(C\subsetneq\widetilde C\). If \(\widetilde g=g\) and \(\widetilde b=b+\delta\) with \(\delta\ge0\), then every \(x\in\widetilde C\) satisfies \(g(x)-b\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint relaxes another on a common domain when its feasible set contains the original feasible set. Increasing the right-hand side by delta permits at most delta additive violation.
assumptions_latex: The constraints \(g(x)\le b\) and \(\widetilde g(x)\le\widetilde b\) are defined on a common domain \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The second constraint relaxes the first exactly when \(C\subseteq\widetilde C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: feasible-set inclusion is the standard definition of constraint relaxation

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded residual system is infeasible exactly when nonnegative row and bound multipliers cancel every variable coefficient while yielding a strictly positive contradiction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\iff\exists y,p,q\ge0:\ A^\top y+p-q=0,\ b^\top y+\ell^\top p-u^\top q>0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates feasibility-preserving relaxations from updates that may empty a residual LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\ge b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\ne\varnothing\). Deleting rows, decreasing their right-hand sides, decreasing \(\ell\), or increasing \(u\), without otherwise changing the system, produces \(\widetilde P\supseteq P\), hence \(\widetilde P\ne\varnothing\). Increasing a right-hand side, tightening a bound, adding a row, or fixing a variable need not preserve feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure relaxation cannot destroy feasibility, whereas restrictive updates can.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Monotonicity Under Pure Relaxation
Feasibility-Loss Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when an iterative fixing or constraint update destroys residual LP feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:Ax\ge b,\ 0\le x\le 1\}\), let \(F_0,F_1\subseteq E\) be disjoint sets fixed respectively to zero and one, and let \(R\) index retained rows. The updated relaxation is \[P'=\{x_{E\setminus(F_0\cup F_1)}:A_{R,E\setminus(F_0\cup F_1)}x\ge b_R-A_{R,F_1}\mathbf1,\ 0\le x\le1\}.\] Feasibility is lost exactly when \(P'=\varnothing\). Equivalently, by Farkas' lemma, loss occurs when some \(y\ge0\) and bound multipliers produce a nonnegative linear combination of the updated left-hand sides whose corresponding right-hand side is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iterative update crosses the feasibility boundary precisely when its residual linear program is empty, equivalently when the updated inequalities admit a Farkas infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P'=\varnothing\) if and only if the updated system has a Farkas infeasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Connectivity Survivable Network Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected cut formulation of minimum-cost survivable network design with pairwise edge-connectivity demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and integral requirements \(r_{uv}\ge0\), edge-connectivity survivable network design seeks a minimum-cost set \(F\subseteq E\) such that every pair \(u,v\in V\) has at least \(r_{uv}\) edge-disjoint \(u\)-\(v\) paths in \((V,F)\). Equivalently, defining \(f(S)=\max\{r_{uv}:u\in S,\ v\notin S\}\), feasibility is \[|F\cap\delta(S)|\ge f(S)\qquad\text{for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V.\] Its standard cut relaxation replaces incidence by \(x\in[0,1]^E\) and requires \(x(\delta(S))\ge f(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost edges so that every vertex pair receives its required number of edge-disjoint paths; equivalently, every separating cut meets the maximum demand it separates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is feasible if and only if \(|F\cap\delta(S)|\ge f(S)\) for every proper nonempty \(S\subset V\).

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S
largest pairwise requirement separated by S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iterative Half-Threshold Rounding for Survivable Network Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic iterative rounding of the edge-connectivity survivable-network cut relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $F\leftarrow\varnothing$ and $i\leftarrow1$. While $F$ is not feasible, define $f_i(S)=f(S)-|\delta(S)\cap F|$, solve LP (11.17) on $E\setminus F$ with requirement function $f_i$ to obtain a basic optimal solution $x$, set $F_i=\{e\in E\setminus F:x_e\ge\tfrac12\}$, update $F\leftarrow F\cup F_i$, and increment $i$. Return $F$ when it is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with no selected edges. While the selected set does not meet the survivable-network requirements, subtract its contribution from every cut requirement, solve the residual cut LP for a basic optimum, and add every remaining edge whose LP value is at least one half. Return the selected set when it becomes feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two \(s\)-\(t\) paths are element-disjoint relative to \(T\) when they share neither an edge nor an internal vertex in \(V\setminus T\); protected terminals may occur internally in several paths. The design variant seeks a minimum-cost subgraph satisfying prescribed lower bounds on these values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Element connectivity packs paths disjoint in edges and unprotected internal vertices and equals the minimum mixed edge/nonterminal separator size.

Element-Connectivity Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise terminal connectivity where edges and nonterminal vertices are failure elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be undirected with terminals \(T\subseteq V\). Two paths between distinct terminals \(s,t\in T\) are element-disjoint when they share neither an edge nor an internal vertex in \(V\setminus T\); internal terminal vertices may be shared. The element connectivity \(\lambda_G^{\mathrm{el}}(s,t)\) is the maximum number of pairwise element-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths. Equivalently, it is the minimum cardinality of a set \(Z\subseteq E\cup(V\setminus T)\) whose deletion separates \(s\) from \(t\). An element-connectivity design with requirements \(r_{st}\) asks for a minimum-cost subgraph satisfying \(\lambda^{\mathrm{el}}(s,t)\ge r_{st}\) for every terminal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Element connectivity counts terminal-to-terminal paths disjoint in edges and nonterminal internal vertices, while allowing terminals to be shared internally.
assumptions_latex: \(T\subseteq V\) is the protected terminal set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_G^{\mathrm{el}}(s,t)\) equals the minimum number of deletable edges and nonterminals separating \(s\) and \(t\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph, let \(D\) be a set of designated unordered pairs \(\{s,t\}\) with \(st\notin E\), let \(c:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and let \(r_{st}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for \(\{s,t\}\in D\). For distinct nonadjacent \(s,t\in V\), the local vertex connectivity \(\kappa_G(s,t)\) is the maximum number of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths. By the vertex form of Menger's theorem, \(\kappa_G(s,t)\) equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(Z\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) such that \(s\) and \(t\) lie in different components of \(G-Z\). The associated design variant seeks a minimum-cost subgraph \(H=(V,F)\), with cost \(\sum_{e\in F}c_e\), satisfying \(\kappa_H(s,t)\ge r_{st}\) for every \(\{s,t\}\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local vertex connectivity is the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths and, for nonadjacent endpoints, equals the minimum internal-vertex separator size. The design variant chooses a minimum-cost subgraph meeting specified requirements on designated pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Connectivity Variants

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(st\in E\), deletion of any \(Z\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) leaves the one-edge path \(st\). Thus no such \(Z\) separates the endpoints, whereas \(\kappa_G(s,t)\) remains finite. The elementary internal-vertex-separator form of Menger's theorem therefore requires nonadjacent endpoints or an explicitly modified adjacency convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For adjacent endpoints, internal-vertex deletion cannot remove the direct edge, so the usual finite separator formula requires a nonadjacency assumption.

children.title: Connectivity-Model Separations
children.top_down_role: Structural plus approximability differences between element-based and vertex-based requirements.

assumptions_latex: All displayed graphs are finite, simple, and undirected.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fully specified witnesses for both strict connectivity-model separations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For edge over element, let \(T=\{s,t\}\) and let the edges be those of the two paths \(s-a-v-c-t\) and \(s-b-v-d-t\). These paths are edge-disjoint, every \(s\)-\(t\) path uses the nonterminal \(v\), and \(\deg(s)=2\); hence \(\lambda^{\mathrm{edge}}(s,t)=2\) and \(\lambda^{\mathrm{el}}(s,t)=1\). For element over vertex, let \(T=\{s,t,z\}\) and use the two paths \(s-a-z-c-t\) and \(s-b-z-d-t\). They are element-disjoint because their only shared internal vertex is protected, every \(s\)-\(t\) path uses \(z\), and \(\deg(s)=2\); hence \(\lambda^{\mathrm{el}}(s,t)=2\) and \(\kappa(s,t)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two explicitly specified path-union graphs witness strict edge-over-element and element-over-vertex connectivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation Witnesses

assumptions_latex: Element-disjoint paths may share internal vertices in the protected terminal set but share neither edges nor internal vertices outside it.

notation.meaning: element connectivity relative to protected set T

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unifies the three connectivity conventions by varying the protected terminal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(s,t\in T_1\subseteq T_2\), every element-disjoint packing relative to \(T_1\) is feasible relative to \(T_2\), so \(\lambda^{\mathrm{el}}_{G,T_1}(s,t)\le \lambda^{\mathrm{el}}_{G,T_2}(s,t)\). With only \(s,t\) protected, element-disjointness is internal vertex-disjointness; with every vertex protected, it is edge-disjointness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Protecting more vertices can only increase element connectivity. Protecting only the endpoints gives vertex connectivity, while protecting every vertex gives edge connectivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity Ordering and Equality Regimes
Connectivity-Model Separations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares edge, element, and vertex connectivity for a protected terminal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For terminals \(s,t\in T\subseteq V(G)\), the three path packings satisfy \[\lambda_G^{\mathrm{edge}}(s,t)\ge\lambda_G^{\mathrm{el}}(s,t)\ge\kappa_G(s,t).\] Both inequalities can be strict. Two edge-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths sharing one nonterminal vertex give \(\lambda^{\mathrm{edge}}=2>1=\lambda^{\mathrm{el}}\). If two otherwise internally disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths share only a third terminal \(z\), then \(\lambda^{\mathrm{el}}=2>1=\kappa\), because \(z\) is protected in the element model but is an internal vertex in the vertex model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge connectivity dominates element connectivity, which dominates vertex connectivity; shared nonterminals and shared protected terminals give strict separations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_G^{\mathrm{edge}}(s,t)\ge\lambda_G^{\mathrm{el}}(s,t)\ge\kappa_G(s,t)\), and either inequality may be strict.

Degree-Bounded Spanning Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost spanning structures subject to local degree upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and bounds \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), the degree-bounded spanning-tree problem asks for a spanning tree \(T\subseteq E\) minimizing \(c(T)=\sum_{e\in T}c_e\) subject to \[|T\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\qquad(v\in V).\] More general degree-bounded spanning structures replace the spanning-tree family by a specified family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) and impose bounds \(\ell_v\le|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b_v\). An instance is feasible only if some member of \(\mathcal F\) satisfies every local bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a minimum-cost spanning tree or related spanning object while respecting prescribed lower and upper bounds on each vertex degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution \(F\in\mathcal F\) satisfies \(\ell_v\le|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b_v\) for every \(v\in V\).

children.title: Crossing Constraint Systems
children.top_down_role: Iterative-rounding settings with intersecting constraint supports lacking laminar organization.

assumptions_latex: For every \(S\in\mathcal C\), \(a_S\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(b_S\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\mathcal C\) is crossing-closed and \(A,B\in\mathcal C\) cross, then \(A\cap B,A\cup B\in\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-indexed constraints whose supports may overlap without containment.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite. Two sets \(A,B\subseteq V\) cross when each of \(A\cap B\), \(A\setminus B\), \(B\setminus A\), and \(V\setminus(A\cup B)\) is nonempty. A family \(\mathcal C\subseteq2^V\) is crossing-closed when \(A\cap B,A\cup B\in\mathcal C\) whenever \(A,B\in\mathcal C\) cross. Given \(m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), vectors \(a_S\in\mathbb R^m\), scalars \(b_S\in\mathbb R\), and a decision vector \(x\in\mathbb R^m\), a crossing constraint system is a set-indexed system \[a_S^\top x\ge b_S\qquad(S\in\mathcal C)\] whose index family contains crossing pairs. When \(\mathcal C\) is crossing-closed, replacing a crossing pair by its intersection and union keeps the replacement indices in \(\mathcal C\). Cut relaxations are a principal example, with \(a_S\) the incidence vector of \(\delta(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossing systems have constraints indexed by overlapping sets for which neither set contains the other; crossing closure retains the intersection and union of every crossing pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Crossing Constraint Systems

children.title: Laminar Constraint Systems
children.top_down_role: Iterative-rounding settings whose constraint supports form nested or disjoint families.

knowledge_statements.title: Laminar Constraint Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-indexed constraints whose supports are nested or disjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal L\subseteq2^V\) is laminar when, for every \(A,B\in\mathcal L\), at least one of \(A\subseteq B\), \(B\subseteq A\), or \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) holds. A laminar constraint system is a system \[a_S^\top x\ge b_S\qquad(S\in\mathcal L)\] indexed by such a family. Inclusion turns \(\mathcal L\) into a forest: the parent of a nonmaximal set is its unique minimal strict superset in \(\mathcal L\). For finite \(V\), every laminar family has at most \(2|V|-1\) distinct nonempty members when \(V\) is included as a root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Laminar constraints are indexed by sets that are always nested or disjoint, so their inclusion structure forms a forest.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal L\) contains distinct nonempty subsets of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every pair \(A,B\in\mathcal L\) is nested or disjoint, and \(|\mathcal L|\le2|V|-1\) when \(V\in\mathcal L\).

children.title: Structural Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Uncrossing, refinement, or restriction regimes that connect crossing systems to laminar structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncrossing transition from crossing tight cuts to a laminar generating family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\ge0\) satisfy \(x(\delta(S))\ge f(S)\) for every proper nonempty \(S\subset V\), where \(f\) is crossing supermodular: \(f(A)+f(B)\le f(A\cap B)+f(A\cup B)\) for crossing \(A,B\). If crossing sets \(A,B\) are tight and the cut-incidence vectors obey the corresponding submodular uncrossing inequality, then \(A\cap B\) and \(A\cup B\) are also tight. Repeated replacement of crossing tight pairs by these uncrossed pairs yields a laminar family whose incidence vectors span the same tight-constraint space, marking the transition from a crossing to a laminar structural regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under crossing supermodularity and cut submodularity, tight crossing constraints can be uncrossed until a laminar family spans the same tight-constraint space.
assumptions_latex: \(x(\delta(S))\ge f(S)\) for every proper nonempty \(S\subset V\).
The applicable cut-incidence uncrossing inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tight-cut space admits a laminar spanning family obtained by repeated uncrossing.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility condition for simplex-to-label rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{t_i}=e_i\) for terminals \(t_1,\ldots,t_k\). Any labeling map \(L:\Delta_k\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) satisfying \(L(e_i)=i\) induces labels \(\ell(v)=L(x_v)\) with \(\ell(t_i)=i\). Consequently, edges whose endpoints have different labels form a feasible multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex rounding map that fixes every simplex vertex preserves all terminal labels and yields a feasible multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell(t_i)=i\) for all \(i\), and \(\{uv\in E:\ell(u)\ne\ell(v)\}\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Fixing Feasibility Invariant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical cut representation of the multiway-cut simplex metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\Delta_k\), \(\frac12\lVert x-y\rVert_1=1-\sum_{i=1}^k\min\{x_i,y_i\}\). If \(\theta\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]\), then also \(\frac12\lVert x-y\rVert_1=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^k\Pr[\mathbf1\{x_i\ge\theta\}\ne\mathbf1\{y_i\ge\theta\}]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half the L1 distance between simplex points equals their missing coordinate overlap and half the expected number of separating coordinate-threshold cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Distance as Coordinate-Threshold Cuts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical single-threshold rounding of the multiway-cut simplex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given x_v\in\Delta_k with x_{t_i}=e_i, sample \theta\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1] and a uniformly random permutation \pi of [k]. For q=1,\ldots,k-1, assign every unassigned v satisfying x_{v,\pi(q)}\ge\theta to label \pi(q); assign all remaining vertices to \pi(k).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use one uniform coordinate threshold and a random terminal order, with the last terminal receiving all unassigned vertices.
assumptions_latex: Every vertex has an explicitly represented point in \Delta_k.
Every terminal is fixed at its corresponding simplex vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell(t_i)=i\text{ for every }i,\text{ and the crossing edges form a feasible multiway cut.}
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Threshold Permutation Simplex Rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime after a simplex solution has been supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After sampling \theta and \pi, scanning at most k-1 coordinates for every vertex assigns all labels in O(k|V|) time. Scanning E then constructs the cut in O(|E|) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One rounding sample and its cut take time linear in the simplex table plus the edge set.
assumptions_latex: The coordinates x_{v,i} are explicitly stored.
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Labeling Runtime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Argmax Simplex Rounding Has Unbounded Edge Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of deterministic largest-coordinate labeling as an LP-relative local rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For 0<\varepsilon<1/2, let x=(1/2+\varepsilon,1/2-\varepsilon) and y=(1/2-\varepsilon,1/2+\varepsilon). Deterministic argmax labeling separates x and y, whereas \frac12\lVert x-y\rVert_1=2\varepsilon. Its edgewise distortion is therefore 1/(2\varepsilon), which is unbounded as \varepsilon\downarrow0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Largest-coordinate labeling can separate arbitrarily close simplex points and has no bounded edgewise distortion.
knowledge_statements.title: Argmax Simplex Rounding Has Unbounded Edge Distortion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected cut guarantee for uniform-threshold permutation rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected nonnegative-cost multiway-cut instance and every feasible simplex solution x, uniform-threshold permutation rounding satisfies \[\mathbb E[c(\delta(\ell))]\le\left(\frac32-\frac1k\right)\frac12\sum_{uv\in E}c_{uv}\lVert x_u-x_v\rVert_1.\] Applied to an optimal simplex solution, it is a (3/2-1/k)-approximation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random threshold-and-permutation rounding for the simplex relaxation of multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For terminals \(t_1,\ldots,t_k\), solve the simplex relaxation assigning each vertex \(v\) a vector \(x_v\in\Delta_k\), with \(x_{t_i}=e_i\), minimizing \(\frac12\sum_{uv\in E}c_{uv}\lVert x_u-x_v\rVert_1\). Sample \(\theta\) uniformly from \((1/2,1)\) and a uniformly random permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). In permutation order except for the last index, assign every unassigned vertex \(v\) satisfying \(x_{v,\pi(j)}\ge\theta\) to terminal \(t_{\pi(j)}\). Assign all remaining vertices to the last terminal. Output the edges whose endpoints receive different terminals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic sequential metric-ball extraction primitive.

The nonempty outputs are disjoint and cover \(V\); edges joining distinct outputs form the induced multicut.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An edge \(uv\) is separated by \(B_s(R)\) only when \(R\) lies between \(d(s,u)\) and \(d(s,v)\). Therefore \(\Pr[|\{u,v\}\cap B_s(R)|=1]\le\min\{1,|d(s,u)-d(s,v)|/(b-a)\}\le\min\{1,d(u,v)/(b-a)\}\).

Then \(\int_a^b c(\delta(B_s(r)))\,dr=\sum_{uv\in E}c_{uv}\ell_{uv}([a,b])\). Consequently some \(r\in[a,b]\) satisfies \(c(\delta(B_s(r)))\le (b-a)^{-1}\sum_{uv}c_{uv}\ell_{uv}([a,b])\le (b-a)^{-1}\sum_{uv}c_{uv}d(u,v)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic metric-LP rounding by extracting balls and deleting their boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite metric space \((V,d)\), nonnegative edge costs \((c_{uv})\), and an admissible radius set \(R\subseteq[0,\infty)\), initialize \(U\leftarrow V\). While \(U\neq\varnothing\), select a center \(s\in U\) and radius \(r\in R\), form \(B_U(s,r)=\{v\in U:d(s,v)\le r\}\), output this ball as the next cluster, and set \(U\leftarrow U\setminus B_U(s,r)\). The radius-selection rule may minimize or bound the boundary cost \(c(\delta(B_U(s,r)))\). The resulting clusters form a partition of \(V\); edges with endpoints in distinct clusters constitute the rounded cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly select a metric ball, output it as a cluster, and remove it. Choosing radii with inexpensive boundaries controls the resulting cut cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Diameter Alone Does Not Control Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary between partition feasibility and probabilistic separation quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\Delta>0\) and \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta\), the two-point metric \(V=\{u,v\}\) with \(d(u,v)=\varepsilon\) has the \(\Delta\)-bounded singleton partition \(\{\{u\},\{v\}\}\), which separates \(u,v\) with probability one. Hence bounded diameter alone implies no universal estimate \(\Pr[\mathcal P(u)\ne\mathcal P(v)]\le C d(u,v)/\Delta\) with fixed \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-diameter partition may always separate two arbitrarily close points, so diameter feasibility alone gives no distance-proportional separation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Diameter Alone Does Not Control Separation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic output object for cluster-based metric rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(\Delta\)-bounded cluster partition of a finite metric space \((V,d)\) is a partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\) such that \(\operatorname{diam}_d(C)\le\Delta\) for every \(C\in\mathcal P\). A random \(\Delta\)-bounded partition is a probability distribution supported on such partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-diameter cluster partition covers every vertex exactly once and gives every cluster diameter at most Delta; randomized clustering is a distribution over these partitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\text{ is }\Delta\text{-bounded}\iff \mathcal P\text{ partitions }V\text{ and }\max_{C\in\mathcal P}\operatorname{diam}_d(C)\le\Delta.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Diameter Cluster Partition
Cluster-Based Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rounding a fractional metric by directly constructing bounded-diameter clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite metric space \((V,d)\), a scale \(\Delta>0\), and a cluster-selection rule, initialize \(U\leftarrow V\). While \(U\neq\varnothing\), choose a nonempty set \(C\subseteq U\) satisfying \(\operatorname{diam}_d(C)\le\Delta\), output \(C\), and replace \(U\) by \(U\setminus C\). When the rule is randomized, it additionally specifies a distribution for which pairwise separation probabilities \(\Pr[u\text{ and }v\text{ are separated}]\) can be bounded in terms of \(d(u,v)/\Delta\). The output incidence vectors of the clusters give an integral partition of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construct disjoint bounded-diameter clusters until every vertex is assigned; probabilistic variants control pair-separation probabilities using fractional metric distances.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(d\) is a metric on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The produced sets are disjoint, cover \(V\), and each have \(d\)-diameter at most \(\Delta\).

children.title: Radius-to-Cluster Interfaces
children.top_down_role: How radius choices induce clusters plus affect separation, coverage, or cost.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact expressive boundary of the fixed-center radius interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(s\), the sets \(B(s,r)\) are nested. A nonempty proper subset \(C\subset V\) equals \(B(s,r)\) for some \(r\ge0\) exactly when \(s\in C\) and \(\max_{x\in C}d(s,x)<\min_{y\notin C}d(s,y)\). The full set is representable by every sufficiently large radius, whereas the empty set is not representable when \(s\in V\) and \(r\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-center radii represent exactly distance-threshold sets containing the center; they do not represent arbitrary clusters.
assumptions_latex: \(s\in V\) is fixed and closed balls with \(r\ge0\) are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=B(s,r)\) is governed exactly by the stated distance-threshold condition and endpoint convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Center Radius Representability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion from a radius to a fixed-center cluster and pair-separation event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(s\in V\), define \(B(s,r)=\{x\in V:d(s,x)\le r\}\). If \(a=d(s,u)\le b=d(s,v)\), then \(B(s,r)\) separates \(u,v\) exactly when \(a\le r<b\). For a nonnegative random radius \(R\), \(\Pr[|B(s,R)\cap\{u,v\}|=1]=\Pr[a\le R<b]\); if \(R\) has continuous distribution function \(F\), this is \(F(b)-F(a)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-ball radius gives a threshold cluster; two points at center-distances a≤b are separated exactly for radii in [a,b).

notation.meaning: closed metric ball centered at s
continuous distribution function of R when invoked

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Ball Radius Interface
Radius-to-Cluster Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface translating ball radii into clusters and boundary events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite metric space \((V,d)\), center \(s\in V\), and radius \(r\ge0\), define the cluster \(C(s,r)=\{v\in V:d(s,v)\le r\}\). For any pair \(u,v\in V\), the ball separates them precisely when \(\mathbf 1_{C(s,r)}(u)\ne\mathbf 1_{C(s,r)}(v)\), equivalently when exactly one of \(d(s,u)\) and \(d(s,v)\) is at most \(r\). Thus a radius-selection rule induces a cluster-selection rule, and a distribution on radii induces pairwise separation probabilities by measuring the radii lying between the two center distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected radius defines a cluster as its metric ball; a pair is separated exactly when the radius lies between its two center distances.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(d\) is a metric on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Radius selection and ball-cluster selection are equivalent through \(C(s,r)=\{v:d(s,v)\le r\}\).

notation.meaning: cluster induced by center s and radius r

The indicator characterization is correct for a closed ball, with separation occurring when the radius is at least the smaller center distance and strictly below the larger one. The conclusion overstates this as equivalence with unrestricted cluster selection: radius selection represents only clusters that are balls about the specified center. With no cited source, the intended interface scope cannot be resolved reliably.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deleted Tree Edges Certify the Output Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact partition and separation certificate for edge-deletion rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a tree \(T=(W,E_T)\) and \(F\subseteq E_T\), the connected components of \(T-F\) partition \(W\). Two vertices \(u,v\) lie in different components exactly when their unique path \(P_T(u,v)\) contains an edge of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleted tree edges yield a component partition and certify pair separation through unique paths.
knowledge_statements.title: Deleted Tree Edges Certify the Output Partition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tree Metrics Decompose into Edge-Cut Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical tree-specific representation underlying cut rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(W,E_T)\) be a tree with lengths \(\ell_e\ge0\). Removing \(e\) induces a bipartition \((A_e,W\setminus A_e)\). For all \(u,v\in W\), \(d_T(u,v)=\sum_{e\in E_T}\ell_e\mathbf1\{|\{u,v\}\cap A_e|=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted tree distance is the nonnegative sum of the cut metrics induced by its edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree Metrics Decompose into Edge-Cut Metrics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding object used by generic tree-metric rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distribution \mathcal D over tree metrics d_T on a set containing V is dominating with expected stretch \alpha for (V,d) if d_T(u,v)\ge d(u,v) for every sampled T and pair u,v, and \mathbb E_T[d_T(u,v)]\le\alpha d(u,v) for every pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dominating random tree never contracts original distances and expands each pair by at most alpha in expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\preceq d_T\text{ almost surely},\qquad \mathbb E[d_T]\preceq\alpha d\text{ pairwise.}
knowledge_statements.title: Dominating Random Tree Embedding

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noncontraction and Stretch Serve Distinct Transfer Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundaries for generic tree-mediated rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Without bounded expected stretch, the two-point metric d(u,v)=1 may be represented by tree distances d_T(u,v)=M with arbitrarily large M, so no uniform distance-linear upper-bound factor follows. Without domination, tree distances d_T(u,v)=\varepsilon<1 can make a tree-side feasibility or lower-bound test ignore almost all of an original unit separation. Thus expected stretch is essential for cost transfer, while domination is essential whenever the reduction relies on noncontraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbounded expansion destroys cost factors, while contraction invalidates reductions that rely on preserving original separations.
assumptions_latex: The claimed guarantees are required uniformly over nonnegative pair coefficients or noncontraction-based feasibility tests.
M can be arbitrarily large and \varepsilon can be arbitrarily small and positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Bounded expected stretch and required noncontraction must be checked separately.}
knowledge_statements.title: Noncontraction and Stretch Serve Distinct Transfer Requirements

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal transfer rule for a tree-rounding cost analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a_{uv}\ge0. If a rounding rule on every sampled tree satisfies \[\mathbb E[Z_T\mid T]\le\gamma\sum_{u<v}a_{uv}d_T(u,v),\] and \mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le\alpha d(u,v), then \[\mathbb E[Z_T]\le\gamma\alpha\sum_{u<v}a_{uv}d(u,v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative analysis linear in tree distances transfers with the embedding's expected-stretch loss.
assumptions_latex: The expected pairwise stretch is at most \alpha.
The conditional tree-rounding bound holds for every sampled tree.

notation.meaning: Cost produced after rounding the sampled tree.

review_flags: Domination is not needed for this upper-bound calculation itself; it is separately needed when feasibility or lower-bound comparisons require noncontraction.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Distance-Linear Transfer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical existence and sampling result for arbitrary finite metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every n-point metric admits a polynomial-time samplable distribution over dominating hierarchically separated tree metrics with expected stretch O(\log n): for a universal C, \[d_T(u,v)\ge d(u,v),\qquad \mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le C\log n\,d(u,v)\] for all pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite metric embeds into a random dominating hierarchical tree with logarithmic expected stretch.
assumptions_latex: (V,d) is a finite metric with n\ge2.
Distances are explicitly represented or available through a polynomial-time oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal D:\ \alpha(\mathcal D)=O(\log n),\text{ and }T\sim\mathcal D\text{ is polynomial-time samplable.}
review_flags: A canonical FRT theorem locator is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Tree-Embedding Theorem
Tree-Metric Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rounding through a distribution of dominating tree metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite metric \((V,d)\) and a distribution \(\mathcal D\) over weighted trees whose leaves contain \(V\), sample \(T\sim\mathcal D\). Apply a tree rounding rule that deletes a specified set \(F_T\subseteq E(T)\); assign two original vertices to the same cluster exactly when they remain connected in \(T-F_T\). If every sampled tree dominates \(d\), meaning \(d_T(u,v)\ge d(u,v)\), and satisfies \(\mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le\alpha d(u,v)\), then any tree-rule analysis linear in tree distances transfers in expectation with multiplicative loss at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embed the fractional metric into a random dominating tree, round by deleting tree edges, and transfer distance-linear guarantees with the embedding’s expected stretch.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and \(d\) is a metric.
\(\mathcal D\) dominates \(d\) and has expected stretch at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deleting \(F_T\) yields an integral partition, with expected distance-linear loss bounded by the tree guarantee times \(\alpha\).

notation.meaning: shortest-path metric of the sampled weighted tree
tree edges deleted by the rounding rule

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is a plausible content kind for Tree-Metric Rounding, but the claimed transfer for any analysis linear in tree distances is not formalized: the relevant objective, coefficients, tree-rounding guarantee, and relation between deleted tree edges and the original problem are unspecified. No source is supplied for either the embedding assumptions or the asserted transfer principle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radius-One Boundary of the Cardinality Estimate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of the stated normalized small-ball estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(r=1\), the spreading inequality yields no upper bound on \(|B(u,1)|\): the derived inequality \(|B|-k\le r(|B|-1)\) reduces to \(k\ge1\). Thus arbitrarily large radius-one balls are compatible with this inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized spreading constraint controls ball size only below radius one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r=1\) gives no finite cardinality bound from the spreading inequality alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Radius-One Boundary of the Cardinality Estimate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality consequence of the stated spreading normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(d\) is a semimetric and \(\sum_{v\in S}d(u,v)\ge |S|-k\) for every \(u\in S\subseteq V\) with \(|S|>k\). For \(0\le r<1\), every ball \(B(u,r)=\{v:d(u,v)\le r\}\) satisfies \(|B(u,r)|\le\left\lfloor\frac{k-r}{1-r}\right\rfloor\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated normalization, a ball of radius below one has at most floor((k-r)/(1-r)) vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is a nonnegative symmetric semimetric with \(d(u,u)=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Spreading Inequalities Bound Small Balls

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization used by the accepted small-ball theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer k\ge1, a semimetric d on finite V is normalized k-spreading if, for every u\in S\subseteq V with |S|>k, \[\sum_{v\in S}d(u,v)\ge |S|-k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized k-spreading semimetric forces every set larger than k to have sufficient total distance from each member.
assumptions_latex: d is nonnegative, symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and has d(u,u)=0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\text{ is normalized }k\text{-spreading}\iff\forall u\in S,\ |S|>k:\ \sum_{v\in S}d(u,v)\ge|S|-k.
review_flags: This is one normalization; other spreading relaxations use different scales and right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Cardinality-Spreading Semimetric

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spreading Alone Does Not Bound Cut Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of a problem-specific objective and charging relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Spreading inequalities constrain only d. If arbitrary nonnegative edge charges c_e are introduced without a relation to a fractional objective, multiplying every charge by M>0 preserves all spreading inequalities and ball-cardinality conclusions while multiplying each nonzero boundary cost by M. Hence spreading alone implies no absolute boundary-cost approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spreading controls metric cardinality but not charged boundary cost unless charges are tied to an objective.
assumptions_latex: At least one considered cluster has a nonempty charged boundary.
Charges are otherwise unconstrained by the semimetric relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Spreading constraints alone imply no finite universal boundary-cost bound.}
knowledge_statements.title: Spreading Alone Does Not Bound Cut Cost
Spreading-Metric Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition rounding from a metric satisfying local spreading inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((V,d)\) be a finite semimetric satisfying spreading inequalities \(\sum_{v\in S}d(u,v)\ge |S|-k\) for every \(u\in S\subseteq V\) with \(|S|>k\). Initialize \(U\leftarrow V\). Repeatedly choose \(u\in U\) and a radius \(r\) from a prescribed interval, output \(B_U(u,r)\), and remove it from \(U\), choosing \(r\) so that the boundary cost is controlled by the fractional metric cost. The spreading inequalities prevent a sufficiently small-radius output ball from containing too many vertices, while iteration produces an integral partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spreading inequalities limit small metric balls; region-growing then extracts capacity-controlled clusters whose boundary cost is charged to the fractional metric.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) is a nonnegative symmetric semimetric satisfying the triangle inequality.
The stated spreading inequalities hold for an integer \(k\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Iterative ball extraction produces an integral partition whose cluster sizes and boundary cost are controlled by the spreading constraints and radius rule.

notation.meaning: vertices of U at semimetric distance at most r from u
target upper scale for cluster cardinality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the Spreading-Metric Rounding leaf, but the normalization of the spreading inequalities, the prescribed radius interval, the cluster-size bound, and the boundary-cost factor are all essential and unspecified. These details vary by relaxation and problem. No source is cited, so the stated algorithmic guarantee is not reliable enough for candidate review.

assumptions_latex: Each instance has an integral feasible set contained in its LP relaxation.
Only ratios with positive denominators are included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every uniform LP-relative rounding factor is at least the corresponding worst-case integrality gap; an unbounded gap excludes every uniform finite factor.

notation.meaning: integral and LP optima of instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family-wise integrality-gap barrier for minimization and maximization LP rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization define \(\operatorname{gap}_{\min}=\sup_{I:z_{LP}(I)>0}z_I(I)/z_{LP}(I)\); for maximization define \(\operatorname{gap}_{\max}=\sup_{I:z_I(I)>0}z_{LP}(I)/z_I(I)\). If rounding guarantees respectively \(z(\widehat x)\le\rho z_{LP}(I)\) or \(z(\widehat x)\ge z_{LP}(I)/\rho\), then \(\rho\) is at least the corresponding gap. If the relevant supremum is unbounded, no uniform finite LP-relative factor exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The worst-case ratio between integral and fractional optima lower-bounds every approximation factor certified against that LP, in both minimization and maximization.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimization and Maximization Integrality-Gap Barriers
Weak-LP Integrality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation barrier imposed by a relaxation’s integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with integral feasible set \(X_I\subseteq X_{LP}\) and nonnegative objective \(c\), define \(z_I(c)=\min_{x\in X_I}c(x)\), \(z_{LP}(c)=\min_{x\in X_{LP}}c(x)\), and \(\operatorname{gap}(X_{LP})=\sup_{c:z_{LP}(c)>0}z_I(c)/z_{LP}(c)\). If an LP-rounding algorithm always maps an optimal fractional solution to an integral solution of value at most \(\rho z_{LP}(c)\), then necessarily \(\rho\ge\operatorname{gap}(X_{LP})\). Hence a family with unbounded gap admits no uniform finite-factor guarantee measured against that relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP’s integrality gap lower-bounds every rounding factor certified against its fractional optimum; an unbounded gap rules out any uniform finite guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with \(X_I\subseteq X_{LP}\).
Objectives are nonnegative and instances considered in the ratio have positive LP optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any universal LP-relative rounding factor \(\rho\) satisfies \(\rho\ge\operatorname{gap}(X_{LP})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct content kind, and the integrality-gap obstruction is mathematically standard. However, the supremum is written over objectives for one fixed pair of feasible sets while the prose also refers to a family of instances; that scope should be tied to an authoritative definition. Because source_refs is empty, the nontrivial barrier claim lacks the required inspectable citation.

assumptions_latex: The linear minimum over \(P\) is attained, and \(X_I\subseteq P\) is the integral feasible set.
\(R_\rho\subseteq P\) is exactly the trigger domain of a specified factor-\(\rho\) local rounding rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{vert}(F_c)\cap R_\rho=\varnothing\), selecting an optimal extreme point cannot invoke the specified factor-\(\rho\) rule.

notation.meaning: face minimizing objective c over P
trigger domain of the specified factor-rho rule

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-relative failure of rounding schemes that require a local property at an optimal LP vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_c=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\). If every vertex of \(F_c\) lies outside \(R_\rho\), then no choice of an optimal extreme point satisfies the specified rule's trigger. This excludes only that rule and factor on that relaxation; it does not exclude changing the relaxation, using nonlocal recovery, accepting another factor, or permitting stated violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If none of the optimal LP vertices satisfies a rounding rule's trigger, optimal-extreme-point selection cannot invoke that rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Roundability Obstruction
Absence of Roundable Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point rounding fails when all optimal vertices violate its local rounding predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a relaxation, \(X_I\subseteq P\) its integral points, and \(R_\rho\subseteq P\) the fractional points from which a specified local rule can produce some \(y\in X_I\) with \(c^\top y\le\rho c^\top x\). If, for some objective \(c\), every vertex in the optimal face \(F_c=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\) lies outside \(R_\rho\), then selecting an optimal extreme point cannot trigger that rule. A successful method must change the relaxation, use nonlocal information, accept a larger factor, or permit violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If no vertex of the optimal LP face satisfies a rounding rule’s trigger, optimal-extreme-point selection cannot yield the promised rounding.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron with integral subset \(X_I\).
The local rounding rule is defined exactly on \(R_\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{vert}(F_c)\cap R_\rho=\varnothing\), the specified optimal-extreme-point rounding scheme cannot certify factor \(\rho\).

notation.meaning: face minimizing the linear objective c over P
points satisfying the local factor-rho rounding predicate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is an appropriate content kind. The core implication is essentially relative to the stipulated domain of a specified rule, but the existence of an optimal face or optimal vertices is not ensured merely by assuming that P is a nonempty polyhedron. The method-relative notion of roundability and the needed bounded-attainment hypotheses require a source before a mathematically stable version can be selected.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The side constraint \(y_1+y_2=1/2\) has fractional feasible points but no integral feasible point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal side constraint that preserves fractional feasibility while eliminating integral feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adding \(y_1+y_2=\tfrac12\) to \([0,1]^2\) leaves, for example, \((y_1,y_2)=(\tfrac12,0)\) feasible. Its intersection with \(\{0,1\}^2\) is empty because an integral left-hand side cannot equal \(\tfrac12\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A half-integral equality can leave the LP feasible while excluding every binary solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral-Feasibility Destruction by a Side Constraint
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Feasibility Destruction by a Side Constraint

assumptions_latex: The rounded variables \(Y_i\) are mutually independent Bernoulli variables with \(\Pr[Y_i=1]=x_i\).
The exact side constraint \(\sum_i a_iY_i=b\) must hold almost surely.

notation.meaning: coefficient of the exact side constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear equality barrier for independent nondegenerate Bernoulli rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Independence gives \(\operatorname{Var}(\sum_i a_iY_i)=\sum_i a_i^2x_i(1-x_i)\). Under the stated nondegeneracy condition this value is positive, whereas an almost-sure equality would have variance zero. Exact preservation therefore requires dependence, deterministic fixing of every relevant coordinate, or an explicitly permitted violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent nondegenerate rounding cannot preserve a nontrivial exact linear equality almost surely because the rounded sum has positive variance.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Rounding Equality Barrier
Side-Constraint Violation Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear side constraints obstruct independent nondegenerate rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let independent Bernoulli variables \(Y_i\) round fractional coordinates with \(\Pr[Y_i=1]=x_i\), and suppose an exact side constraint requires \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_iY_i=b\) almost surely, where \(a_i\in\mathbb R\) and \(\sum_i a_ix_i=b\). Independence gives \(\operatorname{Var}(\sum_i a_iY_i)=\sum_i a_i^2x_i(1-x_i)\). If some \(a_i\ne0\) has \(0<x_i<1\), this variance is positive, so the side constraint cannot hold almost surely. Exact preservation therefore requires dependence, deterministic fixing, or permitted violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent rounding cannot preserve a nontrivial exact linear side constraint almost surely because the rounded weighted sum has positive variance.
assumptions_latex: The rounded coordinates are mutually independent Bernoulli variables.
At least one constrained coordinate has nonzero coefficient and fractional probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[\sum_i a_iY_i=b]<1\); exact preservation requires abandoning nondegenerate independent rounding or relaxing the constraint.

notation.meaning: coefficient in the exact side constraint

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary fits the terminal container. The variance calculation and impossibility result are correct for mutually independent Bernoulli rounding with an exact scalar linear equality. The title is broader than that special case, and no source establishes that this is the intended local scope or supports its placement as the representative side-constraint barrier.

assumptions_latex: The available tight rows are indexed only by \(S=\{1,2\}\) and \(T=\{2,3\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal incidence-vector witness for a nonlaminar tight span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=\{1,2\}\) and \(T=\{2,3\}\), the vectors \(\chi^S=(1,1,0)\) and \(\chi^T=(0,1,1)\) are independent. The sets cross, so every laminar subfamily of \(\{S,T\}\) has at most one member and cannot span their two-dimensional row space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two crossing tight sets on three elements have independent rows, while every available laminar subfamily has only one row.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Nonlaminar Tight-Span Witness

assumptions_latex: Tight constraints are indexed by subsets of a finite ground set.
The rounding proof requires a laminar family spanning the relevant tight-row space.
No valid uncrossing rule supplies tight replacement rows for the crossing pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A laminar tight basis cannot be inferred merely from tightness of crossing constraints.

notation.meaning: crossing members of the tight family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for rounding arguments that require laminarization of tight rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sets \(S,T\) cross when \(S\cap T\), \(S\setminus T\), and \(T\setminus S\) are all nonempty. If tight crossing rows cannot validly be replaced by tight intersection, union, or difference rows, tightness alone does not imply a laminar spanning family. Token-counting or dimension arguments requiring such a family are then unjustified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossing tight constraints do not imply a laminar tight basis unless the relaxation supplies a valid uncrossing operation.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Laminar-Basis Inference
Nonlaminar Tight Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossing tight constraints invalidate rounding arguments requiring a laminar tight basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set-function relaxation, two tight constraints indexed by \(S,T\subseteq V\) are crossing when each of \(S\cap T\), \(S\setminus T\), and \(T\setminus S\) is nonempty. A tight family \(\mathcal F\) is nonlaminar if it contains such a pair. If the constraint system supplies no valid uncrossing operation replacing tight \(S,T\) by tight members among \(S\cap T\), \(S\cup T\), \(S\setminus T\), or \(T\setminus S\), then one cannot infer the existence of a laminar basis of tight constraints. Consequently, token-counting or iterative-rounding steps whose dimension bound requires laminarity are not justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossing tight constraints without a valid uncrossing rule block laminar-basis counting arguments commonly used to expose an integral or large coordinate.
assumptions_latex: Tight constraints are indexed by subsets of a finite ground set \(V\).
The rounding argument under consideration requires a laminar basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonlaminar tightness without uncrossing is a failure boundary for laminar dimension-counting arguments.

notation.meaning: family of tight constraint index sets
crossing members of the tight family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the appropriate content kind. The statement correctly warns that laminar-basis arguments cannot be invoked without a valid uncrossing theorem, but both tightness preservation and the available replacement sets depend on the particular relaxation. No source is provided to support a precise nonlaminar obstruction in the LP-rounding context.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(1/2,1/2)\), so \(x_1+x_2=1\). Independent linear-probability rounding gives each of \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\) probability \(1/4\). Therefore \(\Pr[Y_1+Y_2\ne1]=1/2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variance of a Rounded Linear Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact second-moment formula for independent Bernoulli rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(S=a^\top Y\), independent linear-probability rounding satisfies \[\operatorname{Var}(S)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2x_i(1-x_i).\] In particular, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=x_i(1-x_i)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)=0\) for \(i\ne j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variance of a rounded linear form is the sum of its independent Bernoulli coordinate variances.
knowledge_statements.title: Variance of a Rounded Linear Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint output law of independent linear-probability rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Y_i\) are independent and \(\Pr[Y_i=1]=x_i\), then \[\Pr[Y=y]=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{y_i}(1-x_i)^{1-y_i},\qquad y\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Consequently, for every \(S\subseteq[n]\), \(\mathbb E[\prod_{i\in S}Y_i]=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-probability rounding produces the product Bernoulli law, so joint selection moments factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Bernoulli Distribution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative concentration for the unweighted rounded sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\) and \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\). For \(0<\delta\le1\), \[\Pr[S\ge(1+\delta)\mu]\le\exp(-\delta^2\mu/3),\qquad \Pr[S\le(1-\delta)\mu]\le\exp(-\delta^2\mu/2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rounded cardinality has standard multiplicative Chernoff concentration around the fractional sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Chernoff Bounds for Rounded Cardinality
Linear-Probability Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent Bernoulli rounding with probabilities equal to fractional coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in[0,1]^n\), independently sample \(Y_i\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr[Y_i=1]=x_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), and output \(Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)\). Then \(\mathbb E[Y_i]=x_i\), and for every coefficient vector \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), linearity of expectation gives \(\mathbb E[a^\top Y]=a^\top x\). The basic algorithm stops after all coordinates are sampled; feasibility of coupled constraints is not guaranteed and must be established probabilistically or repaired separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round each coordinate independently to one with probability equal to its fractional value; every linear objective is preserved in expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is integral and satisfies \(\mathbb E[Y]=x\) and \(\mathbb E[a^\top Y]=a^\top x\).

notation.meaning: fractional value and selection probability of coordinate i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind, and the Bernoulli construction and expectation identities are precise and internally consistent. Nonetheless, source_refs is empty. The candidate therefore lacks the required authoritative citation with a specific section, theorem, definition, algorithm, or page locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation count for the coordinatewise capped-scale sampler.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Computing p_i=\min\{1,\alpha x_i\} and independently sampling all n coordinates requires O(n) arithmetic operations and n Bernoulli draws in the unit-cost sampling model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capped scaled-probability rounding is a linear-time one-pass sampler.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic and Bernoulli sampling have unit cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaling Does Not Preserve Packing Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal feasibility boundary for upward-scaled independent probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \alpha>1, the feasible packing point x=(1/2,1/2) for y_1+y_2\le1 yields p_1=p_2=\min\{1,\alpha/2\} under capped scaling. Independent sampling then gives \Pr(Y_1+Y_2>1)=p_1p_2>0. Thus upward probability scaling alone gives no almost-sure packing-feasibility guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing independent selection probabilities can violate even a two-variable packing constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Does Not Preserve Packing Feasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and exponential bounds for hitting a specified subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For p_i=\min\{1,\alpha x_i\} and independent Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i), every S\subseteq[n] satisfies \Pr(\sum_{i\in S}Y_i\ge1)=1-\prod_{i\in S}(1-p_i)\ge1-\exp(-\alpha\sum_{i\in S}x_i).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capped scaling gives an exact product formula for hitting a subset and an exponential lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The Y_i are mutually independent and \Pr(Y_i=1)=\min\{1,\alpha x_i\}.

notation.meaning: sum of rounded indicators indexed by S
sum of fractional coordinates indexed by S

knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Amplification Under Capped Scaling
Scaled-Probability Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent rounding after multiplicatively scaling fractional probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in[0,1]^n\) and a scale \(\alpha>0\), set \(p_i=\min\{1,\alpha x_i\}\). Independently sample \(Y_i\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr[Y_i=1]=p_i\), and output \(Y\). For every nonnegative coefficient vector \(a\), \(\mathbb E[a^\top Y]=\sum_i a_i\min\{1,\alpha x_i\}\le\alpha a^\top x\). Scaling upward increases marginal coverage, while truncation at one prevents invalid probabilities; feasibility and overload must be analyzed for the particular constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiply fractional coordinates by a scale, cap them at one, and independently sample; this increases coverage while potentially increasing resource use.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integral output has marginals \(\Pr[Y_i=1]=\min\{1,\alpha x_i\}\) and nonnegative expected linear cost at most \(\alpha a^\top x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the Scaled-Probability Rounding leaf. An inspectable topic-specific citation is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-style cost of the generic nonlinear transform-and-sample primitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given unit-cost evaluation of f, nonlinear probability rounding of n coordinates uses n evaluations of f, n Bernoulli draws, and O(n) additional operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generic nonlinear sampler is linear-time apart from the cost of evaluating its transfer function.
assumptions_latex: Each evaluation of f and each Bernoulli draw has unit cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Sampling Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which curvature compares a nonlinear probability transfer with the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If f:[0,1]\to[0,1] is concave with f(0)=0 and f(1)=1, then f(t)\ge t for all t\in[0,1]. If f is convex with the same endpoint values, then f(t)\le t. Curvature alone is insufficient: f(t)=t/2 is concave and convex but lies below the identity, while f(t)=(1+t)/2 is concave and convex but lies above it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized concave transfers amplify probabilities and normalized convex transfers suppress them; curvature without endpoint normalization implies neither behavior.
assumptions_latex: The stated comparisons assume f(0)=0 and f(1)=1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ concave}\Rightarrow f(t)\ge t,\qquad f\text{ convex}\Rightarrow f(t)\le t.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature and Identity Comparison

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first and second moments for independently rounded nonlinear probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(f(x_i)) independently, then for every a\in\mathbb R^n, \mathbb E[a^\top Y]=\sum_i a_i f(x_i) and \operatorname{Var}(a^\top Y)=\sum_i a_i^2 f(x_i)(1-f(x_i)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transformed probabilities determine the expectation and variance of every rounded linear form.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear-Transfer Moments
Nonlinear Probability Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent rounding using a nonlinear transfer from fractional values to probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in[0,1]^n\) and a measurable transfer function \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\), set \(p_i=f(x_i)\). Independently sample \(Y_i\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr[Y_i=1]=p_i\), and output \(Y\). Then \(\mathbb E[Y_i]=f(x_i)\) and, for every \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\mathbb E[a^\top Y]=\sum_i a_if(x_i)\). Choosing \(f\) concave may amplify small coordinates, whereas choosing it convex may suppress them; constraint and objective guarantees depend on explicit bounds comparing \(f(t)\) with \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transform each fractional coordinate through a nonlinear probability function and sample independently; guarantees follow from quantitative comparisons between the function and identity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) maps \([0,1]\) into \([0,1]\), and samples are independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is integral with marginals \(\mathbb E[Y_i]=f(x_i)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind, and the marginal and linear-expectation formulas are valid. The assertion that concavity may amplify small coordinates and convexity may suppress them is not secured by concavity or convexity alone; endpoint conditions or explicit comparisons with the identity are needed. With no cited transfer function or source, the intended mathematically correct variant cannot be determined reliably.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Biased independent-rounding approximation for restricted MAX SAT
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected approximation guarantee for MAX SAT instances without negated unit clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let p\in[0,1]. For a MAX SAT instance with no negated unit clauses, independently setting each variable x_i to true with probability p yields a randomized \min\{p,1-p^2\}\text{-approximation algorithm}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For MAX SAT without negated unit clauses, independently setting each variable to true with probability p gives a randomized approximation ratio of min(p, 1 − p²).
assumptions_latex: \text{The MAX SAT instance has no negated unit clauses.}

source_evidence.locator: Random sampling and randomized rounding of linear programs / 5.3. Flipping biased coins / Theorem 5.5

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clause-satisfaction probability under biased independent rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clause-level guarantee for biased independent rounding on restricted MAX SAT instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a MAX SAT instance with no negated unit clauses, let p>\tfrac12 and independently set each variable x_i to true with probability p. Then every clause C satisfies \Pr(C\text{ is satisfied})\geq \min\{p,1-p^2\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For MAX SAT without negated unit clauses, if every variable is independently set to true with probability p greater than one half, every fixed clause is satisfied with probability at least min(p, 1 − p²).
assumptions_latex: \text{The MAX SAT instance has no negated unit clauses.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence guarantee for unrestricted MAX SAT in the biased-rounding context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a randomized \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}\text{-approximation algorithm for MAX SAT}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MAX SAT admits a randomized approximation algorithm with approximation ratio (√5 − 1)/2.
assumptions_latex: \text{The input is a MAX SAT instance.}
