children.title: Load-Balancing Rounding
children.top_down_role: Randomized rounding focused on distributing demand across machines or resources.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized job-assignment conversion underlying machine-load concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_{ij}\ge0\) with \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\) for every job \(j\), independently assign job \(j\) to machine \(i\) with probability \(x_{ij}\). Every job is assigned exactly once, and \(L_i=\sum_jp_{ij}\mathbf1\{A(j)=i\}\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[L_i]=\sum_jp_{ij}x_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent assignment sampling produces a complete integral assignment and preserves every machine load in expectation.
assumptions_latex: For every job, \((x_{ij})_i\) is a probability distribution.

notation.meaning: fractional expected load of machine i

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Assignment Rounding

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expectation Preservation Does Not Control Makespan
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balls-into-bins boundary for independent load-balancing rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) unit jobs, \(n\) identical machines, and \(x_{ij}=1/n\), independent assignment gives expected load \(1\) on every machine, while the maximum load is \(\Theta(\log n/\log\log n)\) with high probability. Hence per-machine expectation preservation alone gives no universal constant makespan bound relative to the fractional value \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent rounding can preserve every expected load while its maximum load grows beyond every constant.
assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) unit jobs and \(n\) identical machines.
Every job is assigned independently and uniformly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expected load of every machine is \(1\), but the maximum load is not bounded by a universal constant with high probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Preservation Does Not Control Makespan

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Assignment Relaxation for Unrelated-Machine Load Balancing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional representation and lower certificate used by load-balancing rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For target load \(T\), use \(x_{ij}\ge0\), \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\) for every job \(j\), \(\sum_jp_{ij}x_{ij}\le T\) for every machine \(i\), and \(x_{ij}=0\) whenever \(p_{ij}>T\). Feasibility is necessary for an integral assignment of makespan at most \(T\); hence the minimum feasible \(T\) lower-bounds optimal makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fractional assignment relaxation distributes every job, limits machine loads, and lower-bounds integral makespan.
assumptions_latex: The job and machine sets are finite.
\(p_{ij}\ge0\) is the processing time of job \(j\) on machine \(i\).

notation.meaning: fraction of job j assigned to machine i
processing time of job j on machine i

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Relaxation for Unrelated-Machine Load Balancing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic slot-matching rounding for unrelated-machine makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible assignment-relaxation solution of load at most \(T\), bucket each machine's fractional jobs into unit-mass slots in nonincreasing processing-time order and find an integral matching of jobs to slots. The resulting machine load is at most \(T+\max\{p_{ij}:j\text{ is assigned to }i\}\). Since pairs with \(p_{ij}>T\) are excluded, the makespan is at most \(2T\). The construction is polynomial-time using bipartite matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slot-matching rounding converts the unrelated-machine assignment LP into a polynomial-time schedule of makespan at most twice the LP value.
assumptions_latex: The assignment relaxation is feasible at value \(T\).
Pairs with \(p_{ij}>T\) have zero fractional assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\max}\le2T\), and the rounded assignment is computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.title: Lenstra–Shmoys–Tardos Assignment Rounding Bound

assumptions_latex: The rounded destinations of distinct jobs are independent.
\(\ell_i=\sum_j p_{ij}x_{ij}\) is the fractional load of machine \(i\).

notation.meaning: fractional expected load on machine i
uniform upper bound on one processing contribution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-load concentration under independent assignment rounding and bounded jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under independent assignment rounding, \(L_i=\sum_j p_{ij}\mathbf 1\{A(j)=i\}\) has expectation \(\mathbb E[L_i]=\ell_i=\sum_jp_{ij}x_{ij}\). If \(p_{ij}\le b\) whenever \(x_{ij}>0\), then for every \(t\ge 0\), \[\Pr[L_i\ge \ell_i+t]\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(b\ell_i+bt/3)}\right).\] Hence, for any finite machine set \(M\), \[\Pr[\max_{i\in M}(L_i-\ell_i)\ge t]\le \sum_{i\in M}\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(b\ell_i+bt/3)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded independent job contributions give Bernstein concentration around each fractional machine load, and a union bound controls the maximum load.
knowledge_statements.title: Load-Balancing Rounding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The concentration property is mathematically coherent and aligned with load-balancing rounding, but the exact Bernstein bound and its assumptions have no cited support. A specific authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Makespan Regimes
children.top_down_role: Guarantee regimes centered on maximum load or completion-time objectives.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\ge 2\) machines with fractional loads \(\ell_i\le T\).
Every eligible processing time is at most \(b\).
Jobs are independently assigned according to a feasible fractional assignment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability additive makespan regimes induced by bounded-contribution concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge 2\), let \(0<\delta<1\), and suppose \(\ell_i\le T\) for every machine while each eligible processing time is at most \(b\). Independent assignment rounding satisfies, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), \[\max_iL_i\le T+\sqrt{2bT\log(m/\delta)}+\frac{2b}{3}\log(m/\delta).\] Thus the rounded makespan is \(T+O(\sqrt{bT\log(m/\delta)})\) when the square-root term dominates, while the additive \(O(b\log(m/\delta))\) regime controls instances containing comparatively large jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With high probability, the rounded makespan is at most the fractional bound plus a square-root deviation and a logarithmic additive term; the relative importance of these terms distinguishes the small-job and comparatively-large-job regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Makespan Regimes

children.title: Facility-Location Rounding
children.top_down_role: Randomized rounding for opening facilities plus assigning clients.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Opening Marginals Do Not Control Nearest-Open Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing why connection analysis needs joint coverage or clustering information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For four facilities with marginals \(1/2\), compare a distribution choosing \(\{1,2\}\) or \(\{3,4\}\) equiprobably with one choosing \(\{1,3\}\) or \(\{2,4\}\) equiprobably. Both preserve every marginal and always open two facilities, but the neighborhood \(\{1,2\}\) is empty with probability \(1/2\) under the first distribution and never empty under the second. Thus marginals and rounded cardinality do not determine nearest-open connection behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opening distributions with identical marginals and totals can have different neighborhood coverage and connection costs.
assumptions_latex: Only individual opening marginals and the rounded total are specified.
Clients connect to an open facility using their neighborhood or distance structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Connection guarantees require additional joint-distribution, clustering, or coverage properties.
knowledge_statements.title: Opening Marginals Do Not Control Nearest-Open Distance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Preservation Preserves Expected Opening Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-independent cost property of marginal-preserving facility opening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite facility set, costs \(f_i\), and rounded indicators \(Y_i\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[Y_i]=y_i\), one has \(\mathbb E[\sum_i f_iY_i]=\sum_i f_i y_i\). Dependence among the indicators does not affect the equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginal-preserving opening rounding preserves total facility-opening cost in expectation regardless of dependence.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Preservation Preserves Expected Opening Cost

assumptions_latex: \(y_i\in[0,1]\) are fractional facility-opening variables with \(\sum_i y_i\ge 1\).
A dependent-rounding primitive preserves marginals and rounds the total to a neighboring integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs a nonempty open set \(S\) and assigns each client to a minimum-cost facility in \(S\).

notation.meaning: fractional opening variable for facility i
connection cost from facility i to client j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic dependent opening followed by nearest-open-facility assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input finite facility and client sets \(F\) and \(C\), opening variables \((y_i)_{i\in F}\) with \(\sum_i y_i\ge 1\), and connection costs \(d(i,j)\). Apply a dependent-rounding primitive to \(y\), obtaining \(Y_i\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb E[Y_i]=y_i\) and \(\sum_iY_i\in\{\lfloor\sum_i y_i\rfloor,\lceil\sum_i y_i\rceil\}\). Set \(S=\{i:Y_i=1\}\). For every client \(j\), choose \(a(j)\in\arg\min_{i\in S}d(i,j)\). Output \(S\) and \(a\); the procedure stops after all clients are assigned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependently round fractional facility openings, then connect every client to a cheapest rounded-open facility; the preserved total ensures that some facility opens.
knowledge_statements.title: Facility-Location Rounding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The procedure is syntactically complete and the neighboring-integer total would make the open set nonempty under the stated sum condition. However, the dependent-rounding primitive and this facility-location application are uncited, and no facility-opening or connection-cost approximation guarantee is established. A specific source is needed to determine whether this is the intended algorithmic variant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Randomized rounding of two facility sets for k-median
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A k-median specialization of facility-location rounding that opens exactly k facilities and assigns every city to an opened facility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A and B be facility sets with |A|=k_1 and |B|=k_2. Form B'\subseteq B by including a closest facility in B for every facility in A, then add facilities from B\setminus B' until |B'|=k_1. With probability a open A, and with probability b=1-a open B'. Independently choose uniformly a set of k-k_1 facilities from B\setminus B' and open them. For a city j connected to i_1\in A and i_2\in B in the two input solutions, connect j to the opened one of i_1 and i_2 when i_2\in B'; when i_2\notin B', connect j to i_2 if it is open, otherwise to i_1 if it is open, and otherwise to the facility i_3\in B' closest to i_1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Map each facility in A to a closest facility in B and pad the resulting set B' to size k1. Randomly open either A or B', and also open a uniformly selected set of k−k1 facilities from the remainder of B. This opens exactly k facilities. Each city is assigned to an appropriate open facility, using the mapped closest facility in B' as a fallback.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected connection-cost bound for k-median rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: City-level expected-cost and computability guarantee for the specified k-median facility-rounding procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every city j, let \operatorname{cost}(j)=a c_{i_1j}+b c_{i_2j}, where b=1-a and i_1,i_2 are its facilities in the two input solutions. If \phi is the integral assignment produced by the specified rounding procedure, then \mathbf{E}[c_{\phi(j)j}]\leq (1+\max\{a,b\})\operatorname{cost}(j). Moreover, this expectation can be computed efficiently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each city, the expected connection cost after the specified rounding is at most (1 plus the larger rounding probability) times its fractional connection cost. The expectation is efficiently computable.

children.title: Network-Design Rounding
children.top_down_role: Randomized rounding for selecting edges, links, or network structures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Cut Size Does Not Certify Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility boundary for independently rounded cut relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a required cut has two crossing edges selected independently with probability \(1/2\) and \(r(S)=1\), then \(\mathbb E[Z_S]=1\) but \(\Pr[Z_S=0]=1/4\). Hence meeting a cut requirement in expectation does not certify realized connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampled cut can fail even when its expected selected size meets the requirement.
assumptions_latex: Two edges cross a required cut and are independently selected with probability \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Z_S]\ge r(S)\) does not imply \(Z_S\ge r(S)\) almost surely or with high probability.

notation.meaning: number of selected edges crossing cut S

knowledge_statements.title: Expected Cut Size Does Not Certify Connectivity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-independent expected-cost property of scaled edge rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_e\ge0\), \(x_e\in[0,1]\), and \(\alpha\ge1\). If \(X_e\in\{0,1\}\) has marginal \(\Pr[X_e=1]=\min\{1,\alpha x_e\}\), then \(\mathbb E[\sum_e c_eX_e]=\sum_e c_e\min\{1,\alpha x_e\}\le\alpha\sum_e c_ex_e\). Independence is unnecessary for this expected-cost inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling fractional edge marginals by alpha increases expected selected cost by at most alpha.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Sampling Cost Bound

assumptions_latex: \(x_e\in[0,1]\) satisfies \(\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge r(S)\) for every required cut \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is \(H=(V,F)\), where each edge belongs to \(F\) independently with probability \(\min\{1,\alpha x_e\}\).

notation.meaning: required number of selected edges across cut S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled independent rounding of a cut-based network-design relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), a feasible fractional vector \(x\in[0,1]^E\), cut requirements \(r(S)\), and a scale \(\alpha>0\). Initialize \(F=\varnothing\). Independently for each edge \(e\), insert \(e\) into \(F\) with probability \(p_e=\min\{1,\alpha x_e\}\). Output \(H=(V,F)\). For every cut \(S\subset V\), the rounded cut size is \(Z_S=|F\cap\delta(S)|\) and satisfies \(\mathbb E[Z_S]=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}p_e\). Feasibility is accepted only if \(Z_S\ge r(S)\) for every required cut; otherwise a separately specified repetition or alteration phase is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale fractional edge values into selection probabilities, sample edges independently, and accept the network only when all required cuts meet their connectivity demands.
knowledge_statements.title: Network-Design Rounding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaled independent sampling step is clear, but the family of required cuts, the meaning and admissible structure of \(r(S)\), and any repetition or alteration mechanism are not sourced. Because those choices determine the applicable network-design model and guarantee, an aligned source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Connection-Cost Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Coupling between selection costs, connection costs, plus connectivity requirements.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expectation Does Not Give Per-Outcome Connection Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating expected connection bounds from deterministic and strong tail guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(B>1\), let \(C=B\) with probability \(1/B\) and \(C=0\) otherwise. Then \(C\ge0\) and \(\mathbb E[C]=1\), while \(C=B\) with positive probability. Thus expectation alone gives neither a finite universal almost-sure ratio nor a tail guarantee beyond consequences such as Markov's inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A good expected connection cost can coexist with rare arbitrarily expensive outcomes.
assumptions_latex: \(C\ge0\) is a random total connection cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite universal almost-sure bound on \(C/\mathbb E[C]\) follows from expectation alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Does Not Give Per-Outcome Connection Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface combining separately controlled opening and connection costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F^*,C^*\ge0\). If randomized opening and connection costs \(F,C\) satisfy \(\mathbb E[F]\le\alpha F^*\) and \(\mathbb E[C]\le\beta C^*\), then \(\mathbb E[F+C]\le\alpha F^*+\beta C^*\le\max\{\alpha,\beta\}(F^*+C^*)\). No independence between \(F\) and \(C\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate expected factors for opening and connection costs combine additively and yield the larger factor for their total.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Part Facility-Cost Aggregation

assumptions_latex: Each client \(j\) is assigned to a random facility \(A(j)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear interface from per-client rounded connection bounds to total expected cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a finite client set, let \(w_j\ge 0\), and suppose a rounding procedure assigns each client \(j\) to a random facility \(A(j)\). If, for every \(j\in C\), \[\mathbb E[d(A(j),j)]\le \beta\sum_i x_{ij}d(i,j),\] then linearity of expectation yields \[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{j\in C}w_jd(A(j),j)\right]\le \beta\sum_{j\in C}\sum_iw_jx_{ij}d(i,j).\] No independence among client assignments is required for this expected-cost interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A per-client expected connection bound automatically gives the same factor for total weighted connection cost, without requiring independent assignments.
knowledge_statements.title: Connection-Cost Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expected-cost interface is precise, matches the terminal context, and correctly does not require independence. It nevertheless contains a nontrivial factor-preservation claim with no citation or standard-field rationale, so a specific source locator is required.

children.title: Dense-Graph Sampling
children.top_down_role: Randomized selection of vertices, edges, or neighborhoods in dense graphs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy, confidence, query, and storage bounds for uniform pair sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the immutable independent uniform pair-sampling estimator \widehat d, if s\ge\lceil(2\varepsilon^2)^{-1}\ln(2/\delta)\rceil, then \Pr(|\widehat d-d(G)|>\varepsilon)\le\delta. Thus O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta)) adjacency queries suffice, independently of |V|; a streaming implementation uses one running count and O(\log s) bits beyond the query representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform pair sampling estimates edge density to additive error using a graph-size-independent number of adjacency queries.
assumptions_latex: Pair samples are independent and uniform with replacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Pair-Sampling Density Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of size-independent relative accuracy under pair sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let p=d(G). For 0<p\le1/2 and fixed constant confidence, estimating p from independent uniform pair queries to relative error \eta\in(0,1) has general Bernoulli sample scale \Theta((\eta^2p)^{-1}). Hence graph-size-independent additive estimation does not yield graph-size-independent relative estimation when p\to0. Under uniform density p\ge c>0, the scale is O((\eta^2c)^{-1}), up to confidence factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative density estimation becomes expensive as density vanishes; a uniform positive density lower bound removes this dependence.
assumptions_latex: Uniform pair queries return independent Bernoulli observations of mean p=d(G).
The \Theta statement uses fixed constant success probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s=\Theta((\eta^2p)^{-1})\text{ is the general constant-confidence relative-error scale}.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive-versus-Relative Density Estimation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-sampling estimator for dense-graph edge density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(S\subseteq V\) uniformly among the subsets of size \(k\ge2\), query all \(\binom{k}{2}\) adjacencies inside \(S\), and output
\[\widehat d_S=\frac{|E(G[S])|}{\binom{k}{2}}.\]
Every unordered vertex pair has the same inclusion probability, so
\[\mathbb E[\widehat d_S]=\frac{|E|}{\binom n2}=d(G).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The edge density of a uniformly sampled induced subgraph is an unbiased estimator of global edge density.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph on \(n\) vertices.

notation.meaning: Subgraph induced by the sampled vertices.
Edge density of the sampled induced subgraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Induced-Subgraph Density Sampling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive concentration for uniform vertex sampling without replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the uniform \(k\)-vertex induced-subgraph estimator and every \(\varepsilon>0\), a bounded-kernel finite-population U-statistic inequality gives
\[\Pr\bigl(|\widehat d_S-d(G)|>\varepsilon\bigr)\le2\exp\bigl(-\lfloor k/2\rfloor\varepsilon^2\bigr).\]
Consequently \(k=O(\bigl(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta)\bigr)\wedge n)\) sampled vertices suffice whenever the requested bound is attainable, using \(O(k^2)\) adjacency queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform induced sample gives graph-size-independent additive density concentration until the required sample reaches the graph size.
assumptions_latex: The sampling and estimator are those of Uniform Induced-Subgraph Density Sampling.
The selected sample size satisfies \(2\le k\le n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Induced-Subgraph Density Concentration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-query estimator for dense-graph edge density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sample vertices \(U_1,\ldots,U_s\) independently and uniformly from \(V\), query their degrees, and output \[\widehat d_{\deg}=\frac1s\sum_{t=1}^s\frac{\deg(U_t)}{n-1}.\] Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat d_{\deg}]=d(G)\), and for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\Pr(|\widehat d_{\deg}-d(G)|>\varepsilon)\le2e^{-2s\varepsilon^2}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly sampled normalized degrees give an unbiased, additively concentrated estimator of edge density.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph with \(n\ge2\).
Independent uniform vertex samples and exact degree queries are available.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Vertex Degree Estimator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample boundary replacing the rejected nonidentifiability claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(s\) independent uniform samples from an edge set of size \(M\),
\[\Pr[\text{no repeated sampled edge}]=\prod_{j=0}^{s-1}\left(1-\frac{j}{M}\right)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{s(s-1)}{2M}\right).\]
Also \(\Pr[\text{some repeated edge}]\le\binom{s}{2}/M\). Hence a collision has constant nontrivial probability precisely on the scale \(s=\Theta(\sqrt M)\). Existing-edge sampling is identifiable in the limit, but it lacks the graph-size-independent additive-density behavior of uniform pair queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform existing-edge samples reveal support size through collisions on the square-root-of-edge-count scale.
assumptions_latex: Samples are independent and uniform with replacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s=\Theta(\sqrt M)\text{ is the constant-probability collision scale}.
knowledge_statements.title: Existing-Edge Sampling Collision Scale

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiable reciprocal-support statistic under labeled uniform sampling from a nonempty edge set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=|E(G)|>0\), and draw labeled edges \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_s\) independently and uniformly from \(E(G)\). For \(s\ge2\), define
\[\widehat q=\binom{s}{2}^{-1}\sum_{1\le a<b\le s}\mathbf1\{Y_a=Y_b\}.\]
Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat q]=1/M\). Thus labeled uniform-edge samples identify reciprocal support size through collisions; estimating density further requires known \(n\) and statistically controlled inversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The collision frequency of uniform labeled edge samples unbiasedly estimates the reciprocal number of edges.
assumptions_latex: The graph has at least one edge.
Samples are independent, labeled, and uniform over the existing edges.
The vertex count \(n\) is known when converting edge count to density.

notation.meaning: The a-th uniformly sampled existing edge.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Edge Collision Statistic

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Always-defined distinct-count estimator of edge-set size from uniform labeled existing-edge samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=\binom n2\), draw \(s\ge1\) labeled edges independently and uniformly from an unknown nonempty edge set of size \(M\le N\), and let \(D\) be the number of distinct sampled edges. Define \(\widehat M\) as the smallest maximizer over integers \(m\in\{D,\ldots,N\}\) of the distinct-count likelihood \[L(m)=\frac{(m)_D}{m^s},\qquad (m)_D=m(m-1)\cdots(m-D+1).\] Then \(\widehat M\) is always defined, including when \(D=s\), and \(\widehat d=\widehat M/N\) is the corresponding clipped density estimate. No accuracy guarantee is implied without a separate support-size analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize the distinct-count likelihood over the known finite range of possible edge counts; the estimator remains defined when all sampled edges are distinct.
assumptions_latex: The graph has known vertex count \(n\) and at least one edge.
Samples are independent, labeled, and uniform over the existing edge set.
\(D\) is the observed number of distinct sampled edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\le\widehat M\le\binom n2,\qquad \widehat d=\widehat M/\binom n2.

notation.meaning: Falling factorial of candidate support size m.
Number of possible unordered vertex pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Clipped Support-Size Maximum-Likelihood Estimator

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Edge-Support Recovery by Coupon Collection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample support recovery from labeled uniform existing-edge samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=|E(G)|>0\), draw \(s\) labeled edges independently and uniformly from \(E(G)\), and let \(D\) be the number of distinct observed edges. Then \[\Pr[D<M]\le M\left(1-\frac1M\right)^s\le Me^{-s/M}.\] Hence \(s\ge M(\ln M+\ln(1/\delta))\) implies exact recovery of \(E(G)\), \(M\), and \(d(G)=M/\binom n2\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual coupon-collector budget recovers the entire labeled edge support with high probability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent pair sampling for estimating the edge density of a dense graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a sample size \(s\ge 1\). Independently draw unordered pairs \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_s\) uniformly from \(\binom{V}{2}\), set \(X_t=\mathbf 1\{Q_t\in E\}\), and output \(\widehat d=s^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^sX_t\). Moreover, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\Pr[|\widehat d-d(G)|>\varepsilon]\le 2\exp(-2s\varepsilon^2).\] Sampling stops after exactly \(s\) pair queries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive stability of dense maximum q-coloring under edge changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) and H=(V,F) share a vertex set. For every coloring \sigma, |\operatorname{val}_G(\sigma)-\operatorname{val}_H(\sigma)|\le|E\triangle F|, and therefore |\operatorname{OPT}_q(G)-\operatorname{OPT}_q(H)|\le|E\triangle F|. If |E|=\Theta(|V|^2), additive error \varepsilon|V|^2 becomes O(\varepsilon) after normalization by |E|.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing t edges changes every coloring value and the optimum by at most t; density converts quadratic additive error into constant normalized error.
assumptions_latex: G and H have the same finite vertex set.

notation.meaning: Symmetric difference of the edge sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Edit Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal baseline for the fixed-q properly-colored-edge objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite undirected graph G=(V,E) and integer q\ge2, independently assigning every vertex a uniform color in [q] properly colors each edge with probability 1-1/q. Hence \mathbb E[\operatorname{val}_G(\sigma)]=(1-1/q)|E| and \operatorname{OPT}_q(G)\ge(1-1/q)|E|.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform random q-coloring properly colors an expected fraction 1−1/q of the edges.

notation.meaning: Number of edges whose endpoints have different colors.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Coloring Baseline

notation.meaning: maximum number of properly colored edges using q colors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization representation of dense maximum q-coloring by properly colored edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and an integer \(q\ge 1\), a coloring is a map \(\sigma:V\to[q]\). Its value is \[\operatorname{val}_G(\sigma)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}\mathbf 1\{\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)\}.\] The dense maximum \(q\)-coloring objective is represented by \[\operatorname{OPT}_q(G)=\max_{\sigma:V\to[q]}\operatorname{val}_G(\sigma).\] Dividing both sides by \(|E|\) when \(|E|>0\) gives the corresponding fraction of properly colored edges without changing the optimizing colorings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum q-coloring chooses a vertex coloring that maximizes the number, or equivalently the fraction, of edges whose endpoints receive different colors.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Coloring

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic conversion of simultaneous sample accuracy into a guarantee for an empirically optimized candidate coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\neq\varnothing\), and suppose \(\sup_{\sigma\in\mathcal H}|\widehat v(\sigma)-v(\sigma)|\le\varepsilon\). If \(\widehat v(\widehat\sigma)\ge\sup_{\sigma\in\mathcal H}\widehat v(\sigma)-\eta\), then \(v(\widehat\sigma)\ge\sup_{\sigma\in\mathcal H}v(\sigma)-2\varepsilon-\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly accurate sampled coloring scores make an approximate empirical optimizer nearly optimal for the true scores.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is nonempty and the displayed suprema are attained or interpreted as suprema.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Estimation Transfers Empirical Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of fixed-family concentration when candidates are generated from the scoring sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A union-bound guarantee established for a deterministic family \(\mathcal H\) does not automatically apply when the scored family is \(\mathcal H(S)\), chosen from the same sample \(S\). Same-sample selection can overfit unsampled edges. Certification requires an independent validation sample or a uniform event over a deterministic superclass containing every possible output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-family concentration cannot automatically certify colorings selected adaptively from the same sample.
assumptions_latex: The candidate family can depend on the observations used to score it.
No simultaneous event has been established over a fixed superclass of all possible outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-family guarantee alone does not certify the adaptively selected coloring.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Class Boundary for Sample Certification

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a finite family of candidate \(q\)-colorings.
\(s\) edges are sampled independently and uniformly from a nonempty edge set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(s\ge (\log(2|\mathcal H|/\delta))/(2\varepsilon^2)\), then all empirical coloring values are within \(\varepsilon\) of their true values with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: true fraction of properly colored edges under coloring sigma
sampled fraction of properly colored edges

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform sample certification for a finite family of candidate colorings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(|E|>0\), and let \(\mathcal H\) be a finite family of colorings. Sample \(s\) edges independently and uniformly from \(E\). For each \(\sigma\in\mathcal H\), let \(\widehat v(\sigma)\) be the sampled fraction whose endpoints receive different colors, and let \(v(\sigma)=\operatorname{val}_G(\sigma)/|E|\). If \[s\ge \frac{\log(2|\mathcal H|/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2},\] then, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), \[|\widehat v(\sigma)-v(\sigma)|\le\varepsilon\quad\text{for every }\sigma\in\mathcal H.\] Thus the sample values form simultaneous additive certificates for all candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enough uniformly sampled edges simultaneously estimate every coloring in a finite candidate family, allowing sampled scores to certify their true scores.
knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-to-Coloring Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous finite-family estimate is mathematically coherent and functions as a probabilistic certificate interface. The exact sample-size bound and sampling assumptions lack any citation, so a source with a theorem, section, or page locator is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-moment condition separating concentration from marginal-only control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i}, where X_{n,i}\in\{0,1\}, and suppose \mathbb E[S_n]/n\to p. If \operatorname{Var}(S_n)=o(n^2), then S_n/n\to p in probability. If the variables in each row have common marginal p and are pairwise independent, then \operatorname{Var}(S_n)=np(1-p) and \Pr(|S_n/n-p|>\varepsilon)\le p(1-p)/(n\varepsilon^2).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subquadratic variance suffices for concentration; pairwise independence supplies it, while preserved marginals alone do not.
knowledge_statements.title: Subquadratic-Variance Concentration Criterion

assumptions_latex: All rounded indicators may be arbitrarily dependent while retaining Bernoulli marginal \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Marginal preservation alone permits \(S_n\in\{0,n\}\), so \(S_n/n\) does not concentrate around \(p\) as \(n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect dependence shows that preserved marginals do not imply concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\), and define \(X_i=Z\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Every indicator has the prescribed marginal \(\Pr[X_i=1]=p\), and \(\mathbb E[S_n]=np\) for \(S_n=\sum_iX_i\). Nevertheless, \[S_n=\begin{cases}0,&Z=0,\\ n,&Z=1,\end{cases}\] so for every \(0<\varepsilon<\min\{p,1-p\}\), \[\Pr[|S_n/n-p|>\varepsilon]=1.\] Hence marginal preservation and expectation control alone cannot yield a vanishing relative-deviation probability; some independence, negative dependence, martingale control, or other concentration hypothesis is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfectly correlated Bernoulli decisions preserve every marginal and the expected sum but exhibit no concentration, marking the boundary of expectation-only rounding guarantees.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Concentration Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The perfect-dependence example correctly expresses a weak-concentration failure boundary, with explicit variables and matching plain and LaTeX statements. Because no evidence or standard-field rationale is supplied, a specific source locator is required before retaining it as candidate-review knowledge.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Requires a Supported Joint Law
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition distinguishing marginal preservation from coupled feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite integral feasible set \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), a randomized output \(Y\) is feasible almost surely exactly when its joint distribution is supported on \(F\): \[\Pr(Y\in F)=1.\] A marginal vector \(x=\mathbb E[Y]\) is realizable by such a feasible joint law if and only if \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(F)\). Coordinate marginals alone do not determine whether a particular joint law has the required support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-sure coupled feasibility is a property of the full joint distribution, not merely its coordinate marginals.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Requires a Supported Joint Law

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact-Cardinality Feasibility Vanishes under Independent Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalable coupled-feasibility obstruction despite fractional convex-hull membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\) be even and \[F_n=\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^ny_i=n/2\right\}.\] The point \(x=(1/2,\ldots,1/2)\) lies in \(\operatorname{conv}(F_n)\). If \(Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) independently, every marginal is preserved, but \[\Pr(Y\in F_n)=\binom{n}{n/2}2^{-n}\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi n}}\longrightarrow0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent rounding preserves every half marginal but satisfies an exact-cardinality constraint with probability tending to zero.

notation.meaning: Binary vectors satisfying the exact-cardinality constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Cardinality Feasibility Vanishes under Independent Rounding
Highly Coupled Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent rounding can violate a coupled constraint despite preserving every coordinate marginal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^2\) and \(x=(1/2,1/2)\in\operatorname{conv}(F)\). Independently round each coordinate by taking \(Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(x_i)\). Then \(\mathbb E[Y_i]=x_i\) for both coordinates, but \(Y=(1,1)\notin F\) with probability \(1/4\). Thus correct marginals and fractional feasibility do not imply feasibility under independently rounded, highly coupled constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible fractional point can have correctly preserved marginals while independent rounding violates a coupled feasibility constraint with positive probability.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct, self-contained, and appropriately classified for this failure-boundary leaf, but the record supplies neither a source nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative condition transferring an expected objective guarantee through feasibility repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let R be a random rounded solution, let A(R) be feasible almost surely, and let f\ge0. If \mathbb E[f(R)]\ge \alpha B and \mathbb E[f(A(R))]\ge \rho\,\mathbb E[f(R)], then \mathbb E[f(A(R))]\ge \alpha\rho B. Feasibility alone supplies no positive objective guarantee without such a retention comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alteration transfers an expected approximation guarantee only through a quantitative objective-retention bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Alteration-Retention Transfer
Objective-Dominating Alterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasibility repair may erase nearly all expected objective value without a retention guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(U_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let each element enter \(R_n\) independently with probability \(1/2\), let \(f(S)=|S|\), and define the feasible family \(F_n=\{S\subseteq U_n:|S|\leq1\}\). The alteration \(A_n(S)=S\) when \(|S|\leq1\) and \(A_n(S)=\varnothing\) otherwise always returns a feasible set. Nevertheless, \(\mathbb E[f(R_n)]=n/2\) and \(\mathbb E[f(A_n(R_n))]=n2^{-n}\), so the retained fraction is \(2^{1-n}\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid repair rule can lose an asymptotically complete fraction of the rounded objective, so feasibility alone provides no approximation guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The objective is the nonnegative cardinality function \(f(S)=|S|\).

notation.meaning: Family of sets of cardinality at most one.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The alteration and both expectations are correct, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. A source specifically supporting the alteration-retention failure phenomenon is still required.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation without Tail Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An expected objective guarantee alone need not yield constant-probability performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each integer \(M\geq2\), define a nonnegative random objective \(Z_M\) by \(Z_M=M\) with probability \(1/M\) and \(Z_M=0\) otherwise. Then \(\mathbb E[Z_M]=1\), whereas \(\Pr(Z_M\geq1/2)=1/M\to0\). Hence a positive lower bound on expectation, without boundedness, concentration, or another tail hypothesis, does not imply any uniform positive probability of attaining even half that expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rare, very large payoff can keep expectation fixed while the probability of attaining half the expectation tends to zero.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rare-payoff counterexample correctly separates expectation from uniform tail probability and fits the leaf, but it has no cited source or standard-field rationale.
