source_witnesses.locator: Randomized Approximation Algorithms in Combinatorial Optimization / 11.3. Semidefinite Programming / Definition 11.4

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recognition of sign embeddings within the unit-vector representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of real unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) is an integral sign embedding exactly when all vectors lie on one common line: there exist a unit vector e and signs \(s_i\in\{-1,1\}\) such that \(v_i=s_i e\) for every i. In that case \(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=s_i s_j\) for all i,j.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit-vector solution represents binary signs exactly when every vector is parallel or antiparallel to one common unit direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists e,\ \|e\|_2=1,\ v_i=s_i e\ \forall i\) exactly characterizes integral sign embeddings.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Line Certificate for Integral Signs

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_i s_j=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), with the relaxation imposing only \(\|v_i\|_2=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard vector relaxation of pairwise products of binary signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary signs \(s_i\in\{-1,1\}\), choose a unit vector \(e\) and represent \(s_i\) by \(v_i=s_i e\), giving \(s_i s_j=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\). The unit-vector SDP relaxation drops the common-line and rank-one requirements and permits arbitrary vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) satisfying \(\|v_i\|_2=1\). Consequently, a quadratic expression \(\sum_{i,j=1}^n c_{ij}s_i s_j\) is relaxed to \(\sum_{i,j=1}^n c_{ij}\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary sign products become inner products; allowing arbitrary unit vectors yields the standard semidefinite vector relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Vector Representations

children.title: Gram-Matrix Representations
children.top_down_role: SDP solutions represented through inner-product matrices of vectors.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|v_i-v_j\|_2^2=X_{ii}+X_{jj}-2X_{ij}\), and an exact realization is obtained from a factorization \(X=V^{\mathsf T}V\).

notation.meaning: Matrix whose columns realize the Gram matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric information and constructive factorization encoded by a finite Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gram matrix records \(\|v_i\|_2^2=X_{ii}\), pairwise inner products \(X_{ij}\), and squared distances \[\|v_i-v_j\|_2^2=X_{ii}+X_{jj}-2X_{ij}.\] If \(X=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\), then \(V=\Lambda_+^{1/2}Q_+^{\mathsf T}\) gives \(X=V^{\mathsf T}V\); its columns form a realization in \(\mathbb R^{\operatorname{rank}(X)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gram matrix determines vector norms, inner products, and pairwise squared distances, and an eigenvalue factorization constructs a minimum-dimensional realization.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Recovery and Construction
Gram-Matrix Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite vector configurations represented by positive-semidefinite matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\), their Gram matrix is \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) with \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\). It satisfies \(X\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq d\). Conversely, every \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) admits a factorization \(X=V^{\mathsf T}V\); taking the columns of \(V\) as vectors recovers \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\). The least possible ambient dimension equals \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is a Gram matrix exactly when it is positive semidefinite; its rank gives the smallest representing dimension.
assumptions_latex: All vector spaces are real and finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\) has a vector Gram representation if and only if \(X\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices.
Matrix whose columns are representing vectors.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional Gram factorization and minimum-dimension rank statement are correct and representation is the proper knowledge kind. No supporting source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Elliptope Representations
children.top_down_role: SDP feasible regions viewed through correlation-matrix geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}\{xx^{\mathsf T}:x\in\{-1,1\}^n\}\subseteq\mathcal E_n\), with strict inclusion for \(n\geq3\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between integral sign correlations and their elliptope relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every \(xx^{\mathsf T}\), \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\), belongs to \(\mathcal E_n\), so \(\operatorname{COR}_{\pm}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\{xx^{\mathsf T}:x\in\{-1,1\}^n\}\subseteq\mathcal E_n\). The inclusion is strict for \(n\geq3\). For \(n=3\), the matrix with diagonal \(1\) and all off-diagonal entries \(-1/2\) is positive semidefinite but violates \(1+X_{12}+X_{13}+X_{23}\geq0\), which every sign-correlation convex combination satisfies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The elliptope contains the convex hull of sign-correlation matrices and is already strictly larger in order three.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Correlation Relaxation Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point spanning criterion and its rank consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathcal E_n\) have a full-span Gram realization \(X_{ij}=v_i^{\mathsf T}v_j\) in \(\mathbb R^r\), where \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\). Then \(X\) is extreme in \(\mathcal E_n\) if and only if \(\{v_iv_i^{\mathsf T}:1\leq i\leq n\}\) spans \(\mathbb S^r\). Consequently, every extreme point satisfies \(r(r+1)/2\leq n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elliptope point is extreme exactly when the outer products in a minimal Gram realization span all symmetric matrices of that rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Rank Criterion

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E_n\) is a compact convex spectrahedron of affine dimension \(n(n-1)/2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic finite-dimensional convex geometry of the elliptope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(\mathcal E_n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:X\succeq0,\operatorname{diag}(X)=\mathbf1\}\) is a nonempty compact convex spectrahedron. Its affine hull is \(\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\operatorname{diag}(X)=\mathbf1\}\), so \(\dim\mathcal E_n=n(n-1)/2\). Every entry satisfies \(|X_{ij}|\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The elliptope is a compact convex spectrahedron with one free coordinate per off-diagonal pair, and every entry lies between -1 and 1.
knowledge_statements.title: Elliptope Convex Geometry
Elliptope Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correlation-matrix form of the unit-vector feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The order-\(n\) elliptope is \(\mathcal E_n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:X\succeq0,\ X_{ii}=1\text{ for every }i\}\). Its elements are precisely feasible correlation matrices for unit-vector SDP variables. Thus any objective linear in pairwise inner products, \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), has the matrix representation \(\langle C,X\rangle\) over \(X\in\mathcal E_n\), where \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The elliptope consists of positive-semidefinite matrices with unit diagonal and represents all unit-vector pairwise inner products.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elliptope definition and its unit-vector objective representation are correct and match the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Gram–Elliptope Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between vector realizations, Gram matrices, plus elliptope points.

assumptions_latex: Representing configurations are real and finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathcal E_n\iff\exists r\leq n\ \exists v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^r:\ \|v_i\|_2=1\text{ for all }i\text{ and }X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\text{ for all }i,j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between elliptope matrices and unit-vector configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq1\). A matrix \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) belongs to \(\mathcal E_n\) if and only if there exist an integer \(r\leq n\) and unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^r\) such that \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\) for all \(1\leq i,j\leq n\). One may take \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\). Two representing configurations that each span their ambient space have the same Gram matrix exactly when a linear isometry maps one configuration to the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elliptope matrices and unit-vector Gram configurations are equivalent, with a minimum representation dimension equal to the matrix rank and full-span representations unique up to a linear isometry.
knowledge_statements.title: Gram–Elliptope Correspondence

children.title: Metric Strengthenings
children.top_down_role: Metric-consistency constraints added to strengthen SDP relaxation geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Strengthenings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semimetric constraints imposed on distances derived from SDP correlations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathcal E_n\), define \(d_{ij}=(1-X_{ij})/2\). The metric strengthening requires, for all distinct \(i,j,k\), \(d_{ij}\geq0\), \(d_{ij}=d_{ji}\), \(d_{ii}=0\), and \(d_{ij}\leq d_{ik}+d_{kj}\). Every rank-one sign matrix \(X=ss^{\mathsf T}\), with \(s\in\{-1,1\}^n\), satisfies these conditions because the resulting \(d_{ij}\) is the cut semimetric indicating whether \(s_i\neq s_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distances derived from an SDP correlation matrix are strengthened by requiring all semimetric axioms, which every integral sign solution satisfies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{ij}\leq d_{ik}+d_{kj}\) for every triple of distinct indices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed semimetric conditions are valid for rank-one sign matrices and condition is an appropriate knowledge kind. The supplied inventory contains no source locator specific to metric SDP strengthenings.

children.title: Triangle-Inequality Strengthenings
children.top_down_role: Triangle-based constraints imposed on induced distances or correlations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separation of all three-index triangle and perimeter inequalities in an explicit distance array.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an explicit symmetric array d, enumerate every unordered triple \(\{i,j,k\}\). For each triple test \(d_{ij}\leq d_{ik}+d_{jk}\), \(d_{ik}\leq d_{ij}+d_{jk}\), \(d_{jk}\leq d_{ij}+d_{ik}\), and \(d_{ij}+d_{ik}+d_{jk}\leq2\). A failed test returns a violated inequality; if no test fails, the entire triangle-and-perimeter family is satisfied. This requires \(O(n^3)\) arithmetic comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerating all index triples exactly separates the triangle and perimeter inequalities in cubic time.
assumptions_latex: A symmetric array \(d\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is given explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The triangle-and-perimeter family is separated exactly in \(O(n^3)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Cubic-Time Triangle-System Separation
Triangle-Inequality Strengthenings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Triangle and perimeter inequalities valid for every cut semimetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every triple of distinct indices \(i,j,k\), strengthen the elliptope relaxation by imposing \(d_{ij}\leq d_{ik}+d_{jk}\) and \(d_{ij}+d_{ik}+d_{jk}\leq2\), together with their index permutations, where \(d_{ab}=(1-X_{ab})/2\). Equivalently, require \(1+\sigma_i\sigma_jX_{ij}+\sigma_i\sigma_kX_{ik}+\sigma_j\sigma_kX_{jk}\geq0\) for every \((\sigma_i,\sigma_j,\sigma_k)\in\{-1,1\}^3\). These inequalities are valid for every integral matrix \(X=ss^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding all triangle and perimeter inequalities cuts fractional elliptope points while retaining every integral cut matrix.

notation.meaning: Cut-distance variable derived from the correlation matrix.
Auxiliary sign selecting a triangle inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The triangle/perimeter system and its signed correlation form are mathematically consistent and valid for integral cut matrices. A specific authoritative locator is absent.

children.title: Strengthening Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Relative relaxation strength across nested families of metric restrictions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper Strengthening Need Not Improve the Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-strictness of objective improvement under proper feasible-region strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let R'\subsetneq R be nonempty feasible regions and suppose the displayed maxima exist. For every maximization objective c, \[\max_{x\in R'}c^{\mathsf T}x\leq\max_{x\in R}c^{\mathsf T}x.\] Proper inclusion does not imply strict inequality: equality holds whenever R' contains an optimizer of R for c.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper strengthening can leave the relaxation value unchanged when it retains an optimizer of the original relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The displayed maxima exist and are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{x\in R'}c^{\mathsf T}x\leq\max_{x\in R}c^{\mathsf T}x\), with equality possible despite \(R'\subsetneq R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Proper Strengthening Need Not Improve the Bound
Strengthening Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested valid constraints produce monotone relaxation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_0\supseteq R_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq R_L\) be SDP feasible regions obtained by successively adding inequalities valid for every integral feasible matrix, and let \(I\subseteq R_\ell\) denote the integral feasible matrices at every level. For a maximization objective \(\langle C,X\rangle\), define \(B_\ell=\max\{\langle C,X\rangle:X\in R_\ell\}\). Then \(B_0\geq B_1\geq\cdots\geq B_L\geq\max_{X\in I}\langle C,X\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successively adding valid constraints yields nested relaxations whose maximization bounds monotonically approach the integral optimum from above.

notation.meaning: Relaxation region at strengthening level ell.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonicity statement follows from the explicitly nested feasible regions and correctly describes a hierarchy property, but no source with a specific hierarchy locator is provided.

children.title: Moment Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted SDP representations indexed by moments or local assignment statistics.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificate paired with a degree-2r moment relaxation for polynomial maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider maximizing f over polynomial constraints \(g_j(y)\geq0\), \(h_k(y)=0\), together with any stated Boolean relations. If, modulo the Boolean ideal, \[\gamma-f=\sigma_0+\sum_j\sigma_j g_j+\sum_k\tau_k h_k,\] where every \(\sigma_j\) is a sum of squares and every displayed product has degree at most \(2r\), then every feasible degree-\(2r\) pseudoexpectation satisfies \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[f]\leq\gamma\). Thus the identity is a verifiable dual upper-bound certificate; equality with the moment optimum requires the usual additional conic-duality regularity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-degree sum-of-squares identity certifies an upper bound for every feasible moment solution; strong-duality equality needs separate regularity.
assumptions_latex: All SOS and multiplier products in the identity have degree at most \(2r\).
The pseudoexpectation satisfies the associated moment, localizing, equality, and Boolean consistency constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[f]\leq\gamma\) for every feasible degree-\(2r\) pseudoexpectation.
knowledge_statements.title: Truncated Sum-of-Squares Upper-Bound Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated moment encoding of polynomial inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}\) be defined through degree \(2r\). For a constraint \(g(y)\geq0\) of degree d, impose \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[gq^2]\geq0\) for every q with \(\deg q\leq r-\lceil d/2\rceil\); equivalently, the corresponding localizing matrix is positive semidefinite. For an equality \(h(y)=0\) of degree e, impose \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[hp]=0\) for every p with \(\deg p\leq2r-e\). A constraint whose degree exceeds \(2r\) contributes no such truncated condition at level r.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial inequalities become positive-semidefinite localizing matrices, while polynomial equalities become linear moment-consistency equations, subject to the truncation degree.
assumptions_latex: \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}\) is defined on polynomials of degree at most \(2r\).
The displayed tests are imposed only when their degree bounds are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[gq^2]\geq0\) and \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[hp]=0\) encode the degree-\(2r\) local consequences of \(g\geq0\) and \(h=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Localizing Constraints for Polynomial Feasibility
Moment Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-bounded pseudoexpectations represented by positive-semidefinite moment matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Boolean variables \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), a degree-\(2r\) moment lifting is a linear functional \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}\) on polynomials of degree at most \(2r\) satisfying \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[1]=1\), \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[q^2]\geq0\) whenever \(\deg q\leq r\), and \(\widetilde{\mathbb E}[(y_i^2-1)p]=0\) whenever \(\deg p\leq2r-2\). Equivalently, the moment matrix indexed by monomials of degree at most \(r\), with entries \(M_{\alpha,\beta}=\widetilde{\mathbb E}[y^{\alpha+\beta}]\), is positive semidefinite and satisfies the Boolean consistency identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A moment lifting replaces Boolean assignments by consistent low-degree pseudo-moments arranged in a positive-semidefinite matrix.
assumptions_latex: Polynomials are real and considered modulo \(y_i^2=1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pseudoexpectation and positive-semidefinite moment-matrix representation is appropriately scoped to real Boolean sign variables, but it lacks an authoritative moment-hierarchy citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Hierarchy Liftings
children.top_down_role: Systematic relaxation families organized by increasing lift levels.

assumptions_latex: At every level, the moment and localizing constraints are the restrictions of an exact full-degree encoding whose level-\(n\) feasible pseudoexpectations are precisely probability distributions supported on \(F\).
\(H_r\) is the projection onto a fixed collection of original moments of the feasible degree-\(2r\) pseudoexpectations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_{r+1}\subseteq H_r\) for every \(1\leq r<n\), and \(H_n=\operatorname{conv}\{m(y):y\in F\}\), where \(m(y)\) is the selected original-moment vector; in particular, \(H_n=\operatorname{conv}(F)\) when the selected moments are the coordinates \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\).

notation.meaning: Projected feasible region at moment level r.
Vector of the selected original moments evaluated at an assignment.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested pseudoexpectation levels tighten fixed projections and recover the integral moment hull at the full Boolean level under an exact constraint encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq1\), let \(F\subseteq\{-1,1\}^n\) be the feasible set of a Boolean optimization problem, and let \(H_r\) be the projection onto a fixed collection of original moments of its feasible degree-\(2r\) pseudoexpectations. Assume the moment and localizing constraints at each level are restrictions of an exact full-degree encoding, so that feasible level-\(n\) pseudoexpectations are exactly probability distributions supported on \(F\). Restricting any feasible degree-\(2(r+1)\) pseudoexpectation to degree \(2r\) yields \(H_{r+1}\subseteq H_r\) for every \(1\leq r<n\). At level \(n\), \(H_n\) is the convex hull of the selected moment vectors of assignments in \(F\); when the projection selects the coordinate moments, \(H_n=\operatorname{conv}(F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher exact moment levels project into lower ones, and the full Boolean level recovers the convex hull of the selected moment vectors of feasible assignments; for coordinate moments this is the feasible-assignment convex hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy Liftings

children.title: Lift-Level Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparisons of relaxation strength, representation size, plus rounding access across levels.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit monomial-basis growth for general and Boolean-quotiented moment matrices; no generic SDP solver-time claim is made.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an order-r moment matrix in n variables, an unquotiented monomial basis has \(N_r^{\mathrm{poly}}=\binom{n+r}{r}\) elements. Modulo the Boolean relations \(y_i^2=1\), a squarefree basis has \(N_r^{\mathrm{Bool}}=\sum_{k=0}^{\min\{r,n\}}\binom{n}{k}\) elements. Both are \(n^{O(r)}\) for fixed r, whereas \(N_n^{\mathrm{Bool}}=2^n\) and \(N_n^{\mathrm{poly}}=\binom{2n}{n}=2^{\Theta(n)}\). Thus polynomial representation size is a fixed-level statement and does not extend uniformly to levels proportional to n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moment matrices are polynomial-size for fixed level, but both ordinary and Boolean-quotiented bases become exponential at full linear-scale levels.
assumptions_latex: The lifting explicitly indexes all degree-at-most-r monomials, using either the ordinary polynomial basis or the squarefree basis modulo \(y_i^2=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_r^{\mathrm{poly}}=\binom{n+r}{r}\), \(N_r^{\mathrm{Bool}}=\sum_{k=0}^{\min\{r,n\}}\binom{n}{k}\); fixed r gives \(n^{O(r)}\), while r=n gives exponential size.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Level Representation-Size Boundary
Lift-Level Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size–strength tradeoff for fixed-level polynomial moment/SOS relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polynomial optimization problem in \(n\) variables, the order-\(r\) moment relaxation uses moments indexed by monomials of degree at most \(2r\) and a moment matrix indexed by monomials of degree at most \(r\). Its matrix dimension is \(\binom{n+r}{r}=n^{O(r)}\), so generic formulation and solution costs grow as \(n^{O(r)}\) for fixed \(r\). If \(U_r\) denotes its optimum for a maximization problem, then \(U_{r+1}\le U_r\), and every integral feasible solution remains feasible at every level. Thus increasing \(r\) strengthens the upper bound while increasing computational cost; exactness occurs whenever some level admits a representing integral solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level r has size polynomial in n for fixed r, produces nested stronger bounds as r increases, and may eventually become exact at substantially greater cost.
assumptions_latex: \(r\in\mathbb N\) and the relaxation contains all moment and localizing constraints required through degree \(2r\).
The original feasible set is encoded by polynomial equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_{r+1}\le U_r\) and the principal moment-matrix dimension is \(\binom{n+r}{r}=n^{O(r)}\).

notation.meaning: order-r relaxation value for a maximization problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits Lift-Level Tradeoffs, and the dimension and nesting claims are broadly standard. However, no source or inspectable locator is supplied. The claim about generic solution cost requires a specified computational model, and the stated exactness condition does not precisely distinguish equality of relaxation values from extraction of a finitely supported integral representing measure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary rounding by one origin-centered isotropic random hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\), sample \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\) and set \(x_i=1\) if \(\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge0\), and \(x_i=-1\) otherwise. For \(\theta_{ij}=\arccos\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), \[\Pr[x_i\ne x_j]=\frac{\theta_{ij}}{\pi}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Label each unit SDP vector by its side of one random central hyperplane; pairwise separation equals normalized angular distance.
assumptions_latex: \text{Zero inner products, a probability-zero event for nonzero }v_i,\text{ are assigned label }1.

notation.meaning: angle between unit vectors i and j

knowledge_statements.title: Single Central-Hyperplane Rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic cost for explicit vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) explicitly represented vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\), sampling one normal and computing all labels takes \(O(nd)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(n)\) output bits, apart from random-number-generation conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With explicit d-dimensional vectors, one-hyperplane rounding takes O(nd) arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Hyperplane Projection Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes probability amplification from deterministic rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sampling finitely many independent hyperplanes and retaining the best observed rounded solution remains randomized whenever at least two retained outputs occur with positive probability. A deterministic guarantee requires an additional deterministic construction, such as an applicable conditional-expectation procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeating random rounding and choosing the best sample may improve success probability, but it does not make the algorithm deterministic.
assumptions_latex: \text{At least two retained outputs occur with positive probability}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Best-of-}R\text{ sampling is randomized, not a derandomization.}
knowledge_statements.title: Repetition Is Not Derandomization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic expectation for objectives linear in pair-separation indicators; no application-specific approximation ratio is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative weights \(w_{ij}\), \[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{\{i,j\}}w_{ij}\mathbf1[x_i\ne x_j]\right]=\sum_{\{i,j\}}w_{ij}\frac{\arccos\langle v_i,v_j\rangle}{\pi}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected value of a weighted cut-style objective is the weighted sum of normalized vector angles.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected Pair-Separation Objective
Single-Hyperplane Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary rounding of unit SDP vectors by one random central hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\). Sample one vector \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\) and output \(x_i=1\) when \(\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge0\), and \(x_i=-1\) otherwise. For every pair \(i,j\), rotational invariance gives \[\Pr[x_i\ne x_j]=\frac{\arccos(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)}{\pi}.\] A deterministic output may be obtained by repeating the sampling rule a prescribed number of times and retaining the feasible rounded solution with the best objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw one isotropic Gaussian normal and label each SDP vector by its side of the resulting origin-centered hyperplane; pairwise separation equals normalized angular distance.
assumptions_latex: Ties, which occur with probability zero, are assigned to label \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output lies in \(\{-1,1\}^n\) and satisfies \(\Pr[x_i\ne x_j]=\arccos(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)/\pi\).

notation.meaning: rounded binary label of vector i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and central-hyperplane separation formula fit the node, but no source or locator is supplied. Repeating randomized trials and selecting the best result does not itself produce a deterministic algorithm; that sentence must be removed or replaced by a genuine derandomization statement supported by a source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outputs the raw partition induced by several central hyperplanes; application-specific merging of cells is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(m\ge1\), independently sample \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\sim N(0,I_d)\) and assign \(c_i=(\operatorname{sgn}\langle g_1,v_i\rangle,\ldots,\operatorname{sgn}\langle g_m,v_i\rangle)\in\{-1,1\}^m\). The signatures partition the vectors into at most \(2^m\) cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several independent central hyperplanes assign each vector a binary sign signature and thereby form at most 2^m cells.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_i\in\{-1,1\}^m\text{ and the signature partition has at most }2^m\text{ cells}.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Sign-Signature Rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic cost of forming raw signatures from an explicit vector representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For explicit vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\), generating all \(m\) Gaussian normals and computing all \(nm\) signs uses \(O(md+ nmd)=O(nmd)\) arithmetic operations and stores \(nm\) signature bits, apart from random-number-generation conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With explicit d-dimensional vectors, raw multiple-hyperplane signatures take O(nmd) arithmetic work and nm bits of signature storage.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Cost

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cell Labels Need Not Be Feasible Problem Labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between the raw geometric partition and application-specific rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The existence of at most \(2^m\) signature cells does not imply a feasible solution to a target \(q\)-label or constrained partition problem. Feasibility after cell merging requires a separately specified map and analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Signatures define geometric cells, but mapping those cells to problem labels can violate the target constraints.
assumptions_latex: \text{The target problem imposes constraints beyond membership in a signature cell.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Raw signatures alone do not certify application-specific feasibility.}
knowledge_statements.title: Cell Labels Need Not Be Feasible Problem Labels

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pairwise distribution before any application-specific cell merging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\theta_{ij}=\arccos\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), \[\Pr[c_i=c_j]=\left(1-\frac{\theta_{ij}}{\pi}\right)^m,\qquad d_H(c_i,c_j)\sim\operatorname{Binomial}\!\left(m,\frac{\theta_{ij}}{\pi}\right).\] In particular, \(\mathbb E[d_H(c_i,c_j)]=m\theta_{ij}/\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two vectors agree on every signature coordinate with the product probability, and the number of separating hyperplanes is binomial.

notation.meaning: angle between the two unit vectors

knowledge_statements.title: Signature Coincidence and Hamming-Distance Laws
Multiple-Hyperplane Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multilabel rounding using the sign pattern of several independent hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and an integer \(m\ge1\). Independently sample \(g_1,
\ldots,g_m\sim N(0,I_d)\), and assign vertex \(i\) the signature \(c_i=(\operatorname{sgn}\langle g_1,v_i\rangle,
\ldots,\operatorname{sgn}\langle g_m,v_i\rangle)\in\{-1,1\}^m\). The signatures define at most \(2^m\) classes. For two vectors with angle \(\theta_{ij}=\arccos\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), independence yields \[\Pr[c_i=c_j]=\left(1-\frac{\theta_{ij}}{\pi}\right)^m.\] Output the signature partition, or map its cells to the required feasible labels by a specified postprocessing rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several independent random hyperplanes map each vector to a sign signature; two vectors share a signature with probability equal to one minus angular distance, raised to m.
assumptions_latex: The hyperplane normals are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method produces at most \(2^m\) cells and \(\Pr[c_i=c_j]=(1-\theta_{ij}/\pi)^m\).

notation.meaning: sign signature assigned to item i
angle between unit vectors i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the node, and the signature-coincidence formula follows from independent central hyperplanes. No supporting source or locator is supplied. The optional mapping from up to 2^m signature cells to feasible labels is application-dependent and must be specified before it can be treated as part of a complete rounding algorithm.

children.title: Biased Hyperplanes
children.top_down_role: Hyperplane distributions with nonuniform orientation or side-selection bias.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased Hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary hyperplane rounding with a nonzero-mean random normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and a bias vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\). Sample \(g\sim N(\mu,I_d)\) and output \(x_i=1\) if \(\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge0\), otherwise \(x_i=-1\). Since \(\langle g,v_i\rangle\sim N(\langle\mu,v_i\rangle,1)\), the marginal label probability is \[\Pr[x_i=1]=\Phi(\langle\mu,v_i\rangle).\] Hence the direction and magnitude of \(\mu\) prescribe correlated marginal biases while the same sampled hyperplane couples all rounded labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shift the Gaussian distribution of the hyperplane normal away from zero; each vector's positive-label probability becomes the normal CDF of its alignment with the bias.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian marginal calculation is mathematically consistent, and an algorithm is a plausible role. No source or locator establishes that this taxonomy uses Biased Hyperplanes specifically for a nonzero-mean normal rather than for threshold-biased or marginal-preserving hyperplane rounding. That convention materially affects the local meaning and requires source confirmation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional on interpreting bias as a nonzero Gaussian mean; it does not define the terminal taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let unit vectors \(v_i\) be the rows of \(V\). Under \(g\sim N(\mu,I_d)\) and \(x_i=1\) iff \(\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge0\), prescribed marginals \(0<p_i<1\) are simultaneously realizable exactly when \((\Phi^{-1}(p_i))_{i=1}^n\in\operatorname{col}(V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under mean-shifted Gaussian normals, desired label probabilities are realizable by one bias vector exactly when their Gaussian quantiles are compatible with the vector matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Attainability Under Mean-Shift Bias

intermediate_metadata.reason: The proposed mean-shift mathematics is sound but deferred because it selects only one of several materially different meanings allowed by the terminal scope. Shifted hyperplanes and combined bias-shift laws were excluded as sibling content.

children.title: Shifted Hyperplanes
children.top_down_role: Affine hyperplanes displaced from the origin before partitioning SDP vectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One affine hyperplane displaced from the origin; item-specific thresholds are excluded because they generally do not describe one hyperplane in the given vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and a common threshold \(t\in\mathbb R\), sample \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\) and set \(x_i=1\) iff \(\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge t\). Conditional on \(g\), this partitions the vectors by the affine hyperplane \(\{z:\langle g,z\rangle=t\}\), and \(\Pr[x_i=1]=1-\Phi(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample a centered Gaussian normal and compare every vector with the same nonzero threshold, producing a partition by one affine hyperplane.
assumptions_latex: t\in\mathbb R\text{ is common to all vectors}.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Threshold Affine-Hyperplane Rounding

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Item-Specific Thresholds Are Not One Affine Hyperplane
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical geometric boundary of the shifted-hyperplane leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Rules \(x_i=1\iff\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge t_i\) with unequal thresholds \(t_i\) generally cannot be represented as classification of all \(v_i\) by one affine hyperplane \(\{z:\langle g,z\rangle=t\}\) in the stated vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using a different threshold for each vector is general threshold rounding, not usually a cut by one shifted hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Item-specific threshold rounding is not, in general, a single affine-hyperplane partition.}
knowledge_statements.title: Item-Specific Thresholds Are Not One Affine Hyperplane

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise law for one common shifted hyperplane; singular correlations are interpreted by continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For unit vectors \(v_i,v_j\), \(\rho=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\in(-1,1)\), and common-threshold rounding at \(t\), \[\Pr[x_i\ne x_j]=2\bigl(\Phi(t)-\Phi_2(t,t;\rho)\bigr).\] At \(t=0\), this reduces to \(\arccos(\rho)/\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation by a common shifted Gaussian hyperplane is a bivariate-normal probability and reduces to normalized angular distance at zero shift.
assumptions_latex: x_k=1\iff\langle g,v_k\rangle\ge t\text{ with one common }t.

notation.meaning: centered bivariate-normal CDF with correlation rho

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Threshold Pairwise Separation
Shifted Hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Thresholded Gaussian rounding by affine rather than central hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and thresholds \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\in\mathbb R\). Sample \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\) and set \(x_i=1\) when \(\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge t_i\), otherwise set \(x_i=-1\). Then \[\Pr[x_i=1]=1-\Phi(t_i).\] With a common threshold \(t_i=t\), the rule cuts the vector configuration by the affine hyperplane \(\{z:\langle g,z\rangle=t\}\); item-specific thresholds realize prescribed marginals by taking \(t_i=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare each Gaussian projection with a nonzero threshold. Common thresholds define an affine hyperplane, while item-specific thresholds can realize chosen marginal label probabilities.
assumptions_latex: Each desired marginal \(p_i\) lies strictly between \(0\) and \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rounded marginal is \(\Pr[x_i=1]=1-\Phi(t_i)\), and choosing \(t_i=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_i)\) realizes \(p_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The thresholded Gaussian rule and its marginal formula are correct for unit vectors, and the algorithm role fits. No source or inspectable locator is supplied. A common threshold represents one affine hyperplane in the stated vector space, whereas item-specific thresholds are a broader threshold-rounding rule; a source must confirm that both variants belong in this exact container.

children.title: Bias–Shift Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes where orientation bias plus affine displacement affect rounding behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Bias–Shift Interaction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-label probabilities when Gaussian normal bias and affine thresholds are both present.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\sim N(\mu,I_d)\), let \(v_i,v_j\) be unit vectors, and round by \(x_k=1\) exactly when \(\langle g,v_k\rangle\ge t_k\). Put \(a_k=t_k-\langle\mu,v_k\rangle\) and \(\rho=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\). Then \[\Pr[x_i=1,x_j=1]=1-\Phi(a_i)-\Phi(a_j)+\Phi_2(a_i,a_j;\rho),\] where \(\Phi_2\) is the centered bivariate-normal distribution function with correlation \(\rho\). Consequently bias and shift interact only through the effective thresholds \(a_k\): pairs \((\mu,t_k)\) producing the same \(a_k\) induce the same joint rounded law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal bias and affine shift combine into effective thresholds. Joint labels are bivariate-normal tail probabilities determined only by those thresholds and the vectors' correlation.
assumptions_latex: \(-1<\rho<1\); boundary cases are interpreted by continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint law depends on \(\mu\) and \(t_k\) only through \(a_k=t_k-\langle\mu,v_k\rangle\).

notation.meaning: correlation of the two Gaussian projections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bivariate-normal tail formula is internally consistent, and representation is an appropriate role for an interaction-regime description. No source or locator supports either the formula in this rounding context or the assertion that effective thresholds completely capture the intended bias-shift regimes of this taxonomy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate-correlation limits of the conditional effective-threshold representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With effective thresholds \(a_i,a_j\), at \(\rho=1\), \(\Pr[x_i=x_j=1]=1-\Phi(\max\{a_i,a_j\})\). At \(\rho=-1\), \(\Pr[x_i=x_j=1]=\max\{0,\Phi(-a_j)-\Phi(a_i)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfectly correlated projections use the larger threshold; perfectly anticorrelated projections can both be positive only when their threshold constraints leave a nonempty interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Correlation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.reason: The effective-threshold formulas are mathematically correct only under one unconfirmed mean-shift convention and are therefore deferred. The locally essential regime taxonomy remains absent. Pure bias and pure affine displacement were excluded as sibling scopes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective Thresholds for Mean-Shifted Gaussian Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional on isotropic Gaussian mean-shift bias and scalar affine thresholds; it does not establish the intended regime taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\sim N(\mu,I_d)\), let \(v_i,v_j\) be unit vectors, and set \(x_k=1\) iff \(\langle g,v_k\rangle\ge t_k\). With \(a_k=t_k-\langle\mu,v_k\rangle\) and \(\rho=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), \[\Pr[x_i=1,x_j=1]=1-\Phi(a_i)-\Phi(a_j)+\Phi_2(a_i,a_j;\rho).\] Thus this joint law depends on \(\mu\) and \(t_k\) only through the effective thresholds \(a_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For isotropic mean-shifted Gaussian normals, bias and displacement combine by subtracting the projected mean from each threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Effective Thresholds for Mean-Shifted Gaussian Rounding

intermediate_metadata.reason: The effective-threshold formulas are mathematically correct only under one unconfirmed mean-shift convention and are therefore deferred. The locally essential regime taxonomy remains absent. Pure bias and pure affine displacement were excluded as sibling scopes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic projection-and-quantization mechanism only; application-specific feasibility, repair, and approximation guarantees are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\), sample \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\), form \(z_i=\langle g,v_i\rangle\), and output \(x_i=Q_i(z)\) for specified measurable quantizers \(Q_i\). For coordinatewise scalar quantization, \(Q_i(z)=q_i(z_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample one isotropic Gaussian direction, project the SDP vectors, and apply a specified measurable quantizer to the correlated projections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x=(Q_1(z),\ldots,Q_n(z))\text{ is a well-defined randomized rounding output}.
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian-Projection Quantization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between the generic geometric sampler and an optimization-specific rounding theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A measurable quantizer of Gaussian projections need not satisfy the target problem's combinatorial constraints, and its covariance description alone implies neither feasibility nor an approximation ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gaussian projection law defines a sampler, but feasibility and approximation quality require a problem-specific quantizer, repair rule, or analysis.
assumptions_latex: \text{The target problem imposes constraints not encoded solely by measurability of the quantizer.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Gaussian projection and quantization alone do not certify feasibility or approximation quality.}
knowledge_statements.title: Quantization Does Not Imply Feasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-free distributional representation of simultaneous Gaussian projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) has row \(v_i^\top\), \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\), and \(z=Vg\), then \(z\sim N(0,VV^\top)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(z_i,z_j)=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\). Hence every measurable rounding law determined by \(z\) depends on the vectors only through their Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simultaneous projections are multivariate normal with the vectors' Gram matrix as covariance, so orthogonal coordinate changes do not alter projection-based rounding.

notation.meaning: matrix whose rows are the SDP vectors

knowledge_statements.title: Gram-Gaussian Representation
Gaussian-Projection Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General rounding obtained by quantizing correlated Gaussian projections of SDP vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\), an integer \(q\ge2\), and a measurable partition \(\mathbb R=B_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}B_q\). Sample \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\), compute \(z_i=\langle g,v_i\rangle\), and output label \(x_i=a\) exactly when \(z_i\in B_a\). Stop after one sample, or repeat independently and retain the best feasible labeling. For every pair, \((z_i,z_j)\) is jointly Gaussian with covariance \(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), so all pairwise label probabilities are Gaussian measures of the corresponding cells \(B_a\times B_b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project all SDP vectors onto one Gaussian direction and quantize the correlated scalar projections using a fixed measurable partition of the line.
assumptions_latex: The sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_q\) are measurable, disjoint, and cover \(\mathbb R\).
Any required feasibility repair or selection rule is specified by the application.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr[x_i=a,x_j=b]=\Pr[(z_i,z_j)\in B_a\times B_b]\), with Gaussian covariance \(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits Gaussian-Projection Rounding, and the covariance statement is correct. No source or locator is supplied. The record defines a broad quantization template rather than a problem-specific rounding algorithm, and any claimed feasible output or best-of-repetitions step depends on an application-specific feasibility rule that is not given.

children.title: Simplex Rounding
children.top_down_role: SDP rounding based on simplex geometry or simplex-induced partitions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic invariances of randomly oriented regular-simplex rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_q\) be the vertices of a centered regular simplex and let \(Q\) be Haar-uniform over isometric embeddings of their span. The labeling \(x_i\in\operatorname*{argmax}_r\langle v_i,Qa_r\rangle\) is invariant under common orthogonal transformations of all input vectors and permutations of the simplex vertices. Hence every fixed nonzero \(v_i\) satisfies \(\Pr[x_i=r]=1/q\). Uniform marginals do not imply that every label occurs in a finite rounded instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly rotated regular simplex treats directions and labels symmetrically, although some labels may be absent from a finite output.
assumptions_latex: Q is Haar-uniform over the relevant isometric embeddings.

notation.meaning: Random isometric embedding of the simplex span.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Label and Rotation Symmetry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two-vertex regular-simplex case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(q=2\), a regular simplex consists of antipodal unit vectors \(a_1=-a_2\). The rule \(x_i\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{r\in\{1,2\}}\langle v_i,Qa_r\rangle\) therefore assigns labels according to the sign of \(\langle v_i,Qa_1\rangle\) and is exactly random-hyperplane rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-label simplex rounding is ordinary random-hyperplane rounding.
knowledge_statements.title: Antipodal Simplex Specialization
Simplex Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multilabel rounding by randomly orienting a regular simplex and selecting the nearest vertex direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and regular-simplex vertices \(a_1,\ldots,a_q\in\mathbb R^{q-1}\) satisfying \(\langle a_r,a_s\rangle=-1/(q-1)\) for \(r\ne s\). Sample a uniformly random isometric embedding \(Q:\mathbb R^{q-1}\to\mathbb R^d\), and assign \[x_i\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le r\le q}\langle v_i,Qa_r\rangle.\] Resolve zero-probability ties by a fixed rule. The output is the conic Voronoi partition induced by a random rotation of the simplex and contains exactly the labels \(1,
\ldots,q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomly rotate a regular simplex and assign each SDP vector to the simplex direction having greatest inner product with it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule returns a labeling \(x\in\{1,\ldots,q\}^n\) determined by a randomly rotated simplex partition.

notation.meaning: vertex direction of the regular simplex
random isometric embedding of the simplex space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits, but no source or locator identifies this random-isometric-embedding construction as the intended simplex-rounding variant. The sentence saying the output contains exactly all labels 1 through q is false if it means every label must occur; the rule only produces a labeling with values in that label set.

children.title: Random-Vector Rounding
children.top_down_role: SDP rounding based on sampled directions, vectors, or vector-valued scores.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic invariances of independent-Gaussian maximum-correlation rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For independent \(g_1,\ldots,g_q\sim N(0,I_d)\), the joint rounded-label distribution is invariant under every common orthogonal transformation of the input vectors and every permutation of the label indices. Consequently, for each fixed nonzero \(v_i\), \(\Pr[x_i=r]=1/q\) for every label \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian maximum-correlation rounding is rotationally invariant and gives every fixed item a uniform marginal label.
assumptions_latex: The Gaussian directions are independent and identically distributed.

notation.meaning: Label maximizing the Gaussian projection of item i.

knowledge_statements.title: Label and Rotation Symmetry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-label specialization of maximum-correlation Gaussian rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For independent \(g_1,g_2\sim N(0,I_d)\), the rule assigning label one when \(\langle g_1,v_i\rangle\ge\langle g_2,v_i\rangle\) is equivalent to testing \(\langle g_1-g_2,v_i\rangle\ge0\). It is therefore random-hyperplane rounding, and for unit vectors \(v_i,v_j\), \[\Pr[x_i\ne x_j]=\frac{\arccos\langle v_i,v_j\rangle}{\pi}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With two labels, independent-Gaussian maximum-correlation rounding is exactly random-hyperplane rounding.
assumptions_latex: g_1,g_2 are independent standard Gaussian vectors.
v_i and v_j are unit vectors.
The Gaussian pair is shared across all items.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Gaussian-Direction Specialization
Random-Vector Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multilabel rounding by maximum correlation with independent Gaussian directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and a label count \(q\ge2\). Independently sample \(g_1,
\ldots,g_q\sim N(0,I_d)\), and output \[x_i\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le r\le q}\langle g_r,v_i\rangle.\] Use a fixed rule for ties, which have probability zero for nonzero \(v_i\). Equivalently, the sampled vectors generate random polyhedral cones, and each \(v_i\) receives the cone's label. The same directions must be shared across all items so that SDP correlations influence their joint labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw one independent Gaussian direction per label and assign each SDP vector to the direction with the largest projection.
assumptions_latex: The Gaussian directions are independent and shared by all items.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure outputs \(x\in\{1,\ldots,q\}^n\) by a random conic partition of \(\mathbb R^d\).

notation.meaning: Gaussian direction associated with label r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum-correlation Gaussian construction is coherent and the algorithm role fits. No source or inspectable locator is supplied, so the intended random-vector-rounding variant and its placement beside simplex rounding cannot be confirmed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If v_i=0, then \langle g_r,v_i\rangle=0 for every label r with probability one. A deterministic tie rule therefore need not preserve uniform label marginals; a symmetric randomized tie rule would be required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero vector creates a permanent tie under maximum-correlation Gaussian rounding.
assumptions_latex: Labels are chosen by maximum Gaussian projection.

children.title: Geometric Partition Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparison of partition geometry, symmetry, plus objective sensitivity across the two families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete higher-label configuration distinguishing the neighboring partition laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take \(q=3\), \(d=2\), and orthogonal unit vectors \(v,w\). Under independent-Gaussian maximum-correlation rounding, the two three-dimensional score vectors are independent, so their labels are independent and uniform; hence \(\Pr[x_v\ne x_w]=2/3\). Under a uniformly rotated regular-triangle partition of the circle, each label occupies an arc of angle \(2\pi/3\). Two directions separated by \(\pi/2\) lie in the same arc with probability \(1/4\), so \(\Pr[x_v\ne x_w]=3/4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For three labels and two orthogonal planar vectors, simplex rounding separates with probability three quarters, while independent-Gaussian maximum-correlation rounding separates with probability two thirds.
assumptions_latex: The simplex orientation is uniform and the Gaussian label directions are independent standard Gaussians.
knowledge_statements.title: Ternary Kernel Separation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact comparison of the two neighboring geometric rounding families when there are two labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q=2\), rotated-simplex rounding assigns labels by the sign of \(\langle a,v_i\rangle\) for a uniform random unit direction \(a\). Independent-Gaussian maximum-correlation rounding assigns label one exactly when \(\langle g_1-g_2,v_i\rangle\ge0\). Since \((g_1-g_2)/\|g_1-g_2\|\) is uniform on the sphere, the two procedures induce the same distribution on binary labelings. Thus, for unit vectors with correlation \(\rho\), both separation probabilities equal \(\arccos(\rho)/\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two labels, simplex and independent-Gaussian maximum-correlation rounding are both random-hyperplane rounding and have identical separation kernels.
assumptions_latex: The sampled randomness is shared across all rounded vectors.

notation.meaning: Correlation of two unit SDP vectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Label Coincidence
Geometric Partition Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of rotationally invariant rounding partitions through their pair-separation kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a random rotationally invariant measurable partition of the unit sphere, and define its separation kernel by \(p_{\mathcal P}(\rho)=\Pr_{\mathcal P}[v\text{ and }w\text{ receive different labels}]\) whenever \(\langle v,w\rangle=\rho\). For unit SDP vectors and nonnegative edge weights, the expected cut value produced by \(\mathcal P\) is \[\mathbb E[W_{\mathcal P}]=\sum_{\{i,j\}}w_{ij}p_{\mathcal P}(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle).\] Hence two geometric rounding families can be compared pointwise through their kernels; if \(p_{\mathcal P}(\rho)\ge p_{\mathcal Q}(\rho)\) for all realized correlations, then \(\mathcal P\) has at least the expected cut value of \(\mathcal Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotationally invariant partition is summarized by its separation probability as a function of correlation; pointwise kernel dominance implies expected cut-value dominance for nonnegative weights.
assumptions_latex: The partition laws are rotationally invariant.

knowledge_statements.title: Hyperplane Rounding for Maximum Cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Goemans–Williamson random-hyperplane conversion of a feasible Max-Cut SDP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible Max-Cut SDP solution represented by unit vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\), sample \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\) and set \(S=\{i:\langle g,v_i\rangle\ge0\}\). Output the cut \(\delta(S)\). For every edge \(\{i,j\}\), \[\Pr[\{i,j\}\in\delta(S)]=\frac{\arccos(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)}{\pi}.\] Therefore its expected weight is \(\sum_{\{i,j\}}w_{ij}\arccos(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)/\pi\), which is at least \(\alpha_{GW}\) times the SDP objective, where \(\alpha_{GW}=\min_{-1\le t<1}\frac{2\arccos(t)}{\pi(1-t)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut vertices by one random origin-centered hyperplane. Each edge is cut with probability equal to its endpoint vectors' angle divided by pi, yielding the Goemans–Williamson ratio.
assumptions_latex: The graph is undirected and has weights \(w_{ij}\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any fixed feasible unit-vector solution, some hyperplane through the origin induces a cut whose weight is at least the average over uniformly random hyperplanes. Consequently, there exists \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \[W(\delta(S))\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}D(v).\] For an optimal SDP solution, this becomes \(W(\delta(S))\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{SDP}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected Goemans–Williamson bound also proves that at least one hyperplane cut attains that bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Guarantee from an Approximate SDP Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-cut guarantee for a feasible vector solution that need not be SDP-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((v_i)_{i\in V}\) be any feasible unit-vector solution of the standard nonnegative-weight Maximum-Cut SDP, with value \(D(v)=\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}}w_{ij}(1-\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)\). Random-hyperplane rounding satisfies \[\mathbb E[W(\delta(S))]\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}D(v).\] Therefore, if \(D(v)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{SDP}(G)\), then \[\mathbb E[W(\delta(S))]\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(G).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The GW factor holds relative to any feasible SDP vector value, and a multiplicatively approximate SDP solution loses only the same multiplicative factor.
assumptions_latex: The vectors are feasible for the standard unit-vector Maximum-Cut SDP.

knowledge_statements.title: Guarantee from an Approximate SDP Solution
Expected-Cut Performance Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard nonnegative-weight Maximum-Cut SDP with random-hyperplane rounding of an optimal SDP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be an undirected graph with \(w_{ij}\ge 0\), and let \((v_i)_{i\in V}\) be an optimal unit-vector solution of the standard Maximum-Cut SDP. Choose a hyperplane through the origin with uniformly random normal and let \(S\subseteq V\) be one of the two induced vertex classes. For every edge \(\{i,j\}\in E\), writing \(\theta_{ij}=\arccos\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), the endpoints are separated with probability \(\theta_{ij}/\pi\). Consequently, \[\mathbb E[W(\delta(S))]=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}\frac{\theta_{ij}}{\pi}\ge \alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(1-\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)=\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{SDP}(G)\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{OPT}(G).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding an optimal Maximum-Cut SDP solution by a uniformly random hyperplane produces a cut whose expected weight is at least the Goemans–Williamson constant times both the SDP optimum and the maximum-cut optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is undirected and \(w_{ij}\ge0\) for every edge.
The unit vectors \((v_i)_{i\in V}\) form an optimal solution of the standard Maximum-Cut SDP.

children.title: SDP Upper-Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Relaxation-based certificates used to benchmark rounded cuts.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_X\frac14\langle L,X\rangle=\min_y\sum_i y_i\), and equality of feasible objectives certifies optimality of both solutions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual certification for the standard finite Max-Cut SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal Max-Cut SDP is strictly feasible because \(X=I\) has unit diagonal and is positive definite. Its dual is \[\min\left\{\sum_{i\in V}y_i:\operatorname{Diag}(y)-\frac14L\succeq0\right\}.\] Both optima are attained and equal. Thus primal-feasible \(X\) and dual-feasible \(y\) with \(\langle L,X\rangle/4=\sum_i y_i\) jointly certify SDP optimality, and \(\sum_i y_i\) upper-bounds every cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized Max-Cut SDP has no primal-dual gap. Matching feasible primal and dual values certify SDP optimality and an upper bound on maximum cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Duality Certificate

assumptions_latex: The graph is undirected with weighted Laplacian \(L\) and nonnegative edge weights.
The primal and dual semidefinite programs are solved to feasible values.

notation.meaning: Dual variables associated with the unit-diagonal constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal relaxation and dual-feasibility certificates for weighted Maximum Cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard relaxation is \[\operatorname{SDP}(G)=\max\left\{\frac14\langle L,X\rangle:X\succeq0,\ X_{ii}=1\text{ for every }i\in V\right\}.\] Every cut incidence vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^V\) yields the feasible matrix \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\), whose objective equals the cut weight; therefore \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)\le\operatorname{SDP}(G)\). Moreover, any \(y\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfying \[\operatorname{Diag}(y)-\frac14L\succeq0\] is a directly checkable dual certificate giving \(\operatorname{SDP}(G)\le\sum_{i\in V}y_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The SDP contains every cut matrix, while any feasible dual matrix supplies a verifiable numerical upper bound on both the SDP and maximum-cut values.
knowledge_statements.title: SDP Upper-Bound Certificates

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_*\) is the unique solution of \(\tan(\theta/2)=\theta\) in \((0,\pi)\), and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}=r(\theta_*)\approx0.878567\).

notation.meaning: Pointwise ratio of hyperplane separation probability to the SDP edge contribution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Analytic characterization of the pointwise tight angle; no global integrality-gap instance is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r(\theta)=\frac{2\theta}{\pi(1-\cos\theta)}\), the unique interior stationary point satisfies \(1-\cos\theta=\theta\sin\theta\), equivalently \(\tan(\theta/2)=\theta\). Its solution is \(\theta_*\approx2.33112\), where \(r\) attains its global minimum \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\approx0.878567\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sharp edgewise constant occurs at the unique positive angle satisfying tan(theta/2) = theta, approximately 2.33112 radians.
knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Angle Characterization

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No universal coefficient \(\beta>\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\) satisfies \(\theta/\pi\ge\beta(1-\cos\theta)/2\) for every \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\).

notation.meaning: Ratio between hyperplane separation probability and an edge's SDP contribution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tightness of the edgewise angle inequality, not a claim about every SDP integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a vector pair at angle \(\theta\), the expected rounded contribution is \(w\theta/\pi\), whereas its SDP contribution is \(w(1-\cos\theta)/2\). Their ratio is \(r(\theta)\), whose minimum is \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\). At any minimizing angle \(\theta_*\), equality holds in the edgewise estimate. Consequently, every \(\beta>\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\) fails at \(\theta_*\), so an analysis obtained only by summing a uniform pointwise comparison cannot prove a larger universal factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The 0.87856 coefficient is sharp for the edgewise angle inequality: an edge at the minimizing angle makes the rounding and SDP comparison exact.
knowledge_statements.title: Rounding–Certificate Tightness

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) have \(w_{ij}\ge0\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted maximum satisfiability and its bounded-width restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weighted MAX-SAT asks for an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) maximizing \(\sum_C w_C\mathbf1[C(x)=\mathrm{true}]\), where \(w_C\geq0\). Weighted MAX-\(k\)SAT restricts every clause to at most \(k\) literals, and weighted MAX-2SAT is the case \(k=2\). Repeated literals and tautological clauses may be simplified without changing the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted MAX-SAT maximizes the total weight of satisfied clauses; MAX-kSAT and MAX-2SAT impose clause-width bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Goemans-Williamson SDP rounding gives a randomized polynomial-time approximation arbitrarily close to 0.87856 for nonnegatively weighted MAX-2SAT.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary randomized baseline for exact-width maximum satisfiability; for clauses of width at most k the uniform width-independent bound is one half.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign every Boolean variable independently and uniformly. Each non-tautological clause containing exactly \(k\) distinct literals is unsatisfied with probability \(2^{-k}\). Therefore \[\mathbb E[W_{\mathrm{sat}}]=(1-2^{-k})\sum_Cw_C\ge(1-2^{-k})\operatorname{OPT}.\] In particular, exact weighted MAX-2SAT has the \(3/4\) baseline. For the at-most-\(k\) convention, clauses of smaller width prevent the same \(1-2^{-k}\) uniform bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform independent assignment satisfies an expected 1 - 2^-k fraction of total weight for exact-k clauses; exact MAX-2SAT therefore has a 3/4 baseline.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Assignment Baseline

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic realization of the independent-assignment guarantee for exact-width weighted MAX-kSAT.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a weighted formula whose non-tautological clauses contain exactly \(k\) distinct literals, process the variables in any order. At each step choose the truth value maximizing the conditional expectation of the ultimately satisfied weight under independent uniform assignments to the remaining variables. The resulting assignment satisfies \[W_{\mathrm{sat}}\ge(1-2^{-k})\sum_Cw_C\ge(1-2^{-k})\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix variables by conditional expectation to deterministically attain the random-assignment MAX-kSAT baseline.
