Balanced Graph Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted two-way cut with a prescribed balance interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have edge costs \(c_e\ge0\), vertex weights \(\mu_v\ge0\), and \(\mu(V)>0\). For \(0<\beta\le1/2\), a set \(S\subset V\) is \(\beta\)-balanced when
\[\beta\mu(V)\le\mu(S)\le(1-\beta)\mu(V).\]
The \(\beta\)-balanced graph-partitioning problem is
\[\min\left\{c(\delta(S)):S\subset V,\ \beta\mu(V)\le\mu(S)\le(1-\beta)\mu(V)\right\},\]
where \(c(\delta(S))\) is the total cost of edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). Both sides of the cut are therefore required to carry a fixed positive fraction of the vertex weight.

children.title: Balance-Constraint Effects

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected or marginal balance does not certify a balanced realized cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu(V)=1\), and let one fair random bit choose \(S=V\) or \(S=\varnothing\). Then every vertex has inclusion probability \(1/2\) and \(\mathbb E[\mu(S)]=1/2\), but every realization has mass \(0\) or \(1\). Thus for every \(0<\beta\le1/2\), expected shore mass and balanced vertex marginals do not imply a positive probability of a \(\beta\)-balanced cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfectly correlated choices can have balanced marginals while producing only the empty or full shore.

Balance-Constraint Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balance prevents the product-demand denominator from becoming arbitrarily small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Normalize nonnegative vertex weights so that \(\mu(V)=1\), and give pair \(\{i,j\}\) product demand \(d_{ij}=\mu_i\mu_j\). For every cut \(S\subset V\), its separated demand is
\[d(S,V\setminus S)=\sum_{i\in S,j\notin S}\mu_i\mu_j=\mu(S)(1-\mu(S)).\]
If \(S\) is \(\beta\)-balanced, then
\[\beta(1-\beta)\le d(S,V\setminus S)\le\frac14.\]
Thus a balance constraint supplies a uniform positive lower bound on the sparsest-cut denominator; without balance, that denominator can approach zero as one side loses vertex mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under product demands, beta-balance keeps separated demand between beta times one-minus-beta and one quarter, excluding vanishing-mass cuts.

notation.meaning: Product demand between vertices i and j.

children.title: Expansion-Based Cut Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cut problems organized by expansion and demand structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of conductance and cardinality-normalized edge expansion on regular graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite unweighted \(d\)-regular graph with \(d>0\), for every \(S\) satisfying \(0<|S|\le|V|/2\), conductance and edge expansion obey \(\phi(S)=h(S)/d\), where \(h(S)=|\delta(S)|/|S|\). Consequently they rank cuts identically in this regime. Without regularity, cardinality and volume normalization need not rank cuts identically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a d-regular graph, conductance is edge expansion divided by d; this equivalence need not hold on irregular graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular-Graph Expansion Equivalence
Expansion-Based Cut Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conductance formulation for volume-normalized expansion cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(w_e\ge0\), weighted degree \(d_v=\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E}w_{uv}\), and volume \(\operatorname{vol}(S)=\sum_{v\in S}d_v\). For every nontrivial set with positive volume on both sides, define its conductance by
\[\phi(S)=\frac{w(\delta(S))}{\min\{\operatorname{vol}(S),\operatorname{vol}(V\setminus S)\}}.\]
The expansion-based cut objective is \(\phi(G)=\min_S\phi(S)\). A threshold regime \(\phi(G)\le\tau\) asks for a cut whose boundary weight is at most \(\tau\) times the volume of its smaller side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conductance divides cut-boundary weight by the smaller side’s volume; low-expansion regimes seek a cut with conductance at most a threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and has nonnegative edge weights.
Only cuts with positive volume on both sides are considered.

children.title: Angular Separation Analysis
children.top_down_role: Certificate analysis expressed through angles among relaxation vectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geodesic structure of angular separation among unit SDP vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For unit vectors \(u,v,w\in\mathbb R^d\), define \(d_{\angle}(u,v)=\arccos\langle u,v\rangle\). This is the geodesic metric on the unit sphere: it is symmetric, vanishes exactly when \(u=v\), and satisfies \[d_{\angle}(u,w)\le d_{\angle}(u,v)+d_{\angle}(v,w).\] Its normalization \(d_{\angle}/\pi\) is therefore also a metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Angular separation is the geodesic metric on the unit sphere, and normalization by pi preserves the metric properties.
knowledge_statements.title: Angular Distance Structure

notation.meaning: Angle between the two SDP vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian random-hyperplane rounding for two unit SDP vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u,v\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be unit vectors with angular separation \(\theta=\arccos\langle u,v\rangle\). For \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\), assign each vector the sign \(s_g(w)=\operatorname{sign}\langle g,w\rangle\), with the zero event assigned arbitrarily. Rotational invariance reduces the event to the plane spanned by \(u\) and \(v\); its probability is
\[\Pr[s_g(u)\ne s_g(v)]=\frac{\theta}{\pi}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gaussian hyperplane separates two unit vectors with probability equal to their angle divided by pi.

children.title: Angle–Correlation Translation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fully specified scalar correspondence for random Gaussian-hyperplane rounding of two unit vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u,v\in\mathbb R^d\) be unit vectors, let \(\rho=\langle u,v\rangle\), and let \(\theta=\arccos\rho\in[0,\pi]\). Draw \(g\sim N(0,I_d)\) and set \(s_g(w)=\operatorname{sign}(\langle g,w\rangle)\), with the zero case assigned arbitrarily. Then \[\Pr[s_g(u)\ne s_g(v)]=\frac{\theta}{\pi}=\frac{\arccos\rho}{\pi}.\] Consequently \(\rho=\cos\theta=\cos(\pi p)\), where p is the separation probability. The map \(p(\rho)=\arccos(\rho)/\pi\) is strictly decreasing on \((-1,1)\), with \(p(1)=0\), \(p(0)=1/2\), and \(p(-1)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Gaussian-hyperplane rounding, correlation, angle, and separation probability translate exactly through cosine and arccosine; greater correlation means lower separation probability.

children.title: Extremal Correlation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Correlation patterns governing best-case or worst-case rounding behavior.

notation.meaning: Gaussian-hyperplane separation probability at correlation rho

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar behavior of hyperplane-separation probability near perfect correlation and anticorrelation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p(\rho)=\pi^{-1}\arccos\rho\), \[p(\rho)\sim \frac{\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}}{\pi}\quad(\rho\uparrow1),\qquad 1-p(\rho)\sim\frac{\sqrt{2(1+\rho)}}{\pi}\quad(\rho\downarrow-1).\] Hence the endpoint deviations have square-root rather than linear scale. In particular, \(p\) is not Lipschitz on \([-1,1]\), and no endpoint Hölder exponent greater than \(1/2\) is possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near correlations plus or minus one, separation-probability deviations scale as the square root of the correlation deviation.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Endpoint Asymptotics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint and orthogonality regimes of the correlation-separation map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The map \(p(\rho)=\pi^{-1}\arccos\rho\) is continuous and strictly decreasing on \([-1,1]\), with
\[p(-1)=1,\qquad p(0)=\frac12,\qquad p(1)=0.\]
For \(|\rho|<1\),
\[p'(\rho)=-\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}.\]
Thus antipodal vectors are always separated, orthogonal vectors are separated with probability \(1/2\), identical vectors are never separated, and endpoint sensitivity is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation decreases from one to zero as correlation increases, with orthogonal vectors at one half and singular endpoint sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremal Correlation Regimes

assumptions_latex: The feasible region is the unit-diagonal elliptope and the objective is identically zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E_n\) contains feasible matrices of rank \(n-1\) and optimal matrices of rank \(1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between existence of high-rank feasible Gram matrices and necessity of high-rank optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), the unit-diagonal elliptope \(\mathcal E_n=\{X\succeq0:\operatorname{diag}(X)=\mathbf1\}\) contains the rank-\(n-1\) regular-simplex Gram matrix from the immutable seed. For the zero objective, however, every point of \(\mathcal E_n\) is optimal, including every rank-one matrix \(xx^{\mathsf T}\) with \(x\in\{\pm1\}^n\). Thus existence of high-rank feasible solutions does not imply that every optimum has high rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectrahedron can contain rank n-minus-one feasible points and rank-one optimal points, so high feasible rank does not establish necessary high optimal rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: High Feasible Rank Does Not Force High Optimal Rank
knowledge_statements.title: High Feasible Rank Does Not Force High Optimal Rank

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an optimal \(X^*\) of rank \(r\) satisfying \(r(r+1)/2\le m\).

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite n-by-n matrices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a low-rank optimum as a function of the number of affine SDP constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a real semidefinite program with nonempty compact feasible region \[\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}.\] For every linear objective, there exists an optimal solution \(X^*\in\mathcal F\) whose rank \(r\) satisfies \[\frac{r(r+1)}2\le m.\] Consequently, some optimum has rank at most \(\left\lfloor(\sqrt{8m+1}-1)/2\right\rfloor\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real SDP with m affine equality constraints and an attained optimum has an optimal solution of rank on the order of the square root of m.
knowledge_statements.title: Barvinok-Pataki Rank Bound

notation.meaning: Gram matrix of the regular simplex

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-simplex family exhibiting unbounded SDP Gram rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(n\ge2\), define
\[X_n=\frac{n}{n-1}I_n-\frac{1}{n-1}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}.\]
Then \(X_n\succeq0\), \(\operatorname{diag}(X_n)=\mathbf{1}\), every off-diagonal entry equals \(-1/(n-1)\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(X_n)=n-1\). Hence \(X_n\) is the Gram matrix of \(n\) unit vectors forming a regular simplex, and feasible unit-vector SDP solutions can require dimension growing linearly with instance size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular-simplex Gram matrices provide unit-vector SDP solutions of rank n minus one, so feasible SDP rank can grow without bound.
knowledge_statements.title: High-Rank SDP Solution Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simplex matrix identities are correct and representation fits the leaf. However, the matrix exhibits feasible solutions having rank n-1; it does not by itself show that an SDP instance requires every relevant feasible or optimal solution to have that rank. A source and narrower wording are required.

children.title: Metric-Only Rounding Barriers
children.top_down_role: Limitations of rounding procedures using only induced metric information.

assumptions_latex: The rounding rule's complete observable input is the same datum \(D\) on instances \(I\) and \(J\).
The rule's admissible output space is common to the two maximization instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every common output distribution has normalized expected value below \(\alpha\) on at least one instance, no \(D\)-only rule is an \(\alpha\)-approximation on both.

notation.meaning: Output distribution determined solely by the observable metric datum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic obstruction for rounding rules whose complete observable input is a labeled metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a randomized rounding rule receive only an observable datum \(D\), such as a labeled SDP metric. If two instances \(I\) and \(J\) expose the same datum, the rule must use the same output distribution \(Q_D\) on both. For a maximization problem with a common admissible output space, if every distribution \(Q\) satisfies \[\min\left\{\frac{\mathbb E_Q[f_I(S)]}{\mathrm{OPT}_I},\frac{\mathbb E_Q[f_J(S)]}{\mathrm{OPT}_J}\right\}<\alpha,\] then no rounding rule depending only on \(D\) can guarantee approximation factor \(\alpha\) on both instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two instances with identical observable metrics but incompatible good outputs certify that no metric-only randomized rule attains the claimed factor on both.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Indistinguishability Barrier

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal observability restriction underlying metric-indistinguishability barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix labeled objects U, an admissible output space \mathcal S, and declared public parameters. A randomized rounding rule is metric-only with respect to a labeled metric datum D=(U,\delta) if its output distribution is a function Q_D only of D and those parameters. Consequently, two instances exposing exactly the same D and public parameters induce the same distribution Q_D.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric-only rule must behave identically on instances presenting the same complete labeled metric and public parameters.
assumptions_latex: The complete observable metric input and all public side information are specified.
Compared instances have a common admissible output space.

notation.meaning: Output distribution determined by observable datum D

review_flags: The restriction is meaningful only after all side information visible to the algorithm is declared.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Only Rounding Rule

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation between relaxation-relative and information-restricted barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An SDP integrality-gap witness compares \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I) with \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I) on each instance and therefore limits every guarantee measured against that relaxation value, regardless of the information used by the rounding algorithm. A metric-indistinguishability witness instead requires distinct instances exposing the same complete observable datum D and limits only algorithms whose output distribution is a function of D. Without additional hypotheses, neither witness is a substitute for the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrality gaps restrict all relaxation-relative rounding, whereas indistinguishable metrics restrict only algorithms denied distinguishing side information.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation-relative benchmark and complete observable datum are explicitly specified.
Approximation direction and normalization are fixed.

notation.meaning: Complete datum observable to the metric-only rounding rule

review_flags: This is a scope separation, not a numerical lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap and Metric-Indistinguishability Separation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sufficient certificate excluding a claimed factor for metric-only randomized rounding on two indistinguishable instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let finite maximization instances \(I,J\) expose the same complete observable datum and have the same finite output set \(\mathcal S\). Define \(r_I(s)=f_I(s)/\operatorname{OPT}_I\) and \(r_J(s)=f_J(s)/\operatorname{OPT}_J\). If some \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) satisfies \[\lambda r_I(s)+(1-\lambda)r_J(s)\leq\alpha\qquad\text{for every }s\in\mathcal S,\] then every output distribution \(Q\) satisfies \[\min\{\mathbb E_Q[r_I(S)],\mathbb E_Q[r_J(S)]\}\leq\alpha.\] Hence no rule determined solely by the shared datum can guarantee a factor greater than \(\alpha\) on both instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixing weight whose pointwise weighted normalized payoff is at most alpha certifies that every common output distribution performs at most alpha on one of two indistinguishable instances.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) is finite and common to both instances.
The instances expose identical complete observable data and public parameters to the metric-only rule.

notation.meaning: Objective values normalized by the respective integral optima
Certificate mixing weight between the two instances
Common output distribution forced by indistinguishability

review_flags: This is a sufficient abstract certificate; a numerical barrier still requires explicit instances, optima, shared observable data, and payoff values.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Instance Distributional Incompatibility Certificate

assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a rounding algorithm whose guarantee uses only a feasible SDP metric.
An instance family has integral optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}\) and relaxation optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality-gap obstruction to guarantees derived solely from an SDP metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a maximization problem and an algorithm \(R\) that rounds a feasible SDP metric to an integral solution. If \(R\) guarantees value at least \(\alpha\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)\) on every instance \(I\), then integral feasibility forces
\[\alpha\le\frac{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)}{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)}\quad\text{for every }I.\]
Therefore
\[\alpha\le\inf_I\frac{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)}{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)},\]
so an SDP integrality-gap family is an unconditional barrier to any stronger metric-based rounding guarantee for that relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integrality gap of an SDP relaxation upper-bounds every universal approximation guarantee obtained by rounding that relaxation's metric.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Only Rounding Barriers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed integrality-gap inequality is correct and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The argument applies to any integral output guarantee measured against this SDP optimum, not specifically to algorithms using only the SDP metric. A family-specific source and precise scope are needed.

children.title: Dimension-Reduction Losses
children.top_down_role: Approximation losses associated with reducing vector dimension before rounding.

notation.meaning: Additive correlation distortion at an endpoint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp rounding loss caused by endpoint correlation distortion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(t)=\pi^{-1}\arccos t\). As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), \[p(1-\varepsilon)-p(1)=\frac{\arccos(1-\varepsilon)}{\pi}\sim\frac{\sqrt{2\varepsilon}}{\pi},\] and symmetrically \[p(-1)-p(-1+\varepsilon)\sim\frac{\sqrt{2\varepsilon}}{\pi}.\] Thus an additive correlation error of order \(\varepsilon\) can cause a rounding-probability error of order \(\sqrt\varepsilon\), so a uniform \(O(\varepsilon)\) loss bound is impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near perfect correlation or anticorrelation, an epsilon correlation error can create a square-root-epsilon rounding-probability error.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Square-Root Loss

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation of correlation distortion into hyperplane-rounding probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p(t)=\pi^{-1}\arccos t\). If \(\rho,\widetilde\rho\in[-1,1]\), \(|\rho-\widetilde\rho|\le\varepsilon\), and \(|\rho|+\varepsilon<1\), then the mean-value theorem gives
\[|p(\widetilde\rho)-p(\rho)|\le\frac{\varepsilon}{\pi\sqrt{1-(|\rho|+\varepsilon)^2}}.\]
No correlation-independent Lipschitz constant exists on all of \([-1,1]\), because \(|p'(t)|\) diverges as \(t\) approaches either endpoint. Thus small dimension-reduction errors can cause disproportionately large probability errors near perfect correlation or anticorrelation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Correlation distortion causes controlled rounding loss away from the endpoints, but no uniform linear bound holds near correlations plus or minus one.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Reduction Losses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mean-value bound and endpoint non-Lipschitz behavior are correct, and property fits the loss-analysis leaf. No inspectable source is supplied for the claimed dimension-reduction interpretation.

children.title: Rank–Metric Failure Interactions
children.top_down_role: Regimes where rank complexity compounds metric insufficiency.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No unit-vector realization in \(\mathbb R^k\) preserves every induced pairwise correlation or squared distance exactly.

notation.meaning: Rank and minimum exact Gram-representation dimension

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for reducing below Gram rank while preserving all unit-vector correlations or distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\succeq0\) have unit diagonal and rank \(r\), and set \(D_{ij}=2-2X_{ij}\). If \(k<r\), there are no unit vectors \(w_1,\ldots,w_n\in\mathbb R^k\) satisfying \(\|w_i-w_j\|_2^2=D_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\). Thus every reduction below rank \(r\) must distort at least one pairwise correlation or squared distance, although the resulting rounding loss depends on where that distortion occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reducing a unit-vector configuration below its Gram rank necessarily changes at least one pairwise metric value.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Rank Reduction Requires Metric Distortion
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Rank Reduction Requires Metric Distortion

assumptions_latex: \(D\) is their complete labeled squared-distance matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}-D/2\), and the minimum exact unit-vector realization dimension is \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\).

notation.meaning: Squared Euclidean distance matrix of the unit vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relation between a complete unit-vector squared-distance matrix, its Gram matrix, and representation rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) be unit vectors, let \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\), and let \(D_{ij}=\|v_i-v_j\|_2^2\). Then \[D_{ij}=2-2X_{ij},\qquad X=\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}-\frac12D.\] Hence the complete labeled squared-distance matrix determines the Gram matrix and its rank. An exact realization of the same unit-vector metric in \(\mathbb R^k\) exists if and only if \(k\ge\operatorname{rank}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For unit vectors, the complete squared-distance matrix determines every Gram correlation and the minimum exact realization dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Vector Metric Determines Gram Rank

assumptions_latex: \(X\succeq0\) with \(X_{ii}=1\) is a Gram matrix of vectors \(v_i\).
Rounding uses one isotropic Gaussian hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of rank-based explanations for pairwise hyperplane rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\succeq0\) satisfy \(X_{ii}=1\), and choose any Gram representation \(X_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\) in dimension \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\). Under isotropic Gaussian-hyperplane rounding,
\[\Pr[s_g(v_i)\ne s_g(v_j)]=\frac{1}{\pi}\arccos(X_{ij}).\]
The right-hand side contains no separate dependence on \(r\). Consequently, high rank alone cannot explain failure for objectives that are sums of pairwise disagreement terms; a genuine rank-related barrier must enter through correlation distortion, global feasibility requirements, or a different rounding rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For pairwise Gaussian hyperplane rounding, rank has no effect beyond the Gram correlations; rank alone therefore cannot create a rounding loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank–Metric Failure Interactions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pairwise separation formula is correct for isotropic Gaussian hyperplane rounding, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The broader conclusion about all sums of pairwise disagreement terms needs a source and should remain explicitly restricted to expected performance under this rounding rule.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary infinite integrality-gap family for the basic Max-Cut SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard Max-Cut SDP, the disjoint union \(I_k\) of \(k\ge1\) triangles satisfies \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I_k)=9k/4\), \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I_k)=2k\), and therefore \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I_k)/\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I_k)=9/8\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint unions of triangles form an infinite family on which the basic Max-Cut SDP has gap 9/8.
assumptions_latex: The standard Max-Cut SDP is \(\max \frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}(1-\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)\) subject to \(\|v_i\|_2=1\).
\(I_k\) is the disjoint union of \(k\ge1\) triangles.
knowledge_statements.title: Triangle Max-Cut SDP Gap Family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal consequence of a maximization SDP integrality-gap family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a maximization algorithm always returns an integral solution of expected value at least \(\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)\), then on a declared family \(\mathcal F\), \[\alpha\le\inf_{I\in\mathcal F}\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)}=\frac1{\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal F)}.\] Thus a family with limiting relaxation-to-integral ratio \(\gamma\) rules out every universal relaxation-relative factor exceeding \(1/\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximization SDP gap family upper-bounds every universal guarantee measured directly against that SDP value.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm always outputs an integral feasible solution.
The guarantee is measured against the same SDP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Relative Approximation Barrier

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Disjoint-Union Preservation of SDP Gap Ratios
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure operation turning an additive gap instance into an infinite family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the integral objective and SDP relaxation decompose additively over disjoint components. If \(I\) satisfies \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)=S\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)=T>0\), then for every \(k\ge1\), \[\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I^{\sqcup k})=kS,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I^{\sqcup k})=kT,\] so the ratio remains \(S/T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For additive problems and relaxations, disjoint copies preserve the SDP integrality-gap ratio.
assumptions_latex: Integral and SDP optimum values are additive over disjoint components.

notation.meaning: Disjoint union of k copies of I.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint-Union Preservation of SDP Gap Ratios

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limiting gap for the standard weighted Goemans-Williamson Max-Cut SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}=\min_{-1\le t<1}\frac{(2/\pi)\arccos(t)}{1-t}\). There exists a sequence of nonnegatively weighted Max-Cut instances \((I_m)\) for which the standard unit-vector SDP satisfies \[\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I_m)}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I_m)}=\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}},\] equivalently \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I_m)/\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I_m)\to1/\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted Max-Cut instances asymptotically attain the reciprocal of the Goemans-Williamson constant as the standard SDP integrality gap.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation is the standard unit-vector Max-Cut SDP.

notation.meaning: Member of the weighted Max-Cut gap family.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotically Sharp Max-Cut SDP Gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size-indexed refinement of a family-wide maximization SDP gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization relaxation and size map \(s(I)\), define \[g(n)=\sup\left\{\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)}:I\in\mathcal F,\ s(I)\le n\right\}.\] Then \(g(n)\) is nondecreasing and \(\sup_n g(n)=\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-size profile is the worst SDP-to-integral ratio among family members of size at most n; it increases to the family gap.

notation.meaning: Worst gap ratio among family members of size at most n.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Size SDP Gap Profile

assumptions_latex: For each instance \(I\), \(0<\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)\le\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)\) in a maximization relaxation.

notation.meaning: Integrality gap of the SDP on the family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization convention for SDP integrality-gap families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a maximization problem with integral optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)\) and SDP-relaxation optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)\), where \(0<\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)\le\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)\), the integrality gap on an instance family \(\mathcal{F}\) is
\[\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal{F})=\sup_{I\in\mathcal{F}}\frac{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{sdp}}(I)}{\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}(I)}.\]
A sequence \((I_n)\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) is an SDP integrality-gap family with limiting gap \(\gamma\) when the displayed ratios converge to \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SDP integrality-gap family consists of instances whose relaxation-to-integral optimum ratios approach a specified limiting worst-case gap.
knowledge_statements.title: SDP Integrality-Gap Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximization integrality-gap convention is precise, and definition is the correct content kind for this topic. No authoritative source with a specific locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Throughout growth, \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\); the output is a primal-feasible support assembled at tight dual constraints.

notation.meaning: Dual slack of primal column j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic dual-growth schema for nonnegative covering linear programs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the covering LP \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,x\ge0\}\), use the dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c,y\ge0\}\). Initialize \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). While some primal row is uncovered, select such a row and increase its dual variable, possibly together with other prescribed active variables, until a dual constraint \((A^{\mathsf T}y)_j=c_j\) becomes tight; then make column \(j\) available to the primal augmentation rule. Stop when the selected columns admit \(Ax\ge b\), optionally apply reverse deletion, and output the resulting \(x\). Dual feasibility is maintained throughout growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow dual variables on uncovered constraints until columns become tight, augment the primal with those columns, and stop after obtaining a feasible cover.

children.title: Primal Object Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection frameworks for constructing an initial primal solution from dual information.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Object Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of dual-tight objects in a binary unit-covering primal-dual schema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the binary covering pair \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax\ge\mathbf 1,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{\mathbf 1^\top y:A^\top y\le c,\ y\ge0\}\). Given a dual-feasible vector \(y\), initialize \(S=\varnothing\) and \(U=\{i:\sum_{j\in S}a_{ij}<1\}\). While \(U\ne\varnothing\), choose an object \(j\notin S\) such that \((A^\top y)_j=c_j\) and \(a_{ij}=1\) for some \(i\in U\), set \(S\leftarrow S\cup\{j\}\), and recompute \(U=\{i:\sum_{j\in S}a_{ij}<1\}\). Return the incidence vector \(x^S\) when \(U=\varnothing\); report failure if no eligible tight object exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a binary unit-covering problem, repeatedly select a dual-tight object covering an uncovered requirement. Return its incidence vector when every requirement is covered, or report failure if no eligible object exists.

notation.meaning: Rows not covered by the selected objects.

source_refs.locator: 5.2 The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 105

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 105

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact success condition for selection restricted to dual-tight objects in binary unit covering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dual-feasible \(y\), let \(T(y)=\{j:(A^\top y)_j=c_j\}\). A cover using only dual-tight objects exists if and only if every row \(i\) has some \(j\in T(y)\) with \(a_{ij}=1\). Under this condition, any procedure that repeatedly selects a tight object covering a currently uncovered row terminates with a feasible cover after at most \(m\) selections. If the condition fails for a row, no tight-object-only selection can cover that row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tight-object selection succeeds exactly when the tight objects collectively cover every requirement; every progress-making execution then uses at most one selection per row.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration selects a previously unselected tight object covering an uncovered row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists S\subseteq T(y):Ax^S\ge\mathbf1\iff \forall i\ \exists j\in T(y)\text{ with }a_{ij}=1.

notation.meaning: Set of primal objects tight under y.

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Object Coverability Criterion

children.title: Feasibility Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Augmentation frameworks that restore or extend primal feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Progress-guaranteed augmentation for an unbounded continuous nonnegative covering system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(z=0\) and \(d=(b-Ax)_+\). While some \(d_i>0\), choose such a row \(i\). If \(a_{ij}=0\) for every \(j\), report infeasibility. Otherwise choose any \(j\) with \(a_{ij}>0\), set \(\delta=d_i/a_{ij}>0\), update \(z_j\leftarrow z_j+\delta\), and recompute \(d=(b-A(x+z))_+\). Each iteration permanently satisfies its chosen row. Therefore the procedure returns a feasible augmentation after at most the number of initially deficient rows, unless it detects an uncovered deficient row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a deficient row and increase any variable covering it until that row is satisfied. With unbounded continuous variables, this takes at most one augmentation per initially deficient row or detects an impossible row.
assumptions_latex: Augmentation variables are continuous, nonnegative, and unbounded above.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At most }|\{i:(Ax)_i<b_i\}|\text{ augmentations produce }A(x+z)\ge b\text{, or expose }i\text{ with }d_i>0\text{ and }a_{ij}=0\ \forall j.

notation.meaning: Positive augmentation satisfying the chosen row.

knowledge_statements.title: Deficient-Row Feasibility Augmentation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Does Not Control Augmentation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary feasibility augmentation can have an unbounded cost ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M>1\), consider \(\min\{z_1+Mz_2:z_1+z_2\ge1,\ z\ge0\}\) from the zero partial solution. Both \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) restore feasibility, but their costs are \(1\) and \(M\). Thus feasibility restoration alone gives no approximation ratio independent of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two augmentations can restore the same covering constraint while differing by an arbitrarily large cost factor.
assumptions_latex: The initial partial solution is zero.

notation.meaning: Arbitrarily large cost of the second augmentation variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Does Not Control Augmentation Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of continuous feasibility augmentation to a residual covering problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}\), \(b,c\ge0\), and a partial vector \(x\ge0\), define \(d=(b-Ax)_+\). A vector \(z\ge0\) makes \(x+z\) feasible for \(A(x+z)\ge b\) if and only if \(Az\ge d\). Hence minimum-cost continuous augmentation is \[\min\{c^\top z:Az\ge d,\ z\ge0\},\] with dual \[\max\{d^\top y:A^\top y\le c,\ y\ge0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous feasibility augmentation is exactly a covering problem for residual deficits, with the associated packing dual providing lower bounds on augmentation cost.
assumptions_latex: Augmentation variables are continuous, nonnegative, and unbounded above.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Covering Formulation
Feasibility Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy augmentation of an incomplete nonnegative covering solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times n}\), \(b,c\ge0\), and a partial solution \(x\ge0\), define deficits \(d_i=(b_i-(Ax)_i)_+\). While some \(d_i>0\), choose \(j\) with \(\sum_i\min\{a_{ij},d_i\}>0\) minimizing \(c_j/\sum_i\min\{a_{ij},d_i\}\). Increase \(x_j\) by \(\delta=\min_{i:a_{ij}>0}d_i/a_{ij}\), recompute \(d\), and continue. Return the augmented vector when \(d=0\); report infeasibility if every denominator is zero while a deficit remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add the most cost-effective object against current deficits, increasing it until a deficient row becomes tight. Stop at feasibility or certify that remaining deficits cannot be covered.
assumptions_latex: \(A\), \(b\), \(c\), and the initial \(x\) are componentwise nonnegative.
Arithmetic and ratio comparisons are exact.

notation.meaning: Residual deficit of covering row i.

children.title: Selection–Augmentation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural tradeoffs between early selection choices and later augmentation costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection–Augmentation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive approximation accounting for a selected core and its augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=x^{\mathrm{sel}}+x^{\mathrm{aug}}\) be feasible for a nonnegative covering minimization problem, and let \(y\) be feasible for its dual. If \(c^\top x^{\mathrm{sel}}\le\alpha b^\top y\) and \(c^\top x^{\mathrm{aug}}\le\beta b^\top y\), then \[c^\top x\le(\alpha+\beta)b^\top y\le(\alpha+\beta)\operatorname{OPT}.\] Thus the certified approximation factor is the sum of the separately established selection and augmentation factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If selection and augmentation cost at most alpha and beta times the same feasible dual value, their combined solution is an alpha-plus-beta approximation.

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate component bounds do not imply a maximum-type combined factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha,\beta\ge1\) and consider \[\min\{x_0+\alpha x_1+\beta x_2:x_0+x_1\ge1,\ x_0+x_2\ge1,\ x\ge0\}.\] The optimum and the value of the feasible dual vector \(y=(1,0)\) are both \(1\). The selected vector \(x^{\mathrm{sel}}=(0,1,0)\) covers the first row, the augmentation \(x^{\mathrm{aug}}=(0,0,1)\) repairs the second row, and their sum is feasible. Moreover, \(c^\top x^{\mathrm{sel}}=\alpha\), \(c^\top x^{\mathrm{aug}}=\beta\), and \(c^\top(x^{\mathrm{sel}}+x^{\mathrm{aug}})=\alpha+\beta\). Thus the separate component bounds alone cannot be replaced by \(\max\{\alpha,\beta\}\) or any universally smaller coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The alpha-plus-beta bound is sharp from separate component estimates alone; a better combined factor requires an additional coupling invariant.
assumptions_latex: Only separate component bounds against a common dual lower bound and feasibility of the combined vector are assumed.

notation.meaning: Variables used by selection and augmentation respectively.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of Additive Selection–Augmentation Accounting

children.title: Augmentation-Cost Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates controlling the approximation contribution of primal augmentation.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation-Cost Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-charge certificate for the cost of feasibility augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a covering minimization problem \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) with dual \(\max\{b^\top y:A^\top y\le c,\ y\ge0\}\). For an augmentation vector \(z\ge0\), a dual-feasible vector \(y\), and \(\beta\ge0\), a family of nonnegative charges \(q_{ij}\) is a \(\beta\)-augmentation certificate if \(c_jz_j\le\sum_iq_{ij}\) for every \(j\) and \(\sum_jq_{ij}\le\beta b_iy_i\) for every \(i\). These finitely checkable inequalities certify \[c^\top z\le\beta b^\top y\le\beta\operatorname{OPT}.\] The certificate does not depend on how \(z\) was constructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative charges covering every augmentation cost and bounded rowwise by beta times the dual contribution certify a beta-scaled augmentation bound.

notation.meaning: Charge from dual row i to augmented object j.

children.title: Reverse-Delete Filtering
children.top_down_role: Reverse-order filtering of provisional primal objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Delete Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-order deletion for an upward-closed feasible set system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\) be the objects inserted by a construction phase, and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) be upward closed. Initialize \(S=E\). For \(t=k,k-1,\ldots,1\), replace \(S\) by \(S\setminus\{e_t\}\) exactly when \(S\setminus\{e_t\}\in\mathcal F\). Return \(S\). The output is feasible and deletion-minimal: for every \(e\in S\), \(S\setminus\{e\}\notin\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan inserted objects in reverse order and delete each one whose removal preserves feasibility. The result is feasible and inclusion-minimal.
assumptions_latex: Membership in \(\mathcal F\) can be tested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal F\) and \(S\setminus\{e\}\notin\mathcal F\) for every \(e\in S\).

notation.meaning: Upward-closed family of feasible object sets.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reverse-delete on an upward-closed family directly preserves feasibility and yields deletion-minimality

children.title: Primal Cleanup Procedures
children.top_down_role: Postprocessing families for converting provisional solutions into admissible outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Cleanup Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-preserving deletion and replacement cleanup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible set \(S\in\mathcal F\) with nonnegative additive cost \(c(S)\), repeatedly apply either a deletion \(S\leftarrow S\setminus D\) or a replacement \(S\leftarrow(S\setminus D)\cup I\) whenever the new set lies in \(\mathcal F\) and has strictly smaller lexicographic potential \((c(S),|S|)\). Stop when no allowed move exists and return \(S\). For finite ground sets, the procedure terminates, preserves feasibility, and never increases cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply feasible deletions or replacements that strictly decrease cost, breaking ties by cardinality. On a finite ground set, cleanup terminates without increasing cost.
assumptions_latex: The ground set and allowed move family are finite.
The initial set belongs to \(\mathcal F\).
Object costs are nonnegative and additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathcal F\), \(c(S_{\mathrm{out}})\le c(S_{\mathrm{in}})\), and no allowed improving move remains.

notation.meaning: Objects removed by a cleanup move.
Objects inserted by a replacement move.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: strict descent on a finite lexicographic potential guarantees termination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Finite strict lexicographic descent supports termination, feasibility preservation, and cost monotonicity, but the generalized deletion-and-replacement procedure has no cited source.

children.title: Redundancy Removal
children.top_down_role: Removal of unnecessary selected objects while preserving required structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle complexity of deletion minimization in an upward-closed feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) be upward closed and \(S\in\mathcal F\). Scan the elements of \(S\) once in any fixed order, deleting \(e\) whenever the current set \(T\) satisfies \(T\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal F\). After at most \(|S|\) membership tests, the returned set \(T\) is feasible and deletion-minimal. If one membership test costs \(\tau_{\mathcal F}\), the oracle running time is \(O(|S|\tau_{\mathcal F})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an upward-closed feasible family, one scan in any order produces a deletion-minimal feasible subset using at most one feasibility test per original element.
assumptions_latex: Membership in \(\mathcal F\) is testable in time \(\tau_{\mathcal F}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\in\mathcal F,\quad T\setminus\{e\}\notin\mathcal F\ \forall e\in T,\quad\text{with time }O(|S|\tau_{\mathcal F}).
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Pass Redundancy Elimination

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion-minimal outputs need not be unique or minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(\mathcal F=\{T\subseteq E:a\in T\text{ or }\{b,c\}\subseteq T\}\). Starting from \(E\), one deletion order can return \(\{a\}\), while another can return \(\{b,c\}\). With \(c_a=2\) and \(c_b=c_c=3/5\), these deletion-minimal outputs cost \(2\) and \(6/5\). Thus deletion minimality implies neither uniqueness nor minimum cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different deletion orders can yield different inclusion-minimal feasible subsets, and an inclusion-minimal output need not be cheapest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{a\}\text{ and }\{b,c\}\text{ are distinct deletion-minimal outputs with costs }2\text{ and }6/5.

notation.meaning: Upward-closed feasible family in the example.

knowledge_statements.title: Order Dependence of Redundancy Removal
Redundancy Removal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of deletion-minimal feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an upward-closed feasible family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\), an element \(e\in S\in\mathcal F\) is redundant in \(S\) when \(S\setminus\{e\}\in\mathcal F\). Repeated removal of redundant elements terminates on finite \(E\) at a set \(S'\subseteq S\) satisfying \(S'\in\mathcal F\) and \(S'\setminus\{e\}\notin\mathcal F\) for every \(e\in S'\). With nonnegative additive costs, \(c(S')\le c(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A redundant object can be deleted without losing feasibility. Repeated deletion produces an inclusion-minimal feasible subset and cannot increase nonnegative additive cost.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(\mathcal F\) is upward closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S'\subseteq S\), \(S'\in\mathcal F\), \(S'\) is deletion-minimal, and \(c(S')\le c(S)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite repeated deletion yields an inclusion-minimal feasible subset

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The redundancy definition and finite deletion-minimality claim are precise and fit the property container, but no source with an inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Cleanup-Cost Control
children.top_down_role: Bounds and charging perspectives for costs introduced during cleanup.

knowledge_statements.title: Cleanup-Cost Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost monotonicity and inherited approximation guarantees under cleanup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_0,S_1,\ldots,S_T\) be feasible primal solutions produced by cleanup moves, with \(c(S_{t+1})\le c(S_t)\) for every \(t<T\). Then \(c(S_T)\le c(S_0)\). Consequently, if a lower-bound certificate \(L\le\operatorname{OPT}\) satisfies \(c(S_0)\le\rho L\), the cleaned solution satisfies \(c(S_T)\le\rho L\le\rho\operatorname{OPT}\); cleanup preserves the original approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any feasibility-preserving cleanup whose moves do not increase cost preserves every approximation guarantee certified for the initial solution.

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound on the optimum.

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation of multiplicative and additive cleanup overhead through an existing lower-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_0\) be an initial solution, \(S_T\) a feasible cleaned solution, and \(L\le\operatorname{OPT}\). If \(c(S_0)\le\rho L\), \(c(S_T)\le\lambda c(S_0)+\Delta\), and \(0\le\Delta\le\gamma L\), where \(\lambda,\rho,\gamma\ge0\), then \[c(S_T)\le(\lambda\rho+\gamma)L\le(\lambda\rho+\gamma)\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicative cleanup loss and additive overhead bounded relative to the certified lower bound transform a rho guarantee into a lambda-rho-plus-gamma guarantee.

notation.meaning: Overhead factor relative to the lower bound.

Relaxed Complementary-Slackness Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative relaxed complementary slackness for covering and packing LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^\top y:A^\top y\le c,\ y\ge0\}\), with \(A,b,c\ge0\). Let primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\) satisfy \(x_j>0\Rightarrow(A^\top y)_j\ge c_j/\alpha\) and \(y_i>0\Rightarrow(Ax)_i\le\beta b_i\), where \(\alpha,\beta\ge1\). Then \[c^\top x\le\alpha\beta b^\top y\le\alpha\beta\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual feasible solutions satisfying alpha- and beta-relaxed complementary slackness yield an alpha-times-beta approximation bound.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is primal feasible and \(y\) is dual feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Feasibility Is Essential for the Approximation Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary showing that relaxed support conditions alone do not make the dual objective a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{Mx_1+x_2:x_1+x_2\ge1,\ x\ge0\}\), whose dual is \(\max\{y:y\le M,\ y\le1,\ y\ge0\}\), where \(M>1\). Let \(x=(1,0)\), \(y=M\), and \(\alpha=\beta=1\). The primal vector is feasible; its positive variable satisfies \((A^{\mathsf T}y)_1=M=c_1\), and the positive dual variable satisfies \((Ax)_1=1=b_1\). Thus the exact support implications hold, but \(y\) is not dual feasible because \(y>1=c_2\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=M>1=\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A costly primal solution can satisfy the support complementary-slackness implications with an infeasible dual vector. Dual feasibility is indispensable because it makes the dual objective a valid lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The covering instance has one requirement and two columns of costs \(M\) and \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The support implications hold, but \(c^{\mathsf T}x=M>\operatorname{OPT}=1\) because \(y\) is not dual feasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Feasibility Is Essential for the Approximation Certificate
Uniform Dual Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repair of multiplicative dual infeasibility by one global scale factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the packing dual \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le c,\ y\ge0\}\), input \(\widehat y\ge0\) and define \(\rho=\max\{1,\max_{j:c_j>0}(A^T\widehat y)_j/c_j\}\), requiring \((A^T\widehat y)_j=0\) whenever \(c_j=0\). Output \(y=\widehat y/\rho\). Then \(y\) is dual feasible and \(b^Ty=b^T\widehat y/\rho\). If a primal-feasible \(x\) satisfies \(c^Tx\le\gamma b^T\widehat y\), then \(c^Tx\le\gammaho\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide every tentative dual variable by the maximum constraint-violation factor. This restores feasibility and converts a gamma charge bound into a gamma-rho approximation.
assumptions_latex: Zero-cost dual constraints have zero load under \(\widehat y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^Ty\le c\), and \(c^Tx\le\gamma b^T\widehat y\) implies \(c^Tx\le\gammaho\operatorname{OPT}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\) is stored explicitly with \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) nonzero entries, then computing \(A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\), scanning all constraint ratios, and forming \(y=\widehat y/\rho\) uses \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)\) arithmetic operations and linear storage for the load and output vectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Uniform-Scaling Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimal global divisor and the zero-cost obstruction for uniform dual repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell=A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\geq0\). If \(\ell_j>0\) for some \(j\) with \(c_j=0\), no finite scalar \(s>0\) makes \(\widehat y/s\) dual feasible. Otherwise define \(\rho=\max\{1,\max_{j:c_j>0}\ell_j/c_j\}\). For every \(s\geq1\), \[A^{\mathsf T}(\widehat y/s)\leq c\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s\geq\rho.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive load on a zero-cost constraint cannot be repaired by finite uniform scaling; otherwise the maximum violation ratio is the smallest feasible divisor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat y/s\) is dual feasible exactly when every zero-cost load vanishes and \(s\geq\rho\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Uniform Repair Factor
Nonuniform Dual Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise repair retaining the largest dominated feasible dual vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a tentative dual vector \(\widehat y\ge0\), compute \[y^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le c,\ 0\le y\le\widehat y\}.\] Output \(y^*\). This coordinatewise clipping repair is dual feasible and retains at least as much objective value as any feasible vector dominated by \(\widehat y\). If \(b^T\widehat y\le\eta b^Ty^*\) and a primal-feasible \(x\) obeys \(c^Tx\le\gamma b^T\widehat y\), then \(c^Tx\le\gamma\eta\operatorname{OPT}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize within the coordinatewise box below the tentative dual vector. The retained dual value determines the approximation loss caused by nonuniform repair.
assumptions_latex: The repair linear program has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^Ty^*\le c\), and the stated accounting inequalities imply \(c^Tx\le\gamma\eta\operatorname{OPT}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Lower Certificates for a Factor-Revealing Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Witnesses that bound a normalized factor-revealing optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho_k=\sup\{C(z):z\in\mathcal Z_k,\ L(z)=1\}\), every feasible normalized \(z\) gives \(C(z)\le\rho_k\). If \(R_k\) contains every normalized encoded configuration and has optimum \(U_k\), then \(\rho_k\le U_k\). Matching bounds determine \(\rho_k\); bounds \(U_k\le\rho\) for all \(k\) imply \(\sup_k\rho_k\le\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible configurations give lower bounds and valid supersets give upper bounds on the revealed factor.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper and Lower Certificates for a Factor-Revealing Program

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness conditions for factor-revealing upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A factor-revealing optimum upper-bounds an algorithm only if every relevant execution is represented or dominated by a feasible configuration. Omitting executions can lower the supremum. For a maximization program, optimizing over a valid superset gives an upper bound, whereas adding constraints not valid for every encoded execution can produce a falsely small factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete execution encoding and the correct relaxation direction are essential for a valid factor bound.
assumptions_latex: The program maximizes a represented worst-case ratio.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Sound upper bounds require execution coverage and valid superset relaxation.}
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding and Relaxation Direction Boundary
Factor-Revealing Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization representation of a worst-case local approximation ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Z_k\) be the feasible configurations of size \(k\) permitted by an algorithm's invariants, and let \(C(z)\ge0\) and \(L(z)>0\) denote the represented charged primal cost and certified lower bound. Define \[\rho_k=\sup_{z\in\mathcal Z_k}\frac{C(z)}{L(z)}.\] If \(\mathcal Z_k\) is closed under positive scaling and \(C\) and \(L\) are positively homogeneous of degree one, then equivalently \[\rho_k=\sup\{C(z):z\in\mathcal Z_k,\ L(z)=1\}.\] If every relevant execution is encoded by some \(z\in\mathcal Z_k\) whose ratio is at least the execution's ratio, then the algorithmic approximation factor is at most \(\sup_k\rho_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor-revealing program maximizes the ratio of represented charged cost to a represented lower bound. Under homogeneous scaling it can be normalized to lower-bound value one, and a complete dominating encoding yields an approximation-factor bound.
assumptions_latex: For the normalized formulation, \(\lambda z\in\mathcal Z_k\), \(C(\lambda z)=\lambda C(z)\), and \(L(\lambda z)=\lambda L(z)\) for every \(z\in\mathcal Z_k\) and \(\lambda>0\).
Every relevant execution has an encoded configuration whose represented ratio is no smaller than the execution ratio.

notation.meaning: Charged primal cost represented by z.
Certified lower bound represented by z.
Worst represented ratio for configurations of size k.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Infeasibility Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative repair of an approximately feasible dual for a covering relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the covering relaxation 
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\geq \mathbf 1,\ x\geq 0\}\]
and its dual 
\[\max\{\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c,\ y\geq0\}.\]
Let \(z\) be an integral feasible solution and let \(y\geq0\) satisfy \(A^{\mathsf T}y\leq \alpha c\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}z\leq \mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}y\), where \(\alpha\geq1\). Then \(y/\alpha\) is dual feasible. Weak duality therefore gives
\[c^{\mathsf T}z\leq \mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}y\leq \alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\leq \alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}.\]
Thus the multiplicative dual infeasibility is charged exactly as an approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling an α-infeasible dual by 1/α makes it feasible; a primal solution bounded by the unscaled dual value is therefore an α-approximation.

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the covering relaxation.
Optimal value of the integral covering problem.

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Dual Feasibility Alone Is Insufficient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary payment condition in dual-infeasibility accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The inequality \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le\alpha c\) controls the dual value but not the cost of an arbitrary feasible integral solution. With two duplicate covering columns of costs \(1\) and \(M\), selecting the expensive column is feasible while \(y=0\) is \(\alpha\)-approximately feasible for every \(\alpha\). A separate inequality such as \(c^{\mathsf T}z\le\gamma\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y\) is therefore necessary; together the two conditions imply
\[c^{\mathsf T}z\le\gamma\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate dual feasibility does not pay for the chosen primal solution; a separate charging inequality is indispensable.
assumptions_latex: \(M>1\), and both columns cover the same requirement.
\(z\) may be any integral feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\mathsf T}y\le\alpha c\not\Rightarrow c^{\mathsf T}z\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT};\quad c^{\mathsf T}z\le\gamma\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y\Rightarrow c^{\mathsf T}z\le\gamma\alpha\operatorname{OPT}.

notation.meaning: factor in the primal-cost payment inequality

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Dual Feasibility Alone Is Insufficient
Weight-Decomposition View
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-ratio composition principle for nonnegative minimization weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}\) be the feasible solutions of a minimization problem, and decompose a nonnegative weight vector as \(c=c^{(1)}+c^{(2)}\). If \(z\in\mathcal F\) satisfies
\[ (c^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}z\leq \alpha\min_{x\in\mathcal F}(c^{(k)})^{\mathsf T}x\qquad(k=1,2), \]
then addition of the two inequalities yields
\[c^{\mathsf T}z\leq\alpha\min_{x\in\mathcal F}c^{\mathsf T}x.\]
The same conclusion holds for any finite decomposition \(c=\sum_{k=1}^{q}c^{(k)}\) when the identical componentwise guarantee holds for every component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution that is α-approximate for every component of a weight decomposition is α-approximate for their sum.

notation.meaning: A component of the objective-weight decomposition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminating recursive local-ratio scheme with reverse-order solution reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\varnothing\neq\mathcal F\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}\), weights \(c\in\mathbb R_{+}^{n}\), and \(\alpha\geq1\), apply a problem-specific recursion rule that, at each nonterminal call, chooses \(d\neq0\) with \(0\leq d\leq c\), sets \(c'=c-d\), and recurses on \(c'\). The rule must be guaranteed to reach a directly solvable base instance after finitely many calls. During reverse reconstruction, produce \(z\in\mathcal F\) so that at each call the returned solution has the required \(\alpha\)-approximation guarantee for the removed component \(d\); the recursive guarantee supplies the corresponding bound for \(c'\). The weight-decomposition principle then supplies the guarantee for \(c=d+c'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively remove simple weight components using a rule that terminates, then reconstruct in reverse order while preserving the componentwise approximation guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Ratio Interpretation of Dual Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A covering-dual increment represented as subtraction from residual primal costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the covering pair with matrix \(A\geq0\), maintain dual vector \(y\geq0\) and residual costs \(r=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\geq0\). Increasing coordinate \(y_i\) by \(\delta\geq0\) changes the residual vector according to
\[r' = r-\delta A_{i*}^{\mathsf T}.\]
Thus a dual-growth step is exactly a local-ratio reduction by the nonnegative weight component \(d=\delta A_{i*}^{\mathsf T}\). The largest feasible increment is
\[\delta^{*}=\min_{j:A_{ij}>0}\frac{r_j}{A_{ij}},\]
with the minimum restricted to finite ratios; at least one affected primal variable becomes tight when \(\delta=\delta^{*}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raising one covering-dual variable subtracts a scaled constraint row from residual primal costs, exactly matching a local-ratio reduction.
assumptions_latex: Row \(i\) has at least one positive entry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update \(y_i\leftarrow y_i+\delta\) is represented by \(r\leftarrow r-\delta A_{i*}^{\mathsf T}\).

notation.meaning: Row i of the covering matrix.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identity follows from the covering dual slack equation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-cost update and maximal feasible increment are internally consistent and the representation role fits the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation for the claimed local-ratio/primal-dual correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Interpretation of Weight Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative row reductions represented as feasible covering-dual growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a sequence of local-ratio reductions subtract scaled covering rows:
\[c=r+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_iA_{i*}^{\mathsf T},\qquad r\geq0,\quad\delta_i\geq0.\]
Define \(y_i=\delta_i\). Then
\[A^{\mathsf T}y=c-r\leq c,\]
so \(y\) is feasible for the dual \(\max\{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c,\ y\geq0\}\). Consequently, every nonnegative weight reduction that is a scaled row of the covering matrix can be read as growth of the corresponding dual coordinate, provided all cumulative residual costs remain nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting nonnegative multiples of covering rows from costs constructs a feasible dual whose coordinates are the reduction amounts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(y=\delta\), one has \(y\geq0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c\).

notation.meaning: Scale of the reduction using row i.
Cost vector remaining after all reductions.
Dual vector induced by the reductions.

The translations are \(r=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\) and verification of the displayed decomposition in the reverse direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative local-ratio row decomposition is exactly a feasible covering dual together with its slack vector.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of a row-decomposition certificate into an approximation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R_{+}^{m\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb R_{+}^{n}\), and \(\alpha\geq1\). Define \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb Z_{+}^{n},\ Ax\geq\mathbf1\}\). Suppose \(c=A^{\mathsf T}y+r\) with \(y\in\mathbb R_{+}^{m}\) and \(r\in\mathbb R_{+}^{n}\), and let \(z\in\mathbb Z_{+}^{n}\) satisfy \(Az\geq\mathbf1\). If \(r^{\mathsf T}z=0\) and \((Az)_i\leq\alpha\) for every \(i\) with \(y_i>0\), then the reduction coefficients \(y\), residual \(r\), and reconstruction multiplicities certify \[c^{\mathsf T}z\leq\alpha\,\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y\leq\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative row decomposition of the costs, zero residual cost on the integral output and row multiplicity at most alpha on the support of the induced dual certify an alpha-approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Correspondence Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic conditions under which local-ratio reductions cease to encode feasible dual growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The covering correspondence requires every reduction to lie in the nonnegative cone generated by rows of \(A\), with nonnegative coefficients and residual \(r=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\geq0\). If any condition fails, the reduction data need not define a feasible dual. For example, with \(A=[1]\) and \(c=[1]\), subtracting \(d=[2]\) leaves \(r=[-1]\). Interpreting the reduction scale as \(y=2\) gives \(A^{\mathsf T}y=2>1=c\), so dual feasibility fails. Likewise, a reduction outside the row cone has no representing vector \(y\geq0\), even if it remains useful in a problem-specific local-ratio recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The correspondence fails when reductions are not nonnegative covering-row combinations or when they drive residual costs negative.
assumptions_latex: The intended dual is \(\max\{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c,\ y\geq0\}\).
Local-ratio reductions are interpreted through \(d=A^{\mathsf T}y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without \(y\geq0\) and \(c-A^{\mathsf T}y\geq0\), local-ratio reduction data does not certify dual feasibility.

notation.meaning: Proposed dual representation of the reduction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient violation-incidence condition for the approximation guarantee of Algorithm 4.3.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\mathcal V(A)$ denote the collection of violated sets returned by $\operatorname{VIOLATION}(A)$. Suppose that, for every infeasible set $A$ and every minimal augmentation $B$ of $A$,
\[
\sum_{T_i\in\mathcal V(A)}|B\cap T_i|\leq\gamma|\mathcal V(A)|.
\]
Then the primal-dual algorithm in Figure 4.3 returns a feasible set $A_{\mathrm{out}}$ and dual vector $y$ satisfying
\[
\sum_{e\in A_{\mathrm{out}}}c_e\leq\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{p}y_i\leq\gamma z_{\mathrm{OPT}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the stated incidence bound holds for every infeasible set and every minimal augmentation, then the uniform-growth reverse-delete algorithm returns a feasible solution costing at most gamma times its dual value and hence at most gamma times optimum.
assumptions_latex: \forall A\ \text{infeasible},\ \forall B\ \text{a minimal augmentation of }A:\ \sum_{T_i\in\mathcal V(A)}|B\cap T_i|\leq\gamma|\mathcal V(A)|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform-Violation Primal-Dual Algorithm with Reverse Deletion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract covering primal-dual procedure using uniform growth over a violation-oracle output; no standalone termination or approximation guarantee is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize $y=0$, $A=\varnothing$, and $\ell=0$. While $A$ is infeasible, let $\mathcal V(A)=\operatorname{VIOLATION}(A)$ and uniformly increase $y_k$ for all $T_k\in\mathcal V(A)$ until some $e_\ell\notin A$ becomes tight:
\[
\sum_{i:e_\ell\in T_i}y_i=c_{e_\ell}.
\]
Add $e_\ell$ to $A$. Once feasibility is reached, examine the inserted elements in reverse order and delete each element whose removal preserves feasibility. Output $A$ and $y$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each infeasible iterate, obtain violated sets from the violation routine and raise their dual variables uniformly until a new element becomes tight. Add it, then reverse-delete redundant elements after reaching feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal V(A)=\operatorname{VIOLATION}(A)\ \text{is defined at each infeasible iterate}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Upon termination, }A\ \text{is feasible and inclusion-minimal under single-element deletion, and }\sum_{i:e\in T_i}y_i\leq c_e\ \forall e\in E.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Cover Primal-Dual Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard dual-growth 2-approximation for minimum-weight vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) with costs \(c_v\geq0\), initialize \(y_e=0\). While an edge \(e=uv\) has neither endpoint tight, increase \(y_e\) until
\[\sum_{e'\ni u}y_{e'}=c_u\quad\text{or}\quad\sum_{e'\ni v}y_{e'}=c_v.\]
After every edge has a tight endpoint, output the set \(C\) of tight vertices, optionally deleting redundant vertices. The vector \(y\) is feasible for the edge-packing dual, \(C\) is a vertex cover, and
\[c(C)=\sum_{v\in C}\sum_{e\ni v}y_e\leq2\sum_{e\in E}y_e\leq2\,
\mathrm{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow uncovered-edge dual variables until endpoints become tight, then return tight vertices; each dual variable is charged at most twice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The output is a vertex cover \(C\) satisfying \(c(C)\leq2\,
\mathrm{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: Dual variable associated with edge e.
Set of tight vertices returned as the cover.
Total cost of vertices in C.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Cover Primal-Dual Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-ascent algorithm for weighted set cover with frequency-dependent charging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For universe \(U\), family \(\mathcal S\), and costs \(c_S\geq0\), initialize \(y_e=0\) and \(C=
\varnothing\). While some element \(e\) is uncovered, increase \(y_e\) until a set \(S\ni e\) becomes tight:
\[\sum_{u\in S}y_u=c_S.\]
Add one such tight set to \(C\), and continue until \(C\) covers \(U\); reverse deletion may then remove redundant sets. Dual feasibility is maintained. If \(f=
\max_{e\in U}|\{S\in\mathcal S:e\in S\}|\), tightness and charging give
\[c(C)\leq f\sum_{e\in U}y_e\leq f\,
\mathrm{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raise uncovered-element dual variables until sets become tight, select tight sets, and charge each element at most its frequency.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(\mathcal S\) are finite and every \(e\in U\) belongs to some set.

notation.meaning: Dual variable associated with element e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The LP pair underlying element-dual growth for weighted set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard weighted set-cover relaxation and its dual are \[\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}c_Sx_S:\sum_{S\ni e}x_S\ge1\ (e\in U),\ x\ge0\right\}\] and \[\max\left\{\sum_{e\in U}y_e:\sum_{e\in S}y_e\le c_S\ (S\in\mathcal S),\ y\ge0\right\}.\] A set becomes eligible for the dual-growth selection rule when its dual constraint is tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fractional set-cover LP is dual to packing nonnegative element weights within every set's cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every dual-feasible \(y\) satisfies \(\sum_e y_e\le\mathrm{OPT}\), and tight set constraints define the method's selection events.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a finite set cover, scanning its sets in reverse selection order and deleting a set whenever the remaining family still covers \(U\) terminates with an inclusion-minimal cover \(C'\subseteq C\). If costs are nonnegative, then \(c(C')\le c(C)\), so every approximation bound established for \(C\) is preserved.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Primal-Dual Algorithm for Weighted Hitting Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-violation dual growth for weighted hitting set, without reverse deletion or a stated approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize $y_i=0$ for $i=1,\ldots,p$ and $A=\varnothing$. While some $T_k$ is not hit by $A$, increase $y_k$ until an element $e\in T_k$ becomes tight,

and set $A\leftarrow A\cup\{e\}$. Output $A$ and $y$.

Frequency-Bounded Set Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-cover instances parameterized by maximum element frequency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A weighted set-cover instance consists of a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^U\), and costs \(c:
\mathcal S\to\mathbb R_{+}\). The frequency of an element \(e\in U\) is
\[f_e=|\{S\in\mathcal S:e\in S\}|.\]
The instance has frequency at most \(f\) when
\[\max_{e\in U}f_e\leq f.\]
Equivalently, in the element-set incidence matrix, every row contains at most \(f\) nonzero entries. This parameter bounds how many selected tight-set costs can charge the same element-dual variable in a primal-dual analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-cover instance is frequency-bounded by f when each element belongs to at most f available sets.
assumptions_latex: Every element of \(U\) lies in at least one member of \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The frequency bound is \(\max_{e\in U}|\{S\in\mathcal S:e\in S\}|\leq f\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-sensitive approximation certificate using dual-weighted element frequencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite weighted set-cover instance \((U,\mathcal S,c)\), define \(f_e=|\{S\in\mathcal S:e\in S\}|\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}=\min\{\sum_{S\in C'}c_S:C'\subseteq\mathcal S\text{ covers }U\}\). Let \(y\in\mathbb R_{+}^{U}\) satisfy \(\sum_{e\in S}y_e\leq c_S\) for every \(S\in\mathcal S\), and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal S\) be a cover consisting only of tight sets. If \(y\neq0\), define \[\rho(y)=\frac{\sum_{e\in U}f_e y_e}{\sum_{e\in U}y_e}.\] Then the pair \((C,y)\) certifies \[c(C)\leq\rho(y)\,\mathrm{OPT},\qquad \rho(y)\leq\max_{e:y_e>0}f_e.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Near-f Integrality Gap at High Frequency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic sharpness family showing that the standard covering relaxation cannot yield a frequency-independent guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix integers \(n\ge f\ge2\). Let the available unit-cost sets be \(S_1,\ldots,S_n\). For every \(f\)-subset \(T\subseteq[n]\), create an element \(e_T\) contained in \(S_i\) exactly when \(i\in T\). Every element has frequency \(f\). An integral cover has size at least \(n-f+1\), while \(x_{S_i}=1/f\) is a fractional cover of value \(n/f\). Therefore \[\frac{\mathrm{OPT}}{\mathrm{OPT}_{LP}}=\frac{f(n-f+1)}{n},\] which approaches \(f\) for fixed \(f\) as \(n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete f-uniform incidence family has covering-LP gap approaching f, independently of tie handling or redundancy deletion.
assumptions_latex: All available sets have unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup \mathrm{OPT}/\mathrm{OPT}_{LP}=f\) over frequency-at-most-\(f\) instances, with the supremum approached by this family.

If a simultaneous-tightness primal-dual rule raises \(y_e\) from \(0\) to \(1\) and selects every newly tight set, all \(f\) sets are selected and the output costs \(f\). Hence the frequency charging bound is attained exactly. When \(f\) grows with input size, this analysis supplies no constant approximation guarantee; tie-breaking, pruning, or a different structural argument is necessary.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact incidence transposition between hypergraph vertex cover and set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite hypergraph \(H=(V,E)\), form a set-cover instance with universe \(E\) and, for each \(v\in V\), the set \(S_v=\{e\in E:v\in e\}\) of cost \(c_v\). Then \(C\subseteq V\) is a hypergraph vertex cover exactly when \(\{S_v:v\in C\}\) covers \(E\), and the two solutions have equal cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hypergraph vertex cover is set cover with hyperedges as universe elements and one incidence set per vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap e\ne\varnothing\ \forall e\in E\iff\bigcup_{v\in C}S_v=E\), with equal objective value.

notation.meaning: Set of hyperedges incident to vertex v.
