assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,E)\) is a finite hypergraph with nonnegative vertex costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{V}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is feasible exactly when \(C\cap e\neq\varnothing\) for every \(e\in E\), and its cost is \(c(C)=\sum_{v\in C}c_v\).

notation.meaning: finite hypergraph with vertices V and hyperedges E

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost vertex covering of hyperedges, not covering vertices by chosen hyperedges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hypergraph vertex cover is a set \(C\subseteq V\) satisfying \(C\cap e\neq\varnothing\) for every \(e\in E\). The minimum-cost hypergraph-covering problem is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in C}c_v:C\subseteq V,\ C\cap e\neq\varnothing\text{ for every }e\in E\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, its integer-programming formulation is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}c_vx_v:\sum_{v\in e}x_v\ge 1\ \text{for every }e\in E,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost vertices that intersect every hyperedge; equivalently, impose one binary covering constraint per hyperedge.

children.title: Local Ratio for Hypergraph Covers
children.top_down_role: Local-ratio approximation frameworks specialized to hypergraph covering.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fully specified polynomial-time local-ratio algorithm for nonnegative-cost hypergraph vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize residual costs \(\bar c=c\), select every vertex with \(\bar c_v=0\), and mark all incident edges covered. While an uncovered edge \(e\) remains, set \(\varepsilon=\min_{v\in e}\bar c_v>0\), replace \(\bar c_v\leftarrow\bar c_v-\varepsilon\) for every \(v\in e\), and select every vertex of e whose residual cost becomes zero, marking all its incident edges covered. Return the selected vertices, optionally deleting redundant vertices in reverse selection order. If \(r=\max_{e\in E}|e|\), the returned cover C satisfies \(c(C)\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}\). With incidence lists, the unpruned phase performs at most \(\min\{|V|,|E|\}\) positive reductions and can be implemented in time linear in the explicit incidence size up to ordinary queue and arithmetic overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly subtract the minimum residual cost on an uncovered edge and select newly zero vertices; the resulting cover is an r-approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,E)\) is finite and has no empty hyperedge.
The input is represented by explicit incidence lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm terminates with a cover \(C\) satisfying \(c(C)\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: Current residual cost of vertex v.
Uniform reduction applied on the chosen uncovered edge.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Edge-Reduction Local-Ratio Algorithm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-sensitive estimate for the uniform cost component supported on one hyperedge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e\) be a nonempty hyperedge and define \(c'_v=\varepsilon\) for \(v\in e\) and \(c'_v=0\) otherwise, where \(\varepsilon\ge0\). For the hypergraph-cover feasible family, \(\mathrm{OPT}(c')=\varepsilon\). Every vertex set \(C\) satisfies \(c'(C)=\varepsilon|C\cap e|\le\varepsilon|e|\). Consequently, when \(|e|\le r\), every feasible C satisfies \[c'(C)\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}(c').\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uniform component on one edge has local approximation factor at most that edge's size, hence at most the rank.
assumptions_latex: The hypergraph has at least one vertex cover.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c=c'+c''\) be nonnegative cost vectors on the same nonempty feasible family. If a feasible solution \(C\) satisfies \(c'(C)\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(c')\) and \(c''(C)\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(c'')\), then \[c(C)\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(c).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution that is an alpha-approximation for both cost components is an alpha-approximation for their sum.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is feasible for the common feasible family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive rank-based local-ratio algorithm for minimum-cost hypergraph vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(C=\varnothing\). If every edge is covered, return \(C\). Otherwise choose an uncovered edge \(e\), let \(\varepsilon=\min_{v\in e}c_v\), and decompose \(c=c'+c''\), where \(c'_v=\varepsilon\) for \(v\in e\), \(c'_v=0\) otherwise, and \(c''=c-c'\). Recursively compute a cover \(C''\) for \((H,c'')\), including every zero-residual-cost vertex required by the recursion, and return the reverse-delete-minimal subset of \(C''\) that covers \(E\). For rank \(r\), the local-ratio bound for each component \(c'\) yields
\[
c(C)\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}(H,c).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly subtract the minimum cost on an uncovered edge, recurse on residual costs, and reverse-delete; the resulting cover is an r-approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Ratio for Hypergraph Covers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact-Complexity Boundary at Ranks One and Two
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact tractability boundary organized by maximum hyperedge cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every nonempty hyperedge has size one, feasibility forces its unique vertex, so an optimum cover is obtained by selecting all forced vertices. If every hyperedge has size at most two, the non-singleton part is an ordinary graph vertex-cover instance after forced singleton edges are handled. Consequently, unweighted hypergraph vertex cover is NP-hard already at rank two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-one covering is exactly trivial, while rank two already contains NP-hard graph vertex cover.
assumptions_latex: The hypergraph is finite and contains no empty hyperedge.
The hardness statement concerns general finite graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank-one instances are exactly solvable in linear incidence time, whereas exact optimization is NP-hard for rank two.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Complexity Boundary at Ranks One and Two

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Near-r Integrality Gap for Rank-r Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp rank-dependent obstruction using complete uniform hypergraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_n^{(r)}\) be the complete \(r\)-uniform hypergraph on \(n\ge r\) vertices with unit vertex costs. Its minimum vertex-cover size is \(n-r+1\), while the fractional assignment \(x_v=1/r\) has optimum value \(n/r\). Thus \[\frac{\mathrm{OPT}}{\mathrm{OPT}_{LP}}=\frac{r(n-r+1)}{n},\] which approaches \(r\) for fixed \(r\) as \(n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete r-uniform hypergraphs have covering-LP gap approaching r, making the rank-r bound asymptotically sharp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The supremum rank-r covering-LP integrality gap is r.

notation.meaning: Complete r-uniform hypergraph on n vertices.

Rank-Sensitive Cover Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite hypergraph \(H=(V,E)\) of rank \(r=\max_{e\in E}|e|\), the rank-based local-ratio algorithm returns a vertex cover \(C\) satisfying
\[
c(C)\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}(H,c).
\]
Thus rank \(2\) gives a factor-two guarantee, every fixed rank gives a constant-factor guarantee, and this guarantee is not constant when the rank grows without a fixed bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank-based analysis guarantees a factor of at most the maximum hyperedge size: rank two gives factor two, fixed rank gives a constant factor, and this particular guarantee is not constant for unbounded rank.

\(r=\max_{e\in E}|e|\), and \(C\) is returned by the rank-based local-ratio hypergraph-cover algorithm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common charging certificate for hypergraph primal-dual and local-ratio analyses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_{e\ni v}y_e\le c_v\) for every vertex, and let \(C\) be a hypergraph cover containing only tight vertices. Then \[c(C)=\sum_{e\in E}|C\cap e|y_e.\] If \(|C\cap e|\le\alpha\) for every edge with \(y_e>0\), then \[c(C)\le\alpha\sum_{e\in E}y_e\le\alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stepwise Equivalence of Dual Growth and Cost Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-level equivalence between edge-supported local-ratio reductions and feasible dual growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For edge updates \((e_t,\varepsilon_t)\) with \(\varepsilon_t\ge0\), applying reductions \(c_v\leftarrow c_v-\varepsilon_t\) for every \(v\in e_t\) yields after each prefix \[\bar c_v=c_v-\sum_{t:v\in e_t}\varepsilon_t.\] The same vector is the slack of \(y_e=\sum_{t:e_t=e}\varepsilon_t\) in the dual constraint at v. Hence \(\bar c\ge0\) is equivalent to dual feasibility, and \(\bar c_v=0\) is equivalent to tightness of the vertex constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of edge-supported cost reductions is identical, prefix by prefix, to increasing the corresponding edge dual variables.
assumptions_latex: No update makes a residual vertex cost negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar c\ge0\iff y\) is dual feasible, and \(\bar c_v=0\iff v\) is dual tight.

notation.meaning: Residual cost, equivalently slack, at vertex v.
Cumulative dual increase assigned to edge e.

knowledge_statements.title: Stepwise Equivalence of Dual Growth and Cost Reduction

assumptions_latex: \(H=(V,E)\) is finite and \(c_v\ge 0\) for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dual increase on edge \(e\) reduces each incident residual cost equally, matching the local-ratio subtraction supported on \(e\).

notation.meaning: dual packing variable for hyperedge e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP correspondence between edge-dual growth and edge-supported local-ratio reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The fractional covering relaxation and its dual are
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}c_vx_v:\sum_{v\in e}x_v\ge1\ (e\in E),\ x\ge0\right\},
\qquad
\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}y_e:\sum_{e\ni v}y_e\le c_v\ (v\in V),\ y\ge0\right\}.
\]
With residual costs \(\bar c_v=c_v-\sum_{e\ni v}y_e\), increasing one \(y_e\) by \(\varepsilon\) subtracts \(\varepsilon\) from every \(\bar c_v\) with \(v\in e\). This is exactly the local-ratio reduction by the cost component supported uniformly on \(e\); a newly tight vertex has \(\bar c_v=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Growing an edge's dual variable subtracts the same amount from all incident vertex costs, exactly matching the corresponding local-ratio reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraph Primal-Dual Correspondence

After replacing \(a_i\) by \(\min\{a_i,b\}\), let \(D_0(0)=0\), \(D_0(t)=+\infty\) for \(1\le t\le b\), and
\[D_i(t)=\min\{D_{i-1}(t),\ c_i+D_{i-1}(\max\{0,t-a_i\})\}.\]
Then \(D_n(b)=\operatorname{OPT}\). The table requires \(O(nb)\) time and \(O(b)\) working space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integral demand and contributions, dynamic programming over capped remaining demand finds an exact optimum in pseudo-polynomial time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical complexity and approximability of binary minimum knapsack with integer input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Binary minimum-knapsack covering with nonnegative integer data is weakly NP-hard. For every \(\varepsilon>0\), it admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme returning a feasible cover \(C\) with
\[c(C)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT},\]
in time polynomial in the binary input length and \(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer minimum knapsack is weakly NP-hard and admits an FPTAS.
assumptions_latex: Contributions, costs, and demand are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak NP-Hardness and FPTAS

assumptions_latex: Items \(i\in[n]\) have sizes \(a_i\ge0\), costs \(c_i\ge0\), and the demand is \(b>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is \(\min\{\sum_i c_ix_i:\sum_i a_ix_i\ge b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

notation.meaning: size or covering contribution of item i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-constraint minimum-cost covering knapsack with binary item selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The minimum-knapsack covering problem selects a subset of items whose total size meets a prescribed demand at minimum cost. Its binary formulation is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_ix_i:\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_ix_i\ge b,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\text{ for every }i\in[n]\right\}.
\]
The instance is feasible exactly when \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i\ge b\). Contributions may be truncated to \(\min\{a_i,b\}\) without changing the feasible binary solutions or the optimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select minimum-cost binary items whose combined contribution reaches the demand; item contributions can be truncated at the demand.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case integrality-gap guarantee for the full knapsack-cover LP of one covering constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_{KC}\) contain \(0\le x_i\le1\) and every knapsack-cover inequality indexed by a deficient set. For every feasible instance with nonnegative costs and contributions,
\[\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{int}}\le2\operatorname{OPT}_{KC}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complete knapsack-cover relaxation for one minimum-knapsack constraint has integrality gap at most two.
assumptions_latex: Every deficient-set knapsack-cover inequality is imposed.

notation.meaning: optimal value of the full relaxation

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Bounded Integrality Gap of the Knapsack-Cover Relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational access to the complete deficient-set inequality family for integer contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in[0,1]^n\), exhaustive separation tests every \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(a(S)<b\). If \(a_i,b\in\mathbb Z_+\), then for each \(t\in\{0,\ldots,b-1\}\), dynamic programming over subsets of total contribution \(t\) can maximize \(\sum_{i\in S}\min\{a_i,b-t\}x_i\). Comparing this maximum with \(\sum_i\min\{a_i,b-t\}x_i-(b-t)\) detects a violated inequality with \(a(S)=t\), yielding a running time polynomial in \(n\) and \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family admits exponential enumeration and, for integer data, exact pseudopolynomial separation by dynamic programming over deficient total contribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a violated knapsack-cover inequality or certifies that none exists, in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(b\).

notation.meaning: total contribution of the deficient set

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Enumeration and Pseudopolynomial Separation

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adding all inequalities \(\sum_{i\notin S}\min\{a_i,b-a(S)\}x_i\ge b-a(S)\) strengthens the basic covering LP without excluding any binary feasible solution.

notation.meaning: total contribution of items in S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Knapsack-cover closure of the basic minimum-knapsack linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(a(S)<b\), define \(r_S=b-a(S)>0\). The strengthened covering relaxation is
\[
\left\{x\in[0,1]^n:\sum_{i\notin S}\min\{a_i,r_S\}x_i\ge r_S\text{ for every }S\subseteq[n]\text{ with }a(S)<b\right\}.
\]
Each displayed inequality is valid for every binary solution satisfying \(\sum_i a_ix_i\ge b\). Taking \(S=\varnothing\) yields the demand-truncated basic covering constraint, while nonempty \(S\) conditions the relaxation on items regarded as already selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strengthen the basic LP by imposing every residual-demand inequality obtained after treating an arbitrary subset as already selected.
knowledge_statements.title: Strengthened Covering Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation of the knapsack-cover relaxation is mathematically consistent and fits the leaf, but the validity and strengthening claims lack a cited source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Builder claim about binary-encoding complexity of the complete inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact separation for the complete knapsack-cover inequality family is weakly NP-hard under binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The builder asserted weak NP-hardness of exact separation.

children.title: Knapsack-Cover Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Certificate structures arising from knapsack-cover enhancements.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible binary cover satisfies \(\sum_{i\notin S}\min\{a_i,r_S\}x_i\ge r_S\).

notation.meaning: contribution of item i truncated at residual demand

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity predicate for a single knapsack-cover inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(a(S)=\sum_{i\in S}a_i<b\), and set \(r_S=b-a(S)\). The knapsack-cover inequality associated with \(S\) is
\[
\sum_{i\notin S}\min\{a_i,r_S\}x_i\ge r_S.
\]
It is a valid strengthening for binary minimum-knapsack solutions: items in \(S\) can supply at most \(a(S)\), so selected items outside \(S\) must supply the residual demand; an individual outside item need not be credited beyond \(r_S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After fixing a subset as selected, truncate every remaining contribution at the residual demand and require those contributions to cover that residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack-Cover Strengthening

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed knapsack-cover inequality is valid under the stated minimum-knapsack setting, and the selected content kind is acceptable for this leaf, but no authoritative source or locator is provided.

children.title: Residual-Demand Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covering subproblems organized by demand remaining after partial selections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility test after conditioning on a partially selected set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(a(S)<b\), set \(r_S=b-a(S)\) and \(a_i^S=\min\{a_i,r_S\}\). The residual binary instance is feasible exactly when
\[\sum_{i\notin S}a_i^S\ge r_S,\]
equivalently when \(\sum_{i\notin S}a_i\ge r_S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-residual instance is feasible exactly when all remaining items together can meet its residual demand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\in\{0,1\}^{[n]\setminus S}:\sum_{i\notin S}a_i^Sx_i\ge r_S\iff\sum_{i\notin S}a_i^S\ge r_S.

notation.meaning: remaining contribution capped at residual demand

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Feasibility Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order relation between residual instances induced by nested selected sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(S\subseteq T\subseteq[n]\) and both are deficient, then
\[0<r_T\le r_S,\qquad \min\{a_i,r_T\}\le\min\{a_i,r_S\}\quad(i\notin T).\]
If \(a(T)\ge b\), the residual demand after \(T\) is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Further conditioning cannot increase residual demand or any surviving capped coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_T\le r_S\text{ and }a_i^T\le a_i^S\text{ whenever both residuals are positive}.

notation.meaning: residual demands after S and T

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Under Further Conditioning
Residual-Demand Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual instance induced by conditioning on a partially selected item set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a set \(S\subseteq[n]\) regarded as already selected, if \(a(S)\ge b\), then the residual demand is zero. If \(a(S)<b\), define \(r_S=b-a(S)>0\) and \(a_i^S=\min\{a_i,r_S\}\) for every \(i\notin S\). The positive-residual covering constraint is
\[
\sum_{i\notin S}a_i^Sx_i\ge r_S.
\]
An item with \(a_i\ge r_S\) has residual coefficient \(a_i^S=r_S\), while an item with \(a_i<r_S\) has residual coefficient \(a_i^S=a_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected set either meets the demand already or induces a positive residual problem in which every remaining contribution is capped at the residual demand.
assumptions_latex: Items \(i\in[n]\) have contributions \(a_i\ge0\), the demand satisfies \(b>0\), and \(S\subseteq[n]\).
The remaining selection variables satisfy \(x_i\in[0,1]\) for \(i\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(a(S)<b\), the residual problem has demand \(r_S=b-a(S)>0\), coefficients \(a_i^S=\min\{a_i,r_S\}\), and constraint \(\sum_{i\notin S}a_i^Sx_i\ge r_S\); if \(a(S)\ge b\), its residual demand is zero.

notation.meaning: total contribution of the selected set S
contribution of item i truncated at the residual demand
selection variable for remaining item i

children.title: Steiner-Forest Approximation
children.top_down_role: Primal-dual moat-growing frameworks for Steiner-forest problems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model boundary of the factor-two theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The classical theorem assumes an undirected graph, nonnegative edge costs, and pairwise edge-connectivity demands. It does not by itself extend to directed Steiner forest, internally vertex-disjoint requirements, or arbitrary non-uncrossable cut functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The factor-two theorem is confined to nonnegative undirected pair-connectivity instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The classical }2\text{-approximation has the stated model scope.}
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Guarantee Scope

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Factor Two Relative to the Cut Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical undirected Steiner-forest approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected Steiner-forest instance with nonnegative edge costs, the classical primal-dual moat-growing algorithm with its prescribed pruning phase returns a feasible forest \(F\) and a feasible moat dual \(y\) satisfying \[c(F)\le2\sum_S f_D(S)y_S\le2\,\mathrm{LP}^*\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical pruned moat-growing algorithm returns a forest costing at most twice the demand-cut LP optimum and hence twice the integral optimum.
assumptions_latex: The classical Steiner-forest moat-growing and pruning rules are used.

notation.meaning: optimum of the Steiner-forest demand-cut relaxation
dual moat assignment produced by the algorithm

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Two Relative to the Cut Relaxation

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph with costs \(c_e\ge0\) and terminal pairs \((s_i,t_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A primal-dual moat-growing algorithm returns a feasible forest \(F\) with \(c(F)\le2\,\mathrm{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: cost of an optimal Steiner forest

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical undirected Steiner-forest factor-two primal-dual guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and undirected, let \(c_e\ge0\), and let \((s_i,t_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be terminal pairs. There exists a polynomial-time primal-dual moat-growing algorithm that constructs an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) such that every \(s_i\) and \(t_i\) lie in the same connected component of \((V,F)\) and
\[
\sum_{e\in F}c_e\le2\,\mathrm{OPT},
\]
where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the minimum cost of any edge set satisfying all pairwise connectivity requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical moat-growing primal-dual algorithm computes, in polynomial time, a Steiner forest costing at most twice optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Steiner-Forest Approximation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem has the standard undirected, nonnegative-cost scope and states a polynomial-time factor-two guarantee, but no source specifically supporting the moat-growing Steiner-forest theorem is cited.

children.title: Generalized Connectivity Requirements
children.top_down_role: Network-design settings with connectivity requirements beyond a single terminal set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrary Boolean Cut Functions Need Not Be Structured
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary separating cut covering from the proper uncrossable class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(V=\{1,2\}\), the function with \(f(\{1\})=1\) and \(f(S)=0\) otherwise is not symmetric. On \(V=\{1,2,3,4\}\), setting \(f(\{1,2\})=f(\{2,3\})=1\) and all other values to zero violates uncrossability. Thus cut-cover inequalities alone impose neither property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit Boolean functions show that symmetry and uncrossability do not follow from having cut-cover constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Boolean Cut Functions Need Not Be Structured

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural hypotheses used by the undirected generalized-forest framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:2^V\to\{0,1\}\) is proper when \(f(\varnothing)=f(V)=0\), \(f(S)=f(V\setminus S)\), and \(f(A\cup B)\le\max\{f(A),f(B)\}\) for disjoint \(A,B\). It is uncrossable when \(f(A)=f(B)=1\) implies either \(f(A\cap B)=f(A\cup B)=1\) or \(f(A\setminus B)=f(B\setminus A)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper Boolean requirements are symmetric and disjoint-union closed; uncrossability preserves one standard uncrossing pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is proper and uncrossable exactly when the displayed axioms hold.}

notation.meaning: Boolean requirement on the cut indexed by S

knowledge_statements.title: Proper and Uncrossable Boolean Requirements

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Demand-Pair Requirements Form a Proper Uncrossable Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural inclusion of Steiner-forest demand cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For undirected demand pairs \(D\), let \(f_D(S)=1\) exactly when \(S\) separates at least one pair. Then \(f_D\) is proper and uncrossable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Demand-pair cut indicators satisfy the properness and uncrossability axioms.

notation.meaning: indicator that a cut separates a demand pair

knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Pair Requirements Form a Proper Uncrossable Class

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected, with nonnegative edge costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is characterized by \(|F\cap\delta(S)|\ge f(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: connectivity requirement across vertex cut S
edges with exactly one endpoint in S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-requirement formulation supporting the standard undirected moat-growing framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A selected edge set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfies the generalized connectivity requirement \(f\) when
\[
|F\cap\delta(S)|\ge f(S)\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.
\]
Here symmetry means \(f(S)=f(V\setminus S)\). The uncrossing condition requires that whenever \(f(A)=f(B)=1\), either \(f(A\cap B)=f(A\cup B)=1\), or \(f(A\setminus B)=f(B\setminus A)=1\). Sets with \(f(S)=1\) are active connectivity cuts until the selected edges cross them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized connectivity is expressed by cut demands; symmetry and uncrossability organize the violated cuts used by moat-growing algorithms.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Connectivity Requirements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut condition and stated symmetry convention are coherent, but the exact uncrossability convention and its applicability to the intended moat-growing framework require a specific source.

children.title: Demand-Pair Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Connectivity instances organized by terminal-pair demands.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-time verification and violated-cut extraction for a proposed solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute the connected components of \((V,F)\). Then \(F\) satisfies all demands if and only if \(s_i\) and \(t_i\) have the same component label for every \((s_i,t_i)\in D\). This takes \(O(|V|+|F|+|D|)\) time. If a pair fails, the vertex set of the component containing one endpoint is a violated demand cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connected components verify all demand pairs in linear time, and a failed pair yields a violated cut.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq E\) and \(D\) is a finite list of demand pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Pair Feasibility Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp existence condition before optimization is considered.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying every pair in \(D\) if and only if each \(s_i,t_i\) lie in the same connected component of \(G\). Infeasibility is certified by a union \(S\) of components of \(G\) with \(\delta_G(S)=\varnothing\) that separates a demand pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The instance is feasible exactly when no demanded pair is separated by the input graph's components.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite set of demand pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists F\subseteq E\text{ satisfying }D\iff \forall(s_i,t_i)\in D,\ s_i\sim_G t_i.

notation.meaning: the endpoints lie in the same component of G

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Graph Feasibility Boundary
Demand-Pair Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut representation of pairwise connectivity in undirected Steiner forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the demand-cut function by
\[
f_D(S)=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if some }(s_i,t_i)\in D\text{ has exactly one endpoint in }S,\\
0,&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
An edge set \(F\subseteq E\) connects \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) for every \((s_i,t_i)\in D\) if and only if
\[
|F\cap\delta(S)|\ge f_D(S)\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V.
\]
Thus Steiner-forest feasibility is a binary cut-covering system over the cuts that separate at least one demand pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge set connects every terminal pair exactly when it crosses every cut that separates at least one demanded pair.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\{(s_i,t_i)\}_{i=1}^{k}\subseteq V\times V\) is a finite set of demand pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An edge set \(F\subseteq E\) connects every pair in \(D\) exactly when \(|F\cap\delta(S)|\ge f_D(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: finite set of terminal demand pairs
indicator that cut S separates at least one demand pair
set of graph edges with exactly one endpoint in S

children.title: Moat–Connectivity Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Connections between moat structure and generalized connectivity obligations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable lower bound supplied by a moat assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(y_S\ge0\) and \(\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\) for every edge, then \(\sum_S f(S)y_S\) is at most the cost of every feasible fractional or integral cut cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every dual-feasible moat assignment certifies a lower bound on network cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Feasibility Lower-Bound Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tight-Edge Growth Alone Has No Ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation between dual feasibility and approximation charging.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\) have \(m\) incident unit-cost edges \(su_1,\ldots,su_m\), and require only that \(s\) connect to \(u_1\). Setting \(y_{\{s\}}=1\) makes every incident edge tight and is dual feasible. Selecting all \(m\) tight edges gives cost \(m\) although the dual value and optimum are one. Hence tight-edge selection without a specified pruning and crossing bound has no universal approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A star instance permits arbitrarily many tight redundant edges, so tightness and dual feasibility alone give no approximation ratio.
assumptions_latex: The graph is the stated undirected unit-cost star.

notation.meaning: the set of all m star edges

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Edge Growth Alone Has No Ratio

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual interface underlying moat growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relaxation \[\min\{\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e:x(\delta(S))\ge f(S)\ (S\subseteq V),\ x\ge0\}\] has dual \[\max\{\sum_{S\subseteq V}f(S)y_S:\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\ (e\in E),\ y\ge0\}.\] A positive \(y_S\) is a moat budget, and an edge is tight when the budgets of the cuts it crosses sum to its cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moats are dual cut variables, and tight edges saturate their dual constraints.

notation.meaning: dual moat variable for cut S

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Covering LP and Moat Dual

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is undirected with costs \(c_e\ge0\), and \(f:2^V\to\{0,1\}\) specifies required cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual moat growth preserves \(\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\); tight edges merge moats until no required cut remains uncovered.

notation.meaning: dual moat variable for cut S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic primal-dual interface between active connectivity cuts, dual moats, and tight edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(F=\varnothing\) and \(y_S=0\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). At each iteration, identify the inclusion-minimal connected components \(S\) of \((V,F)\) with \(f(S)=1\) and no selected edge crossing \(S\); declare them active and increase their \(y_S\) uniformly while maintaining
\[
\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\qquad(e\in E).
\]
When an edge becomes tight, add it to \(F\) and merge the incident components. Stop when no active component remains, then reverse-delete redundant selected edges. Output the pruned set \(F\), which covers every required cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow dual variables on active violated cuts, add edges when their dual constraints become tight, merge components, and finally prune redundant edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Moat–Connectivity Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact moat-growing variant cannot be validated from the record. Its assumptions do not state the symmetry or uncrossability conditions used by the neighboring framework, and the active-component and reverse-delete rules require authoritative specification.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical growth-and-pruning template for proper constrained forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with F=\varnothing and y=0. A component C of (V,F) is active when f(C)=1. Raise the dual variables of all active components uniformly until an edge joining distinct components becomes tight, add a tight joining edge, and update the components. Continue until no component is active. Then scan added edges in reverse order and delete each edge whose deletion preserves x_F(\delta(S))\geq f(S) for every S\subseteq V.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow all active component moats until a joining edge becomes tight, merge components, and reverse-delete redundant edges.
assumptions_latex: f is a proper zero-one requirement function.
Active components and the next tight-edge event can be found in polynomial time.

notation.meaning: Dual variable of an active component.

review_flags: oracle requirements must support polynomial identification of active components and tight events
knowledge_statements.title: Proper-Function Moat-Growing Algorithm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical guarantee for the proper-function constrained-forest algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For n=|V|\geq2, the standard moat-growing and reverse-delete algorithm returns a constrained forest F together with a feasible dual y satisfying \[c(F)\leq\left(2-\frac{2}{n}\right)\sum_{S\subseteq V}f(S)y_S\leq\left(2-\frac{2}{n}\right)\operatorname{OPT}.\] With polynomial-time access to the required component and tight-edge events, the algorithm runs in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard proper constrained-forest moat-growing algorithm is a polynomial-time (2−2/n)-approximation.
assumptions_latex: The required active-component and tight-edge operations are polynomial-time implementable.
knowledge_statements.title: Goemans–Williamson Approximation Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional cut relaxation and packing dual for proper constrained forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cut relaxation is \[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e:x(\delta(S))\geq f(S)\ \text{for all }S\subseteq V,\ x\geq0\right\}.\] Its dual is \[\max\left\{\sum_{S\subseteq V}f(S)y_S:\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\leq c_e\ \text{for all }e\in E,\ y\geq0\right\}.\] Every dual-feasible y is therefore a lower-bound certificate for every integral constrained forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constrained-forest cut relaxation has a dual packing required cuts into edge-cost capacities.
knowledge_statements.title: Constrained-Forest Cut Relaxation and Dual
Goemans–Williamson Constrained-Forest Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The proper-function formulation underlying moat-growing constrained-forest algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and let \(f:2^V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfy \(f(V)=0\), \(f(S)=f(V\setminus S)\), and \(f(A\cup B)\leq\max\{f(A),f(B)\}\) for disjoint \(A,B\subseteq V\). A constrained forest is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(|F\cap\delta(S)|\geq f(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). The associated optimization problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in F}c_e:F\subseteq E,\ |F\cap\delta(S)|\geq f(S)\ \text{for all }S\subseteq V\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained forest is an edge set crossing every cut declared active by a symmetric proper zero-one requirement function; the associated problem seeks such an edge set of minimum cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and \(c_e\geq0\) for every \(e\in E\).
\(f\) is a proper zero-one cut-requirement function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is feasible exactly when \(|F\cap\delta(S)|\geq f(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\).

notation.meaning: Edges with exactly one endpoint in S.
Whether cut S must be crossed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical rooted primal-dual growth with edge and penalty events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rooted PCST, grow dual values on active connected components not containing r. Continue until either an edge constraint becomes tight, in which case add an eligible tight edge and merge components, or a penalty constraint becomes tight, in which case deactivate the affected component. After growth, prune tight edges and inactive branches not needed to connect the surviving vertices to r. The resulting tree is feasible for the rooted objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow active moats until an edge or penalty becomes tight, then merge or deactivate components and prune the resulting tight-edge forest.
assumptions_latex: A root r and the rooted PCST convention are fixed.
G is finite and all costs and penalties are nonnegative.
The standard rooted moat-growth and pruning rules are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is connected, contains }r,\text{ and pays penalties for every }v\notin V_T.
review_flags: authoritative rooted PCST algorithm locator required
knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Collecting Moat-Growing Scheme

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial approximation status for rooted and rootless vertex-penalty PCST.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard rooted primal-dual algorithm runs in polynomial time and returns T with \[c(T)+\pi(V\setminus V_T)\leq2\operatorname{OPT}_r.\] For the rootless convention of the immutable seed, run the rooted algorithm once for each possible root and also compare the empty solution; the cheapest candidate is a polynomial-time 2-approximation. PCST is NP-hard through its Steiner-tree special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rooted and rootless prize-collecting Steiner tree admit polynomial-time factor-two approximations, while the problem remains NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and edge costs and penalties are nonnegative.
The rooted or rootless feasibility convention is fixed.
review_flags: the exact historical theorem and implementation locator should be supplied
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Factor-Two Approximation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal witness that fixed-root and rootless formulations need not have equal optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V=\{r,v\}, let edge rv have cost 1, and set \pi_r=0 and \pi_v=1. In the rootless formulation, the singleton tree \{v\} has value 0. In the formulation rooted at r, either v is omitted and penalty 1 is paid or edge rv is bought for cost 1, so \operatorname{OPT}_r=1. Thus a fixed-root instance is not interchangeable with the rootless instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-vertex instance separates the rootless optimum from the optimum with a prescribed root.
assumptions_latex: The rootless objective charges penalties for omitted vertices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), edge costs \(c_e\geq0\), and vertex penalties \(\pi_v\geq0\), a prize-collecting Steiner tree solution is either a nonempty connected subgraph \(T=(V_T,E_T)\) or, by convention, the empty solution with \(V_T=E_T=\varnothing\). knowledge_statements.title: Feedback Vertex Set Primal-Dual Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic cycle-packing primal-dual scheme for weighted undirected feedback vertex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with weights \(w_v\geq0\), initialize \(S=\varnothing\) and \(y_C=0\) for every cycle \(C\). While \(G-S\) contains a cycle, choose such a cycle \(C\) and increase \(y_C\) until some \(v\in C\) first satisfies \(\sum_{C'\ni v}y_{C'}=w_v\); add one such tight vertex to \(S\). After no cycle remains, inspect selected vertices in reverse order and delete any vertex whose removal preserves the feedback-vertex-set property. Output the resulting inclusion-minimal set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow dual weight on residual cycles until vertices become tight, select tight vertices, and reverse-delete redundant selections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G-S\) is acyclic, so the output \(S\) is an inclusion-minimal feedback vertex set.

notation.meaning: Dual variable associated with cycle C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Low-high-degree-cycle primal-dual algorithm for feedback vertex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The second primal-dual procedure chooses a cycle containing few vertices of current degree at least three.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $n=|V|$. Initialize $y_C=0$ for every cycle $C$ and $S=\varnothing$, and repeatedly delete vertices of degree one. While the current graph contains a cycle, find a cycle $C$ containing at most $2\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ vertices whose current degree is at least $3$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Improved primal-dual algorithm for undirected feedback vertex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual growth selects tight vertices, removes vertices absent from all residual cycles, and reverse-deletes redundant selected vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(y\leftarrow0\), \(F\leftarrow\varnothing\), \(S\leftarrow V\), and \(\ell\leftarrow0\). While \(F\) is not feasible and \(G(S)\) contains a cycle, increment \(\ell\); increase \(y_S\) until some \(v_\ell\in S\) satisfies \[\sum_{C:v_\ell\in C}\bigl(d_C(v_\ell)-b_C(v_\ell)\bigr)y_C=w_{v_\ell};\] set \(F\leftarrow F\cup\{v_\ell\}\); let \[T=\{v\in S:v\text{ lies on no cycle in }G(S\setminus\{v_\ell\})\};\] and set \(S\leftarrow S\setminus(\{v_\ell\}\cup T)\). Set \(F'\leftarrow F\). For \(k=\ell,\ldots,1\), remove \(v_k\) from \(F'\) whenever \(F'\setminus\{v_k\}\) is feasible. Return \(F'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raise the dual variable of the current residual set until a vertex becomes tight, select that vertex, and discard vertices lying on no remaining cycle. Then examine selected vertices in reverse order and remove each one whose deletion preserves feasibility.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected graph with vertex weights }w_v
\text{A feasible set intersects every cycle of }G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: BBF Weight-Reduction Algorithm for Minimum-Weight Feedback Vertex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm statement only; its factor-two guarantee is recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize $F=\varnothing$, recursively remove vertices of degree at most $1$, and set $i=1$. While a disjoint or almost-disjoint cycle $\Gamma$ exists, set $\delta=\min_{v\in\Gamma}w(v)$, replace $w(v)$ by $w(v)-\delta$ for $v\in\Gamma$, and record $(G_i,w_i)$ with $G_i=\Gamma$ and $w_i(v)=\delta$ on $\Gamma$. Then set
\[\delta=\min_{v\in V}\frac{w(v)}{d(v)-1},\]
replace $w(v)$ by $w(v)-\delta(d(v)-1)$ for every remaining vertex, record $G_i=G$ and $w_i(v)=\delta(d(v)-1)$, and recursively remove vertices of degree at most $1$. If vertices remain, repeat the cycle-reduction phase. Otherwise, form $F$ from the vertices whose reduced weight is zero, remove redundant vertices from $F$, and output $F$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The BBF algorithm recursively removes low-degree vertices, reduces weights on disjoint or almost-disjoint cycles, applies a degree-minus-one proportional weight reduction to the residual graph, and repeats. When the residual graph is empty, it selects zero-reduced-weight vertices and removes redundancies.
assumptions_latex: \text{vertices of degree at most one are recursively removed before proportional updates}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is the minimal feedback vertex set output by the stated BBF weight-reduction procedure}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cyclomatic vertex weights and their lower bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cyclomatic weight construction for weighted feedback vertex set approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define $\delta_G(v)=\operatorname{cyc}(G)-\operatorname{cyc}(G-v)$. If $F=\{v_1,\ldots,v_f\}$ is a feedback vertex set, $G_0=G$, and $G_i=G-\{v_1,\ldots,v_i\}$, then $\operatorname{cyc}(G)=\sum_{i=1}^f\delta_{G_{i-1}}(v_i)\leq\sum_{v\in F}\delta_G(v)$. A vertex-weight function is cyclomatic if $w(v)=c\,\delta_G(v)$ for every vertex and some $c>0$; for such weights, $c\,\operatorname{cyc}(G)\leq\mathrm{OPT}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cyclomatic decrease of a vertex is the loss of cyclomatic number caused by deleting it. Along an ordered feedback vertex set these decreases telescope to the graph's cyclomatic number and are at most their corresponding values in the original graph. Weights proportional to those original decreases therefore give a lower bound on the optimum feedback vertex set weight.
assumptions_latex: F=\{v_1,\ldots,v_f\}\text{ is a feedback vertex set of }G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Layering algorithm for weighted feedback vertex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-reduction decomposition followed by reverse inclusion-minimal extension; the meaning of \(\delta_H\) is inherited from the surrounding source context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(H\leftarrow G\), \(w'\leftarrow w\), and \(i\leftarrow0\). While \(H\) is not acyclic, set \(c=\min_{u\in V(H)}\{w'(u)/\delta_H(u)\}\), \(G_i\leftarrow H\), \(t_i\leftarrow c\,\delta_{G_i}\), and \(w'\leftarrow w'-t_i\); then replace \(H\) by the subgraph of \(G_i\) induced by vertices \(u\) satisfying \(w'(u)>0\), and increment \(i\). Set \(k\leftarrow i\), \(G_k\leftarrow H\), and \(F_k\leftarrow\varnothing\). For \(i=k,\ldots,1\), extend \(F_i\) to a feedback vertex set \(F_{i-1}\) of \(G_{i-1}\) by adding an inclusion-minimal set from \(V_{i-1}\setminus V_i\). Output \(F_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm repeatedly removes a maximal residual-weight layer defined using the source's delta function, retains the positive-residual induced subgraph, and then traverses the layers backward while minimally adding removed vertices to obtain a feedback vertex set of the original graph.
assumptions_latex: w\text{ is the input vertex-weight function}
\delta_H\text{ has the meaning and domain specified in the surrounding source context}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_0\text{ is the algorithm's output feedback vertex set for }G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge Cuts Do Not Model Internal-Vertex Survivability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary of the edge-connectivity cut interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two edge-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths share a single internal vertex \(v\), using otherwise distinct vertices and edges. Every \(s\)-\(t\) cut has at least two edges, but deleting \(v\) disconnects \(s\) from \(t\). Thus the edge-cut requirement two does not certify two internally vertex-disjoint paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two edge-disjoint paths may share an articulation vertex, so edge-cut constraints do not characterize vertex connectivity.
assumptions_latex: The two paths are edge-disjoint and have the sole common internal vertex \(v\).
knowledge_statements.title: Edge Cuts Do Not Model Internal-Vertex Survivability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional primal-dual interface for undirected edge-connectivity design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Relaxing integrality gives \[\min\{\sum_ec_ex_e:x(\delta(S))\ge f(S)\ (\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V),\ x\ge0\}.\] Its dual is \[\max\{\sum_Sf(S)y_S:\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\ (e\in E),\ y\ge0\}.\] Every dual-feasible \(y\) lower-bounds the integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The survivable cut relaxation has one dual price per cut, and every feasible dual certifies a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Survivable Cut Relaxation and Dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncrossing structure of maximum separated-pair requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric nonnegative pair requirements and \(f(S)=\max\{r_{uv}:u\in S,v\notin S\}\), \[f(A)+f(B)\le\max\{f(A\cap B)+f(A\cup B),\ f(A\setminus B)+f(B\setminus A)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum separated-pair requirements obey the skew-supermodular uncrossing inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Skew-Supermodularity of Pairwise Cut Requirements
Survivable Network Design Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-covering integer formulation for pairwise edge-connectivity requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have costs \(c_e\geq0\) and symmetric integral requirements \(r_{uv}\geq0\). Define \(f(S)=\max\{r_{uv}:u\in S,\ v\in V\setminus S\}\), with an empty maximum equal to zero. The survivable network-design interface is \[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e:x(\delta(S))\geq f(S)\ \text{for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V,\ x\in\mathbb{Z}_+^E\right\}.\] For zero-one \(x\), the constraints require the selected subgraph to contain at least \(r_{uv}\) edge-disjoint paths between every pair \(u,v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise edge-connectivity requirements become covering constraints demanding enough selected capacity across every separating cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(\delta(S))\geq\max_{u\in S,v\notin S}r_{uv}\) for every nontrivial cut characterizes the cut interface.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Set-Cover Embedding in Nonmetric UFL
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural boundary showing that unrestricted connection costs contain weighted set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible weighted set-cover instance with universe \(J\), sets \(S_i\), weights \(f_i\geq0\), and \(W=\sum_i f_i\), construct a UFL instance with one facility per set, one client per element, and \[c_{ij}=\begin{cases}0,&j\in S_i,\\W+1,&j\notin S_i.\end{cases}\] Then every optimal UFL solution uses only zero-cost assignment edges, its open facilities form a set cover, and its cost equals the cover weight. Hence the two instances have the same optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary nonmetric UFL exactly contains weighted set cover through zero-cost membership edges and prohibitive nonmembership edges.
assumptions_latex: The weighted set-cover instance is feasible and finite.

notation.meaning: Sum of all set weights, used to choose a prohibitive connection cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Set-Cover Embedding in Nonmetric UFL

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional opening-and-assignment relaxation for finite uncapacitated facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard UFL relaxation is \[\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}f_i y_i+\sum_{i\in I,j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_i x_{ij}=1\ (j\in J),\ 0\leq x_{ij}\leq y_i,\ y_i\geq0\right\}.\] Restricting \(x_{ij},y_i\) to binary values recovers the discrete formulation, and every fractional optimum has an equally good representative with \(0\leq y_i\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard relaxation fractionally opens facilities and assigns clients only to open facility mass; binary variables recover discrete UFL.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\leq\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{UFL}}\), and the binary restriction represents UFL.

notation.meaning: Fraction of client j assigned to facility i.

knowledge_statements.title: Standard UFL Linear Relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Jain–Vazirani guarantee for metric uncapacitated facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If connection costs are induced by a metric on facilities and clients, the Jain--Vazirani primal-dual facility-location algorithm runs in polynomial time and returns an integral solution of cost at most \(3\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}\), and therefore at most \(3\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{UFL}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical Jain–Vazirani primal-dual method is a polynomial-time 3-approximation for metric UFL.
assumptions_latex: Connection costs are restrictions of a metric on \(I\cup J\).

notation.meaning: Cost returned by the Jain–Vazirani algorithm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven dual growth and conflict filtering for metric uncapacitated facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\alpha_j=0\) and make every client active. Raise all active \(\alpha_j\) uniformly. An active client becomes connected and inactive upon reaching an already tight facility; when \(\sum_j(\alpha_j-c_{ij})_+=f_i\), declare facility \(i\) temporarily open, connect its active contributing clients, and make them inactive. After all clients are inactive, form the conflict graph on temporarily open facilities, joining facilities that share a contributing client; open a maximal independent set. Connect each client to its selected temporary facility if that facility was retained, and otherwise to a retained conflicting facility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grow client prices until facilities become tight, prune conflicting temporary facilities with a maximal independent set, and reconnect clients to retained facilities.
assumptions_latex: Connection costs are induced by a metric on \(I\cup J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The returned solution is feasible and has cost at most }3\sum_j\alpha_j\le3\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Jain–Vazirani Metric-UFL Construction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual and lower-bound certificates for the standard UFL relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual of the standard UFL relaxation is \[\max\sum_{j\in J}\alpha_j\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \alpha_j\le c_{ij}+\beta_{ij}\ (i,j),\quad \sum_j\beta_{ij}\le f_i\ (i),\quad \beta_{ij}\ge0,\quad \alpha_j\in\mathbb R.\] Eliminating \(\beta\) gives \(\sum_j(\alpha_j-c_{ij})_+\le f_i\) for every facility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Client prices are feasible when their positive excess above each facility's connection costs does not exceed its opening cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\sum_j\alpha_j=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}},\text{ and every feasible }\alpha\text{ is a lower-bound certificate.}

notation.meaning: client contribution toward opening facility i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Event Bound for Dual-Growth UFL
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic-operation bound for the finite Jain–Vazirani growth phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the event-driven metric-UFL dual-growth construction, each client becomes inactive at most once and each facility is declared tight at most once. Thus at most |J|+|I| state-changing events occur. Recomputing every client contribution and every candidate facility-tightening time after each event uses O(|I||J|(|I|+|J|)) rational arithmetic operations and polynomial space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There is at most one deactivation per client and one tightening per facility, so direct event scanning is polynomial in arithmetic operations.
assumptions_latex: The costs are nonnegative rational numbers.
Simultaneous events are processed together using a fixed tie rule.
The bound counts exact rational arithmetic operations rather than unit-cost bit operations.
review_flags: The displayed bound is an arithmetic-operation bound; a concrete bit-complexity statement requires an encoding-level event implementation.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Event Bound for Dual-Growth UFL
Uncapacitated Facility Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite uncapacitated facility-location formulation without metric assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be facilities and \(J\) clients. Facility \(i\) has opening cost \(f_i\geq0\), and assigning client \(j\) to \(i\) costs \(c_{ij}\geq0\). An uncapacitated facility-location solution consists of \(F\subseteq I\) and a map \(\sigma:J\to F\); no bound is imposed on \(|\sigma^{-1}(i)|\). Its cost is \[\sum_{i\in F}f_i+\sum_{j\in J}c_{\sigma(j),j}.\] The problem minimizes this cost over nonempty \(F\) when \(J\ne\varnothing\), with the empty solution permitted when \(J=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Open any number of facilities and assign every client to an open facility, minimizing opening plus assignment cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-growth and conflict-pruning algorithm for UFL
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual facility-selection procedure for uncapacitated facility location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(v=w=0\), \(S=D\), and \(T=\varnothing\). While \(S\ne\varnothing\), uniformly increase \(v_j\) for \(j\in S\) and \(w_{ij}\) for \(j\in S\) and \(i\in N(j)\) until either some \(j\in S\) neighbors a facility in \(T\), or some \(i\notin T\) has the tight constraint \(\sum_{j\in D}w_{ij}=f_i\). In the first case remove such \(j\) from \(S\); in the second add \(i\) to \(T\) and remove \(N(i)\) from \(S\). Then set \(T'=\varnothing\). Repeatedly choose \(i\in T\), add it to \(T'\), and delete every \(h\in T\) for which some \(j\in D\) satisfies \(w_{ij}>0\) and \(w_{hj}>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm grows active clients' dual values and applicable facility cost shares until clients reach selected facilities or facility constraints become tight. It then greedily prunes tight facilities so that retained facilities do not share a positively contributing client.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ and }D\text{ define an uncapacitated facility-location instance}
\sum_{j\in D}w_{ij}\le f_i\text{ is maintained during dual growth}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T'\subseteq T\quad\text{and}\quad \nexists i\ne h\in T',\ j\in D:\ w_{ij}>0\land w_{hj}>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-fitting algorithm for uncapacitated facility location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-growth facility-opening procedure using doubled facility-opening costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\alpha_j=0\) for every \(j\in D\), \(S=D\), \(X=\varnothing\), and \(\widehat f_i=2f_i\) for every \(i\in F\). While \(S\neq\varnothing\), increase all \(\alpha_j\), \(j\in S\), uniformly until either \(\alpha_j=c_{ij}\) for some \(j\in S\) and \(i\in X\), or \(\sum_{j\in S}(\alpha_j-c_{ij})_++\sum_{j\notin S}(c(j,X)-c_{ij})_+=\widehat f_i\) for some \(i\in F\setminus X\). In the first case remove such a \(j\) from \(S\). In the second case add such an \(i\) to \(X\) and remove every \(j\in S\) with \(\alpha_j\geq c_{ij}\). Finally, open all facilities in \(X\) and assign each client to a closest facility in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raise the values of all active clients uniformly. Remove a client when its value reaches its connection cost to an already selected facility; select a new facility when accumulated contributions reach twice its opening cost, and remove all active clients neighboring it. Finally open the selected facilities and assign every client to a closest selected facility.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is the facility set and }D\text{ is the client set}
f_i\text{ is the opening cost of facility }i
c_{ij}\text{ is the connection cost from client }j\text{ to facility }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\subseteq F\text{ is opened, and every }j\in D\text{ is assigned to a closest facility in }X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cardinality Lagrangean Dual and Convex-Envelope Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best scalar-multiplier bound and its exactness boundary for the discrete cardinality profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(q)=\min\{A(F):|F|=q\}\) for \(q=1,\ldots,|I|\), and define \(L_k(\lambda)=\min_q\{g(q)+\lambda(q-k)\}\). Equality holds exactly when \((k,g(k))\) is lower-hull supported; otherwise the scalar Lagrangean dual has a positive cardinality gap.

For a multiplier \(\lambda\geq0\), define \[L(\lambda)=\min_{\varnothing\ne F\subseteq I}\bigl(A(F)+\lambda(|F|-k)\bigr).\] Every cardinality-feasible set \(F\) with \(|F|=k\) is feasible in the inner minimization with unchanged objective; hence \(L(\lambda)\leq\operatorname{OPT}_k\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic connection between uniform facility penalties and k-median relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A(F)=\sum_{j\in J}\min_{i\in F}c_{ij}\), define the uniform-penalty facility-location value \(U(\lambda)=\min_{F\ne\varnothing}(A(F)+\lambda|F|)\). The Lagrangean relaxation of the k-median constraint \(|F|=k\) satisfies \[L_k(\lambda)=\min_{F\ne\varnothing}\bigl(A(F)+\lambda(|F|-k)\bigr)=U(\lambda)-\lambda k.\] Thus any optimizer of the uniform-penalty facility-location problem also optimizes the inner k-median relaxation at the same multiplier, and its facility count determines the relaxed cardinality violation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(q)=\min_{|F|=q}A(F)\). A cardinality \(k\) occurs among the minimizers of \(A(F)+\lambda|F|\) for some scalar \(\lambda\) if and only if \((k,g(k))\) lies on the lower convex envelope of \(\{(q,g(q)):1\leq q\leq|I|\}\). Multiplier-Sensitive Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concavity and monotone facility counts under a uniform opening multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U(\lambda)=\min_{F\ne\varnothing}(A(F)+\lambda|F|)\). Then \(U\) is nondecreasing, concave, and piecewise affine on \([0,\infty)\). Moreover, if \(0\leq\lambda_1<\lambda_2\) and \(F_t\) minimizes \(A(F)+\lambda_t|F|\) for \(t\in\{1,2\}\), then \[|F_1|\geq|F_2|.\] On any interval where a single facility set \(F\) remains optimal, \(U\) has slope \(|F|\); at a breakpoint, the one-sided slopes are facility counts of optimal solutions on the adjacent regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing the facility multiplier cannot increase the number of facilities in an optimal solution; the value function is concave and piecewise affine.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and \(A(F)\in\mathbb{R}\) for every nonempty \(F\subseteq I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U\) is concave and piecewise affine, and optimal facility counts satisfy \(|F_1|\geq|F_2|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Feasible Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificate for a minimization primal and maximization dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the covering primal and packing dual \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\geq b,\ x\geq0\},\qquad \max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c,\ y\geq0\}.\] For any primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\), \[b^{\mathsf T}y\leq c^{\mathsf T}x.\] Consequently, a displayed dual-feasible vector \(y\) is a directly verifiable lower-bound certificate: checking \(y\geq0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\leq c\) certifies \(b^{\mathsf T}y\leq\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm P}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any feasible maximization-dual solution supplies a checkable lower bound on every feasible primal solution and on the primal optimum.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary weak duality for covering and packing linear programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard weak-duality certificate and its content kind fits exactly, but no authoritative LP-duality citation or locator is attached.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp factor at least one that converts a tentative nonnegative packing dual into a feasible dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell_j=(A^{\mathsf T}y)_j\), with \(y\ge0\) and \(c_j\ge0\), and define \[r_j=\begin{cases}\max\{0,\ell_j\}/c_j,&c_j>0,\\0,&c_j=0\text{ and }\ell_j\le0,\\+\infty,&c_j=0\text{ and }\ell_j>0.\end{cases}\qquad \rho_\star=\max\{1,\max_j r_j\}.\] For an allowed scaling factor \(\rho\ge1\), \(y/\rho\) is dual feasible exactly when \(\rho\ge\rho_\star\), provided \(\rho_\star<\infty\). Positive load on a zero-cost constraint prevents repair by any finite uniform factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum load-to-cost ratio, floored at one and with zero-cost obstructions treated explicitly, is the least permitted uniform repair factor.
assumptions_latex: Uniform certificate factors are restricted to \(\rho\ge1\).

Then \(y/\rho\) is feasible for the packing dual. If additionally \(c^{\mathsf T}x\leq b^{\mathsf T}y\), the pair \((x,y)\) certifies \[\frac{b^{\mathsf T}y}{\rho}\leq\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm P}\quad\text{and}\quad c^{\mathsf T}x\leq\rho\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm P}.\] Verification requires only the displayed primal feasibility, scaled dual inequalities, and cost comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Charging Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local accounting certificate bounding primal cost by a dual lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(J\) be finite sets, let \(c_i\ge 0\) for every \(i\in F\), let \(z_j\ge 0\) for every \(j\in J\), and suppose \(\sum_{j\in J}z_j\le \operatorname{OPT}\). For \(\alpha\ge 0\), a matrix \(q=(q_{ij})_{i\in F,j\in J}\) is an \(\alpha\)-charging certificate if \[q_{ij}\ge 0,\qquad c_i\le \sum_{j\in J}q_{ij}\ \ (i\in F),\qquad \sum_{i\in F}q_{ij}\le \alpha z_j\ \ (j\in J).\] Such a certificate establishes \[c(F):=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\le \alpha\sum_{j\in J}z_j\le \alpha\operatorname{OPT}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite selected objects and lower-bound witnesses, nonnegative charges that cover every selected cost and load each witness by at most α times its contribution certify an α-approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Charging–Cost-Sharing Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between aggregate shares and a disaggregated charging matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(J\) be finite, let \(c_i\ge0\) for \(i\in F\), let \(z_j\ge0\) for \(j\in J\), and let \(\alpha\ge0\). There exists a nonnegative matrix \(q=(q_{ij})_{i\in F,j\in J}\) satisfying \[c_i\le\sum_{j\in J}q_{ij}\ \ (i\in F),\qquad \sum_{i\in F}q_{ij}\le\alpha z_j\ \ (j\in J)\] if and only if there exist nonnegative shares \((\xi_j)_{j\in J}\) satisfying \[\sum_{i\in F}c_i\le\sum_{j\in J}\xi_j,\qquad \xi_j\le\alpha z_j\ \ (j\in J).\] Thus disaggregated charging and aggregate cost-sharing certificates have the same factor \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite nonnegative data, a charging matrix with factor α exists exactly when aggregate cost shares with factor α exist.

children.title: Cross-Subsidy Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where cost transfers invalidate local charging interpretations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp quantitative condition ensuring that retained shares recover retained cost after deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For retained objects \(R\), write \(c(R)=\sum_{i\in R}c_i\) and \(\xi(R)=\sum_{i\in R}\xi_i\). If \(c_i,\xi_i\ge0\) and \(\xi(R)\ge\lambda c(R)\) for some \(\lambda>0\), then \[c(R)\le\lambda^{-1}\xi(R).\] The factor \(\lambda^{-1}\) is sharp when equality holds. If no uniform positive \(\lambda\) exists, no finite recovery factor follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive uniform lower bound on retained shares relative to retained cost gives the sharp reciprocal recovery factor; allowing that fraction to vanish permits unbounded recovery loss.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is finite and \(c_i,\xi_i\ge0\) for all \(i\in R\).

notation.meaning: cost and assessed share of object i

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Retained-Subsidy Condition
Cross-Subsidy Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate budget balance need not survive deletion of subsidizing components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take independently removable objects \(a,b\), each of cost \(1\), with assessments \(\xi_a=2\) and \(\xi_b=0\). Then \[\xi_a+\xi_b=c_a+c_b=2,\] so aggregate budget balance is exact. If conversion retains only \(b\), its available share is \(0\) although its cost is \(1\); no finite \(\beta\) satisfies \(c_b\le\beta\xi_b\). Thus deletion-based conversion requires subset budget balance, cross-monotonicity, or an explicit bound on lost subsidy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact global balance can hide complete underpayment of a retained component, so conversion needs subsetwise control of cross-subsidy.
assumptions_latex: Only aggregate budget balance is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite subset-recovery factor follows from aggregate budget balance alone.

children.title: Laminar Dual Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical representation and recognition test for explicitly listed laminar dual support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L\) be a finite family of subsets of \(V\). It is laminar if and only if every nonmaximal \(S\in\mathcal L\) has a unique smallest strict superset \(p(S)\in\mathcal L\), the resulting parent links form an inclusion forest, and sets at incomparable nodes are disjoint. Pairwise containment-or-disjointness checks recognize this structure in time polynomial in the explicit representation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite laminar support is exactly an immediate-inclusion forest whose incomparable nodes represent disjoint sets.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal L\) is a finite explicitly represented family of subsets of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal L\text{ is laminar exactly when its immediate-inclusion structure is such a forest.}

knowledge_statements.title: Inclusion-Forest Representation
Laminar Dual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible cut-packing dual supported on nested or disjoint sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(G=(V,E)\), costs \(c_e\ge0\), and requirements \(f(S)\ge0\), consider the cut-cover relaxation \[\min\left\{\sum_ec_ex_e:x(\delta(S))\ge f(S)\ (S\subset V),\ x\ge0\right\}.\] A laminar dual certificate is \(y_S\ge0\) satisfying \[\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e\quad(e\in E),\] such that \(\mathcal L:=\{S:y_S>0\}\) is laminar. Its value \(\sum_Sf(S)y_S\) is a verifiable lower bound on every feasible primal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A laminar certificate is a feasible cut-packing dual whose positive sets are nested or disjoint and whose value lower-bounds optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Moat Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-growth certificate interpreting positive cut variables as moat widths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y_S\ge0\) be a feasible cut-packing dual and let \(F\subseteq E\) be primal feasible. Interpreting \(y_S\) as moat width, suppose every \(e\in F\) is tight and the moat-edge incidence obeys \[c_e=\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S,
\qquad
\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le\alpha\sum_Sf(S)y_S.\] Then \[c(F)\le\alpha\sum_Sf(S)y_S\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}.\] These displayed equalities and inequalities form an independently checkable moat certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible moat widths pay tight selected edges; bounded moat-edge incidence certifies the approximation factor.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncrossing theorem for symmetric skew-supermodular cut requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and let \(f\ge0\) be symmetric and skew-supermodular. Thus, for crossing \(A,B\), at least one of \[f(A)+f(B)\le f(A\cap B)+f(A\cup B),\qquad f(A)+f(B)\le f(A\setminus B)+f(B\setminus A)\] holds. If the cut-packing dual \[\max\left\{\sum_Sf(S)y_S:\sum_{S:e\in\delta(S)}y_S\le c_e,
\ y\ge0\right\}\] attains an optimum, then it has an optimum \(y^*\) whose positive support is laminar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For symmetric skew-supermodular requirements, an optimal cut-packing dual can be chosen with laminar positive support.
assumptions_latex: The finite cut-packing dual attains its optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is optimal \(y^*\) for which \(\{S:y_S^*>0\}\) is laminar.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a substantive uncrossing theorem. A precise source is required to confirm whether symmetry, skew-supermodularity, the indexed cut family, and the stated dual constraints suffice for the claimed laminar optimal support.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Builder-proposed iterative laminarization based only on a bounded strict potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proposed claim asserts that repeated objective-preserving uncrossing transfers terminate after finitely many steps whenever they strictly increase a bounded real-valued potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proposed finite-termination implication is not valid from bounded strict potential increase alone.
assumptions_latex: Each transfer preserves dual feasibility and objective value.
A bounded real-valued potential strictly increases at every transfer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Finite termination does not follow from these assumptions alone.}
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Uncrossing Procedure

intermediate_metadata.reason: The essential positive theorem remains materially uncertain, and the Builder's added finite-termination claim is mathematically unsupported because bounded strict increase alone permits infinite sequences. Laminar-certificate semantics, moat accounting, and crossing-family obstructions remain excluded to the adjacent siblings.

children.title: Crossing-Family Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Constraint families where crossing structure obstructs laminar or moat certification.

knowledge_statements.title: Crossing-Family Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Without uncrossing closure, optimal dual support can be necessarily crossing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,2,3,4\}\), \(A=\{1,2\}\), and \(B=\{2,3\}\). Then \(A\cap B\), \(A\setminus B\), \(B\setminus A\), and \(V\setminus(A\cup B)\) are all nonempty, so \(A\) and \(B\) cross. Consider the covering program \[\min\{x_A+x_B:x_A\ge1,\ x_B\ge1,\ x_A,x_B\ge0\}\] and its dual \[\max\{y_A+y_B:0\le y_A\le1,\ 0\le y_B\le1\}.\] The unique dual optimum is \(y_A=y_B=1\), so every optimal dual solution has crossing, nonlaminar support \(\{A,B\}\). The indexed constraint family contains no intersection, union, or difference member that could support an uncrossed replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint family containing only two genuinely crossing members can force both associated dual variables to be positive when it contains no uncrossed replacement members.
assumptions_latex: The indexed constraint family is exactly \(\{A,B\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every optimal dual solution has crossing, nonlaminar support.

notation.meaning: crossing members of the constraint family
