knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Dual Congestion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation accounting fails under unbounded reuse of one dual contribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(k\ge1\), let a lower-bound certificate consist of one witness \(z=1\), and let conversion select \(k\) unit-cost objects, each charged wholly to that witness. Then \[c(F_k)=k,
\qquad \rho_k:=\frac{\sum_{i\in F_k}q_i}{z}=k.\] Every object is locally paid, yet no constant \(\alpha\) satisfies \(c(F_k)\le\alpha z\) for all \(k\). Constant-factor conversion therefore requires a uniform bound on overlap, reuse, or incidence congestion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paying every object locally is insufficient when arbitrarily many objects reuse the same dual witness.
assumptions_latex: There is no uniform bound on witness reuse.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Cleanup-Cost Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unpriced feasibility repair can dominate the certified intermediate cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(k\ge1\), suppose an intermediate solution \(F_k^0\) has certified cost at most \(1\) but leaves \(k\) independent defects. If each defect requires a distinct unit-cost repair object, every feasible cleanup \(R_k\) satisfies \[c(R_k)\ge k,
\qquad c(F_k^0\cup R_k)
\ge k.\] Hence the ratio of final cost to the intermediate certificate is unbounded. A valid conversion must charge cleanup to new dual growth, bound the number of repairs, or prove a constant-cost completion lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cheap certified intermediate solution gives no approximation guarantee when repairing its independent defects costs arbitrarily much.
assumptions_latex: The certificate for \(F_k^0\) has value at most \(1\).
The \(k\) defects require distinct unit-cost repairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cleanup-to-certificate ratio is at least \(k\) and is unbounded.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmetric Assignment Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reassignment bounds fail without a triangle inequality or comparable detour condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a,b\) be facilities and \(j\) a client, with assignment costs \(d(a,j)=1\) and \(d(b,j)=M\), where \(M>0\) is arbitrary. Suppose an intermediate solution assigns \(j\) to \(a\), but cleanup deletes \(a\) and forces assignment to \(b\). Then reassignment cost grows from \(1\) to \(M\). Without a metric inequality relating \(d(b,j)\) to previously paid connections or facility-to-facility movement, no instance-independent constant bounds this increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without metric structure, deleting a facility can force a client's assignment cost to increase by an arbitrary factor.
assumptions_latex: Cleanup deletes \(a\) and leaves \(b\) as the only feasible assignment.

children.title: Capacity Barriers
children.top_down_role: Obstructions caused by hard capacities in primal-dual approximation frameworks.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-oblivious conversion may require arbitrarily expensive overflow repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(n\ge2\). For each \(M>0\), consider \(n\) unit-demand clients and two facilities \(a\) and \(b\). Facility \(a\) has capacity \(n-1\) and opening cost \(0\); facility \(b\) has capacity \(1\) and opening cost \(M\). All connection costs are \(0\), assignments are unsplittable, and \(b\) is the only facility available for overflow from \(a\). A capacity-oblivious intermediate assignment sending all \(n\) clients to \(a\) has accounted cost \(0\) but exceeds its capacity by one. Every feasible repair must open \(b\), and therefore has additional cost at least \(M\). As \(M\) is arbitrary, intermediate assignment cost alone cannot bound capacity-repair cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any fixed number of at least two clients, a one-unit capacity violation can force an arbitrarily expensive overflow facility opening that a capacity-oblivious intermediate accounting did not price.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge2\) is an integer and clients have unit demand.
Assignments are unsplittable, connection costs are zero, and \(b\) is the only overflow facility.
Facility \(a\) has capacity \(n-1\) and opening cost \(0\); facility \(b\) has capacity \(1\) and opening cost \(M>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mandatory repair cost is at least \(M\), which is unbounded while the intermediate accounted cost remains \(0\).

notation.meaning: opening cost of the overflow facility

children.title: Side-Constraint Barriers
children.top_down_role: Obstructions introduced by additional feasibility restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Side-Constraint Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of automatic side-feasibility preservation under deletion-based capacity repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite and let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\) be a side-feasible family. If \(\mathcal F\) is not downward closed, then some \(S\in\mathcal F\) and \(T\subset S\) satisfy \(T\notin\mathcal F\); hence deletion is not, in general, a side-feasibility-preserving repair operation. Moreover, a deletion-only capacity repair can fail completely: take \(E=\{e\}\), \(\mathcal F=\{\{e\}\}\), consumption \(a(e)=1\), original capacity \(B=1\), and reduced capacity \(B'=0\). The original set \(\{e\}\) is feasible, while its only capacity-feasible subset under \(B'\) is \(\varnothing\notin\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-downward-closed side constraints are not automatically preserved by deletion. In particular, a singleton requirement and a reduced zero capacity give an instance in which no deletion-only repair preserves the side constraint.
assumptions_latex: Capacity repair may only delete selected elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deletion alone does not universally guarantee both capacity feasibility and membership in \(\mathcal F\).

notation.meaning: Original set and one of its subsets
Original and reduced capacities in the counterexample

review_flags: The mathematical obstruction has been made precise.
A supporting source for this approximation-conversion failure boundary is still required.

children.title: Capacity–Constraint Interactions
children.top_down_role: Compounded limitations arising from capacities plus auxiliary constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility threshold for one additive capacity combined with an exact-cardinality requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(1\le k\le |E|\), and let \(a_e\ge0\). If \(a_{(1)}\le\cdots\le a_{(|E|)}\) are the ordered consumptions, then there exists \(S\subseteq E\) with \(|S|=k\) and \(\sum_{e\in S}a_e\le B'\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^k a_{(i)}\le B'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact-k selection fits the capacity exactly when the k smallest consumptions fit. This sharpens the seed's sufficient infeasibility test based on a common positive lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists S\subseteq E:\ |S|=k,\ a(S)\le B'\iff \sum_{i=1}^k a_{(i)}\le B'\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Cardinality–Capacity Feasibility Threshold
Capacity–Constraint Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An exact feasibility conflict between a tightened capacity and a cardinality side constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\), and assign each \(e\in E\) a consumption \(a_e\ge a_{\min}>0\). Define \(a(S)=\sum_{e\in S}a_e\). Every set satisfying \(|S|=k\) has \(a(S)\ge k a_{\min}\). Consequently, if a reduced capacity satisfies \(B'<k a_{\min}\), no set satisfies both \(|S|=k\) and \(a(S)\le B'\). This can destroy joint feasibility even when some cardinality-\(k\) set was feasible under the original capacity \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every k-element set consumes at least k times the minimum element consumption. Reducing capacity below that threshold makes the cardinality constraint and capacity constraint incompatible, even if they were compatible before the reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no \(S\subseteq E\) satisfying both \(|S|=k\) and \(a(S)\le B'\).

notation.meaning: Positive lower bound on element consumption

review_flags: The threshold statement is now mathematically explicit.
A supporting source for its role in the intended conversion family is still required.

children.title: Bicriteria Escape Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximation regimes permitting controlled relaxation of restrictive constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resource Augmentation Is Not Exact Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal separation between a capacity-relaxing bicriteria output and feasibility for the original capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\beta>1\). Let \(E=\{e\}\), \(\mathcal F=2^E\), \(B=1\), \(a(\varnothing)=0\), \(a(\{e\})=\beta\), \(f(\varnothing)=0\), and \(f(\{e\})=1\). Then \(\operatorname{OPT}(B)=0\), while \(S=\{e\}\) satisfies \(f(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(B)\) and \(a(S)=\beta B\). Thus \(S\) is a valid \((1,\beta)\)-bicriteria output but is infeasible for the original capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid bicriteria output with capacity factor greater than one need not be feasible for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource Augmentation Is Not Exact Feasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order structure of bicriteria guarantees when the exact-capacity benchmark is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\operatorname{OPT}(B)\ge0\) and \(S\) is an \((\alpha,\beta)\)-bicriteria solution. For every \(0<\alpha'\le\alpha\) and \(\beta'\ge\beta\), \[f(S)\ge\alpha'\operatorname{OPT}(B),\qquad a(S)\le\beta'B.\] Hence \(S\) is also \((\alpha',\beta')\)-bicriteria. The case \(\beta=1\) preserves exact capacity, while \(\alpha=1\) preserves the exact-capacity benchmark value under resource augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative benchmark, guarantees weaken monotonically as objective quality decreases or allowed capacity increases; beta one means exact capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Bicriteria Monotonicity and Boundary Cases
Bicriteria Escape Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria approximation allowing controlled capacity violation while retaining exact side-constraint feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be finite, let \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\) be the side-feasible family, and let \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) and \(a:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) denote the objective and consumption. For \(B\ge 0\), define \(\mathrm{OPT}(B)=\max\{f(T):T\in\mathcal F,\ a(T)\le B\}\), assuming this feasible set is nonempty. Given \(0<\alpha\le 1\) and \(\beta\ge 1\), an \((\alpha,\beta)\)-bicriteria solution is a set \(S\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \(f(S)\ge\alpha\mathrm{OPT}(B)\) and \(a(S)\le\beta B\). Thus only the capacity requirement is relaxed; membership in \(\mathcal F\) remains exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alpha-beta bicriteria solution preserves the side constraints, obtains at least an alpha fraction of the exact-capacity optimum, and uses at most beta times the capacity.
assumptions_latex: The set \(\{T\in\mathcal F:a(T)\le B\}\) is nonempty.

notation.meaning: Optimal value under exact capacity B

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard bicriteria-approximation convention specialized to capacity relaxation.
A supporting source locator remains required.

children.title: Local-Search Approximation
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood design, locality-gap certificates, efficient approximate local optimality, classical problem families, geometric regimes, and failure boundaries.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Local Search Heuristics for k-Median and Facility Location Problems
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Local Search Heuristics for k-Median and Facility Location Problems

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle scan that finds an improving single exchange or certifies local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(|E|=n\) and \(S\subseteq E\). Enumerate every addition \(S\cup\{e\}\) with \(e\notin S\), every deletion \(S\setminus\{d\}\) with \(d\in S\), and every swap \((S\setminus\{d\})\cup\{e\}\) with \(d\in S\) and \(e\notin S\). There are \(n+|S|(n-|S|)\) candidates. After rejecting infeasible candidates, the scan either returns one with larger objective value or certifies that \(S\) is locally optimal in the single-exchange neighborhood. With unit-cost feasibility and objective-value queries, the scan uses \(O(n^2)\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic oracle scan of all additions, deletions, and one-for-one swaps finds an improvement or certifies single-exchange local optimality.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility and objective values are available through unit-cost oracle queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At most }n+|S|(n-|S|)\text{ candidates are tested, hence }O(n^2)\text{ oracle calls suffice.}
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Exchange Enumeration and Certificate
Single-Exchange Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-search neighborhoods generated by changing at most one selected and one unselected element.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be finite and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\) be the feasible family. The single-exchange neighborhood of \(S\in\mathcal F\) is
\[N_1(S)=\{T\in\mathcal F:|S\setminus T|\le 1,\ |T\setminus S|\le 1,\ T\ne S\}.\]
Thus a neighbor is obtained by one feasible addition, deletion, or one-for-one swap. For an objective \(f\) to be maximized, \(S\) is single-exchange locally optimal when \(f(S)\ge f(T)\) for every \(T\in N_1(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-exchange neighbor differs by at most one deletion and at most one addition; local optimality excludes every improving feasible move of this form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_1(S)\) consists exactly of feasible nontrivial additions, deletions, and one-for-one swaps.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical symmetric-difference definition of a one-exchange local-search neighborhood.
A directly supporting local-search source locator is needed for certification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise and the definition kind fits the neighborhood leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw candidate bound before feasibility filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n=|E|\) and \(s=|S|\), the number of distinct nontrivial deletion-insertion choices with budgets \((p,q)\) is at most \[\left(\sum_{i=0}^{p}\binom{s}{i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=0}^{q}\binom{n-s}{j}\right)-1.\] For fixed \(p,q\), this is \(O(n^{p+q})\); if the budgets grow with the input, this formula gives no polynomial bound with a fixed exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed exchange budgets give polynomially many raw candidates, while growing budgets need not.
assumptions_latex: Deletion and insertion subsets are explicitly enumerated.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Budget Enumeration Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood obtained by deleting and inserting bounded numbers of elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\in\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) and integers \(p,q\ge0\) with \(p+q>0\), define \[N_{p,q}(S)=\{T\in\mathcal F:T\ne S,\ |S\setminus T|\le p,\ |T\setminus S|\le q\}.\] A solution is \((p,q)\)-locally optimal when no member of this neighborhood strictly improves the chosen objective orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded multi-exchange removes at most p selected elements and inserts at most q unselected elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\in N_{p,q}(S)\Rightarrow |S\setminus T|\le p\text{ and }|T\setminus S|\le q.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Multi-Exchange Neighborhood

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise hierarchy induced by increasing deletion and insertion budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0\le p\le p'\) and \(0\le q\le q'\), then \[N_{p,q}(S)\subseteq N_{p',q'}(S).\] Therefore every \((p',q')\)-local optimum is also a \((p,q)\)-local optimum for the same objective orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing either budget enlarges the neighborhood and strengthens local optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(p\le p'\) and \(q\le q'\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Exchange Nesting

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent radius description for equal-cardinality feasible families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If all members of \(\mathcal F\) have equal cardinality, then \(|S\setminus T|=|T\setminus S|\) for \(S,T\in\mathcal F\). Consequently, \[T\in N_{k,k}(S)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T\ne S\text{ and }|S\triangle T|\le2k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an equal-cardinality family, a bounded k-for-k exchange is exactly a nontrivial feasible move of symmetric-difference distance at most 2k.
assumptions_latex: All members of \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) have equal cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\in N_{k,k}(S)\iff T\ne S\text{ and }|S\triangle T|\le2k.
knowledge_statements.title: Equal-Cardinality Symmetric-Difference Form
Bounded Multi-Exchange Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhoods formed by exchanging bounded numbers of selected and unselected elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p,q\) be nonnegative integers, not both zero. For \(S\in\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\), the bounded \((p,q)\)-exchange neighborhood is
\[N_{p,q}(S)=\{T\in\mathcal F:T\ne S,\ |S\setminus T|\le p,\ |T\setminus S|\le q\}.\]
A maximization solution \(S\) is \((p,q)\)-locally optimal for objective \(f\) if \(f(S)\ge f(T)\) for all \(T\in N_{p,q}(S)\). When \(p,q\) are fixed constants, exhaustive neighborhood inspection uses at most \(O(|E|^{p+q})\) candidate subsets before feasibility and objective evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded multi-exchange removes at most p elements and adds at most q; fixed bounds give a polynomial-size enumerable neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every neighbor changes at most \(p\) selected and \(q\) unselected elements.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard bounded-exchange neighborhood and direct candidate-count estimate.
A directly supporting local-search source locator is needed for certification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-exchange definition and fixed-parameter candidate-count estimate are plausible, but neither has a cited locator. The complexity sentence also extends beyond the core definition and requires support.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw candidate count before feasibility filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n=|E|\) and \(s=|S|\), there are \(n-s\) additions, \(s\) deletions, and \(s(n-s)\) swaps before feasibility filtering. Thus at most \[n+s(n-s)=O(n^2)\] candidates are inspected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The elementary neighborhood has at most n plus s times n-minus-s raw candidates.
assumptions_latex: Candidates are explicitly generated before feasibility filtering.
knowledge_statements.title: Add–Delete–Swap Candidate Count

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialization for downward-closed and equal-cardinality feasible families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal F\) is downward closed, then \(S\setminus\{d\}\in\mathcal F\) for every \(d\in S\). If every member of \(\mathcal F\) has the same cardinality, no one-element addition or deletion is feasible and \(N_{\mathrm{ads}}(S)=N_{\leftrightarrow}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Downward closure guarantees deletions, while equal feasible cardinality eliminates additions and deletions and leaves only swaps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F\text{ downward closed}\Rightarrow N_-(S)=\{S\setminus\{d\}:d\in S\};\quad \mathcal F\text{ equicardinal}\Rightarrow N_{\mathrm{ads}}(S)=N_{\leftrightarrow}(S).
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Move Collapse Under Cardinality Structure
Add–Delete–Swap Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The elementary neighborhood separating addition, deletion, and swap move classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\in\mathcal F\subseteq 2^E\), define
\[N_{\mathrm{ads}}(S)=N_{+}(S)\cup N_{-}(S)\cup N_{\leftrightarrow}(S),\]
where \(N_{+}(S)=\{S\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal F:e\in E\setminus S\}\), \(N_{-}(S)=\{S\setminus\{d\}\in\mathcal F:d\in S\}\), and \(N_{\leftrightarrow}(S)=\{(S\setminus\{d\})\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal F:d\in S,\ e\in E\setminus S\}\). A maximization solution is locally optimal for this neighborhood precisely when none of these three move classes contains a strictly improving feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The neighborhood is the union of all feasible one-element additions, deletions, and one-for-one swaps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{ads}}(S)\) contains exactly the feasible add, delete, and swap neighbors of \(S\).

A directly supporting local-search source locator is needed for certification.

children.title: Path Exchanges
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood moves supported on path-shaped exchange structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Exchanges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange moves whose support is a path in a problem-specific exchange graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S,T\in\mathcal F\), and let \(H(S,T)\) be an exchange graph with vertex set \(S\triangle T\), whose edges encode the problem's admissible exchange incidences. A path exchange supported by a simple path \(P\) of \(H(S,T)\) replaces
\[S\quad\text{by}\quad S\triangle V(P).\]
The path is admissible when \(S\triangle V(P)\in\mathcal F\). Its gain for a maximization objective \(f\) is \(f(S\triangle V(P))-f(S)\); it is improving exactly when this quantity is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path exchange flips membership of the elements along a simple exchange-graph path, provided the resulting solution remains feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(H(S,T)\) is a specified exchange graph on \(S\triangle T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An admissible path \(P\) defines the feasible neighbor \(S\triangle V(P)\).

children.title: Cycle Exchanges
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood moves supported on cyclic exchange structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Exchanges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange moves whose support is a cycle in a problem-specific exchange graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S,T\in\mathcal F\), and let \(H(S,T)\) be an exchange graph on \(S\triangle T\). A cycle exchange supported by a simple cycle \(C\) of \(H(S,T)\) replaces \(S\) by \(S\triangle V(C)\). The cycle is admissible when \(S\triangle V(C)\in\mathcal F\). For a maximization objective \(f\), its gain is \(f(S\triangle V(C))-f(S)\), and local optimality against cycle exchanges requires this gain to be nonpositive for every admissible cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle exchange flips all elements on an exchange-graph cycle; local optimality forbids every feasible cycle having positive gain.
assumptions_latex: \(H(S,T)\) is a specified exchange graph on \(S\triangle T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admissible cycle \(C\) induces the feasible exchange \(S\triangle V(C)\).

children.title: Component Exchanges
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood moves replacing connected or separable solution components.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Exchanges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange moves supported on a connected component of an exchange structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S,T\in\mathcal F\), let \(H(S,T)\) be an exchange graph on \(S\triangle T\). If \(K\) is a connected component of \(H(S,T)\), the associated component exchange maps \(S\) to \(S\triangle V(K)\). It is admissible precisely when \(S\triangle V(K)\in\mathcal F\). Componentwise analysis is valid only when the exchange structure ensures that the chosen component can be flipped independently; connectedness alone does not imply feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Structure Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitioning a symmetric difference into independently analyzable exchange supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An exchange-structure decomposition of \(S,T\in\mathcal F\) is a partition
\[S\triangle T=Q_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}Q_m\]
such that each support \(Q_i\) induces an allowed path, cycle, or component exchange and \(S\triangle Q_i\in\mathcal F\). Its incidence difference decomposes as

Any stronger conclusion—such as additive objective gain or simultaneous feasibility of several exchanges—requires corresponding separability or compatibility assumptions.

children.title: Nonoblivious Potentials
children.top_down_role: Local-search potentials differing from the original optimization objective.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of potential-based moves and local optima under strictly increasing transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\), let \(N\) be a neighborhood map, and let \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be strictly increasing. For \(\Psi=g\circ\Phi\), \(\Psi(T)>\Psi(S)\) if and only if \(\Phi(T)>\Phi(S)\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\) and \(T\in N(S)\). Hence \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\) induce the same improving moves and locally optimal states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly increasing transformation of a nonoblivious potential preserves all improving moves and local optima.
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Equivalent Nonoblivious Potentials
Nonoblivious Potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local search driven by a surrogate potential designed to imply guarantees for the original objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a feasible family, let \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) be the original objective, and let \(N\) be a neighborhood map with \(N(S)\subseteq\mathcal F\). A nonoblivious potential is a function \(\Phi:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) used to evaluate local moves instead of using \(f\) alone. A state \(S\in\mathcal F\) is \(\Phi\)-locally optimal when \(\Phi(S)\ge\Phi(T)\) for every \(T\in N(S)\). An algorithm that halts exactly when no neighbor has larger potential returns such a state. An approximation guarantee for \(f(S)\) requires a separate result connecting \(\Phi\)-local optimality to the original objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonoblivious local search evaluates moves with a surrogate potential. Halting when no neighbor improves that potential certifies potential-local optimality, while an objective approximation requires a separate analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the stopping rule finds no \(T\in N(S)\) with \(\Phi(T)>\Phi(S)\), then \(\Phi(S)\ge\Phi(T)\) for every \(T\in N(S)\); this alone does not imply \(f(S)\ge f(T)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic termination of strict ascent over a finite state space, not specific to nonoblivious potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be finite. Starting from \(S_0\in\mathcal F\), suppose an algorithm repeatedly chooses \(S_{i+1}\in N(S_i)\) with \(\Phi(S_{i+1})>\Phi(S_i)\). Then no state is revisited and at most \(|\mathcal F|-1\) moves occur. If termination occurs exactly when no improving neighbor exists, the terminal state is \(\Phi\)-locally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict ascent over a finite state space terminates after at most one fewer moves than there are states.
review_flags: DEFER_CANONICAL_HOME: This is a generic finite local-search termination fact, not primarily a property of nonoblivious potentials.

Nestedness implies \(|N_k^I(S)|\le|N_{k+1}^I(S)|\), but alone gives no polynomial bound in the encoded input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quality improves monotonically with neighborhood inclusion, while explicit checking scales with neighborhood cardinality and need not remain polynomial.
assumptions_latex: One listed-candidate check costs at most \(\tau(I)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization analogue of the accepted maximization hierarchy property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a positive minimization objective, suppose \(N_k^I(S)\subseteq N_{k+1}^I(S)\) for every instance \(I\) and feasible \(S\). If \(L_k(I)\) is the set of radius-\(k\) local minima, then \(L_{k+1}(I)\subseteq L_k(I)\). Hence, whenever defined, \[\operatorname{gap}_{\min}(k)=\sup_I\max_{S\in L_k(I)}\frac{f_I(S)}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}\] satisfies \(\operatorname{gap}_{\min}(k+1)\le\operatorname{gap}_{\min}(k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger nested neighborhoods leave fewer local minima and cannot worsen the worst-case minimization locality gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a neighborhood rule \(N\) for a maximization problem and a factor \(\alpha\ge 1\). A tight local-optimum construction is a sequence of instances \((I_t)_{t\ge 1}\), with objective functions \(f_t\), designated feasible solutions \(S_t\), and optimal solutions \(O_t\), such that \[f_t(T)\le f_t(S_t)\quad\text{for every }T\in N_{I_t}(S_t),\qquad f_t(S_t)>0,\] and \[\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f_t(O_t)}{f_t(S_t)}=\alpha.\] If one finite instance attains the ratio, the sequence may be constant. Such a family establishes that the worst-case locality gap under \(N\) is at least \(\alpha\), and hence no uniformly smaller approximation factor holds for all \(N\)-local optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight construction gives local optima whose ratios to global optima approach alpha, proving that no smaller factor holds uniformly for the chosen neighborhood rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Tight Local-Optimum Constructions

Suppose instances \(I_t\) have optimal solutions \(O_t\) and designated \(N\)-local minima \(S_t\) such that \(f_t(O_t)>0\), \[f_t(S_t)\le f_t(T)\quad(T\in N_{I_t}(S_t)),\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f_t(S_t)}{f_t(O_t)}=\alpha.\] Then the worst-case minimization locality gap of \(N\) is at least \(\alpha\). If an \(\alpha\)-upper bound is known, that bound is tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local minima whose cost ratios approach alpha prove that no uniformly smaller minimization locality-gap factor is possible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a finite nonempty feasible family, let \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\), and let \(N(S)\subseteq\mathcal F\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\). Starting from \(S_0\in\mathcal F\), at iteration \(t\) choose any \(S_{t+1}\in N(S_t)\) satisfying \(f(S_{t+1})>f(S_t)\). No feasible solution can recur, so the process terminates after at most \(|\mathcal F|-1\) improving moves. Its terminal solution \(S_T\) satisfies \(f(S)\le f(S_T)\) for every \(S\in N(S_T)\). The iteration bound can be exponential in the encoded input length when \(|\mathcal F|\) is exponential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict improvement over a finite feasible set terminates at a local maximum after at most one fewer moves than the number of feasible solutions, although this need not be polynomial in the input length.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that strict improvement alone does not ensure termination without finite state space or another well-founded ranking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F=\mathbb N\), \(N(t)=\{t+1\}\), and \(f(t)=t\). Starting at \(0\), the unique trajectory \(0,1,2,\ldots\) strictly improves at every step and never terminates. Thus the finite-state hypothesis in exact-improvement termination cannot be dropped without replacing it by a well-founded progress condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an infinite feasible space, strict objective improvement can continue forever.
assumptions_latex: The objective is unbounded above along the permitted trajectory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(t+1)>f(t)\ \text{for all }t\in\mathbb N,\qquad \text{but the trajectory does not terminate}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite nonempty feasible family \(\mathcal F\), an objective \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\), a scale \(M>0\), a threshold \(\varepsilon>0\), a neighborhood map \(N\) with \(N(S)\subseteq\mathcal F\), and an initial solution \(S_0\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \(f(S_0)>0\). Define \(g(S)=f(S)/M\). At iteration \(t\), choose any \(T\in N(S_t)\) satisfying \[g(T)\ge (1+\varepsilon)g(S_t),\] set \(S_{t+1}=T\), and stop if no such \(T\) exists. Since \(M>0\), the acceptance rule is equivalent to \(f(T)\ge(1+\varepsilon)f(S_t)\). The process terminates on the finite family, and its output \(S\) satisfies \(f(T)<(1+\varepsilon)f(S)\) for every \(T\in N(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale the objective by a positive constant, accept only neighbors improving it by a factor of at least one plus epsilon, and stop at a multiplicatively epsilon-local optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Improvement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration complexity of multiplicative scaled improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After \(K\) multiplicative-improvement updates, \(f(S_K)\geq(1+\varepsilon)^Kf(S_0)\). If all reachable values are at most \(U\), then \(K\leq\lfloor\log(U/f(S_0))/\log(1+\varepsilon)\rfloor\). Since \(\log(1+\varepsilon)\geq\varepsilon/(1+\varepsilon)\), the displayed secondary bound follows. Polynomial per-iteration work therefore gives polynomial total time whenever \((1+1/\varepsilon)\log(U/f(S_0))\) is polynomially bounded in the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative improvements yield a logarithmic objective-ratio update bound with inverse dependence on epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Growth Iteration Bound

knowledge_statements.title: Thresholded Improvement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-threshold local search for finite maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite, let \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(N:S\to 2^S\), fix \(\tau>0\), and initialize \(x_0\in S\). At iteration \(t\), choose any \(y\in N(x_t)\) satisfying \(f(y)-f(x_t)\geq\tau\) and set \(x_{t+1}=y\); stop if no such neighbor exists. The output \(x\) satisfies \(f(y)-f(x)<\tau\) for every \(y\in N(x)\). If \(f(z)\leq U\) for every \(z\in S\), at most \(\lfloor(U-f(x_0))/\tau\rfloor\) updates occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept moves gaining at least the threshold. The output has no neighbor gaining as much as the threshold, and the number of updates is at most the available objective range divided by the threshold, rounded down.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)-f(x)<\tau\) for every \(y\in N(x)\), after at most \(\lfloor(U-f(x_0))/\tau\rfloor\) updates.

assumptions_latex: There exist \(c\in\mathbb R\) and \(\gamma>0\) such that \(f(S)\subseteq c+\gamma\mathbb Z\).
The additive-threshold rule accepts gains at least \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0<\tau\leq\gamma\Longrightarrow\bigl[x\text{ is \(\tau\)-terminal}\iff x\text{ has no strictly improving neighbor}\bigr],\quad\text{whereas \(\tau>\gamma\) need not have this property}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-local-optimality boundary determined by objective granularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every objective value lies in \(c+\gamma\mathbb Z\) for some \(\gamma>0\). Every strict positive gain is then at least \(\gamma\), so for \(0<\tau\leq\gamma\), a state has no neighbor gaining at least \(\tau\) exactly when it has no strictly improving neighbor. This fails for \(\tau>\gamma\): with states \(x,y\), \(y\in N(x)\), \(f(x)=c\), and \(f(y)=c+\gamma\), thresholded search may stop at \(x\) although \(y\) strictly improves it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Thresholded local optimality equals exact local optimality when the threshold does not exceed the objective lattice spacing, and can be weaker above it.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Versus Objective Granularity

children.title: Scaling–Threshold Interaction
children.top_down_role: Effects of scaling choices on meaningful improvement thresholds.

assumptions_latex: The multiplicative acceptance rule compares \(g(y)\) with \((1+\varepsilon)g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure-scale invariance and translation failure for multiplicative thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g=af\) with \(a>0\), a move satisfies \(g(y)\geq(1+\varepsilon)g(x)\) exactly when \(f(y)\geq(1+\varepsilon)f(x)\). Adding a translation generally changes the accepted moves because \(af(y)+b\geq(1+\varepsilon)(af(x)+b)\) contains the additional term \(\varepsilon b\). For example, \(f(x)=1\), \(f(y)=2\), and \(\varepsilon=1/2\) define an accepted move, whereas for \(g=f+100\), \(g(y)=102<\tfrac32\,101\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative improvement is invariant under positive scaling but generally not under translation of the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplicative Scale Invariance and Translation Boundary
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Scale Invariance and Translation Boundary
Scaling–Threshold Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation of additive thresholds under positive affine objective scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and define \(g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(g(x)=a f(x)+b\), where \(a>0\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}\). For every \(x,y\in X\), \(g(y)-g(x)=a(f(y)-f(x))\). Hence a move meets an additive threshold \(\tau_g\) for \(g\) exactly when it meets the threshold \(\tau_f=\tau_g/a\) for \(f\). Positive scaling preserves thresholded moves when the threshold is scaled by the same factor, while translation has no effect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive objective scaling multiplies every improvement and its corresponding threshold by the same factor; translation has no effect.

children.title: Granularity–Quality Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Approximation and running-time effects of coarse improvement granularity.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(x_0\in S\), and \(f(z)\leq U\) for every \(z\in S\).
\(\mathrm{OPT}\leq\alpha f(x)+\beta\Delta(x)\) for every \(x\in S\), where \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint running-time and additive-quality accounting for threshold granularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, additive-threshold local search performs at most \(\lfloor(U-f(x_0))/\tau\rfloor\) updates and terminates at \(x\) with \(f(x)>(\mathrm{OPT}-\beta\tau)/\alpha\). Consequently, for any desired numerator loss \(\eta>0\), choosing \(\tau=\eta/\beta\) yields \(f(x)>(\mathrm{OPT}-\eta)/\alpha\) after at most \(\lfloor\beta(U-f(x_0))/\eta\rfloor\) updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reducing the permitted additive quality loss strengthens the guarantee but increases the generic update bound inversely with that loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Granularity Runtime-Quality Frontier
Granularity–Quality Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic conversion of residual local gain into approximation quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization problem with feasible set \(S\), objective \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\), and neighborhood map \(N:S\to 2^S\), define \(\Delta(x)=\sup(\{0\}\cup\{f(y)-f(x):y\in N(x)\})\), and suppose \(\Delta(x)<\infty\). Assume \(\mathrm{OPT}\leq\alpha f(x)+\beta\Delta(x)\) for every \(x\in S\), where \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\geq0\). If thresholded search stops at \(x\) with \(\Delta(x)<\tau\), then \(f(x)>(\mathrm{OPT}-\beta\tau)/\alpha\). Thus the threshold contributes at most \(\beta\tau/\alpha\) to the resulting additive quality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If global suboptimality is controlled by the largest residual local gain, stopping below a coarser threshold introduces a proportional additive term in the quality guarantee.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative conventions for positive maximization and minimization objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). For maximization with \(f(x)>0\), \(x\) is multiplicatively \(\varepsilon\)-locally optimal if \(f(y)\le(1+\varepsilon)f(x)\) for every \(y\in N(x)\). For minimization with positive neighbor values, it is multiplicatively \(\varepsilon\)-locally optimal if \(f(x)\le(1+\varepsilon)f(y)\) for every \(y\in N(x)\). At \(\varepsilon=0\), both reduce to exact local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative approximate local optimality excludes neighboring improvements by a factor greater than one plus epsilon.

Under the positivity assumptions for multiplicative comparisons, multiplicative \(\varepsilon\)-local optimality is unchanged by this scaling.

Approximate Local Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive approximate local optimality for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a feasible set, let \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(N:S\to 2^S\) be a neighborhood map. For \(\varepsilon\geq0\), a point \(x\in S\) is an additive \(\varepsilon\)-local optimum if \(f(y)\leq f(x)+\varepsilon\) for every \(y\in N(x)\). Equivalently, no permitted one-step move improves the objective by more than \(\varepsilon\). The case \(\varepsilon=0\) is exact local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution is approximately locally optimal when no permitted neighbor improves its objective by more than the additive tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is an additive \(\varepsilon\)-local optimum if and only if \(f(y)-f(x)\leq\varepsilon\) for every \(y\in N(x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation boundary between a small neighborhood and an efficiently searchable neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial bound on \(|N_I(x)|\) does not alone imply polynomial-time best-neighbor evaluation: neighborhood members must also be generable or optimizable over from the supplied encoding. Efficient Neighborhood Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time best-neighbor evaluation condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an encoded instance and encoded feasible solution \(x\), a best-neighbor evaluator either returns \(y\in N(x)\) satisfying \(f(y)\geq f(z)\) for every \(z\in N(x)\), together with the gain \(f(y)-f(x)\), or reports that \(N(x)=\varnothing\). The neighborhood is efficiently evaluable when this task, objective evaluation, and exact comparison with an encoded rational threshold take time polynomial in the instance, solution, and threshold encoding lengths. Under this condition, for every encoded rational \(\tau\geq0\), testing whether any neighbor gains more than \(\tau\) and producing such a neighbor when one exists take polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neighborhood is efficiently evaluable when a best neighbor and its gain can be found and compared with an encoded threshold in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: Instances and feasible solutions have finite encodings.
Objective values and encoded rational thresholds can be compared exactly in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every encoded rational \(\tau\geq0\), one can decide in polynomial time whether there exists \(z\in N(x)\) with \(f(z)-f(x)>\tau\), and return such a neighbor when it exists.

assumptions_latex: Every performed move strictly increases \(\Phi\) by at least \(\delta>0\).
All states reachable from \(x_0\) satisfy \(L\leq\Phi(x)\leq U\).
One iteration costs at most \(q(n)\) time.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient progress condition for polynomial total local-search time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a local-search trajectory start at \(x_0\), and suppose a potential \(\Phi\) is bounded by \(L\leq\Phi(x)\leq U\) on every reachable state. If each update increases \(\Phi\) by at least \(\delta>0\), then the number of updates is at most \(\left\lfloor(U-\Phi(x_0))/\delta\right\rfloor\). If an update costs at most \(q(n)\), total time is \(O(q(n)(1+(U-L)/\delta))\); in particular, it is polynomial when \(q(n)\) and \((U-L)/\delta\) are polynomially bounded in the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomially bounded potential range divided by a guaranteed minimum improvement yields polynomially many local-search updates.

assumptions_latex: Feasible solutions have encodings of length polynomial in the instance length.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between polynomial local-search primitives and polynomial convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every encoded instance \(I\), suppose one can construct an initial solution \(x_0\in\mathcal F(I)\) in polynomial time and, for every \(x\in\mathcal F(I)\), either find in polynomial time a neighbor \(y\in N_I(x)\) with \(f_I(y)>f_I(x)\) or report that no such neighbor exists. These guarantees bound the work of one improvement query but do not bound the number of successive improving states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial-time initialization and improvement queries do not by themselves make the full improvement trajectory polynomial.

Polynomial Local-Search Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential improvement paths despite efficient move evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq1\), let \(S_n=\{0,1,\ldots,2^n-1\}\), encode states in \(n\) bits, set \(f(i)=i\), and let \(N(i)=\{i+1\}\) for \(i<2^n-1\), with \(N(2^n-1)=\varnothing\). Objective and neighbor evaluation are polynomial-time, and every move strictly improves \(f\). Nevertheless, exact-improvement local search from \(0\) performs \(2^n-1\) moves. Polynomial per-move work and finite termination therefore do not imply polynomial total time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A succinct chain of exponentially many improving states shows that efficient move evaluation alone does not make local search polynomial-time.

assumptions_latex: The multiplicatively thresholded metric k-means algorithm is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Rational-Input Convergence for Metric k-Means

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Squared-Metric k-Means LP Relaxation and Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional assignment lower bound for finite-candidate metric k-means.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_{ij}=w_jd(i,j)^2\). The standard relaxation minimizes \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) subject to \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\), \(x_{ij}\le y_i\), \(\sum_i y_i=k\), and \(x,y\ge0\). Its dual maximizes \(\sum_j\alpha_j-k\lambda\) subject to \(\alpha_j\le c_{ij}+\beta_{ij}\), \(\sum_j\beta_{ij}\le\lambda\), \(\beta_{ij}\ge0\), with \(\alpha_j,\lambda\) free. Thus every dual-feasible solution lower-bounds the integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-candidate squared-metric assignment LP and its dual give a lower bound for metric k-means.
assumptions_latex: \(F,C\) are finite, \(d\) is a metric, and \(w_j\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Dual client values, assignment slacks, and cardinality price

review_flags: Equivalent dual sign conventions are possible.
knowledge_statements.title: Squared-Metric k-Means LP Relaxation and Dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global exact-optimization boundary for the finite squared-metric model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Computing a globally optimal finite metric \(k\)-means solution is NP-hard. Polynomial enumeration of every fixed-radius exchange therefore yields only a local optimum unless additional structure is assumed or \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite metric k-means is NP-hard although each fixed-size swap neighborhood is polynomially searchable.
assumptions_latex: The finite metric instance and \(k\) are part of the input.
review_flags: An authoritative hardness locator would improve provenance.
knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness of Finite Metric k-Means
Metric k-Means Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Thresholded p-swap search for squared metric cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite sets \(F\) and \(C\), a metric \(d\) on \(F\cup C\), weights \(w_j\geq0\), integers \(k,p\geq1\), and \(\tau\geq0\), initialize \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|=k\). Define \(\Phi(S)=\sum_{j\in C}w_j\min_{i\in S}d(j,i)^2\). While there exist \(A\subseteq S\) and \(B\subseteq F\setminus S\) with \(|A|=|B|\leq p\) and \(\Phi(S)-\Phi((S\setminus A)\cup B)>\tau\), perform the swap. Return \(S\) when no such swap exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange at most p centers whenever squared metric clustering cost decreases by more than the threshold, stopping at a thresholded p-swap local optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(F,C\) are finite and \(d\) is a metric on \(F\cup C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(A\subseteq S\) and \(B\subseteq F\setminus S\) with \(|A|=|B|\leq p\), \(\Phi(S)-\Phi((S\setminus A)\cup B)\leq\tau\).

children.title: Euclidean k-Means Local Search
children.top_down_role: Local-search approximation specialized to Euclidean k-means instances.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact continuous-center characterization for one Euclidean k-means cluster.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty weighted cluster \(P\), let \(W=\sum_{x\in P}w_x>0\) and \(\mu=W^{-1}\sum_{x\in P}w_xx\). For every \(z\in\mathbb R^d\), \(\sum_{x\in P}w_x\|x-z\|_2^2=\sum_{x\in P}w_x\|x-\mu\|_2^2+W\|z-\mu\|_2^2\). Hence \(\mu\) is the unique minimum-cost center for the fixed cluster.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-weight Euclidean cluster is optimally represented by its weighted centroid, with an exact squared-displacement penalty for every other center.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Centroid Identity

assumptions_latex: Candidate centers and clients are finite subsets of Euclidean space.
\(S\) is an exact p-swap local optimum for the squared Euclidean objective.
review_flags: Finite-candidate discrete guarantee; unrestricted continuous-center search requires a separate implementation or candidate-discretization result.
A positive stopping threshold requires an additional error term and is not covered by this exact-locality statement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-candidate Euclidean specialization of the squared-metric p-swap locality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every exact \(p\)-swap local optimum \(S\) for finite-candidate Euclidean \(k\)-means satisfies \(\Phi(S)\leq(3+2/p)^2\mathrm{OPT}\). Consequently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), a sufficiently large constant \(p=O(1/\varepsilon)\) yields a \((9+\varepsilon)\)-approximation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-candidate Euclidean p-swap local optimum has factor (3+2/p)^2, approaching 9 for large constant swap size.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean p-Swap Locality Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Candidate Swap Enumeration and Threshold Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood size and finite convergence for discrete Euclidean p-swap search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(p\), the number of admissible exchanges is \(\sum_{q=1}^{p}\binom{k}{q}\binom{|F|-k}{q}=O(k^p|F|^p)\). If every accepted exchange decreases the nonnegative objective by more than \(\tau>0\), a run from \(S_0\) performs fewer than \(\Phi(S_0)/\tau\) exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-size finite-candidate swaps are polynomially enumerable, and a positive additive threshold bounds the number of accepted moves.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted move decreases \(\Phi\geq0\) by more than \(\tau>0\).
review_flags: The iteration bound can be pseudopolynomial in binary input length.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Candidate Swap Enumeration and Threshold Termination

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between finite-candidate and unrestricted continuous-center local search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If replacement centers range over all of \(\mathbb R^d\), even the one-swap neighborhood is uncountable. The centroid identity optimizes a center only after its client cluster is fixed and therefore does not supply finite enumeration of swaps whose assignments may change. Finite enumeration requires a finite candidate set, a justified discretization, or an exact improvement oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The centroid formula alone does not make unrestricted continuous-center swaps finitely searchable.
assumptions_latex: Assignments may change after a swap.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Center Neighborhood Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes unrestricted centers from the finite-candidate regime used by enumerable swap search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite weighted set C\subset\mathbb R^d and k\ge1, continuous Euclidean k-means minimizes \(\sum_{j\in C}w_j\min_{z\in S}\|j-z\|_2^2\) over finite S\subset\mathbb R^d with 1\le|S|\le k. Given a finite F\subset\mathbb R^d with k\le|F|, finite-candidate Euclidean k-means restricts S to subsets of F. Therefore \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{continuous}}\le\operatorname{OPT}_F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean k-means may use arbitrary centers or a finite candidate set; directly enumerable swaps require the latter or a separate oracle.
assumptions_latex: In the candidate regime, F is finite and k\le|F|.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous and Finite-Candidate Euclidean k-Means

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable certificate for the exact finite-candidate Euclidean p-swap guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S\subseteq F have |S|=k. If exhaustive inspection verifies \Phi((S\setminus A)\cup B)\ge\Phi(S) for every A\subseteq S and B\subseteq F\setminus S with 1\le|A|=|B|\le p, then S is an exact p-swap local optimum and \Phi(S)\le(3+2/p)^2\operatorname{OPT}_F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible candidate-center set with no improving p-swap certifies the finite-candidate Euclidean locality bound.
assumptions_latex: The Euclidean p-Swap Locality Guarantee applies.

notation.meaning: Optimal value with centers restricted to F

review_flags: This certificate compares against the finite-candidate optimum, not the unrestricted continuous-center optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Candidate Euclidean Locality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomially convergent rational finite-candidate variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational C,F\subset\mathbb Q^d, fixed p, and 0<\eta<1, repeatedly accept a p-swap S' satisfying \Phi(S')\leq(1-\eta)\Phi(S). Stop immediately at zero cost; otherwise stop when no such swap exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-candidate Euclidean swaps with a fixed relative-improvement threshold avoid magnitude-dependent additive descent.
assumptions_latex: C,F\subset\mathbb Q^d are finite and weights are nonnegative rationals.
review_flags: This finite-candidate algorithm does not search unrestricted continuous replacement centers.
Its stopping condition is weaker than exact p-swap locality.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicatively Thresholded Finite-Candidate Euclidean Swaps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Encoding-Time Convergence of Euclidean Thresholded Swaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity consequence of rational squared-distance separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Squared distances between rational input points are rational with polynomial encoding length. If \Phi_{\min}>0 is the least positive feasible objective, geometric descent makes at most \[\left\lceil\frac{\log(\Phi(S_0)/\Phi_{\min})}{-\log(1-\eta)}\right\rceil\] accepted moves. For fixed p, exhaustive neighborhood inspection gives \[T=|F|^{O(p)}\operatorname{poly}(|C|,d,B,1/\eta).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational squared distances make fixed-p multiplicative finite-candidate Euclidean local search polynomial-time.
assumptions_latex: The multiplicatively thresholded finite-candidate algorithm is used.
B is the rational input encoding length.

notation.meaning: Least positive feasible finite-candidate objective value

review_flags: The bound does not include an unrestricted continuous-center improvement oracle.
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Time Convergence of Euclidean Thresholded Swaps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General-input exact-computation boundary complementary to Euclidean local-search guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact Euclidean \(k\)-means is NP-hard when \(k\) is part of the input even in the plane, and it is NP-hard for \(k=2\) when the dimension is part of the input. Thus the centroid identity solves a fixed-cluster subproblem but not the global partition-and-center problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centroids optimize fixed clusters, but globally optimal Euclidean k-means is NP-hard when either the number of centers or dimension is allowed to vary in the stated regimes.
assumptions_latex: Input coordinates have finite rational encodings.
For planar hardness, \(k\) is part of the input; for two-means hardness, dimension is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Exact Euclidean }k\text{-means is NP-hard in these general-input regimes}.
review_flags: The two distinct restricted-regime hardness statements require authoritative locators.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Euclidean k-Means Hardness Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-center coordinate descent, distinct from finite-candidate p-swap search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given centers \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\in\mathbb R^d\), repeatedly assign every positive-weight point to a nearest center using a fixed tie rule, then replace each positive-weight nonempty cluster's center by its weighted centroid. Empty clusters follow a fixed declared rule. Each completed assignment or centroid step weakly decreases \(\Phi=\sum_xw_x\min_r\|x-z_r\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lloyd's method alternates nearest-center assignment and centroid recomputation without increasing Euclidean k-means cost.
assumptions_latex: Tie and empty-cluster handling are fixed in advance.
review_flags: Lloyd fixed points need not be p-swap local optima.
knowledge_statements.title: Lloyd Assignment–Centroid Descent

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Termination Condition for Lloyd Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination boundary for finite data with ties and empty clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite data there are finitely many labeled assignments. If every accepted change of assignment or center configuration strictly decreases \(\Phi\), Lloyd descent terminates after finitely many accepted changes at a configuration in which every point is assigned to a nearest center and every positive-weight nonempty cluster center is its centroid. Arbitrary equal-cost tie changes or empty-cluster reseeding do not satisfy this conclusion without an anti-cycling rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict descent ensures finite Lloyd termination; unrestricted equal-cost tie or reseeding changes may not.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted configuration change strictly decreases the objective.
Cluster labels and tie handling are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{strict accepted descent}\Longrightarrow\text{finite termination at an assignment--centroid fixed point}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Termination Condition for Lloyd Descent
Euclidean k-Means Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete Euclidean p-swap search with squared distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite \(C,F\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), weights \(w_j\geq0\), integers \(k,p\geq1\), and \(\tau\geq0\), initialize \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|=k\). Let \(\Phi(S)=\sum_{j\in C}w_j\min_{i\in S}\|j-i\|_2^2\). Repeatedly replace \(A\subseteq S\) by \(B\subseteq F\setminus S\), where \(|A|=|B|\leq p\), whenever the replacement decreases \(\Phi\) by more than \(\tau\). Return \(S\) when no qualifying exchange exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Swap at most p candidate centers whenever weighted squared Euclidean cost decreases beyond the threshold.

children.title: Metric–Euclidean Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Differences in neighborhood analysis across metric and Euclidean settings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit boundary showing that the general metric regime is strictly broader than Euclidean distance instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The four-point star metric with center \(o\), three leaves \(a,b,c\), distances \(d(o,a)=d(o,b)=d(o,c)=1\), and pairwise leaf distances \(2\) is a finite metric but has no isometric embedding into any Euclidean space. Indeed, equality in \(\|a-b\|_2\leq\|a-o\|_2+\|o-b\|_2\) would force each pair of leaf vectors from \(o\) to be antipodal, which three distinct leaves cannot satisfy simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A four-point star metric is a concrete finite metric that cannot be realized isometrically by Euclidean distances.
knowledge_statements.title: Non-Euclidean Finite Metric Witness
Metric–Euclidean Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean instances form a restricted subclass of metric squared-distance instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(C,F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), define \(d(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2\). Then \(d\) is a metric, and every center set \(S\subseteq F\) has identical cost \(\sum_{j\in C}w_j\min_{i\in S}d(j,i)^2=\sum_{j\in C}w_j\min_{i\in S}\|j-i\|_2^2\) in the metric and Euclidean formulations. Their discrete swap neighborhoods therefore coincide. Conversely, a general finite metric need not admit an isometric embedding into any Euclidean space, so Euclidean geometric arguments do not automatically extend to arbitrary metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite Euclidean instances are metric instances with identical squared costs and swaps, but general metrics need not possess a Euclidean realization.
assumptions_latex: Both formulations use the same candidate centers and squared-distance objective.

notation.meaning: Euclidean metric induced by the norm

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Dimension-Sensitive Regimes
children.top_down_role: Euclidean local-search behavior organized by ambient or intrinsic dimension.

assumptions_latex: The candidate set \(G\subset\mathbb R^d\) is explicitly available and has \(m\) points.
The current solution contains exactly \(k\) centers.
A move exchanges equally many selected and unselected centers, with exchange size at most \(p\).

notation.meaning: number of admissible swaps of size at most p

review_flags: Naive objective recomputation costs \(O(|C|kd)\) arithmetic operations per resulting k-center set; faster incremental evaluation requires additional data structures.
Bit complexity additionally depends on coordinate, weight, and accumulator encodings.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined candidate-grid, swap-size, and coordinate dependence of exhaustive Euclidean neighborhood search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicit candidate set \(G\) of size \(m\), a \(k\)-center solution has \(\binom{k}{r}\binom{m-k}{r}\) exchanges replacing exactly \(r\) centers. Hence exhaustive \(p\)-swap search examines \(N_p=\sum_{r=1}^{\min\{p,k,m-k\}}\binom{k}{r}\binom{m-k}{r}\) moves. This is polynomial in \(m\) for fixed \(p\), but not when \(p\) is part of the input. With explicit coordinates, naive evaluation of each resulting solution takes \(O(|C|kd)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite k-center solution has a polynomial-size p-swap neighborhood only for fixed p; explicit Euclidean evaluation also carries linear coordinate-dimension cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension and Swap-Neighborhood Enumeration
Dimension-Sensitive Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension dependence of Euclidean grid candidate enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\geq1\), \(R>0\), \(h>0\), and \(G=h\mathbb{Z}^d\cap[-R,R]^d\). Each coordinate has exactly \(2\lfloor R/h\rfloor+1\) admissible values, so \(|G|=(2\lfloor R/h\rfloor+1)^d\). Consequently, the number of candidate evaluations in exhaustive grid enumeration is polynomial in the numeric quantity \(R/h\) when \(d\) is fixed, but exponential in \(d\) when dimension is variable. If each candidate can be evaluated in polynomial time, the same distinction applies to total enumeration time, measured in these parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean candidate grid has size exponential in dimension. Its enumeration uses polynomially many candidate evaluations in the numeric grid-width ratio for fixed dimension, but exponentially many when dimension varies.
assumptions_latex: Any total-time claim additionally assumes polynomial-time evaluation of each candidate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|G|=(2\lfloor R/h\rfloor+1)^d\), which is polynomial in the numeric quantity \(R/h\) for fixed \(d\) and exponential in variable \(d\).

children.title: Capacitated Location Local Search
children.top_down_role: Local-search neighborhoods for location problems with facility capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Location Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exchange local search for metric capacitated facility location with hard capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given facilities \(F\), clients \(D\), opening costs \(f_i\), capacities \(u_i\), demands \(d_j\), and metric assignment costs \(c_{ij}\), initialize a feasible pair \((S,\sigma)\), where \(S\subseteq F\), \(\sigma:D\to S\), and \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}d_j\le u_i\) for every \(i\in S\). Fix an exchange radius \(p\in\mathbb N\). Repeatedly choose \(R\subseteq S\) and \(A\subseteq F\setminus S\) with \(|R|,|A|\le p\), and a feasible reassignment \(\sigma':D\to(S\setminus R)\cup A\), whenever this strictly decreases \(\sum_{i\in S}f_i+\sum_{j\in D}c_{\sigma(j)j}\). Stop when no such exchange exists and output the resulting \(p\)-local optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly exchange at most p open and closed facilities and feasibly reassign clients, stopping when no exchange reduces opening plus assignment cost.
assumptions_latex: \(c\) is a metric on facilities and clients.
\(d_j,u_i\ge 0\) and an initial hard-capacity-feasible solution is supplied.
Each improving exchange and its reassignment can be identified exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S,\sigma)\) is feasible and admits no strictly improving exchange with \(|R|,|A|\le p\).
review_flags: exact capacitated-location local-search variant requires a supporting source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but no citation identifies the intended hard-capacitated facility-location neighborhood. In addition, the displayed cost uses the current set and assignment rather than explicitly comparing the candidate cost on (S\setminus R)\cup A with the current cost. A source and source-aligned formulation are required.

children.title: Bicriteria Location Local Search
children.top_down_role: Location approximations permitting controlled relaxation of a secondary criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Bicriteria Location Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local search permitting multiplicative capacity violation while optimizing facility and assignment cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a capacity factor \(\beta\ge1\) and exchange radius \(p\). Starting from \((S,\sigma)\) satisfying \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}d_j\le\beta u_i\) for every \(i\in S\), search over exchanges \((R,A)\) with \(R\subseteq S\), \(A\subseteq F\setminus S\), and \(|R|,|A|\le p\). Accept an exchange only if some reassignment \(\sigma':D\to(S\setminus R)\cup A\) remains \(\beta\)-capacity-feasible and strictly lowers total opening and assignment cost. Terminate when no accepted exchange exists. Relative to a hard-capacity optimum of cost \(\mathrm{OPT}_1\), an output costing at most \(\alpha\mathrm{OPT}_1\) is called an \((\alpha,\beta)\)-bicriteria solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local search maintains beta-relaxed capacities; its quality records both cost relative to the hard-capacity optimum and the permitted capacity factor.
assumptions_latex: The comparison optimum obeys the original capacities \(u_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a \(p\)-local optimum under capacity factor \(\beta\); if its cost is at most \(\alpha\mathrm{OPT}_1\), it has bicriteria guarantee \((\alpha,\beta)\).
review_flags: source needed for the intended bicriteria local-search specialization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is appropriate, but the intended bicriteria local-search specialization has no source. The statement also uses F, D, f_i, u_i, d_j, and assignment costs without introducing them locally. The exact neighborhood and guarantee should be reconstructed from an authoritative citation.

children.title: Capacity-Violation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between objective quality and permitted capacity violation.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) is a fixed class of capacitated-location instances with fixed assignment and facility-opening conventions.
\(\mathrm{OPT}_1(I)\) denotes the optimum under the original capacities.
review_flags: The instance class must fix demand divisibility and facility-opening conventions before attainable pairs from different results are compared.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal meaning of a multiplicative objective/capacity bicriteria guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm \(A\) has bicriteria guarantee \((\alpha,\beta)\) on \(\mathcal I\) if, for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), it returns a solution of cost at most \(\alpha\mathrm{OPT}_1(I)\) whose load at every facility \(i\) is at most \(\beta u_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost-capacity bicriteria guarantee bounds cost against the original hard-capacity optimum and bounds every facility load by a common multiple of its original capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Capacity Bicriteria Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tradeoff Frontiers Require Fixed Modeling Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on comparisons among bicriteria guarantee pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Changing demand divisibility, permission to open multiple copies, the hard-capacity benchmark, the instance class, or the algorithm class changes the attainable region itself. Guarantee pairs obtained under different conventions need not belong to, or be comparable through, one function A_*(\beta).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity tradeoff points are comparable only when all modeling and benchmark conventions remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Different modeling conventions define different attainable regions unless an explicit reduction relates them.}
knowledge_statements.title: Tradeoff Frontiers Require Fixed Modeling Conventions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested representation making the bicriteria frontier well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance class \mathcal I and algorithm class \mathcal A independently of \beta. Let \[\mathcal R=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in[1,\infty)^2:\exists A\in\mathcal A\text{ having guarantee }(\alpha,\beta)\text{ on }\mathcal I\}.\] Define its upward closure \mathcal R^+=\{(\alpha',\beta'):\exists(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal R,\ \alpha'\ge\alpha,\ \beta'\ge\beta\} and lower frontier A_*(\beta)=\inf\{\alpha:(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal R^+\}. Then A_* is nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix all conventions, close attainable guarantees upward, and take the least cost factor at each capacity factor.
assumptions_latex: The same instance class, benchmark, demand and opening conventions, and algorithm class are used for every \beta.

notation.meaning: Lower cost frontier at capacity factor beta.

knowledge_statements.title: Attainable Cost-Capacity Region
Capacity-Violation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of the best attainable cost factor as capacity relaxation increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\beta\ge1\), let \(A(\beta)\) be the infimum of all \(\alpha\) for which the specified algorithm family always returns a solution of cost at most \(\alpha\mathrm{OPT}_1\) while every facility \(i\) receives demand at most \(\beta u_i\). If \(1\le\beta_1\le\beta_2\), every solution feasible under factor \(\beta_1\) is feasible under factor \(\beta_2\). Consequently, the attainable tradeoff frontier is monotone: \[A(\beta_2)\le A(\beta_1).\] Thus allowing greater capacity violation cannot worsen the best cost guarantee available to the same algorithm family, although a particular parameterized implementation need not realize the frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The best attainable cost factor is nonincreasing as the permitted multiplicative capacity violation grows.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathrm{OPT}_1\) is measured using the original hard capacities.
The infimum defining \(A(\beta)\) ranges over a fixed algorithm family and instance class.

notation.meaning: best attainable cost factor at capacity factor beta

review_flags: standard monotonicity argument; local source locator unavailable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the tradeoff leaf. The monotonicity is valid only when the admissible algorithm-and-guarantee class at beta_2 contains every method admissible at beta_1; the phrase 'fixed algorithm family' does not explicitly establish that closure. No source is supplied for the intended frontier definition.

children.title: Hard-Capacity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limitations of local-search neighborhoods under strict capacity enforcement.

assumptions_latex: The proposed open set is fixed.
Demands are splittable, or all demands and capacities are integral with unit-demand clients.
Assignment eligibility is represented by facility-client arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A feasible reassignment exists}\Longleftrightarrow\text{the assignment network has a flow of value }\sum_jd_j.
review_flags: For arbitrary unsplittable demands larger than one, ordinary max flow is only a relaxation and its cuts are not a complete feasibility test.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive and negative reassignment certificates in flow-representable assignment regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Build a network with source-to-client capacity \(d_j\), eligible client-to-facility arcs, and facility-to-sink capacity \(u_i\). In the splittable regime, and in the integral unit-demand regime by flow integrality, a capacity-feasible reassignment exists exactly when the maximum flow has value \(D=\sum_jd_j\). Otherwise a minimum cut of capacity below \(D\) certifies that some client-side demand cannot be accommodated by its eligible facilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splittable and unit-demand reassignment feasibility is exactly a maximum-flow test; a deficient cut certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Feasibility Certificates

assumptions_latex: Every client demand is fully assigned under the instance's integral or fractional assignment convention.
Facility capacities are hard and may not be exceeded.

notation.meaning: assignment amount or indicator from facility i to client j

review_flags: The domain of x must match the instance's splittable or unsplittable demand convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global feasibility obligation for every strict-capacity exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proposed open set \(S\), a hard-capacitated exchange is feasible only if there is a coupled assignment \(x\) satisfying every client-coverage equation and every facility-load inequality. Independently choosing each client's cheapest open facility is therefore not a valid exchange rule unless the resulting assignment also satisfies these inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard-capacity exchange is valid only together with a complete post-exchange assignment satisfying every client and facility constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Reassignment Requirement

assumptions_latex: \(n\geq2\) clients have unit demand and are unsplittable.
Distances are induced by the Euclidean line.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-metric counterexample to independent nearest-open reassignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Place facilities at \(b=0\) and \(a=1\) on the real line, with capacities \(u_b=n-1\) and \(u_a=n\). Place the \(n\) distinct clients at distinct coordinates in \((0,1/4)\). Every client is strictly nearer to \(b\) than to \(a\), so nearest-open assignment with both facilities open sends all \(n\) clients to \(b\) and violates its capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even in a strict Euclidean metric, assigning every client to its nearest open facility can overload a hard-capacitated facility.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Metric Nearest-Assignment Overload
Hard-Capacity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nearest-facility reassignment ceases to preserve feasibility under hard capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(n\ge2\) unit-demand clients, facilities \(a,b\), capacities \(u_a=n\) and \(u_b=n-1\), and distances satisfying \(c_{bj}=0<c_{aj}=1\) for every client \(j\). Opening both facilities and assigning every client to its nearest open facility sends load \(n\) to \(b\), violating \(u_b\). Hence an exchange analysis that opens facilities and independently assigns each client to its cheapest open facility is invalid for hard-capacitated location. Feasibility requires a coupled reassignment respecting all load inequalities; uncapacitated projection or nearest-open arguments cannot be transferred without this additional step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With hard capacities, independently assigning clients to their nearest open facility can overload one facility, so every exchange needs a coupled feasible reassignment.
assumptions_latex: Capacities are hard: no load above \(u_i\) is permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nearest-open reassignment loads \(b\) by \(n>u_b=n-1\) and is infeasible.
