knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-size exchange guarantee for unweighted set packing of bounded set size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge3\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). There exists a constant exchange bound \(t=t(k,\varepsilon)\) such that the following holds. For a family \(\mathcal F\) of sets of cardinality at most \(k\), let \(P\subseteq\mathcal F\) be a pairwise-disjoint packing having no improving exchange \((X,Y)\) with \(X\subseteq P\), \(Y\subseteq\mathcal F\setminus P\), \(|X|+|Y|\le t\), \((P\setminus X)\cup Y\) pairwise disjoint, and \(|Y|>|X|\). If \(P^*\) is a maximum-cardinality packing, then \[|P^*|\le\left(\frac{k}{2}+\varepsilon\right)|P|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded-rank unweighted set packing, sufficiently large constant-size exchange optimality gives a k/2 plus epsilon approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Set-Packing Exchanges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded exchange local search for maximum-weight packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite set family \(\mathcal F\), weights \(w:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), a feasible packing \(P\subseteq\mathcal F\), and radius \(t\in\mathbb N\), repeatedly choose \(X\subseteq P\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathcal F\setminus P\) such that \(|X|+|Y|\le t\), \((P\setminus X)\cup Y\) is pairwise disjoint, and \(w(Y)>w(X)\), where \(w(Z)=\sum_{S\in Z}w(S)\). Replace \(P\) by \((P\setminus X)\cup Y\). Stop when no such exchange exists and output \(P\). The output is \(t\)-exchange-local with respect to total weight, not merely cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange bounded collections of packed and unpacked sets whenever feasibility is preserved and the total inserted weight exceeds the removed weight.
assumptions_latex: The initial family \(P\) is pairwise disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every feasible exchange with \(|X|+|Y|\le t\), one has \(w(Y)\le w(X)\).

notation.meaning: total weight of a subfamily Z

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid and let \(B_1,B_2\) be bases. knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Degree Spanning Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization of the maximum vertex degree over all spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the minimum-degree spanning-tree value is \[\Delta^*(G)=\min\left\{\max_{v\in V}\deg_T(v):T\subseteq E\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\right\}.\] A minimum-degree spanning tree is any spanning tree \(T^*\) attaining this minimum. Here degree refers to degree in the selected tree, not degree in the ambient graph. The optimization objective is the largest tree degree; it is distinct from minimizing total edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-degree spanning tree minimizes the largest vertex degree among all spanning trees of a connected graph.

notation.meaning: degree of vertex v in tree T

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a spanning tree of \(G\), let \(k=\Delta(T)\), let \(D_k\) be any nonempty subset of the degree-\(k\) vertices of \(T\), and let \(D_{k-1}\) be any subset of the degree-\((k-1)\) vertices. Let \(F\) be the edges of \(T\) incident to \(D_k\cup D_{k-1}\), and let \(\mathcal C\) be the \(|F|+1\) connected components of \(T-F\). If every edge of \(G\) joining two distinct components of \(\mathcal C\) has at least one endpoint in \(D_k\cup D_{k-1}\), then \(\Delta(T)\leq \mathrm{OPT}+1\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the minimum achievable maximum degree of a spanning tree of \(G\).

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Bounded Spanning Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spanning-tree feasibility under vertex-specific upper bounds on tree degrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected undirected graph and let \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) assign vertex bounds. A degree-bounded spanning tree is a set \(T\subseteq E\) such that \((V,T)\) is connected and acyclic and \(\deg_T(v)\le b(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). In the weighted version, edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R\) are given and the objective is to minimize \(c(T)=\sum_{e\in T}c(e)\) over all degree-bounded spanning trees. An instance is infeasible when no spanning tree satisfies all bounds simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-bounded spanning tree obeys a prescribed upper bound on each vertex degree; the weighted problem minimizes edge cost among such trees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible trees are exactly the spanning trees \(T\) satisfying \(\deg_T(v)\le b(v)\) for all \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on the tree degree of vertex v

Before filtering, at most \(\sum_{r=2}^{k}\binom nr(2r-1)!!\) pairings are inspected. Thus an improving exchange can be found, or local optimality certified, in \(n^{O(k)}\) time for fixed \(k\); this statement does not give polynomial time when \(k\) is part of the input.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Deleting \(r\) edges \(D\) from an undirected tour leaves path components and \(2r\) exposed endpoint incidences; an isolated vertex created by two adjacent deletions contributes two incidences. A set \(A\) of \(r\) inserted edges is a feasible exchange exactly when it restores degree two at every vertex and makes \((T\setminus D)\cup A\) connected, hence one Hamiltonian cycle. Candidate endpoint pairings that create loops, duplicate unavailable edges, incorrect degrees, or multiple cycles are rejected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tour exchange reconnects the endpoint incidences exposed by deleted edges and is feasible exactly when the result is one degree-two connected spanning cycle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical nontrivial two-edge exchange for an undirected tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the cyclic order contains edges \(\{a,b\}\) and \(\{c,d\}\) as \(a,b,\ldots,c,d,\ldots,a\), deleting those nonadjacent edges and inserting \(\{a,c\}\) and \(\{b,d\}\) yields the nontrivial feasible two-opt reconnection. In cyclic-order form it reverses the segment from \(b\) through \(c\), and its cost change is \(c_{ac}+c_{bd}-c_{ab}-c_{cd}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric two-opt move deletes two nonadjacent tour edges, reconnects across them, and reverses the intervening segment.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Opt Segment Reversal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification for three pairwise nonadjacent deleted edges in a symmetric tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Delete three pairwise nonadjacent edges from an undirected Hamiltonian cycle. The deletion produces three path components with six exposed endpoints. Up to reversal of the whole tour, the feasible reconnections consist of the original tour, three nonidentity reconnections equivalent to a two-opt segment reversal, and four genuine three-opt reconnections that replace all three deleted adjacencies. Thus conventions must distinguish the seven nonidentity reconnections from the four genuine three-opt classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three nonadjacent deleted tour edges have seven nonidentity reconnections: three are two-opt-equivalent and four are genuine three-opt moves.
assumptions_latex: The three deleted tour edges are pairwise nonadjacent.
A reconnection must produce one Hamiltonian cycle.
review_flags: Three-opt counting conventions vary when adjacent deletions, orientations, or two-opt-equivalent reconnections are included.
An authoritative locator should confirm the intended convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Three-Opt Reconnection Classes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive local search under the declared at-most-k edge-exchange convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a Hamiltonian cycle \(T\) and fixed radius \(k\), repeatedly enumerate all sets of at most \(k\) deleted tour edges and all reconnections that restore one Hamiltonian cycle. Replace \(T\) by any strictly cheaper resulting tour, or by the cheapest improving neighbor in the best-improvement variant. Stop when no improving neighbor exists; the returned tour is \(k\)-exchange-local.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate feasible reconnections within the fixed exchange radius and accept improving tours until local optimality.
assumptions_latex: The instance has finitely many Hamiltonian cycles.
The at-most-\(k\) symmetric-difference convention is used.
review_flags: Finite termination does not imply a polynomial number of accepted moves.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Fixed-Radius Tour-Exchange Descent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit reconciliation of two fixed-radius tour-exchange conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a tour \(T\), define \(\mathcal N^{=r}(T)=\{T':T'\text{ is a tour and }|T\setminus T'|=|T'\setminus T|=r\}\). Define \(\mathcal N^{\le k}(T)=\bigcup_{r=1}^{k}\mathcal N^{=r}(T)\). Thus local optimality for \(\mathcal N^{\le k}\) is equivalent to local optimality for every \(\mathcal N^{=r}\), \(1\le r\le k\); local optimality only for \(\mathcal N^{=k}\) need not exclude improving smaller exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At-most-k exchange is the union of the exactly-r neighborhoods for r up to k, so it requires local optimality at every smaller radius.
assumptions_latex: Tours use the same vertex set and additive edge costs.
Exchange size is measured by deleted and inserted edges in the symmetric difference.

notation.meaning: Tours differing from T by exactly r deleted and r inserted edges
Tours reachable by exchanges of size at most k

review_flags: Named k-opt conventions vary across sources; the superscripts explicitly fix the convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactly-r and At-Most-k Tour-Exchange Conventions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Planar Euclidean structural consequence of two-opt local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a tour through points in \(\mathbb R^2\) with Euclidean edge lengths, if two tour edges with four distinct endpoints cross properly in their interiors, deleting them and inserting the feasible uncrossing pair strictly shortens the tour. Consequently, a two-opt local optimum has no properly crossing tour edges. Collinear and endpoint degeneracies require non-strict tie handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar Euclidean two-opt local optimum has no proper edge crossing because uncrossing is an improving two-opt move.
assumptions_latex: Tour costs are Euclidean lengths in \(\mathbb R^2\).
The crossing edges have four distinct endpoints and intersect properly.
review_flags: This property is Euclidean and does not extend to arbitrary metric cost tables.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Two-Opt Uncrossing Property
Traveling-Salesman Exchange Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The symmetric-difference neighborhood underlying fixed-radius tour exchanges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a complete undirected graph and let \(T\subseteq E\) be a Hamiltonian cycle. For \(k\in\mathbb N\), the \(k\)-exchange neighborhood of \(T\) is \[\mathcal N_k(T)=\left\{T'\subseteq E:T'\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle},\ |T\setminus T'|=|T'\setminus T|\le k\right\}.\] For edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb R\), the tour \(T\) is \(k\)-exchange-local if \(c(T)\le c(T')\) for every \(T'\in\mathcal N_k(T)\). A move deletes at most \(k\) tour edges and inserts the same number while restoring one Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-exchange replaces at most k tour edges and reconnects the result into a Hamiltonian cycle; local optimality compares all such tours.
assumptions_latex: Edge costs are additive over tours.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is \(k\)-exchange-local exactly when \(c(T)\le c(T')\) for every \(T'\in\mathcal N_k(T)\).
review_flags: standard k-exchange definition; authoritative locator unavailable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind is appropriate and the symmetric-difference neighborhood is internally precise. No authoritative locator is supplied, so the use of 'k-exchange' for deleting and inserting at most k edges, rather than another common k-opt convention, cannot be tied to the intended source.

knowledge_statements.title: Survivable-Network Exchange Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-exchange local search constrained by cut-based survivability requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), edge costs \(c_e\ge0\), and integral cut requirements \(r(S)\ge0\) for nonempty proper \(S\subset V\), initialize an edge set \(H\subseteq E\) satisfying \(|H\cap\delta(S)|\ge r(S)\) for every such \(S\). Fix \(p\in\mathbb N\). Repeatedly select \(X\subseteq H\) and \(Y\subseteq E\setminus H\) with \(|X|,|Y|\le p\) such that \((H\setminus X)\cup Y\) satisfies every cut requirement and has strictly smaller total cost. Replace \(H\) by this set. Stop when no improving feasible exchange exists and output the resulting \(p\)-exchange-local survivable network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange bounded groups of edges only when every survivability cut remains satisfied and total edge cost decreases.
assumptions_latex: An initially feasible survivable edge set is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output satisfies \(|H\cap\delta(S)|\ge r(S)\) for every proper nonempty \(S\subset V\) and admits no improving feasible \(p\)-exchange.

notation.meaning: cut edges with exactly one endpoint in S
required number of selected edges across the cut

review_flags: generic survivable-network exchange scheme needs a source for the intended problem variant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the local-search leaf, but no source identifies this cut-requirement model as the intended survivable-network variant or supports the selected p-exchange neighborhood. The generic scheme should not be treated as sourced mathematical knowledge without such a locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Partitioning Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-preserving vertex moves and swaps for balanced cut minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E,w)\), initialize a bipartition \((A,B)\) with \(A\cup B=V\), \(A\cap B=\varnothing\), and \(\bigl||A|-|B|\bigr|\le1\). Its cut cost is \(W(A,B)=\sum_{uv\in E:\,u\in A,\,v\in B}w_{uv}\). Repeatedly perform either a single-vertex move that preserves the balance condition or a swap of one vertex of \(A\) with one vertex of \(B\), provided the operation strictly decreases \(W(A,B)\). Stop when neither type of improving operation exists and output \((A,B)\). The output is locally optimal for this move-and-swap neighborhood, without implying global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move or swap vertices while preserving near-equal part sizes, accepting only operations that reduce the weighted cut.
assumptions_latex: The initial bipartition satisfies the balance condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No balance-preserving single-vertex move or one-for-one swap strictly decreases \(W(A,B)\).

notation.meaning: total weight of edges crossing the partition

review_flags: standard local-search formulation; authoritative graph-partitioning locator unavailable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is suitable, and the stated move-and-swap rule is coherent for near-balanced bipartition cut minimization. Graph partitioning has several distinct balance constraints, objectives, and standard neighborhoods; no source establishes that this is the intended variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Exchange Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic bounded-job-exchange local search for a finite scheduling problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite job set, \(\mathcal F\) a nonempty finite set of feasible schedules, \(C:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) a minimization objective, and \(k\in\mathbb N\). For \(S\in\mathcal F\), define \(N_k(S)\) as the schedules obtainable by changing the machine, position, or start-time decisions of at most \(k\) jobs while preserving feasibility. Initialize with \(S_0\in\mathcal F\). At iteration \(t\), choose any \(S_{t+1}\in N_k(S_t)\) satisfying \(C(S_{t+1})<C(S_t)\). Stop when no such schedule exists and output \(S_t\); then \(C(S_t)\le C(S')\) for every \(S'\in N_k(S_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly apply a feasible improving exchange involving at most k jobs; termination returns a schedule locally optimal for that exchange neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The neighborhood \(N_k(S)\) can be searched or supplied by an oracle.

notation.meaning: Feasible schedules differing from S in decisions for at most k jobs.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite strict-improvement local search and its stopping condition are definitional

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Approximation of Last-Job Relocation Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation guarantee for identical-parallel-machine makespan scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scheduling jobs on identical parallel machines to minimize makespan, the local-search procedure that repeatedly moves a last-finishing job to a machine on which it would finish earlier is a \(2\)-approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The last-finishing-job relocation procedure is a 2-approximation for minimizing makespan on identical parallel machines.
assumptions_latex: \text{The machines are identical and the objective is makespan minimization.}
\text{The schedule returned by the specified local-search procedure admits no prescribed improving relocation of its selected last-finishing job.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Euclidean Dimension Implies Bounded Doubling Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation to the doubling-metric sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every subset of \(\mathbb R^d\) with Euclidean distance has doubling constant at most \(5^d\), hence doubling dimension at most \(d\log_2 5\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-dimensional Euclidean metrics have uniformly bounded doubling dimension.
review_flags: The numerical constant is conventional rather than sharp.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Euclidean Dimension Implies Bounded Doubling Dimension

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-dimensional growth property used by geometric local-exchange analyses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\subseteq B_2(x,R)\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be \(r\)-separated. Then \(|Y|\leq(1+2R/r)^d\). Consequently every radius-\(R\) Euclidean ball admits an \(r\)-net and an \(r\)-ball cover of size at most \((1+2R/r)^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-dimensional Euclidean ball contains only polynomially many separated points at a fixed scale ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Packing and Covering Bound
Bounded-Dimensional Euclidean Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean metric instances whose ambient dimension is independent of input size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite metric instance \((X,d_X)\) is bounded-dimensional Euclidean if there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) and an injective embedding \(\varphi:X\to\mathbb R^d\) such that \(d_X(x,y)=\lVert\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)\rVert_2\) for all \(x,y\in X\). The dimension \(d\) is fixed over the instance family and does not grow with \(|X|\). Consequently, every Euclidean ball of radius \(r>0\) is coverable by at most \(O_d(1)\) balls of radius \(r/2\), a geometric property commonly used to bound local-exchange interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The points embed isometrically into a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space; fixed dimension also gives uniformly bounded ball-covering complexity.
assumptions_latex: The ambient dimension \(d\) is fixed across the instance family.

notation.meaning: A constant depending only on d.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-dimensional Euclidean metrics and their constant doubling property are standard definitions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Doubling Does Not Imply Euclidean Isometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict boundary with the bounded-dimensional Euclidean sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unit-edge shortest-path metric of the four-cycle \(C_4\) has bounded doubling dimension but is not isometric to any Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-doubling metric need not admit an isometric Euclidean embedding.
knowledge_statements.title: Doubling Does Not Imply Euclidean Isometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure properties under restriction and rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((X,d)\) has doubling constant \(\lambda\), every subspace \((Y,d|_{Y\times Y})\) has doubling constant at most \(\lambda^2\), while \((X,cd)\) has the same doubling constant for every \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subspaces and uniform rescalings of bounded-doubling metrics remain bounded-doubling.
review_flags: The factor two accommodates the requirement that covering centers lie in the subspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Hereditary and Scale-Invariant Doubling Structure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scale sparsity consequence of bounded doubling dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((X,d)\) has doubling constant \(\lambda\), \(Y\subseteq B(x,R)\), and distinct points of \(Y\) have distance greater than \(r\), then \(|Y|\leq\lambda^{\lceil\log_2(2R/r)\rceil}\). For \(D=\log_2\lambda\), this is \((R/r)^{O(D)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded doubling dimension limits separated points in a ball at every scale ratio.

notation.meaning: r-separated subset of a radius-R ball

review_flags: Open-versus-closed ball conventions affect only boundary cases.
knowledge_statements.title: Doubling Packing Bound
Doubling Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric spaces with a uniform finite-scale covering bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric space \((X,d)\) has doubling constant \(\lambda\) if every ball \(B(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)\le r\}\), for every \(x\in X\) and \(r>0\), can be covered by at most \(\lambda\) balls of radius \(r/2\) whose centers lie in \(X\). Its doubling dimension is \(\operatorname{ddim}(X)=\log_2\lambda_*\), where \(\lambda_*\) is the least admissible doubling constant. A family has bounded doubling dimension when \(\sup_X\operatorname{ddim}(X)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every radius-r ball can be covered by a uniformly bounded number of radius-r/2 balls; the base-two logarithm of the least bound is doubling dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{ddim}(X)=\log_2\lambda_*,\qquad \lambda_*:=\min\{\lambda:B(x,r)\text{ has an }r/2\text{-cover of size at most }\lambda\}.\]

notation.meaning: Closed metric ball of radius r centered at x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the ball-cover definition of doubling dimension is standard
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar Metrics Need Not Be Doubling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between planar representation and bounded metric growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the unit-edge planar star \(K_{1,n}\), the radius-one ball centered at its hub requires \(n+1\) radius-\(1/2\) balls to cover. Thus its doubling constant is at least \(n+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Planarity alone does not bound doubling dimension.
assumptions_latex: The star edges have unit length.
knowledge_statements.title: Planar Metrics Need Not Be Doubling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical balanced-separator structure of the graph representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists an absolute constant \(c\) such that every planar graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices has a vertex set \(Z\) with \(|Z|\leq c\sqrt n\) and every component of \(G-Z\) has at most \(2n/3\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every planar graph has a square-root-size balanced vertex separator.
review_flags: A source locator is desirable for this named theorem.
knowledge_statements.title: Planar Separator Theorem
Planar Graph Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path metrics induced by nonnegatively weighted planar graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a planar graph with edge lengths \(\ell:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For vertices \(u,v\) in the same connected component, define \(d_G(u,v)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}\ell(e)\). The pair \((V,d_G)\) is a planar graph metric when \(G\) is connected and distinct vertices have positive shortest-path distance. A metric on \(X\) is induced by a planar graph if \(X\subseteq V\) and its distances equal the restriction of \(d_G\) to \(X\times X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar graph metric is the shortest-path distance of a connected, nonnegatively weighted planar graph, possibly restricted to designated vertices.
assumptions_latex: Distinct vertices have positive shortest-path distance.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted shortest-path metrics and planar graph restrictions are standard
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minor-Free Metrics Need Not Be Doubling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between minor exclusion and metric growth control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unit-edge star \(K_{1,n}\) excludes \(K_3\) as a minor. Its radius-one ball about the center requires \(n+1\) radius-\(1/2\) balls to cover, so its doubling constant is at least \(n+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-minor-free graph metrics can have unbounded doubling dimension.
assumptions_latex: All star edges have length one.
knowledge_statements.title: Minor-Free Metrics Need Not Be Doubling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural separator property of the graph representation underlying this metric regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed graph \(H\), there is a constant \(c_H\) such that every \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) with \(H\not\preccurlyeq G\) has a vertex set \(Z\) with \(|Z|\leq c_H\sqrt n\) for which every component of \(G-Z\) has at most \(2n/3\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every graph excluding a fixed minor has a square-root-size balanced separator.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has \(n\) vertices and excludes \(H\) as a minor.
review_flags: A source locator is desirable for this named theorem.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Minor Separator Theorem
Minor-Free Graph Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path metrics represented by graphs excluding a fixed minor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite graph \(H\). Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected graph with an edge-length map \(\ell:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\), and define \(d_G(u,v)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}\ell(e)\). If \(d_G(u,v)>0\) for all distinct \(u,v\in V\) and \(H\) cannot be obtained from \(G\) by deleting vertices, deleting edges, and contracting edges, then \((V,d_G)\) is an \(H\)-minor-free graph metric. A family is fixed-minor-free when \(H\) is independent of \(|V|\). For \(X\subseteq V\), the restriction of \(d_G\) to \(X\times X\) is an \(H\)-minor-free graph metric restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An H-minor-free graph metric is the genuine shortest-path metric of a connected nonnegatively weighted graph that excludes the fixed graph H as a minor; the metric may also be restricted to designated terminals.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is fixed across the instance family.
Distinct vertices have positive shortest-path distance.

notation.meaning: H is a graph minor of G.
Shortest-path metric induced by G and its edge lengths.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-minor exclusion and positively separating weighted shortest-path metrics are standard definitions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating geometric decompositions from valid local-search certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every indexed region, the proposed replacement must satisfy the optimization constraints and lie within the allowed exchange radius. If a regional replacement is infeasible or outside the neighborhood, local optimality supplies no inequality for it; the aggregate certificate is invalid unless the region is modified or its error is explicitly charged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separator is insufficient by itself: every regional replacement used in the sum must be a feasible allowed local move.
assumptions_latex: Local optimality is asserted only over a specified feasible neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (A_i,B_i)\notin\mathcal N(L)\Longrightarrow\text{local optimality supplies no exchange inequality}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exchange-Feasibility Requirement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp algebraic boundary of the separator summation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(\varepsilon<1\) is necessary for the stated multiplicative conclusion. If \(\varepsilon\geq1\), the aggregate inequality \((1-\varepsilon)C(L)\leq\alpha C(O)\) yields no finite upper bound on \(C(L)/C(O)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary charges must consume strictly less than the local cost for the summation argument to yield a ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Charge Absorption Threshold

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange-family interface underlying separator-supported aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let regions specify feasible exchanges \((A_i,B_i)\), with \(A_i\subseteq L\) removed and \(B_i\subseteq O\) inserted. If aggregation covers every local cost with total coefficient one, charges each comparison object with total coefficient at most \(\alpha\), and incurs total boundary charge at most \(\varepsilon C(L)\) for \(0\leq\varepsilon<1\), then the regional nonimprovement inequalities certify \(C(L)\leq\alpha(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}C(O)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible regional exchanges yield a global certificate when they cover local cost, have bounded comparison overlap, and incur small boundary charge.
assumptions_latex: Every regional replacement belongs to the feasible local-search neighborhood.
Aggregation coefficients and charges are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Overlap Regional Exchange System
Separator-Supported Exchange Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-summation principle converting local exchange inequalities and separator charges into a global approximation bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) and \(O\) be a local and comparison solution, let \(C\) be their nonnegative cost function, and let \(I\) be a finite index set. Suppose a separator decomposition produces nonnegative charges \(l_i,o_i,b_i\) for every \(i\in I\), with \(\sum_{i\in I}l_i=C(L)\), \(\sum_{i\in I}o_i\le\alpha C(O)\), and \(\sum_{i\in I}b_i\le\varepsilon C(L)\), where \(\alpha\ge0\) and \(0\le\varepsilon<1\). If each separator-supported feasible exchange and local optimality imply \(l_i\le o_i+b_i\), then \((1-\varepsilon)C(L)\le\alpha C(O)\), and hence \(C(L)\le\alpha(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}C(O)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many separator regions, local exchange inequalities sum to a global approximation guarantee when comparison charges have bounded overlap and boundary charges consume less than the local solution's cost.
assumptions_latex: All charges and costs are nonnegative.
Each indexed replacement is a feasible local-search exchange.

notation.meaning: Finite index set of separator regions.
Local-solution and comparison-solution charges for region i.
Overlap factor and relative boundary-charge bound.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the conclusion follows from the stated finite charge inequalities by summation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization counterpart of the minimization locality-gap definition, including zero-valued local optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonnegative maximization family, let \(\operatorname{LOC}(I)=\{S:C_I(S)\ge C_I(S')\text{ for all }S'\in N_I(S)\}\). Define the ratio of a local optimum by \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)/C_I(S)\), with value \(+\infty\) when \(C_I(S)=0<\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), and omit the indeterminate case \(C_I(S)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\). The locality gap is the supremum of these ratios and is unbounded exactly when ratios exceed every finite \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximization, the locality gap compares the global optimum with local-optimum value; a zero-valued local optimum against a positive optimum already gives an infinite gap.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a maximization problem with nonnegative objective values.
Only instances with finite optimum are included.

notation.meaning: Set of locally optimal feasible solutions for instance I.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximization Locality-Gap Convention
Unbounded Locality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal criterion for failure of any uniform approximation ratio under a chosen neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem family \(\mathcal I\) with neighborhood map \(N_I\), let \(\operatorname{LOC}(I)=\{S:C_I(S)\le C_I(S')\text{ for all }S'\in N_I(S)\}\). Its locality gap is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\sup_{S\in\operatorname{LOC}(I)}C_I(S)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), restricted to instances with \(0<\operatorname{OPT}(I)<\infty\). The gap is unbounded precisely when, for every \(M>0\), some instance has a locally optimal solution \(S\) satisfying \(C_I(S)>M\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neighborhood has unbounded locality gap when locally optimal solutions can exceed the global optimum by every prescribed factor.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
Only instances with finite positive optimum are included.

notation.meaning: Neighborhood of solution S on instance I.
Set of locally optimal feasible solutions.
Global optimum value on instance I.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard supremum-based definition of locality gap
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes existence of a long improvement path from pivot-rule and rule-independent lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_I\) be the finite directed strict-improvement graph of instance \(I\), and fix a start \(S_0\). Existence of a path of length \(2^{\Omega(|I|)}\) proves only that some admissible trajectory is exponentially long. A deterministic pivot rule \(P\) has an exponential lower bound only when its selected trajectory from a specified encoded start has that length. Every pivot rule is forced to take exponentially many moves from \(S_0\) only when every path from \(S_0\) to a sink has exponential length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One exponentially long improvement path does not make every execution exponential; rule-specific and rule-independent lower bounds require stronger quantifiers.
assumptions_latex: \(G_I\) is finite and contains exactly the permitted strict-improvement arcs.
\(P\) selects an outgoing arc whenever the current state is not a sink.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_Q|Q|\ge 2^{c|I|}\ \not\Rightarrow\ |Q_P(S_0)|\ge2^{c|I|},\qquad \min_{Q:S_0\leadsto\mathrm{sink}}|Q|\ge2^{c|I|}\Rightarrow\text{every pivot rule takes exponentially many moves}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Quantifier Boundary for Exponential Trajectories
Exponentially Long Improvement Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-complexity obstruction for strict-improvement local search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each instance \(I\), form the directed improvement graph whose vertices are feasible solutions and whose arcs are pairs \(S\to S'\) with \(S'\in N_I(S)\) and \(C_I(S')<C_I(S)\). The neighborhood family admits exponentially long improvement paths if there are a constant \(c>0\) and infinitely many input sizes \(n\) for which an instance of encoding length at most \(n\) has a simple directed path containing at least \(2^{cn}\) arcs. Thus strict descent guarantees termination but not polynomially many iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly improving local-search moves can form paths exponential in the encoded input size, so finite termination alone gives no polynomial iteration bound.
assumptions_latex: Every instance has finitely many feasible solutions.
Accepted arcs strictly decrease the objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood-Evaluation Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational obstruction to implementing one nominal local-search iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \(I\), a feasible solution \(S\), and a threshold \(\delta>0\), define the improvement-neighborhood decision problem as determining whether there exists \(S'\in N_I(S)\) such that \(C_I(S')\le C_I(S)-\delta\). Neighborhood-evaluation hardness occurs when this decision problem is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions, even though feasibility and \(C_I(S')\) are polynomial-time verifiable. In that regime, a polynomially bounded neighborhood description does not by itself yield a polynomial-time local-search step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local-search neighborhood is evaluation-hard when deciding whether it contains a sufficiently improving feasible solution is NP-hard despite easy verification of candidates.
assumptions_latex: Instances, solutions, and \(\delta\) have finite binary encodings.
Candidate feasibility and objective values are polynomial-time verifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{Decide whether }\exists S'\in N_I(S):C_I(S')\le C_I(S)-\delta\text{ is NP-hard}.\]

notation.meaning: Neighborhood of S for instance I.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Handles triangle violations not captured by ratios restricted to positive two-link cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(d(x,y)+d(y,z)=0\) but \(d(x,z)>0\), then no finite \(\lambda\) satisfies \(d(x,z)\le\lambda(d(x,y)+d(y,z))\). Thus the finite patching factor is properly represented by \(\inf\{\lambda\ge0:d(x,z)\le\lambda(d(x,y)+d(y,z))\text{ for all }x,y,z\}\), equivalently by a supremum using the conventions \(a/0=\infty\) for \(a>0\) and \(0/0=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive direct cost joined by two zero-cost links makes every finite metric-patching constant fail and must count as an infinite triangle violation.
review_flags: clarifies the zero-denominator case omitted by a positive-denominator supremum
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Denominator Triangle Violations
Metric-Assumption Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies loss of exchange-analysis control when the triangle inequality is weakened or absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonnegative symmetric dissimilarity \(d\) with \(d(x,x)=0\), define its triangle-violation factor by \(\tau(d)=\sup_{x,y,z:d(x,y)+d(y,z)>0}d(x,z)/(d(x,y)+d(y,z))\). A metric has \(\tau(d)\le1\). Any local-exchange argument that replaces a direct connection \((x,z)\) by the two-link connection \((x,y),(y,z)\) incurs the bound \(d(x,z)\le\tau(d)(d(x,y)+d(y,z))\). Consequently, if \(\tau(d)\) is unbounded over the instance family, this patching step yields no uniform constant approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a uniform triangle-inequality bound, rerouting through exchanged objects can cost an arbitrarily large multiple, invalidating constant-factor patching analyses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sup_I\tau(d_I)=\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{the displayed patching inequality supplies no uniform constant factor}.\]
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the violation-factor inequality follows directly from its definition

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Induced Exchange Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local optimality caused by infeasibility of small exchanges under hard capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a capacitated assignment problem with feasible solutions \(\mathcal F\), objective \(C\), and a neighborhood \(N_k(S)\) permitting changes to at most \(k\) opened resources or assigned demand groups. A solution \(S\in\mathcal F\) exhibits a capacity-induced \(k\)-exchange barrier if every improving modification affecting at most \(k\) such objects violates a capacity constraint, while some feasible modification affecting at least \(k+1\) objects has lower cost. Then \(S\) is locally optimal in \(N_k\) although a coordinated larger exchange improves it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hard capacities can make every small improving exchange infeasible even when a larger coordinated reassignment is feasible and cheaper.
assumptions_latex: Capacity constraints are hard feasibility constraints.
\(N_k(S)\) changes at most \(k\) resources or demand groups.
At least one larger feasible improving modification exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C(S)\le C(S')\text{ for all }S'\in N_k(S),\qquad \exists T\in\mathcal F:C(T)<C(S).\]
